A federal museum run as one of the Museus Ibram under the Instituto Brasileiro de Museus.

n: Museu de Arte Brasileira da FAAP

Run by the Fundação Armando Alvares Penteado (FAAP), the private foundation that also runs the FAAP university, theatre and cinema.

Posts annual management reports for 2020 to 2024 with an independent audit report; funded by a business levy and names no sponsors.
A regional administration of Sesc Brasil, whose Departamento Nacional is the national executive body, in the same commerce system as Senac.

Member of Arts Collaboratory. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: University gallery. Footer logos show Dalhousie University, the Canada Council for the Arts and the City of Halifax. No sponsor or donor list is published.

An academic support unit of Dalhousie University, housed in the Dalhousie Arts Centre.

The university gallery of the Université du Québec à Montréal, which the site names as a partner.

Grew from Norman MacKenzie's 1936 bequest to the Regina campus of the University of Saskatchewan, now the University of Regina, and keeps close ties to it. Member of AAMD.

Kunsthal Charlottenborg belongs to the Schools of Visual Arts of the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts.

f: Carlsberg Foundation and Ny Carlsberg Foundation (DKK 750M each in March 2026 for restoration) plus a state operating grant. Augustinus Fonden gave DKK 1.53M in 2025 for a Gauguin purchase.
w: Flags: Tobacco. Augustinus Fonden's investment arm holds over 25% of Scandinavian Tobacco Group (cigars, pipe tobacco).
x: FY2025 income DKK 137.0M: about 23 percent state grants, 28 percent foundations and donations, 42 percent tickets, events and shop (årsregnskab 2025, p. 12).
It posts yearly reports and signed accounts for 2018 to 2025, names its board, and thanks eleven funders by name in the 2021 report.

f: 716k visitors in 2024. Kulturstyrelsen grant DKK 36.1M (about 26%); 2024 backers include Augustinus Fonden, A.P. Møller foundations, Ny Carlsbergfondet, Realdania, Novo Nordisk Fonden and Villum Fonden.
w: Flags: Tobacco. Augustinus Fonden paid for many 2024 acquisitions and DKK 2M for the 2026 Freud show. Its investment arm holds over 25% of Scandinavian Tobacco Group.
x: FY2025 income DKK 143.8M before art-purchase grants: about 25 percent Kulturstyrelsen grant; the other 75 percent, net revenue of 105.7M, is not split in the report (årsrapport 2025, p. 37).
It posts annual reports for 2008 to 2025 with audited accounts, names its six board members and lists 2024 sponsors and foundations.

n: Centro de Arte Contemporáneo de Quito
f: Run by the Fundación Museos de la Ciudad, a nonprofit acting on commission of the Quito municipality. Admission is free. No sponsors are named.
w: Housed in the old military hospital, San Juan district. Part of the Sistema de Museos Quito. No controversy found.
x: The foundation running it posts yearly accountability reports from 2016 to 2025 with budgets and transparency files; it names no funders and no board.
Run by the Fundación Museos de la Ciudad, which also operates the Museo de la Ciudad, Museo del Carmen Alto, Museo Interactivo de Ciencia and Yaku water museum.

f: No funder list is published. The Arab Fund for Arts and Culture lists a 2024 CiC project under Egypt's National Cultural Opportunities Fund. Cairo artists depend on foreign grants.
w: Non-profit founded in 2004. Lost its downtown Cairo premises and moved to Garden City, describing persistent pressure; no state funder is involved.
x: Its archived site publishes no reports, accounts or funder list, and says a board of trustees exists without naming it.

f: Space set up with support from Young Arab Theatre Fund, Foundation for Arts Initiatives, Abbara, Roberto Cimetta Fund, Netherlands Embassy in Cairo and AFAC through a Swiss SDC grant.
w: Artist collective since 2005; runs the Cairo Video Festival. AFAC lists a 2019 North Africa Cultural Program grant. No current budget is published.
x: Names its founding supporters in one undated About sentence and lists no board; it publishes no annual reports or accounts.

f: State museum owned by Egypt's Ministry of Culture, in the National Cultural Centre in Zamalek. Opened 1927. No sponsors are named.
w: Holds more than 13,000 works. Ahram Online reported a partial closure; no removed or censored works are documented.
x: No official site was found; searches returned only third-party pages, so no reports, accounts, funder list or board are published that we could find.

f: Art Museum of Estonia budget: state operating grant, own income, project grants, sponsors. Thanked: Ministry of Culture, Cultural Endowment, Gambling Tax Council, Tallink, Liviko, Akzo Nobel Baltics.
w: Thank-you page also lists Eesti Rahvusringhääling, Merko Ehitus, Nordecon and Viru Keskus. No Eesti Energia link found.
x: A thank-you page names about 30 funders and partners without a year and the About page lists the supervisory board; no reports or accounts.
Kumu is the main building of the Art Museum of Estonia, whose other four museums are Kadriorg, Mikkel, Niguliste and Adamson-Eric.

f: Founders Elias Sime and Meskerem Assegued began buying land in 2013 with their own money and sales of Sime's art. Dire Dawa city gave the Harla land in 2007.
w: No donor, grant or sponsor appears in The Reporter or Wikipedia. The museum opened in March 2019.
x: It publishes no reports, accounts or board; its home page names four sponsors in one undated line beside an opening-day video.

n: EMMA Espoo Museum of Modern Art
f: City of Espoo is the chief financier. Main corporate partners are JCDecaux and Länsiväylä. Works closely with the Saastamoinen Foundation, a forest-industry family foundation whose collection is shown there.
w: Run by the EMMA Art Museum Foundation, set up in 2002. The Wirkkala Rut Bryk Foundation collection is also shown.
x: Posts activity reports for 2006 to 2024 with key financial figures, names its two main corporate partners and lists its board; no full statements.

Run by the EMMA Art Museum Foundation inside Exhibition Centre WeeGee, where it shows the Saastamoinen Foundation, Wirkkala-Bryk and Kakkonen collections beside KAMU Espoo City Museum. Member of Suomen museoliitto.

f: Owned and run by the Amos Anderson Fund (formerly Konstsamfundet). Helsingin Sanomat is main partner; Genelec and Bauer Media Outdoor are partners.
w: The fund took its new name in autumn 2025. A December 2020 staff petition on racism led to an equality project. No funder objection found.
x: Shows its main partner and partners as logos, names its owner the Amos Anderson Fund, and publishes no reports, accounts or board list.
Owned and run by the Amos Anderson Fund (formerly Konstsamfundet), which also runs the Söderlångvik museum in Dragsfjärd. Member of Gallery Climate Coalition, Suomen museoliitto.

f: The private Gösta Serlachius Fine Arts Foundation (1933) maintains the museums. Its board seats go to the Serlachius family association and art bodies. No income sources are published.
w: Tried the foundation page, exhibition credits, the sustainability page and state museum subsidy lists. No funder roster found.
x: The foundation page names its seven board members, but no annual report, accounts or donor list is posted on the museum site.
Maintained by the Gösta Serlachius Fine Arts Foundation, whose board seats go to the Serlachius family association, Åbo Akademi and two Finnish art bodies. Member of Res Artis, Suomen museoliitto.

f: Set up in 2010 after Luc Hoffmann backed it. Maja Hoffmann, a Roche heir, chairs the board, which includes the Mayor of Arles. Partners: Hiscox, Blackwall Green, Christie's.
w: Roche is a pharmaceutical group, no flag category. Maja Hoffmann also chairs the LUMA Foundation behind LUMA Arles.
x: Names its institutional partners, corporate partners and sponsors on a partners page and lists its board of directors; no annual reports or accounts are posted.
Lists the Van Gogh Museum, Musée Réattu, Musée Estrine and Abbaye de Montmajour as institutional partners, and belongs to Van Gogh Europe, Plein Sud and Sud Contemporain.

f: Funded by the LUMA Foundation of Maja Hoffmann, a Roche heir. Artnet put the total project cost at about EUR 150M.
w: Gentrification critique of the Arles project; Le Monde (25 June 2021) said Gehry's tower sits badly with the foundation's environmental and local values.
x: States that it was created and funded by the LUMA Foundation of Maja Hoffmann, and publishes no reports, accounts, donor list or board.

Created in 2013 as the arm of the LUMA Foundation that runs the Parc des Ateliers; hosts Atelier LUMA and Offprint, and Les Rencontres d'Arles signed the 2008 site agreement. Member of Gallery Climate Coalition.

n: Frac des Pays de la Loire
f: State through DRAC Pays de la Loire and Région Pays de la Loire. Main patron Fondation Sodebo since 2012; Collection RAJA backed the 2024 Veilhan show.
w: Food and packaging patrons. No flagged funder, protest or censorship found.
x: Names its main patron Sodebo and a 2024 project patron on its patronage page, and names its president and staff; no reports, accounts or board.

f: Ministry of Culture and DRAC, City of Dijon, Région Bourgogne-Franche-Comté, Côte-d'Or council. Private partners: DVF, Groupe Roger Martin, art foundations, Friends of Le Consortium.
w: Groupe Roger Martin is a family civil-engineering firm. The €1.65M budget figure in the first text is unconfirmed. No flagged funder or protest found.
x: Names its public funders, Friends and main private supporters, and lists the association's three-person executive board; no annual reports or accounts are posted.

f: Région Grand Est and the Ministry of Culture (DRAC Grand Est), named as its tutelles in the 2025 Frac booklet. Run as an association. Patron names are not published.
w: Its patronage page invites donors but names none.
x: Lists its board of directors in a 2025 booklet on its site; patron names are not published, and no annual reports or accounts are posted.
Works in a standing three-Frac network with Frac Alsace and Frac Champagne-Ardenne in the Grand Est; Platform membership is mapped separately. Member of Platform.

f: French state (DRAC Bourgogne-Franche-Comté), Région Bourgogne-Franche-Comté, City of Montbéliard and Pays de Montbéliard Agglomération.
w: The page names no sponsors or patrons. Public money only; no censorship or protest found.
x: Names its four public funders in its About text; publishes no annual reports, accounts, private sponsors or board list.
Member of d.c.a., Seize Mille, TRAC, Bla!, MÔM'ART and Une ouverture pour l'art, and the local relay for the Nouveaux Commanditaires.

f: Created in 1984 by Cartier SA and funded by Cartier, part of Richemont. Moved to a new Jean Nouvel site at the Palais-Royal, reopening 25 October 2025.
w: In 2023 Yanomami leaders and anthropologist Bruce Albert criticised Cartier's greenwashing use of a Yanomami photo. Cartier removed it and called it an oversight.
x: No annual report, accounts, funder list or board is posted; the site names its founder, a president and a managing director only.

n: Musée de la Chasse et de la Nature
f: Private museum run by the public-interest Fondation François Sommer, set up by François and Jacqueline Sommer. A Friends association funds acquisitions. No corporate sponsor list is published.
w: The foundation is chaired by Henri de Castries. The 155k visitor figure is not confirmed. No protest or boycott found.
x: Neither the museum nor Fondation François Sommer posts annual reports, accounts, a donor list or its board; only the Friends association names its own directors.
Run by the Fondation François Sommer, which also runs the Domaine de Belval in the Ardennes and the Club de la Chasse et de la Nature.

f: French state, plus patrons: Fondation Engie, Richard Mille, Ruinart, Swiss Life, Matmut, Revolut, Hugo Boss, G7. Exhibition partners include Havaianas and Vlisco.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Fondation Engie is named in the footer as annual supporter and in the Sustainable Palais programme. Engie sells gas.
x: It posts activity reports for 2020 to 2025 off its main menu, naming its board and 2025 supporters, with budget totals but no full accounts.

f: DRAC Grand Est, Région Grand Est, Collectivité européenne d'Alsace and the City of Strasbourg. One listed patron, SAS Neunreiter. Residency partners are foreign art centres.
w: European centre for contemporary artistic action, in the former Neunreiter store. No protest or censorship found.
x: No annual report or accounts; the about page names the elected board, four public funders, five networks and one patron (SAS Neunreiter), all undated.
Belongs to d.c.a., Arts en résidence, Bla!, Plan d'Est and Tôt ou t'art; its board seats go to Mudam, HEAR and the Strasbourg museum's Friends; five foreign residency partners.

f: Run directly by Région Occitanie with the State (Ministry of Culture, DRAC Occitanie). Sète city, Sète Agglopôle and Hérault department are partners. No private sponsors.
w: The partners page names no sponsor or patron. No censorship or protest found.
x: Run by Région Occitanie, which posts budgets 2020 to 2026 and names 158 elected councillors; the Crac itself lists only public partners, undated.
Managed by Région Occitanie, which also runs the MRAC Occitanie in Sérignan and the Narbovia museum; part of the Plein Sud network of southern art venues.

f: French state public establishment. Dior, The American Friends of Versailles and the Société des Amis de Versailles funded the Salon de Diane ceiling, reopened June 2026.
w: Dior's parent LVMH drew €518M of tax relief for its Paris foundation, criticised by the Cour des comptes in 2018. Epstein links here are venue-only. See the Epstein cross-reference.
x: In September 2018 Epstein emailed Jack Lang and his daughter Caroline about a venue for the 2019 Pritzker Architecture Prize ceremony, writing that Pritzker wanted "something unique this time". The ceremony was held at the Palace of Versailles in May 2019; nothing shows Epstein arranged it. Pritzker, whose family runs the prize, kept writing to Epstein after his 2008 conviction and has said he "exercised terrible judgment in maintaining contact". Pritzker stepped down as Hyatt executive chairman on 16 February 2026.
Posts annual reports 2003 to 2024 and names its board; shows no donor roster, since donors are engraved in the Château and credited per project.
A public establishment governing the château, Trianon, Marly, the carriage museum and Opéra Royal; founding member and president of the Association of European Royal Residences.

n: Kropka (Belarusian community space; listed in place of 'Krokva')
f: Grants from unnamed international foundations cover about two thirds of costs (TOL, 2024). Visitors can donate. One paid coordinator is funded by donor organisations.
w: Closed 10 Jan 2025. Its team cited fewer Belarusians in Georgia and Georgian laws, including the foreign influence law (Pozirk).
x: No site, reports, accounts, funder list or board were found for Kropka, and press says the Tbilisi space closed in January 2025.

f: Founder Irena Popiashvili told Artforum in 2018 that most funding comes from private donors, with a small share of municipal funds. Neither is named.
w: Roving space founded in 2018. Wayback copies of its 2025 pages name no donors.
x: Its archived site has one About paragraph naming two founders; no reports, accounts, supporters or board appear.

f: German Federal Foreign Office paid for PerspAKTIV residencies in 2022 to 2023 and 2023 to 2025. The Visegrad Fund supports Secondary Archive. CEC ArtsLink runs a residency with it.
w: Anti-war platform partners include European Cultural Foundation, Goethe-Institut and Swedish Institute. No full funder roster is published.
x: A small initiative with no annual report, accounts or board posted; funders such as the Federal Foreign Office appear only in project credits.

f: Berlin Senate Department for Culture and Social Cohesion, KW Friends, Berlin LOTTO-Foundation (bought the buildings), Schering Stiftung, Casa Camper. Julia Stoschek Collection is a programme partner.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. Two artists withdrew from the 2024 Poetics of Encryption show as part of Strike Germany. KW marked their names struck out.
x: The institute names its 27-member board and its main funders in text, but publishes no annual reports or accounts.
KW shares its association, Kunst-Werke Berlin e.V., with the Berlin Biennale, its sister organisation, and lists the Berlin Program for Artists as a partner. Member of Deutscher Museumsbund.

f: Federal government pays 71% of the Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation's €275M operating budget, Berlin 14%, other Länder 7%. Sparkassen-Finanzgruppe is main sponsor, renewed in 2017.
w: The budget is the umbrella foundation's, not SMB alone. The Sparkassen renewal page dates from 2017; no newer sponsor list was found.
x: Parent SPK posts annual reports 2016 to 2025 and budget figures; SMB names only supporter groups and patrons undated, and no council members.

A body of the Stiftung Preußischer Kulturbesitz, sibling of the Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin; runs about twenty museums including the Nationalgalerie sites, Pergamonmuseum and Museumsinsel houses. Member of ASEMUS, Deutscher Museumsbund.

f: Nearly 1,000 members plus eleven corporate partners: Sparkasse Bielefeld, Hörmann, DMG MORI, Dr. Wolff, Gundlach, Bautra, Wannenmacher, Enderweit, jablgo, PGW Pecunia, Comspace.
w: Founded 1929 and member-run. No Stadtwerke, energy or arms funder found. Board chair Andreas Wannenmacher.
x: No annual report or accounts; the about page lists the five-person Vorstand and shows eleven undated corporate partner logos.

f: Over 1,000 members. Project funders: Kunststiftung NRW, NRW culture ministry, Stadt Bonn, Sparkasse KölnBonn, Kulturstiftung des Bundes, Kemmler Foundation, Art Explora, Volksbank Bonn Rhein-Sieg.
w: Funders read from exhibition credits. The Kunstverein does not publish its core budget.
x: No annual report, accounts or funder roster; the about page lists the ten-person Vorstand, and exhibition pages credit funders such as Stadt Bonn per show.

f: Run by the Kunstverein in Bremen. Funders include Senator für Kultur, Senatskanzlei, Sparkasse Bremen, EY, Hermann Reemtsma Stiftung, Fritz Thyssen Stiftung, Hollweg Stiftung and Kaefer.
w: Flags: Tobacco. Hermann Reemtsma Stiftung was set up in 1988 by the son of cigarette maker Hermann F. Reemtsma, so its money is tobacco-family money.
x: The Kunsthalle shows 22 funders as undated logos and publishes no annual report, accounts or board list.
The Kunsthalle Bremen is still run privately by the Kunstverein in Bremen, which has over 11,000 members. Member of ADKV, Deutscher Museumsbund.

f: A museum of the City of Cologne, founded 1976 with the Peter and Irene Ludwig donation. The Ludwig Foundation, the Friends and the Gesellschaft für Moderne Kunst support it.
w: An undated partner list names Eni beside long-closed firms such as Sal. Oppenheim. No current energy or arms funder found.
x: FY2023 costs EUR 18.8M: about 75 percent City of Cologne general budget (net), 15 percent earned, 10 percent grants and allocations (Jahresabschluss 2023, Teilergebnisrechnung 0402).
A Cologne city museum with no report or board of its own; the city posts accounts 2008 to 2023; it names 41 partners, undated.
A museum of the City of Cologne; its partners page names the Peter und Irene Ludwig Stiftung, which researches and expands the Ludwig Collection shown there. Member of Deutscher Museumsbund.

n: Kunstverein für die Rheinlande und Westfalen
f: City of Düsseldorf and de Haen-Carstanjen & Söhne support it. Stadtwerke Düsseldorf is its permanent partner.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Stadtwerke Düsseldorf sold 6,300 GWh of gas in 2025 and runs gas-fired plants at Lausward. EnBW owns 54.95%, the city 25.05%.
x: The Kunstverein names its eight-person board and advisory board, shows sponsors as undated logos, and posts no annual report or accounts.

f: City of Frankfurt culture office (permanent), Hessian science and arts ministry for 2022 to 2026, Stiftung Giersch (2006 building), Städelschule Portikus e.V., cooperation partner THE FLAG since 2025.
w: Part of the Städelschule art academy. The first text's Helaba and Wüstenrot Stiftung are not on the page. No protest or censorship found.
x: No annual report, accounts or board; the about page names the City of Frankfurt, the Hessian ministry (2022 to 2026), Stiftung Giersch and THE FLAG.
Part of the Städelschule, the Hochschule für Bildende Künste in Frankfurt, which hosts its legal notice; the Städelschule Portikus e.V. supports it.

f: Hamburg's Behörde für Kultur und Medien supports it; the Claussen-Simon-Stiftung backed the Whispers show. Part of Kunstmeile Hamburg.
w: Municipal exhibition hall for contemporary art. The Kemmler Foundation named earlier is on none of the pages opened.
x: A non-profit gGmbH that posts no annual report, accounts or board; the home page credits the Hamburg culture authority and Kunstmeile Hamburg by logo.
Run by Kunsthaus Hamburg gGmbH, whose shareholders include BBK Hamburg, Griffelkunst-Vereinigung and Neue Kunst in Hamburg; member of Kunstmeile Hamburg and host of Stadtkuratorin Hamburg.

f: State of Lower Saxony funds it; NDR is cultural partner. 32 corporate partners listed in 2026 include Talanx, Hannover Rück, GETEC Gruppe, NORD/LB, Bertelsmann, Deutsche Messe and VHV Versicherungen.
w: Talanx, a 2026 partner, drew an Insure Our Future campaign over Trans Mountain cover (2020). GETEC Gruppe now runs grids and renewables.
x: No annual report or accounts; it names 32 corporate partners undated and lists a ten-person board plus about 30 advisory board members.

f: Kulturstiftung des Bundes, Brandenburg science and culture ministry, Teltow-Fläming district, Mittelbrandenburgische Sparkasse. Kunststrom sales of biomass electricity part-finance the art programme.
w: Former coal power station now runs on locally sourced biomass. Spanner Re2, a biomass firm, gives support. No fossil or arms funder found.
x: Its site (kunststrom.com) posts no annual report, accounts, funder list or board; the legal notice names only a managing director, Pablo Wendel.
Run by the non-profit Performance Electrics gGmbH, led by Pablo Wendel and Helen Turner; no museum, parent or network is named on its own pages. Member of Gallery Climate Coalition.

f: Mainzer Stadtwerke and Mainzer Fernwärme head the partner list, with the City of Mainz, Volksbank Darmstadt-Mainz, Rheinhessen Sparkasse and a state ministry.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Mainzer Stadtwerke supplies gas, runs a gas grid and owns half of KMW, whose power plant burns natural gas.
x: The Kunsthalle names 14 partners with Mainzer Stadtwerke first, but posts no annual report, accounts or board, and its operating foundation lists no officers.
Kunsthalle Mainz is a member of the Mainzer Wissenschaftsallianz. Member of Deutscher Museumsbund.

f: City of Mannheim, Hans-Werner and Josephine Hector (€50M for the Hector building) and their foundations, the Förderkreis, and a Stifterkreis of 57 persons, foundations and firms.
w: Hector is an SAP co-founder. Stifterkreis members are not named on the site. No protest, boycott or censorship found.
x: No annual report or accounts; support pages name the Hector family and foundations, and the Stifterkreis page lists the foundation council and executive board, undated.

f: Landeshauptstadt München Kulturreferat funds the house. Sponsors: Dallmayr, Aqua Monaco, Dompierre, Mondino Aperitivo, Schnitzer&, Karin und Uwe Hollweg Stiftung, Biehler von Dorrer Stiftung, Stiftung Stark.
w: Over 2,200 members. Süddeutsche Zeitung is media partner. Sponsor names read from logos on the Supporters page.
x: No annual report or accounts; the board page names nine members and the sponsors page shows eleven logos with no names or dates.
Names fifteen co-production partners on its institution page, among them Kunsthalle Zürich, Frac Lorraine, Casco Art Institute, S.M.A.K., White Columns, Museo Tamayo and the Whitney. Member of ADKV.

f: City of Munich gallery. On 18 September 2025 the council accepted gifts from Beisheim Stiftung, Pro Helvetia, Art Mentor Foundation Lucerne and Herbert Schuchardt-Stiftung.
w: A Förderverein supports acquisitions. The 371k visitor figure is not confirmed. No energy or arms funder, protest or censorship found.
x: FY2024 costs EUR 15.0M: about 77 percent City of Munich general budget (net), 20 percent admission and other fees, 3 percent grants from other bodies (Haushaltsplan 2026, product 36252200).
A Munich city gallery with no report or board of its own; the city posts consolidated accounts, and the gallery names six foundations, undated.
Shown on its site as Lenbachhaus and Kunstbau, its second exhibition space; the footer links to the Kunstareal site and the City of Munich. Member of Deutscher Museumsbund.

f: Municipal institution of the City of Münster's Kulturamt. Residence NRW+ fellowships are paid equally by the NRW culture ministry and Kunststiftung NRW, with Pro Helvetia. A Freundeskreis helps.
w: No corporate sponsors are named. No Stadtwerke or arms funder, protest or censorship found.
x: Part of the City of Münster's culture office; the city posts annual accounts 2010 to 2024, while the Kunsthalle lists no funders or board.

f: Exhibition house of the City of Oldenburg. Stiftung Niedersachsen funds three media-art grants of €12,500 each. Edith Ruß's donation made the house possible; Elisabeth Brand's legacy furnished it.
w: Donors Edith Ruß and Elisabeth Brand died in 1993; both were NSDAP members. The council renamed the house on 24 February 2025.
x: An exhibition house of the City of Oldenburg: no report, funder list or board of its own, and the city posts annual accounts.

f: Museen der Stadt Recklinghausen, NRW culture ministry, Kunststiftung NRW, Sparkasse Vest, Ruhrfestspiele (city and DGB union federation), Förderverein für Bildende Kunst; WDR 3 media partner.
w: Banks do fund shows, so it is not free of sponsors. Sparda is named for its jazz series. No energy or arms funder found.
x: A city museum with no report or board of its own; the city posts audited accounts, and the site shows four undated funder logos.
Credited to the Museen der Stadt Recklinghausen, with the Ikonen-Museum shown beside it, and carries the Zwanzig Museen Ruhrkunst logo in its footer. Member of ADKV, Deutscher Museumsbund.

f: Private foundation from 2006. Funded through the EU and OACPS ACP-EU Culture programme (AWA consortium with Institut français) and the British Council Digital Collaboration Fund.
w: Runs the Centre for Clay and Textiles in Wa. The funders page gives no years. No oil, mining or other flagged funder found.
x: No annual report or accounts; the Funders page names the EU, British Council and Google Arts and Culture, undated, and six board members are listed.
Member of the Arts Collaboratory network, runs the Wa Centre in northern Ghana, and co-runs the ARTIFY programme with the University of Ghana Business School. Member of Arts Collaboratory.

n: EMST National Museum of Contemporary Art
f: Hellenic Ministry of Culture subsidy: €4.2M in 2023, €5.0M in 2024, €6.8M in 2025 (Greek Parliament). Stavros Niarchos Foundation gave €3M to open the building in 2020.
w: 2018 director dismissal by the culture minister and 2026 mismanagement claims by MPs are governance disputes, not funding. Footer sponsors: SNF, Samsung.
x: No annual report or accounts; the footer shows undated logos for the Culture Ministry, SNF and Samsung, and the site names a nine-member administrative board.
NEON's partners page says it has supported EMST since 2012; EMST's own site names only the Hellenic Ministry of Culture and sponsors. Member of CIMAM.

f: Private non-profit founded by collector Dimitris Daskalopoulos (food conglomerate Delta/Vivartia). The Art Newspaper says he alone funded its €1M Tobacco Factory renovation. NEON says it spent almost €6M.
w: NEON announced in April 2026 that it ends activity by 2027, with a last show by Michael Rakowitz.
x: No annual report, accounts, funder list or board; the partners page names cultural partners, and the about page says only that NEON is a non-profit.
Founded in 2013 by Dimitris Daskalopoulos; its partners page names Whitechapel Gallery, EMST, Museum of Cycladic Art, Hellenic Children's Museum, Greek National Opera and Outset Greece.

f: Greek Ministry of Culture supervises and funds it: €210,000 in 2020 and €240,000 over three years for acquisitions. Greece and the EU regional fund also co-fund its Biennale.
w: Krasnyanskaya, Moscow gallerist, headed its support council in 2019; AVC Charity funded its archive project that year. OpenSanctions has no match for her or Cheglakov.
x: No annual report, accounts or sponsor list found; the about page names the management board chair, vice chair, seven members and the general director.

An integrated public institution formed in November 2018 from five museums: Modern Art (Costakis Collection), Contemporary Art, Photography, the Experimental Center for the Arts and Museum Alex Mylona.

f: Fundación Paiz, a family foundation. Main sponsors: Epson, Pinturas Volcán, Marcas Mundiales. Others: Don Arturo, Cemaco, Copa Airlines, Hertz. Allies include Guatemala's culture and foreign ministries and INGUAT.
w: Sponsor logos read from the archived 24th Bienal page (Oct 2025). Run by the foundation since 1978.
x: Neither the Bienal nor Fundación Paiz posts a report, accounts or donor list; the foundation page names only its board president, María Regina Paiz.
Organised by the Fundación Paiz, which also runs the Centro Cultural Fundación Paiz and the Colección de Arte Paiz. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: Open Society Foundations paid a final package in 2024 as it closed its national foundations. Kellogg, Ford and Citi-CAF fund it; the diaspora fund Ayiti Demen raised $609,068.
w: The EU, AFD and USAID have withdrawn. Gang violence closed Martissant Park to the public.
x: Posts annual reports 2016 to 2024 that name funders and an external audit; the board is listed at five members. No financial statements are posted.
FOKAL lists the Centre d'Art, Parc de Martissant, Kiskeyart and the Bibliothèque Monique Calixte as its affiliated structures; Open Society Foundations is its main funder.

f: Run by Atis Rezistans artists with British curator Leah Gordon. The site links sponsor pages for 2015, 2017 and 2019 but names no sponsors. No budget is published.
w: Biennial on the Grand Rue, Port-au-Prince; Atis Rezistans also took part in documenta fifteen in 2022. No controversy found.
x: Its edition pages name sponsors in text for 2015, 2017 and 2019, but there are no annual reports, accounts or board list.
Hosted by the artists' collective Atis Rezistans in two Port-au-Prince neighbourhoods every two years since 2009. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: HK government (Arts Capacity Development Funding Scheme, Arts Development Council), foundations, Bloomberg, Goldman Sachs Gives, Morgan Stanley, Tai Kwun, patrons. The annual auction is a large share of the budget.
w: Flags: Gambling. Sponsor Tai Kwun is run by the Hong Kong Jockey Club. Its Charities Trust funded AAA's Ha Bik Chuen archive project, 2016 to 2019.
x: Its site lists its board and a named donor board with no date; it publishes no annual reports or accounts.

n: CHAT (Centre for Heritage, Arts and Textile)
f: Non-profit Mill6 Foundation, founded by Vanessa Cheung. Founding donor: D. H. Chen Foundation. Main donor: Nan Fung Group, the property group that owned the mills.
w: Opened 16 March 2019 in a former Nan Fung cotton mill. ANTEPRIMA partners on the textile art prize. No Jockey Club or government funder found.
x: No annual report or accounts; it names two donors, undated, and lists eight directors of Mill 6 Foundation, mostly Nan Fung Group executives.
CHAT is run by the non-profit Mill6 Foundation, from the former Nan Fung Textiles cotton mill at The Mills in Tsuen Wan.

f: Yenn and Alan Lo Foundation, Sunpride Foundation and Cheng-Lan Foundation lead the 2025 gala list. Galleries such as Gagosian, Zwirner and White Cube give; annual benefit auction and Patrons' Circle.
w: No flagged funder, protest or censorship found. No public grant is listed on its current supporter pages.
x: No annual report or accounts; it names benefactors of its 2025 gala and an undated patrons' circle, and lists a nine-person board plus advisors.
Para Site runs a residency programme with Triangle Network and HANGAR Lisbon, a fellowship exchange with Delfina Foundation, and the Unconditional Trust grant with Asia Art Archive.

f: 2023: state budget subsidy HUF 384.9M of HUF 838.9M revenue; NKA state cultural fund grants HUF 80.3M; Ludwig Foundation Aachen EUR 55,000 for the collection; Magyar Telekom digital support.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. In 2019 the museum took down János Brückner's Orbán portrait. Artnet called it censorship under political pressure; the director cited public reaction.
x: FY2025 income HUF 743.8M: about 66 percent state funding, 13 percent company and foreign donors, 21 percent own revenue (éves költségvetési beszámoló 2025, forms 01, 02, 04).
The museum posts narrative reports for 2005 to 2025 and budget accounts for 2011 to 2025, shows two undated logos, and names no board.

The Ludwig Museum began inside the Hungarian National Gallery, holds Ludwig Foundation works on long-term deposit, sits in the Müpa building and commissions Hungary's Venice Biennale presence. Member of CIMAM.

f: City of Reykjavik paid ISK 543.6M in 2023. Own income was ISK 160.8M: tickets 46%, shop 25%, grants 16%, venue hire 9%, other 5%.
w: City-run museum with three sites. A three-year Museum Council grant pays for a research post.
x: FY2023 income ISK 704M: about 77 percent City of Reykjavik contribution, 23 percent own income, mostly tickets and shop (annual report 2023, p. 11).
Posts its 2023 annual report; its parent City of Reykjavik posts consolidated annual accounts. No sponsor list, and no current board for the museum.
Reykjavík Art Museum runs three sites, Hafnarhús, Kjarvalsstaðir and Ásmundarsafn, and names Reykjavík Arts Festival, DesignMarch and Iceland Airwaves as festival partners.

f: Built 1952 on Sir Cowasji Jehangir's gift in memory of his son. A committee chaired by Adi H. Jehangir manages it; no sponsors or ongoing funders are listed.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. In April 2013 the gallery and Mumbai police made Eleena Banik remove two goddess paintings. In 2006 it had a student cover a nude sculpture.
x: The gallery names its management committee with chairman Adi Jehangir, but publishes no reports, accounts or sponsors.

f: Artist-run since 1997. Top supporters: Prince Claus Fund, Goethe-Institut New Delhi and Ford Foundation; capital circle includes Apeejay Trust, Inlaks India Foundation, Weikfield; benefactor Sangeeta Jindal.
w: Benefactor Sangeeta Jindal (JSW Foundation): JSW is mostly steel; its power arm is about 5% of group revenue (US$1.1B of US$23B).
x: No annual report or audited accounts, only foreign-contribution filings from 2012; it names donors by tier, undated, and lists an eight-member board plus advisors.
Khoj began in 1997 with Triangle Arts Trust, set up the South Asian Network for the Arts in 2004 with Vasl and others, and co-runs a curatorial programme with Goethe-Institut.

f: Founded 1998 by artist Sunaryo with direction and support from the Selasar Sunaryo Foundation. Its site names no sponsors; foreign partners are unnamed.
w: Nonprofit art space in Bandung. No flagged funder, protest or censorship found. Earlier partner names (Goethe-Institut, Japan Foundation, British Council) are not on its site.
x: Its site posts no annual report, accounts, sponsor list or board; a 2010 ASEF profile names only the Selasar Sunaryo Foundation.
Selasar Sunaryo Art Space was set up in 1998 by the artist Sunaryo with direction and support from the Selasar Sunaryo Foundation.

n: Cemeti Institute for Art and Society
f: Residency costs are paid by partner funders: Mondriaan Fund (2024), Goethe-Institut Indonesia and National Arts Council Singapore. Prince Claus Fund network partner since 2018. Operating budget not published.
w: KADIST and AFIELD gave Cemeti the 2024 Art Space Grant. No supporters page or annual report exists on cemeti.art.
x: Its site names the Mondriaan Fund as a 2024 residency partner and shows five founders and staff; no reports or accounts are posted.

f: Arts Council, Carlow County Council and Carlow LEO are the named funders. No sponsors are listed.
w: No flagged funder, protest or censorship found.
x: No annual reports; posts 2024 financial statements and a nine-member board with appointment years; funders appear as undated logos.
VISUAL is a project of the non-profit company Carlow Arts Centre Ltd, and Carlow College donated the site for its building.

f: State-funded national cultural institution (Department of Culture, Communications and Sport). Founder Members: KPMG, AIB, BAM Ireland, O'Flynn Group and O'Flynn Exhams Solicitors; tourism bodies Pure Cork and Ireland's Ancient East.
w: Closed to the public since 22 September 2024 for redevelopment; reopening is planned for 2028. No protest or censorship found.
x: FY2024 income EUR 3.85M: about 91 percent Department of Culture grants (30 percent capital), 1 percent donations and sponsorship, 1 percent earned (audited statements, p. 29).
Posts annual reports 2010 to 2024 and financial statements 2016 to 2024, lists ten board members, and names three partners with other funders by logo.

Crawford Art Gallery is a National Cultural Institution run by a state-created company; while closed for redevelopment it tours its Collection, including long displays at Hillsborough Castle and Emo Court.

f: FY2025 income €871k: UCC subvention €428k, Arts Council €192k, other grants €13k, gifts €41k, plus shop, education and hire.
w: Gifts (€41k) and corporate sponsors are not named. Founding donor Lewis Glucksman was a Lehman banker; banks are allowed. No controversy found.
x: FY2025 income EUR 871K: about 49 percent university subvention from UCC, 22 percent Arts Council, 5 percent gifts, 19 percent earned, rest other grants (audited accounts p. 16).
No annual report; posts 2025 audited financial statements and a 2025 board list, and names University College Cork and the Arts Council as funders.
The Glucksman is part of University College Cork and hosts the UCC Art Collection. Member of CIMAM, Gallery Climate Coalition.

f: FY2025 income €695k: Arts Council €378k, Trinity College Dublin €141k, sponsorship €19k, patrons €12k, plus €121k other income mostly from Ireland at Venice 2026 partners.
w: Director's Circle includes Kerlin Gallery and mother's tankstation. The accounts do not name the Venice 2026 partners. No flagged funder or protest found.
x: FY2025 income EUR 695K: about 55 percent Arts Council, 20 percent Trinity College Dublin, 9 percent donors and sponsors, 5 percent earned, 12 percent Venice and events (accounts p. 18).
No annual report; posts 2025 audited accounts, lists a ten-member board, and names its Arts Council and Trinity College support plus tiered patrons, undated.
The Douglas Hyde Gallery is the contemporary gallery of Trinity College Dublin, which co-funds it with the Arts Council.

f: Run by Dublin City Council, the main funder; the Hugh Lane Gallery Trust (charity RCN20040185) takes private donations. No corporate sponsors listed.
w: Closed 28 September 2025 for refurbishment lasting at least three years. The 2018 to 2023 strategy targeted EUR 350,000 a year in new revenue.
x: hughlane.ie blocked the check; parent Dublin City Council posts annual reports 2016 to 2025 and audited accounts 2015 to 2025.
Hugh Lane Gallery is run by Dublin City Council and shares the 39 paintings of the Sir Hugh Lane Bequest with the National Gallery in London under a 2021 partnership.

f: Arts Council is principal funder. Grants from Dublin City Council, Culture Ireland and others; corporate partners Henry J Lyons, Arthur Cox and Dublin Port; RTÉ Supporting the Arts.
w: No flagged funder, protest or censorship found.
x: FY2025 income EUR 821K: about 71 percent Arts Council and Dublin City Council, 12 percent donors, sponsors and friends, 15 percent studio and event income (audited accounts p. 19).
No annual report; posts 2025 audited accounts and a 13-member board, and names its Arts Council principal funder, grant funders and three corporate partners, undated.
TBG+S runs paired residency exchanges with Tokyo Arts and Space, HIAP Helsinki, Bétonsalon Paris, ISCP New York, Cité Internationale des Arts and Moly-Sabata, plus Irish partners such as RHA.

f: Not-for-profit initiative founded 2005. Exhibitions are funded by the Arts Council and the Waterford City & County Council Arts Grant; an older page also lists the Henry Moore Foundation.
w: No sponsors are named. No flagged funder, protest or censorship found.
x: No annual report, accounts or board; the about page credits the Arts Council and the Waterford City and County Council arts grant, undated.

f: €345,000 from the 2025 Arts Centre Funding scheme. Its site names no sponsors; the footer funder logos are an image.
w: Houses the Niland Collection. No flagged funder, protest or censorship found.
x: FY2024 income EUR 665K: about 76 percent public funding (Arts Council 50 percent, Sligo County Council 18 percent), 2 percent foundations and donors, 21 percent earned (audited accounts p. 16).
No annual report; posts 2024 audited accounts and a 15-member board with company secretary, and a footer funder-logo image with no names or date.
The Model programmes its weekly film series with Sligo Film Society and holds the Niland Collection.

f: Founders Comune di Bergamo and TenarisDalmine gave EUR 1.10M in 2021, TenarisDalmine EUR 430k of it. IGT Italia backs the 2025 Cattelan show; sponsors include SABO, Carvico and Bonaldi Motori.
w: Flags: Gambling. TenarisDalmine makes oil and gas drilling pipe, a supplier not counted as a fossil-fuel funder. Lottery and gaming firm IGT backed the 2025 Cattelan show.
x: FY2025 income EUR 2.07M: about 36 percent Comune di Bergamo and Almenno grants, 48 percent TenarisDalmine, donations and sponsors, 10 percent tickets and sales (bilancio consuntivo 2025).
It posts yearly accounts for 2017 to 2025 that name 27 private funders for 2025, and lists its board, but no separate annual report.
GAMeC shows exhibitions at the Palazzo della Ragione and offers a joint visit with the Accademia Carrara. Member of AMACI.

f: City of Bologna museum, run by Istituzione Bologna Musei. Main sponsor Hera Group (2025 show, ART CITY 2026). Trust per l'Arte Contemporanea: BolognaFiere, two foundations, donor Gruppo Unipol.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Hera Group's gas area (distribution, sales, district heating) was 28.9% of Group EBITDA in the first nine months of 2025, its largest of four areas.
x: A city unit, MAMbo publishes no reports or accounts of its own; its Trust page names its founding funders and a trustee, undated.

f: 2025 plan EUR 4.39M: Province of Bolzano EUR 3.73M, Ministry of Culture EUR 73k, Fondazione Cassa di Risparmio EUR 77k, shop EUR 70k. Tickets bring EUR 134k a year.
w: Private foundation of the Province and Museion Private Founders. Partner logos include Sparkasse and Plank; none from flagged sectors.
x: FY2025 income EUR 4.45M: about 91 percent public funding (mostly the Province of Bolzano), 3 percent private sponsorship, 5 percent earned (audited accounts pp. 16 and 17).
No annual report; the foundation's transparency portal posts annual accounts 2022 to 2025 and its six-member board, while partners appear as undated logos.
Museion has been a private-law foundation since 2006, set up by the Province of Bolzano and the Museion Private Founders, the former Museion Association. Member of AMACI, CIMAM.

f: State museum under the Ministry of Culture. Donors include Veronica Atkins (€4.5M, Boboli amphitheatre), Edwin L. Wiegand Foundation ($1M, Vasari Corridor), Ferragamo (€600k, 2014) and Fondazione CR Firenze.
w: Contract workers protested before Botticelli's Venus on 5 April 2026 over outsourced jobs. Climate activists hit its paintings in 2022 and 2024; no funder targeted.
x: FY2025 income EUR 78.0M: about 4 percent state transfers, 1 percent donations and sponsorship, 95 percent tickets, concessions and loan fees (rendiconto 2025, entrate).
No annual report; its transparency portal posts accounts for 2023 to 2026 and a five-member board, and the donation page names donors, mostly undated.
The Uffizi Galleries bring together the Uffizi, Palazzo Pitti and the Boboli Gardens, joined in 2014, with the Vasari Corridor and the Galleria d'Arte Moderna inside them.

f: Chaired by Miuccia Prada. 2019 revenue was €25.2M from tickets, catalogues and sponsorship contracts; it received no donations that year.
w: Prada withdrew its Pradamalia figurines in December 2018 after blackface criticism and boycott calls. Miuccia Prada, foundation president, is a Prada Group executive director.
x: FY2019 net revenues EUR 25.2M from tickets, guided tours, catalogues and sponsorship contracts; no donations received; no split of the revenue lines is published.
Posts an institutional report covering 2017 to 2019 with summary financials and its board; it names no sponsors and reports no donations in 2018.
Fondazione Prada has three Italian venues: the Milan site, the Osservatorio in Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II, and Ca' Corner della Regina in Venice.

f: Founded and supported by Pirelli, its only named backer; Marco Tronchetti Provera chairs it. Technical sponsors include K-Way and M&C Saatchi Milano.
w: On 4 June 2026 Grizzly Research alleged Pirelli's Russian plants serve Rostec, a sanctioned group owning 25% of Pirelli Tyre Russia. Pirelli denies it.
x: No annual report or accounts; the about page names Pirelli as founder, three technical sponsors, and a board with chairman Marco Tronchetti Provera, undated.
Pirelli HangarBicocca is a non-profit foundation conceived and supported by Pirelli, and works with the University of Milano-Bicocca under a 2015 convention.

f: Fondazione Donnaregina belongs to the Campania Region. Public funds were EUR 3.4M at end of 2021, mostly from the Region; EUR 4.7M from the Region was expected for 2022.
w: Il Sole 24 Ore said the museum depends on public money and has no dedicated fundraising (Dec 2022).
x: FY2025 income EUR 4.70M: about 95 percent public contributions (Regione Campania, cohesion funds, ministry), 4 percent ticketing and services; no private income line (audited accounts p. 3).
No annual report; the foundation's transparency portal posts accounts 2019 to 2026 and names its board, while the site lists no sponsors or donors.
Madre is governed by the Fondazione Donnaregina per le arti contemporanee, set up in 2004. Member of AMACI.

f: 2025 public funds EUR 2.58M: Comune di Prato 1.31M, Regione Toscana 0.77M, Ministry of Culture 0.50M. Partners: Fondazione CR Prato, PwC, Unicoop Firenze.
w: Founded by the Comune di Prato and sustained by Regione Toscana. PwC is the corporate sponsor; no private amounts are published.
x: FY2024 income EUR 3.44M, but the accounts put EUR 2.29M of founder and supporter funds, public and private together, on one line, so no public share is stated.
Posts annual reports 2016 to 2024 and accounts 2016 to 2026, lists a seven-member board, and names its partners and sponsors, including PwC, undated.
Centro Pecci was founded in 1988 by the Pecci family and the Luigi Pecci Contemporary Art Association; since 2015 the public foundation FACT supports it. Member of AMACI.

f: Ministry of Culture EUR 14.0M in 2025, Regione Lazio 350k, Enel 600k as a promoter member, sponsors KME and Bulgari. Eni pays EUR 48,750 for archive work.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Protest or boycott, Campaigned name. On 27 October 2025 six artists withdrew and six collectives called a boycott over Eni, Leonardo and Gaza. MAXXI's 2025 accounts show no Leonardo money.
x: FY2025 income EUR 21.8M: about 73 percent public grants (Ministry of Culture 14.0M), 12 percent sponsorship and private gifts, 13 percent tickets and rentals (bilancio 2025, p. 48 and notes).
It posts yearly accounts for 2020 to 2025 with a management report and names its board, but sponsors are undated logos.
MAXXI is run by Fondazione MAXXI and has a second site, MAXXI L'Aquila. Member of AMACI, CIMAM.

f: 2023 income €5.6M: public grants €3.2M (Regione Piemonte, Turin, Rivoli), private grants €1.3M (Fondazione CRT, CRC, Compagnia di San Paolo); Intesa Sanpaolo and Lavazza Group are partners.
w: Francesca Lavazza chairs the board. Fondazione Magnetto funds a restoration. No flagged funder, protest or censorship found.
x: FY2025 income EUR 5.0M: about 57 percent public grants (Regione Piemonte, Turin, Rivoli, ministry), 28 percent private (foundations, patrons, friends), 14 percent earned (rendiconto p. 7).
Rivoli posts yearly accounts and activity reports for 2017 to 2025 with auditors' reports, names its board, and names funders and sponsors in the accounts.

Castello di Rivoli runs Villa Cerruti as a venue, holds works on long-term loan from Fondazione CRT's art foundation and from Fondazione Rivetti, and names Gallerie d'Italia as partner. Member of AMACI, CIMAM.

f: Private foundation led by founder Patrizia Sandretto Re Rebaudengo. Named partners: Regione Piemonte, Fondazione CRT, Compagnia di San Paolo and Asja (renewable energy). No amounts published.
w: Partner Asja, founded by board member Agostino Re Rebaudengo, held 10% of palm-oil firm Poligrow in 2015. SOMO and Indepaz accuse Poligrow of land accumulation.
x: FY2025 income EUR 2.94M: about 73 percent private contributions, 13 percent public contributions, 12 percent earned (bilancio sociale 2025, p. 21).
FSRR posts a yearly social report with accounts for 2021 to 2025, names its board, and names four partners on an undated page.
Fondazione Sandretto Re Rebaudengo promoted the national Comitato Fondazioni Arte Contemporanea in 2014, which its founder Patrizia Sandretto Re Rebaudengo presides.

n: Official. Unofficial. Belarus (Belarus at the Venice Biennale, 2026 collateral event)
f: No sponsors or public funders named. Commissioned and organised by Belarus Free Theatre, an exiled company based in London; M+B Studio, Venice, produced the exhibition.
w: Belarus bans Belarus Free Theatre. In March 2025 Minsk put co-founder Mikalai Khalezin on a wanted list for creating an extremist group.
x: A one-off Venice event run by Belarus Free Theatre, so the theatre's Companies House accounts and trustee list apply; no funder is named.
Presented by Belarus Free Theatre as a collateral event of the 61st Venice Biennale, held in the church of San Giovanni Evangelista.

f: 2024 budget: public funds EUR 33.1M; tickets, sales and sponsorship 31.4M. 2026 donors include Getty, Ford, Batia and Idan Ofer and the Helis Foundation; Bvlgari and illycaffè are lead sponsors.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott, Fossil fuels, State censorship or punishment. The Helis Foundation (Helis oil family) and Getty are 2026 donors. The EU cancelled a EUR 2M grant over Russia's pavilion in July 2026.
x: The Gulf Labor Coalition occupied the Israeli Pavilion for an hour, also protesting labour on the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi. The city shut Iceland's pavilion, Christoph Büchel's mosque in a disused church, calling it a public-safety threat.

US cables record the USSR's protest against the 1977 Biennale's programme on East European dissent; Soviet ambassador Ryjov attacked it publicly in Florence on 18 November. Embassy Rome says Parliament's slow approval of funds confined the programme to old film reruns and photo displays.
FY2025 income EUR 58.0M: about 56 percent public contributions, 15 percent sponsorship and donations, 27 percent tickets and services (bilancio 2025, conto economico and nota integrativa).

Art Not Genocide Alliance, On the Making of the May 8 Strike at the 61st Venice Biennale (e-flux, 2026): The Alliance describes a 24-hour walkout by cultural workers, joined by Italian unions, in support of Palestine and workers' rights. It argues that the Biennale's governance and funding push political risk onto precarious artists and staff, enable artwashing and depend on underpaid workers. Antonia Majaca, What Did the Golden Lion Die Of? On Judgment and Disavowal at the Venice Biennale (e-flux, 2026): Majaca argues that when the 2026 jury excluded states whose leaders face International Criminal Court charges, La Biennale replaced the prize with a public vote. She links its Mussolini-era concession structure and a Qatar Museums donation for a pavilion to a spread of responsibility. See the What the field says case study.
It posts audited accounts for 2020 to 2025, names its board and auditors, and lists 2026 donors by name, but no separate annual report.
The Biennale keeps its own Historical Archives of Contemporary Arts (ASAC) and runs the Biennale College training project. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: Government gallery of Jamaica. The 2022 Kingston Biennial was backed by the Culture Ministry, CHASE Fund, Tourism Enhancement Fund, GraceKennedy, Berger Paints and AC Hotel Kingston.
w: CHASE Fund and the Tourism Enhancement Fund are public funds. No flagged funder, protest or censorship found.
x: As a division of the Institute of Jamaica, it publishes no reports, accounts, funder list or board on its own site.
The National Gallery of Jamaica is a division of the Institute of Jamaica, alongside the National Museum Jamaica, Natural History Museum, Music Museum and Liberty Hall.

f: FY2023 outturn JPY 883.5M: prefecture general revenue 481.4M, prefectural bonds 131.0M, transfers 130.8M, fees 69.9M, other 70.4M. Supportship club members co-fund programmes.
w: Prefectural museum, opened 2006. Shows are backed by local media; FY2023 corporate credits were Dai Nippon Printing, Abeism and Yamato Transport.
x: FY2023 outturn JPY 883.5M: about 84 percent prefectural funds (481M general revenue, 131M bonds, 131M fund transfers), 8 percent fees and charges (annual report p. 84).
The museum posts yearly reports from 2006 to 2023 with budget and outturn tables, and an undated list of corporate supporters, but no board list.
Aomori Museum of Art works with the Aomori Contemporary Art Centre, Hirosaki Museum of Contemporary Art, Towada Art Center and Hachinohe Art Museum through the Aomori Gokan project.

f: The foundation says it runs mainly on admission income. Founded 1968 by the Fujisankei Group (Fuji Television, Sankei Shimbun, Nippon Broadcasting); 173 firms paid for construction. Donations accepted.
w: No current corporate donor list is published. No flagged funder, protest or censorship found.
x: The foundation posts statutes and a dated board list but no annual report, accounts or donor list; it says admissions fund most of its work.
The Hakone Open-Air Museum was opened in 1969 by the Fujisankei Communications Group and is run by the Chokoku-no-mori Art Foundation, set up for it.

f: Pola Art Foundation, set up in May 1996 with the personal assets of Tsuneji Suzuki of the Pola founding family; a public-interest foundation since July 2010.
w: Its site names no other sponsors and does not state POLA ORBIS support or admissions income. No flagged funder, protest or censorship found.
x: FY2025 income JPY 4.93B: about 83 percent endowment dividends, 16 percent earned museum revenue, 1 percent other; no grant or donation line (net-assets statement).
The Pola Art Foundation posts business reports for FY2021 to FY2025, balance sheets and net-asset statements, and a board list; it names no donors.
Pola Museum of Art is run by the Pola Art Foundation, established in 1996, and was built from the collection of Pola head Tsuneshi Suzuki.

n: Hiroshima City Museum of Contemporary Art
f: FY2024 report: City of Hiroshima, plus grants from the Agency for Cultural Affairs, Ogasawara Foundation and Asahi Shimbun Foundation. No corporate sponsors.
w: Chim↑Pom solo show cancelled after their Oct 2008 'Pika' skywriting over Hiroshima drew public backlash. 2026 Mel Chin show co-run with Asahi Shimbun.
x: The city museum posts yearly reports for FY2017 to FY2024 that credit funders per show, but shows no accounts and no board list.
Hiroshima City MOCA has mutual cooperation agreements with eleven partner museums in western Japan, among them the Hiroshima Prefectural Art Museum and the Suntory Museum of Art.

f: Ohara Art Foundation. Official partners (1 April 2026) include Kurabo, Kuraray, Chugoku Bank, Sanyo Shimbun, ENEOS Mizushima refinery, Okayama Gas, Yokoyama Sekiyu and Japan Tobacco, plus over 200 other firms.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Tobacco. ENEOS Mizushima refinery, Okayama Gas and Yokoyama Sekiyu sell fuel or gas. Japan Tobacco is a tobacco partner. All are on the 2026 list.
x: FY2024-25 income JPY 531M: about 85 percent admissions and sales, 6 percent subsidies, 1 percent donations; official-partner funding is not shown as a separate line (正味財産増減計算書).
Its foundation posts yearly business reports for 2024 and 2025, financial statements and a director list; partners are logos dated April 2026.
The museum is held by the Ohara Art Foundation and runs a joint school membership with the Kurashiki Kokokan archaeological museum.

f: Mito City endowed the Mito Arts Foundation with ¥100M and designated it manager. Supporters include Suntory, NEC, Joyo Bank, Genden Fureai Ibaraki Foundation and petroleum retailer Yoshida Sekiyu.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Yoshida Sekiyu sells petroleum products at 23 ENEOS-brand outlets in Ibaraki and also runs Orix car rental, TSUTAYA and car leasing.
x: FY2024-25 income JPY 1.07bn: about 55 percent subsidies, 11 percent admissions and fees, 3 percent donations; 24 percent commissioned work and 4 percent project grants, payers not named.
The foundation posts business reports and accounts for 2012 to 2024, shows 22 supporters as undated logos, and lists no directors.
Art Tower Mito is run by the Mito Arts Foundation and includes the Mito Chamber Orchestra, its concert hall, theatre and gallery.

f: Built by the Benesse Foundation, funded by Benesse Corporation (Fukutake family). EFU Investments and a BPEA EQT fund bought 70.1% of Benesse in March 2024.
w: Benesse is the only named funder. No flagged funder, protest or censorship found.
x: The Fukutake Foundation, which runs the art, lists yearly plans and reports from FY2007 and a dated board; no donor list is published.
The Fukutake Foundation and Benesse Corporation run Benesse Art Site Naoshima, whose museums span Naoshima, Teshima and Inujima; it takes part in the Setouchi Triennale.

f: Okayama City, Okayama Prefecture and the Ishikawa Foundation lead the executive committee. Stripe International and Chugoku Bank are corporate partners. Foundation president Yasuharu Ishikawa directs the Summit.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. Citizens petitioned the city council and prefecture in 2021 and 2022 over harassment allegations against Ishikawa. Both were rejected; he directs the 2025 edition.
x: The 2025 summit site names its executive committee, sponsors and supporting agencies by name, but posts no reports or accounts.

The Okayama Art Summit is run by an executive committee with the Okayama Culture Zone Liaison Council, the Consortium of Universities in Okayama and Okayama University as affiliated bodies. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: SIAF2027 organiser: City of Sapporo executive committee. Supporters: Agency for Cultural Affairs (FY2026), Swiss Embassy, Japan Foundation for Regional Art-Activities, Kao Foundation, CLAIR. Partners: Wacom, Sony, Kokuyo.
w: Seven initiative partners are named, among them Sony Group and Wacom. They co-create programmes; no budget amounts found.
x: FY2023 festival-year income JPY 570M: about 84 percent City of Sapporo contribution, 4 percent sponsors, 6 percent tickets, 6 percent other (executive committee settlement).
Sapporo's city site posts the festival committee's reports and settled accounts for FY2020 to FY2024, its member roster of May 2025, and named partners.

SIAF2027 is staged in Sapporo venues including the Hokkaido Museum of Modern Art, Hokkaido Museum and SCARTS, with JAGDA Hokkaido and Dialogue on Art and Technology as Official Partners. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: Run by the Foundation Arc-en-Ciel, set up in 1977 by Toshio Hara. Corporate supporting members (November 2021) include MUFG Bank, Mori Building, Takasago Thermal Engineering and Ikaho Country Club.
w: Much of its energy comes from solar power. No flagged funder, protest or censorship found.
x: Hara Museum ARC names eight corporate supporters as of November 2021 but posts no annual reports, accounts or board list.
Hara Museum ARC is run by the Foundation Arc-en-Ciel and succeeds the foundation's Hara Museum of Contemporary Art in Tokyo, which closed in January 2021.

f: Executive committee led by Kagawa Prefecture and the Fukutake Foundation. Sponsors (Feb 2025): Japan Tobacco, Cosmo Oil, Okayama Gas, Shikoku Electric Power, Chari-Loto, Kawasaki Heavy Industries, Mitsui & Co.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Tobacco, Gambling. Chari-Loto sells online keirin race bets. Okayama Gas is a gas utility and Cosmo Oil a refiner. Japan Tobacco is a tobacco maker.
x: The festival lists over 200 sponsors and donors as of February 2025 and names its executive committee, but posts no reports or accounts.
The Setouchi Triennale executive committee includes the chairman and honorary chairman of the Fukutake Foundation. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: FY2024 committee budget JPY 359.9M: tickets 105.3M, donations and sponsors 91.6M, Agency for Cultural Affairs and JAC 70.0M, art fund 41.0M, Tokamachi 39.0M, Tsunan 5.1M.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. TEPCO's Niigata office, the Fukushima Daiichi operator, gave staff and a venue in kind in 2024.
x: FY2024 income JPY 359.9M: about 32 percent city, town and national grants, 26 percent donations and sponsors, 31 percent tickets and tours, 11 percent art fund (総括報告書).
The committee posts summary reports for 2018, 2022 and 2024 with accounts and officers, and the support page names sponsors without a date.
The triennale is run by the NPO Echigo-Tsumari Satoyama Collaborative Organisation, whose head offices sit in the KINARE museum and Matsudai Nohbutai. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: Run by the Issey Miyake Design Culture Foundation. October 2026 corporate partners: Mitsui Fudosan, Miyake Design Studio, Issey Miyake Inc and Shiseido as main partners, plus 20 other firms.
w: Main partner Mitsui Fudosan co-develops Jingu Gaien; ICOMOS issued a Heritage Alert on 5 September 2023 and a petition drew about 225,000 signatures.
x: The site names 4 main and 20 other corporate partners, undated, and the Miyake foundation lists officers, but no reports or accounts.
21_21 DESIGN SIGHT was founded by Issey Miyake, credits The Miyake Issey Foundation in its footer, and shares a ticket discount with the Suntory Museum of Art at Tokyo Midtown.

f: Run by the Ishibashi Foundation, set up in 1956 by Bridgestone founder Shojiro Ishibashi, who gave it his art collection. Known as the Bridgestone Museum of Art before.
w: Bridgestone's Firestone unit was sued in 2005 over child labour on its Liberian plantation; the Seventh Circuit ruled for Firestone in 2011.
x: The Ishibashi Foundation, Artizon's operator, posts reports from 2019, balance sheets for 2020 to 2025 and a dated officer list, but no donor list.
Artizon Museum, formerly the Bridgestone Museum of Art, is managed by the Ishibashi Foundation, which also runs its sister museum, the Ishibashi Museum of Art in Kurume. Member of CIMAM.

f: Public-interest foundation; its site names no donors or sponsors. Chairman Koichi Nezu is honorary chairman of Tobu Department Store; councillor Yoshizumi Nezu chairs Tobu Railway.
w: The claim that it takes no Tobu Group donations is not on its site. No flagged funder, protest or censorship found.
x: FY2025 income JPY 1.15B: about 67 percent earned (exhibitions, research, real estate), 31 percent endowment income, 1 percent membership fees, 0.2 percent public grants (settlement p. 7).
Nezu posts yearly reports from FY2012, settled accounts and a full list of directors and councillors, and names no donors or sponsors.
The Nezu Museum is run by the Nezu Museum Foundation, established in 1940 under the founder's will.

f: Its 2026 shows are run and paid for by the Tokyo Metropolitan Foundation for History and Culture (Tokyo government). The Korean Embassy and Cultural Center back one show.
w: As Tokyo Wonder Site (2006-07), it was at the centre of a nepotism row over Governor Ishihara's son's paid role, raised in the Tokyo assembly.
x: Its operator, the Tokyo history and culture foundation, posts reports for FY2017 to FY2025, accounts for FY2020 to FY2025, a board list and named donors.

The Tokyo Metropolitan Foundation for History and Culture runs Tokyo Arts and Space, which swaps artists with eight overseas partners, including Temple Bar Gallery + Studios and WIELS. Member of Res Artis.

f: Founded by Shizuko Watari in 1990 out of her Galerie Watari; the owner's residence is in the building. No sponsors or funder list are published.
w: Self-funded family museum with no published budget. No flagged funder, protest or censorship found.
x: The private museum's site lists membership tiers but no annual reports, accounts, donor names or board.

f: Municipal museum run for Towada City by Nanjo and Associates Group. August 2026 corporate members include Towada Gas. City FY2018 records show ¥17.7M siting funds and a ¥5M grant.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Towada Gas sells gas and kerosene and is a top-tier S course member. The claim that nuclear grants built the museum is not confirmed.
x: The centre lists its corporate members as of August 2026, but posts no annual reports or accounts and names no board.
Towada Art Center is one of five Aomori art museums in the AOMORI Art Project, with the Aomori Museum of Art, ACAC, Hirosaki MoCA and Hachinohe Art Museum.

n: Yamaguchi Center for Arts and Media (YCAM)
f: FY2021 programme budget ¥305M: 88.7% Yamaguchi City, 3.3% Agency for Cultural Affairs grants. The 2026 show is funded by the same two. No sponsors.
w: The latest published budget breakdown is FY2021. Corporate links are commissioned R&D only (Sony CSL, Mitsukoshi Isetan). No controversy found.
x: FY2021 programme income JPY 305M: about 92 percent Yamaguchi City subsidies and Agency for Cultural Affairs grants, 8 percent tickets and fees (annual report p. 2).
YCAM posts annual reports for FY2009 to FY2021 with a programme outturn table, but no funder list and no named board.
YCAM is run by the Yamaguchi City Foundation for Cultural Promotion, a public interest incorporated foundation.

f: FY2024 income ¥1.10B: ¥881M city management fee through the Yokohama Arts Foundation, ¥91M own projects, ¥23M fees, ¥40M city support. Five HEART to ART corporate partners.
w: FY2024 visitors 340,288. HEART to ART firms: NTT Technocross, KSP, Japan Real Estate Investment Corporation, Joytec, Yokohama Shinkin Bank. No flagged funder or protest found.
x: FY2024 income JPY 1.10B: about 84 percent City of Yokohama (management fee plus support), 11 percent earned, 5 percent mixed sponsorship, subsidy and donations (settlement p. 19).
The museum posts reports and settled accounts for FY2020 to FY2024 and names corporate supporters, undated; its operator posts a dated board list.
Yokohama Arts Foundation operates the Yokohama Museum of Art from 2023 to 2033, and the museum's exchange division manages the Yokohama Triennale, centred on the museum. Member of CIMAM.

f: Private non-profit founded in 1988 by artist Suha Shoman and run by the Khalid Shoman Foundation, set up by the Shoman family. No funder list is published.
w: Arab Bank, founded by the Shoman family, lost a 2014 US terror-financing verdict (overturned 2018). No source shows the bank funds Darat al Funun.
x: Its site posts no annual reports, accounts, funder list or board; it names only the Khalid Shoman Foundation as its parent.
Credited in its site footer to The Khalid Shoman Foundation. Member of CIMAM.

f: No current funder list found. Mimeta named Makan a partner in March 2012. Makan describes itself as an independent non-profit space.
w: Latest source found is from 2012. No supporters page found.
x: Makan's old website is gone and no reports, accounts, funders or board are posted anywhere found.

f: Founder Michael Armitage said in 2021 that funding was his responsibility, with help from White Cube. In 2022 he thanked unnamed individuals, institutions and galleries. No list is published.
w: Non-profit founded 2020; included in the 2026 Venice Biennale. The support and donate pages return 404.
x: Its site posts no annual reports, accounts, funder list or board; partners appear only inside event descriptions.

f: Latvian Ministry of Culture, State Culture Capital Foundation, Riga City Council, Altum and EU social-entrepreneurship co-financing; project supporters KRASO, Kokmuiža and Media Port.
w: Absolut and Valmiermuiža from the first text are not on its homepage. No flagged funder, protest or censorship found.
x: Kim? names its two board members and posts its statutes, but no annual report, accounts or sponsor list; shows carry their own supporter credits.
Kim? is a founding partner of the Contemporary Art Library and works with CAC Vilnius, KAI Tallinn and Färgfabriken Stockholm in a Nordic-Baltic network on gardens and climate.

f: Small NGO. Major benefactors: Robert A. Matta Association, Foundation for Arts Initiatives, Andy Warhol Foundation, Norwegian Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Teiger Foundation; Sfeir Semler Gallery is a patron.
w: The supporters page lists no corporate or Gulf funder. Sharjah Art Foundation, named in the old note, is not on it.
x: Ashkal Alwan names four trustees and its benefactors on an undated page, but its Annual Reports section is empty and no accounts appear.

Ashkal Alwan names 21 international partners, among them Serpentine, Delfina Foundation and Wexner Center, six Beirut partners including Beirut Art Center, and belongs to the Arts Collaboratory network. Member of Arts Collaboratory.

f: The museum earns up to 50% of its budget; sponsors, donors and members cover the rest. Tesonet Foundation is strategic patron; Svyturys, Hostinger and PLC Panorama are major partners.
w: Patron Antanas Guoga (listed 2022 to 2026) sold TonyBet's Lithuanian arm in 2016. Paradise Papers (2017) showed he hid the sale of iBus Media.
x: MO posts annual reports for 2018-19 to 2025, names its patrons and partners on an undated page, and lists an advisory board, but no accounts.

f: Private contributions, residency subscriptions and event rentals, per Reform.news. Zolak does not seek grants and runs a crypto bar.
w: Belarusian exile venue in a former ELFA factory, Vilnius. The team aims for financial stability without grants.
x: Zolak's site lists spaces, prices and rules, with no annual report, accounts, funder names or board.

f: Financially supported by the Ministère de la Culture, in partnership with Les Amis des Musées d'Art et d'Histoire Luxembourg. No other sponsors are named.
w: The name comes from the 1882 Casino Bourgeois club building, bought by the State in 1959. No sponsor, protest or censorship found.
x: Casino Luxembourg names its nine-member board and shows logos of its ministry funder and its friends' association, but posts no reports or accounts.
Luxembourg state and civil society sit on its board; it names Les Amis des Musées as partner and the University of Luxembourg for a 2025/26 post-master's programme.

f: No funder list is published. Yayasan ILHAM, a nonprofit, has run it since 2019; IB Tower Sdn Bhd ran it from 2015. Ilham Tower is owned via Daim family firms.
w: Anti-corruption agency MACC seized Ilham Tower on 18 December 2023 and again in June 2025, and moved to forfeit it in June 2025.
x: Yayasan ILHAM, the non-profit that runs it, posts no reports, accounts, funders or board; its About pages name staff only.
Run since 1 January 2019 by the non-profit Yayasan ILHAM.

f: Mali's Ministry of Culture organises and the Institut français co-produces. Royal Air Maroc is a long-time partner. No full funder list is published.
w: African photography biennale since 1994. The 15th edition runs 26 November 2026 to 26 January 2027. No protest or censorship found.
x: The festival site names its 2026 partners, led by Mali's culture ministry, with earlier editions filterable, but posts no reports, accounts or board.
Co-organised and co-produced by Mali's Ministry of Culture and the Institut français; the biennial's own domain no longer serves its pages.

f: UNAM university museum, part of its Dirección General de Artes Visuales since 2005. No corporate sponsor found.
w: Entrepreneur Daniel Mont paid for the 1953 building by Mathias Goeritz. UNAM bought and reopened it in 2005. No protest or censorship found.
x: El Eco has no records of its own; owner UNAM posts audited annual accounts for 2022 to 2025 and names its governing boards.
A UNAM museum run through the university's Coordinación de Difusión Cultural and its Dirección General de Artes Visuales, which also runs MUAC.

f: Fundación Jumex runs the museum with no board, funded by profits of the Grupo Jumex juice company. Admission is free.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. In 2015 the foundation cancelled a Hermann Nitsch show; critics called it censorship. Cuauhtémoc Medina said in 2020 the family cancelled and imposed programmes.
x: The museum's foundation posts no reports, accounts, funder list or board; the site names only Grupo Jumex as the source of support.
Museo Jumex is the main platform of the Fundación Jumex Arte Contemporáneo and shows works from Colección Jumex.

f: UNAM university museum under its Coordinación de Difusión Cultural. No sponsors named in the sources.
w: Sol Henaro has directed it since 2024. A Juan Gabriel show due 28 May 2026 was postponed with no reason given.
x: The Chopo's site names no sponsors; owner UNAM posts audited accounts for 2022 to 2025 and names its governing boards.
A UNAM museum listed under the university's Coordinación de Difusión Cultural beside MUAC and Museo Experimental El Eco.

n: Museo de la Ciudad de México
f: Public museum run by the Mexico City Ministry of Culture. No sponsors found.
w: A federal judge suspended Fabián Cháirez's show in April 2025 after an amparo suit. The city culture ministry defended the show.
x: The museum's page on the ministry portal posts no reports, accounts, funders or board; the ministry publishes ministry-wide Glosa reports for 2019 to 2023.

f: Corporate art collection of FEMSA, founded 1977 and managed by FEMSA staff. FEMSA runs OXXO stores and the Coca-Cola FEMSA bottler.
w: Residents of San Cristóbal de las Casas, Chiapas marched in 2017 to cancel the Coca-Cola FEMSA plant's water concession; permits cost 2,600 pesos each.
x: The collection is part of FEMSA, which files an annual report and a 20-F with audited accounts and names its board.

f: State museum run by the Oaxaca state patronato for cultural and tourist units. No sponsors named.
w: Temporary exhibitions only, no permanent collection. The state government began rehabilitating the colonial building. No protest or censorship found.
x: No museum or agency site could be opened, so its reports, accounts, funders and board could not be checked.

f: Fundación Amparo, set up by banker Manuel Espinosa Yglesias, funds the museum. Colección FEMSA co-presents an exhibition there from 26 September 2026; the museum site names no sponsors.
w: Name to know: FEMSA. Residents of San Cristóbal de las Casas marched in April 2017 to cancel Coca-Cola FEMSA's water concession.
x: Owner Fundación Amparo posts a 2025 activities report; neither site shows accounts, donors or a board, only a staff directory.
Founded through Fundación Amparo in 1991 by Manuel Espinosa Yglesias and his daughter; the site names no network and no standing partner institution.

f: Artist-founded non-profit (Bosco Sodi, 2014); 2026 sponsors: Harp Helú, Home Depot, Teka, Grupo Habita, Tequila 1800, Punta Pájaros, Nirox Foundation.
w: Allowed money named: alcohol (Tequila 1800), retail (Home Depot), hotels/property (Grupo Habita, Punta Pájaros), banking family (Harp Helú).
x: Casa Wabi thanks its sponsors with an undated page of logos and lists staff directors, but posts no annual reports, accounts or board.
Founded on the initiative of artist Bosco Sodi; runs two other spaces under its name, Casa Wabi Sabino in Mexico City and Casa Nano in Tokyo.

f: Federal state company under Mexico's culture ministry. Modified budget MXN 132.9M for January to September 2025, of which MXN 88.0M accrued. A private patronato supports it.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. More than 250 Tijuana artists and writers boycotted the centre and its director Virgilio Muñoz for about three years, to 2011.
x: The centre posts federal budget and spending reports by quarter, but no annual report, funder list or board.

f: Municipal museum of Zapopan, run through the municipal culture institute. The museum's site names no sponsors.
w: Free public contemporary art museum. The old domain mazmuseo.com now carries casino spam links; the municipal site is maz.zapopan.gob.mx.
x: The municipal museum's site lists exhibitions, programmes and a contact address, with no annual reports, accounts, sponsor names or board.

f: Mongolian state-owned museum, created by Council of Ministers resolution in 1965 and listed under the National Centre for Cultural Heritage. No budget or sponsor list published.
w: Opened 23 July 1966 and holds over 16,000 objects. State-owned; no budget or sponsor list is published.
x: Its own site is down; parent body NCCH posts activity reports for 2006 to 2022 but no accounts, funders or board.
A Mongolian state museum listed under the National Centre for Cultural Heritage; no network, branch or partner museum is named. Member of ASEMUS.

f: Run under Maroc Premium Foundation, which has overseen the Casablanca Biennale and the Essaouira art centre since 2014. No funder list is published.
w: Artist residency near Essaouira founded in 2008 by Mostapha Romli. The ifitry.ma site no longer resolves.
x: It has no site of its own; its parent biennale shows 2021 partner logos without names, with no reports, accounts or board.
Part of the Maroc Premium Foundation, which also oversees the Essaouira art centre, the Casablanca International Biennale and the BIC Project Space.

f: Structural patron NOMAD (2015 to now). Project partners 2013 to 2023: AFAC, British Council, Goethe-Institut, Pro Helvetia, US Embassy, Stimuleringsfonds, Fondation Jardin Majorelle, Kamel Lazaar Foundation.
w: Artist-run space and residency in the Marrakech medina since 2013. The partner list stops at 2023, and patron NOMAD is not identified on the site.
x: Its About page names structural patron NOMAD (2015 to now) and partners for 2013 to 2023; no annual report, accounts or board.
Lists Marrakech Biennale, Fondation Jardin Majorelle, Fondation Dar Bellarj, Le Cube and Goethe-Institut Marokko among its 2013 to 2023 partners.

f: Fondation Alliances, set up in 2009 by Othman Lazraq, funds it. The Lazraq family runs the listed property developer Alliances. No other funder is named.
w: Opened 2016 in Marrakech. In April 2015 Alliances shares were suspended twice during debt talks and a conservatory seizure sought by a Holmarcom unit.
