x: MACAAL's site covers exhibitions, mission and visits, and links its founder, Fondation Alliances, but posts no reports, accounts, funder list or board.
A project of the Fondation Alliances, which set up and funds the museum; no network or partner museum is named on its site.

f: Sponsors in 2025: Moza Banco, Nedbank, Standard Bank and the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation. Prize partners include Óbidos council, the Portugal-Mozambique Chamber of Commerce and Camões.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. The Gulbenkian Foundation, endowed by oilman Calouste Gulbenkian, backed a 2025 drama workshop and is a listed sponsor.
x: FY2025 income MZN 22.4M: about 64 percent sponsorship (Cultivarte projects, Gulbenkian, Standard Bank), 36 percent sales and rentals; no government grant line (Relatório e Contas 2025, pp. 8-10).
It posts activity reports for 2022 to 2025, accounts for 2019 and 2023 to 2025, a 2025 sponsor list and its three founders.

f: State-owned art gallery. Bank Windhoek partners on its 2025/2026 Triennial. No other sponsor is named on the site.
w: In March 2014 the gallery asked artist Paolo Solari Bozzi to withdraw photos of Himba girls; he pulled the whole show. The gallery denied censorship.
x: FY2024-25 income NAD 9.81M: about 90 percent Ministry of Education, Arts and Culture, 7 percent earned, 2 percent foundation and donor money (audited statements p. 56).
NAGN posts annual reports for 2019/20 to 2024/25 with audited statements, names its seven trustees, and names its strategic partners in the latest report.

f: 2022 edition: Nepal Ministry of Culture, Prince Claus Fund, World Bank, EU, US, Australian, Swiss and Indian embassies, Toyota, Himalayan Bank. 2026: Italian Ministry of Culture grant, EUR 35,739.
w: The current supporters page lists only the organisers, so the 2022 roster is the latest full list. No excluded names on it.
x: The current Triennale site lists only its two organisers as supporters, with patrons empty, and posts no reports, accounts, funder list or board.

Organised by the Siddhartha Arts Foundation, with the Nepal Academy of Fine Arts as co-organiser in 2026; venues include the Nepal Art Council, Patan Museum and Siddhartha Art Gallery. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: Mondriaan Fonds and Amsterdams Fonds voor de Kunst fund it for 2025 to 2028. Ammodo, the city's districts, Fonds voor Cultuurparticipatie and Cultuurfonds add project money.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. In 2015 the board dismissed director Lorenzo Benedetti. Curatorial Programme tutors asked it to resign and withdrew. An Amsterdam inquiry found the board fell short.
x: FY2025 income EUR 1.37M: about 80 percent public subsidies (Amsterdam arts fund, Mondriaan Fund, city), 13 percent private funds and donations, 7 percent earned (jaarrekening p. 91).

Irene De Craen, WW#14 Appels en peren (artists shown at De Appel, 2015): De Craen reads the board's 14 September 2015 dismissal of director Lorenzo Benedetti as a sign of managerial culture in the arts. She notes no visual artist sits on De Appel's board and says funding now turns on figures, citing a Mondriaan Fund application. Charles Esche, Lorenzo Benedetti deve lasciare definitivamente il De Appel. A deciderlo è La Corte del distretto di Amsterdam. Posizione che solleva una questione cruciale nel mondo dell'arte (artists shown at De Appel, 2015): Exibart reports on 4 December 2015 that the Curatorial Programme tutors, among them Esche, Filipovic, Martinez and Ruf, backed Benedetti, asked De Appel's board to resign and withdrew from the programme until it was renewed. Exibart gives no signatory count. See the What the field says case study.
De Appel posts annual reports for 2008 to 2025 with accounts, names its supervisory board, and names its funders in the 2025 report.
Member of Dutch and Amsterdam sector networks: MOKER, BKNL, ACI, Adamnet and the library and archive networks NADD and OKBN. It names no parent, founder or university. Member of Museumvereniging.

f: Ministry of OCW, Amsterdams Fonds voor de Kunst, Stadsdeel Oost and VriendenLoterij Fonds, per its about page.
w: Decolonial art platform founded in 2009. The Rabo ArtLab project is in no source I opened.
x: Framer Framed names its six-member supervisory board and four public funders on undated pages, but posts no annual reports or accounts.
Framer Framed names no parent; it is a board member of the Amsterdam cultural network ACI, De Zaak Nu and MOKER/P_Oi.

f: €37.5M income (2024), City of Amsterdam 62%. VriendenLoterij is main partner; IMC, ABN AMRO, Mastercard, Polestar and Teijin are loyal partners; Ammodo and the Mondriaan Fund also give.
w: ABN AMRO is a loyal partner (2024 report). It paid €480M in 2021 to settle a Dutch money-laundering case covering 2014 to 2020.
x: FY2024 income EUR 37.5M: about 63 percent public (City of Amsterdam 62 percent), 10 percent private and sponsors, 27 percent earned (annual report summary p. 7).

Sven Lütticken, Propositional Politics (BAK, 2025): Lütticken says BAK's propositions programme grew from working inside neoliberalised Dutch funding, and faults it for never defining a proposition. He says the Stedelijk Museum relies on high-profile donors and has not answered Gaza in its programme, and he wants documenta's terms of success challenged. Not Surprised Collective, Stedelijk Museum Fails to Loan Artwork by Ahmet Ögüt to Protect Students in Amsterdam (artists shown at De Appel, 2024): Thirteen signatories say the Stedelijk refused their 28 May 2024 request to lend Ahmet Ögüt's Bakunin's Barricade to protect protesting students, offered replicas and a talk instead, and put its own interests ahead of human rights. See the What the field says case study.
The Stedelijk's 2024 report summary, on its own file host, names partners and gives a financial overview with an auditor's opinion; its website blocked checks.

Its 2024 annual summary calls Centraal Museum and Bonnefanten sister museums and records joint acquisitions for Collectie Nederland; its own site is behind a bot challenge. Member of CIMAM, Gallery Climate Coalition, Museumvereniging.

f: Run by Stichting Musea Arnhem since 2014 on an annual Gemeente Arnhem subsidy (€2.6M in 2011). No sponsors named in the sources I opened.
w: Reopened on 13 May 2022 after a delayed renovation. No protest or censorship found.
x: FY2024 income EUR 8.49M: about 70 percent public (Gemeente Arnhem 63 percent), 5 percent private, 25 percent earned (jaarverslag 2024, p. 47).
Museum Arnhem posts annual reports for 2012 to 2024, links full accounts, names its supervisory board, and names six funds undated.
Run by Stichting Musea Arnhem; its 2022 to 2027 plan names Museum Het Valkhof, Rozet and ArtEZ as partners and the Musea Bekennen Kleur platform as a network. Member of Museumvereniging.

f: Eindhoven municipality, Mondriaan Fund, Ammodo, Creative Europe and the Promotors foundation; VriendenLoterij, a public charity lottery, is also listed as a supporter.
w: No fossil, arms or gambling-operator funder listed. In 2011 Eindhoven councillors pushed grant cuts and a wider audience; no outcome is documented.
x: It names funds and donors on undated pages, but posts only 2012 and 2013 annual reports, no accounts and no board.
A partner in the L'Internationale confederation of European museums; its Promotors foundation gathers private donors and is a funder, not an affiliate. Member of L'Internationale, Museumvereniging.

f: Provinsje Fryslân gives fixed subsidy; OCW and VriendenLoterij support; Windpark Fryslân is a named partner, with Fonds 21, Mondriaan Fonds, Cultuurfonds, VSBfonds, Turing and Wetterskip Fryslân.
w: Director Kris Callens left in February 2025; the museum cited transgressive behaviour. ING and ABN AMRO are not on the current partners page.
x: FY2024 income EUR 7.1M: about 53 percent public subsidy (Fryslan province, ministry), 25 percent other contributions, 20 percent earned (annual report 2024, finance tables).
The Fries Museum posts annual reports for 2003 to 2024, links full accounts on an ANBI site, names partners undated, and lists its supervisory board.
One organisation with Keramiekmuseum Princessehof, and it includes the Fries Verzetsmuseum as a part of the museum. Member of Museumvereniging.

f: Gemeente Leiden, Province of South Holland and OCW fund it. Its thanks page also names BankGiro Lottery, Mondriaan Fonds, Ammodo, BNG Cultuurfonds, VSBfonds and Fonds 21.
w: The thanks page lists all donors since founding, including the tobacco-family Niemeijer Fonds, undated, so it is not counted. No protest found.
x: De Lakenhal posts annual reports for 2007 to 2025 that name its funds and partners, but shows no accounts and no board list.
A 2014 cooperation agreement ties it to the Rijksmuseum, and it works closely with Universiteit Leiden, which has a room in the museum. Member of Museumvereniging.

f: Province of Limburg, the culture ministry and VriendenLoterij give structural support. Mondriaan Fund, Ammodo and others add project money. Over 150,000 visitors a year.
w: Ammodo backs its 2024 to 2026 shows by Mirga-Tas and Al Solh. No protest or censorship found.
x: FY2025 income EUR 10.0M: about 73 percent structural public subsidy (Limburg, ministry, municipality), 7 percent other grants and gifts, 20 percent earned (jaarverslag pp. 106 to 107).
Bonnefanten's ANBI page posts annual reports with accounts for 2017 to 2025 and names its supervisory board; the 2025 report names its funders.

Pairs its The Studio solo shows with six-month residencies at the Jan van Eyck Academie under the Limburg Beeldende Kunst Stipendium, set up by the Province in 2018. Member of CIMAM, Museumvereniging.

f: Dutch Ministry of Education, Culture and Science and the Municipality of Middelburg, the two supporters named on its site. A Friends scheme takes donations.
w: No corporate sponsor or fund is named on its site. The Province of Zeeland, named in the first draft, is not listed there.
x: FY2025 income EUR 1.47M: about 96 percent public subsidies (OCW, Middelburg, Zeeland province), 4 percent earned, 0.2 percent private (jaarverslag p. 59).
Vleeshal posts annual reports and accounts for 2019 to 2025, names its supervisory board, and names its two public funders on an undated page.
Vleeshal keeps its publications library on long-term loan to the Zeeuwse Bibliotheek; the site names no network or parent beyond its own foundation. Member of Museumvereniging.

f: The Ministry of OCW, VriendenLoterij and the Helene Kröller-Müller Fonds are named in the site footer. No corporate sponsor is named.
w: The cited 2024 visitor-count page is gone; the 280,000 figure is unconfirmed. No protest or censorship found.
x: FY2025 income EUR 18.6M: about 51 percent ministry subsidy, 12 percent private funds, lotteries and sponsors, 38 percent earned (jaarrapport 2025, pp. 52 to 53).
The museum posts annual reports with accounts for 2017 to 2025, names its supervisory board, and names its main funders in the 2025 report.

f: Income €2.7M (2025), €1.9M of it subsidy from Rotterdam and OCW. Ammodo, Niemeijer Fonds, Droom en Daad, Mondriaan Fonds, VSBfonds, ELJA, Elise Mathilde and Zabawas also give.
w: Flags: Tobacco, Protest or boycott. Niemeijer Fonds was founded by a Groningen tobacco manufacturer's daughter. A 2017 open letter demanded the Witte de With name go; renamed 2021.
x: FY2025 income EUR 2.7M: 70 percent subsidies, 20 percent donations and private funds, 10 percent earned and indirect income (jaarverslag 2025, staat van baten en lasten).
It posts annual reports for 2020 to 2025, the 2025 accounts, a named supervisory board and a 2025 thank-you list of funders.
Shares its Witte de Withstraat building with CBK Rotterdam's TENT space and, since 2024, Hiphophuis. Formerly Witte de With Center for Contemporary Art. Member of Museumvereniging.

f: Ministry of OCW and Gemeente Rotterdam give annual support. Droom en Daad funded the Santos warehouse; the Wertheimer legacy, Fonds 21, Rabobank Rotterdam Fonds and others add project money.
w: Droom en Daad (Van der Vorm family) bought the Santos warehouse. Its 2018 Boijmans offer, about €40M, failed in May 2019 over two board seats.
x: FY2025 income EUR 8.59M: about 70 percent public subsidies (ministry, Rotterdam, others), 25 percent private funds and lotteries, 5 percent earned (jaarrekening pp. 31 to 32).
It posts annual reports for 2018 to 2025 with audited accounts, a named 2025 funder appendix, ANBI forms and a named supervisory board.

f: Gemeente Den Haag owns the collection and subsidises the museum. VriendenLoterij gives €500,000 a year. Mondriaan Fonds, Vereniging Rembrandt, Aronson Antiquairs and several funds also give.
w: Funds on the page include Fonds 21, Fonds1818, Turing and Debman Foundation. No regional bank, Shell, ING or BNG is named.
x: FY2025 income EUR 22.4M: about 62 percent public subsidies (mostly Gemeente Den Haag), 7 percent private funds and lotteries, 31 percent earned (jaarverslag pp. 37 to 38).
It posts annual reports for 2017 to 2025 with a balance sheet and income statement, names its funders each year, and lists the supervisory board.
Runs Fotomuseum Den Haag and KM21, its contemporary art space, alongside the Kunstmuseum; the annual report covers all three together. Member of CIMAM, Museumvereniging.

f: VriendenLoterij has backed the museum since 2008 and paid €579,767 in 2025. Stichting Abramsen-Koedam co-presents its sculpture prize. Friends and Rabo ClubSupport votes add income.
w: The researcher's BNG, Aegon and other names come from 2018 and 2019 reports, so they are not current. BNG is state-owned; no protest found.
x: FY2024 income EUR 3.09M: about 55 percent earned, 45 percent gifts, funds and sponsors; the museum reports no structural government subsidy (jaarverslag p. 37).
Its ANBI page posts annual reports 2017 to 2024, yearly accounts 2012 to 2025 and a named board; the 2024 report names about 30 funders.
Names no parent or network; the Stichting Abramsen-Koedam awards the Per Abramsen Sculpture Prize in cooperation with the museum. Member of Museumvereniging.

f: Private museum run by a foundation built on the estate of Jan de Pont. It takes no municipal subsidy and sought no government or fund support.
w: Nearly 75,000 visitors in 2023. De Pont was a lawyer and businessman linked to Tilburg's wool industry. No sponsor named.
x: Its site states the foundation is self-funded and audited, posts a two-year income summary only, lists a five-member board, and names no funders or reports.

f: Culture ministry (64%), Utrecht (31%) and one-off grants (1%) paid 97% of €1.98M income in 2024. Both ended funding from 2025 and income fell to €538k. Utrecht grants Basecamp €62,500 yearly for 2027–28.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. Utrecht ended its subsidy from 2025 despite a positive report, BAK says. The Council for Culture advised ending state funding. Four institutions wrote in support.
x: FY2025 income EUR 537,608: about 85 percent public subsidies (all incidental, no structural funding), 15 percent earned, under 1 percent donations (jaarrekening 2025, p. 19).

Sven Lütticken, Propositional Politics (BAK, 2025): Lütticken says BAK's propositions programme grew from working inside neoliberalised Dutch funding, and faults it for never defining a proposition. He says the Stedelijk Museum relies on high-profile donors and has not answered Gaza in its programme, and he wants documenta's terms of success challenged. See the What the field says case study.
Its ANBI page posts annual reports 2021 to 2025 with balance sheets, names seven funders in an undated list, and lists the supervisory board.

f: Structural support from Mondriaan Fund, City of Utrecht and Stichting DOEN via Arts Collaboratory.
w: The site names no corporate sponsor and gives no years for the support. No protest or censorship found.
x: FY2024 income EUR 203K: about 59 percent City of Utrecht subsidy, 18 percent Arts Collaboratory foundation, 23 percent other income and project payments (financieel verslag p. 13).
Its Foundation page says annual and financial reports sit in a public Dropbox folder; the About page names three funders, the Team page the board.
Casco names the Arts Collaboratory network as the route for its Stichting DOEN support; it is run by its own foundation, Stichting Casco, with a supervisory board. Member of Arts Collaboratory.

f: Gemeente Utrecht, VriendenLoterij and the Ministry of OCW are named on the museum's sponsor page. No corporate sponsor is named.
w: The page gives no amounts or dates for the three. No protest or censorship found.
x: FY2025 income EUR 18.4M: about 53 percent city and ministry subsidy, 38 percent earned, 7 percent fund contributions (public and private mixed), 2 percent other private (jaarverslag p. 74).
It posts annual reports and accounts for 2018 to 2025 and a named supervisory board; the 2025 report lists funders and corporate partners by name.
Runs the miffy museum and the Rietveld Schröder House alongside its main building; the site names no network or university tie. Member of Museumvereniging.

f: Creative New Zealand (NZ$637k a year, 2027 to 2029) and Auckland Council lead; Chartwell Trust, Foundation North, Goethe-Institut and Wesfarmers partner; Pub Charity gave NZ$4,000 (year not found).
w: Wesfarmers owns Bunnings, Kmart and Officeworks. Its chemicals, energy and fertilisers division holds Kleenheat, which retails natural gas in Western Australia.
x: FY2025 income NZD 902K: about 73 percent Creative New Zealand, 13 percent other grants (council and trusts), 9 percent donors, 3 percent earned (performance report p. 7).
It posted its audited 2025 annual report in September 2026, names partners and circle donors on its support page, and lists its Tiaki trustees.

f: 497,998 visitors (2024-25). Run by Tātaki Auckland Unlimited for Auckland Council. Partners include BMW, Van Cleef & Arpels, HSBC, Anthony Harper, Baker Tilly; trusts include Chartwell and Mackelvie.
w: HSBC backed A Century of Modern Art in 2025. HSBC agreed a $1.92 billion US penalty in December 2012 over money-laundering failures.
x: Parent Tataki Auckland Unlimited posts audited annual reports 2021 to 2026 and its board; the gallery's own 2024-25 review names partners and trusts.

Owned and operated by Tātaki Auckland Unlimited within the Auckland Council group; it holds the Mackelvie Trust, Edmiston Trust, Chartwell Trust and Thanksgiving Foundation collections on loan. Member of CIMAM.

f: Core funding from the Waitākere Ranges Local Board (Auckland Council). It also takes gifts from a Benefactors Collective and sponsors, none named.
w: Its site names no sponsor or trust. Income was NZ$1.17M in the year to June 2024.
x: FY2023-24 income NZD 1.17M: about 61 percent service delivery grants and contracts, 15 percent donors and members, 19 percent earned (charities register annual return).
No annual reports on its site; the NZ register holds returns to June 2024. One council funder is named; the About page lists the board.
Te Uru grew from the Lopdell House Society's gallery in Titirangi; its funding comes from the Waitākere Ranges Local Board of Auckland Council, and the site names no network.

f: Christchurch City Council; the Christchurch Art Gallery Foundation raises acquisition funds. Partners are JBWere (foundation partner) and Anthony Harper (major partner), plus hotel, design and drinks suppliers.
w: No gaming-machine trust, SkyCity or fossil company is listed on the support page.
x: A council unit with no reports or accounts of its own; partner logos only, no board. Its Foundation files returns on the NZ register.

f: Dunedin City Council gallery. Gallery Partners are Creative New Zealand, Quartz Reef and Craigs Investment Partners; the DPAG Society buys works.
w: Founding partners in 1996 included Mobil Oil New Zealand and the Lotteries Board; neither is a current funder.
x: A council unit with no reports or accounts of its own. Its supporters page names gallery partners and benefactors; staff are listed, no board.

f: Hutt City Council provides most funding. The Dowse Foundation, set up in 2003, raised $2M. Corporate partners in 2025: Dulux, Tuatara Brewery, Almighty.
w: The Foundation's founding partners, from its 2003 campaign, include NZ Community Trust and Pub Charity, gaming-machine trusts; no current gaming-trust funding found.
x: A council museum: its Foundation site names supporters and trustees but posts no reports. The museum and council sites were blocked.

f: NZ$85M revenue (2024-25), Crown 52%. Its current partners page lists Panasonic, Bloomberg, Samsung, MyLotto and gaming-machine trusts PubCharity and Lion Foundation.
w: Flags: Gambling. Both raise money from gaming machines. Named Te Taiao | Nature grant partners at its 2019 opening and again in the 2024-25 annual report.
x: FY2024-25 revenue NZD 85.0M: about 52 percent Crown funding, 6 percent donations and sponsorship, 32 percent commercial, exhibition and rental revenue (annual report 2024/25, p. 36 and note 3).
It posts annual reports from 2000-01 to 2024-25 with Auditor-General accounts, names its eight board members and lists partners without a date.

f: Whanganui District Council ($26.1M) led the NZ$79.4M rebuild with the Ministry for Culture and Heritage, Lottery Grants Board, Provincial Growth Fund, Stout Trust and other unnamed trusts.
w: Nearly NZ$11M came from community and private trusts and individuals, mostly unnamed. No Lion Foundation, Pub Charity, NZCT or SkyCity is named.
x: Parent Whanganui District Council posts audited annual reports 2017 to 2025; the gallery's partners page names funders and its Trust page names nine trustees.

f: Founded 2007 by Bisi Silva with her own money. A March 2022 Sotheby's benefit auction raised US$1M toward a permanent home in Yaba. It publishes no funder list.
w: Its site names no donors or partners. The claim of foundation-only funding, never Nigerian state or corporate money, has no source.
x: Its site names its trustees and staff, but posts no annual report, accounts or funder list.
Runs the multi-year Finland-Africa Platform for Innovation pilot, pairing its Àsìkò Art School with Rejmyre Art Lab's Nordic Studio, with Uniarts Helsinki as contact.

f: Federal Government through the National Commission for Museums and Monuments; IHS Nigeria, a telecom-tower company, funded a 2026 renovation. A Ford Foundation refit stalled.
w: Reopened April 2026 after renovation. No NNPC, Shell, TotalEnergies or Dangote money found.
x: A federal museum with no records of its own; the parent commission's site posts no annual reports, accounts, funder list or governing council.
One of the 53 national museums run by Nigeria's National Commission for Museums and Monuments, the federal agency that manages them.

f: Ministry of Culture, City of Bergen, Vestland county, Arts Council Norway, Fritt Ord, Sparebanken Norge, Nordic Council of Ministers, Bergesen Foundation, Westfal-Larsen fund and EGD Holding.
w: No Equinor, Aker, Fredriksen, Norsk Tipping or other flag-category funder is named on its supporter list.
x: FY2025 operating income NOK 22.2M against costs of NOK 22.6M; the register and annual report give no split between public grants, private gifts and own revenue.
Its About page names 21 supporters and the 2026 board; accounts for 2023 to 2025 sit in the Norwegian register, with no annual report.

Founded in 1838 as Bergens Kunstforening; lists about 80 partners, among them KODE, Astrup Fearnley Museet, Nasjonalmuseet, Van Abbemuseum, KW Institute, ZKM, Bergen Assembly and the University of Bergen.

f: 2025 income: 59% public grants, 9% sponsors, 16% project gifts, 17% own revenue. Main partners: Sparebankstiftelsen DNB and DNV (NOK 2M a year, 2024 to 2026).
w: DNV GL halted Nord Stream 2 certification work in November 2020 after US sanctions threats. No campaign or objection aimed at DNV found.
x: FY2025 income NOK 66.6M: the annual report gives 59 percent public grants, 9 percent sponsors, 16 percent project gifts and 17 percent own revenue, without amounts.
It posts annual reports for 2013 to 2025 naming funders and its board; accounts for 2023 to 2025 are in the Norwegian register.

Its programme names ongoing collaborations with the Ultima festival, Dextra Musica and Bærum kulturskole; its own partners page shows logos only and names no parent or network. Member of CIMAM. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: Christen Sveaas, his investment company Kistefos AS and Christen Sveaas' art foundation; Riksantikvaren, local and county councils and savings-bank foundations.
w: Kistefos AS invests in offshore services, shipping, banks and property. Oilfield and supply services are no flag.
x: FY2025 ordinary income NOK 42.0M: about 10 percent public, 51 percent donations, 39 percent earned; owner companies also gave NOK 97M for sculptures and buildings (annual report, note 8).
It posts annual reports 2010 to 2025 with full accounts and names funders; the site names only the board chair, the register the rest.
Kistefos shows the art collection of Christen Sveaas' Kunststiftelse, an art foundation set up in 2019 by the museum's founder, Christen Sveaas.

f: Norwegian Ministry of Culture and Equality, the Thomas Fearnley, Heddy and Nils Astrup and Hans Rasmus Astrup foundations, and Sparebankstiftelsen DNB; sponsors EGD Holding and The Thief.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Protest or boycott. Oil firm Lundin Norway sponsored 2012 to 2019. Kunstkritikk's editor called it image laundering. Swedish prosecutors won leave to sue Lundin's management over Sudan.
x: FY2025 operating income NOK 70.8M, of which 32 percent is sales revenue; the register summary does not split the other 68 percent between state grant, foundation gifts and sponsors.
The museum posts no annual report, but its accounts are in Norway's register, its board is named and funders and sponsors are listed undated.
Shows the private Astrup Fearnley Collection. The site names no network, university or sibling institution.

f: Ministry of Culture and Oslo municipality operating grants. Sparebankstiftelsen DNB gave NOK 40M in 2024 to start rehabilitation. Fritt Ord and Bergesenstiftelsen also give.
w: The foundation needs NOK 186M to rehabilitate the building before its 100th anniversary in 2030.
x: FY2023 income NOK 23.3M: about 59 percent state and Oslo operating grant, 11 percent sales; the other NOK 6.9M is not split in the accounts (annual reports 2023 and 2024).
It posts annual reports 2015 to 2024 with accounts, a named funder section and the board; filings for 2023 to 2025 are in the register.
An artist-founded house whose Council seats eight Norwegian artists' associations, with Norske Billedkunstnere in the chair; its own pages name no parent institution.

f: Ministry of Culture and Equality, Stavanger municipality, Kulturdirektoratet (Arts Council Norway) and Rogaland county, plus Fritt Ord, Bergesenstiftelsen and Sparebankstiftelsen SR-bank.
w: Supporters come from the About page. No annual accounts with figures were found.
x: FY2025 operating income NOK 6.5M against costs of NOK 10.1M; no split between public grants, private gifts and own revenue is published in the documents read.
It posts annual reports 2018 to 2025, an undated supporter list and its board; accounts for 2023 to 2025 sit in the Norwegian register.
Its About Us page names thirteen partner institutions in Norway, the UK, the US and Switzerland, among them Kunstnernes Hus, MUNCH, Goldsmiths CCA, Spike Island and Bluecoat.

f: Punjab and federal government bodies; lead sponsor Habib Bank; star sponsors Barjeel Art Foundation, Bareeze and ICCI; partners include Nishat, PIA, Dulux and Careem.
w: The sponsor page is undated and shows logos only. No oil, gas, arms, tobacco or gambling sponsor is listed; no censorship or boycott found.
x: FY2023-24 income PKR 64.9M: about 94 percent public (Government of Punjab, Embassy of France), 2 percent private donation, 4 percent bank interest (financial statements, note 10).
Its Financials page posts reports 2015 to 2025 and statements 2015 to 2024, its Board page lists the board, and sponsors appear as logos.
Its home page says Lahore will host the International Biennial Association's 14th General Assembly during the opening of Lahore Biennale 04 in March 2027. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: Building (about US$24M, 2016) paid by 30-plus Palestinian families, Qattan Foundation, Bank of Palestine and the Arab Fund; Aliph funded a 2022 studio. No current donor list.
w: Independent of Taawon since 2021. The claim that it takes no Palestinian Authority money has no source.
x: It posts annual reports for 2020 to 2022, a named founding-donor list and eleven board directors; no separate audited accounts found.

f: Sponsored by Al Risan Art Museum. It aimed to raise $90,000 for its artists through institutional partnerships and donations (2024). The Istanbul pavilion ran on private and artist support.
w: Artist-led project launched in 2024 with over 60 Palestinian artists. In January 2025 it protested Bloomberg Philanthropies' funding of the ICA's New Contemporaries.
x: The biennale's own site posts no reports, accounts, named funders or organising team; its support page only asks for donations and artwork purchases by email.
Shown through host pavilions: Depo Istanbul, Leitrim Sculpture Centre, Recess in New York, Lofos Art Project in Greece and All All All in Denmark.

f: Income £2.6M in 2025. Al-Qattan Charitable Trust, Qattan family gifts, Save the Children (68% of external income), Drosos, Taawon, Enabel, Art Fund, Arts Council England.
w: Barclays is a banker, not a funder. The 2025 accounts name no BP money. Trust funding paused in 2025 pending a Jersey licence.
x: FY2025 income GBP 2.6M: about 77 percent donations and grants, 18 percent investment income, 4 percent earned; spending was GBP 7.0M, met from reserves (accounts 2025, SOFA).
It posts annual reports from 2005 to 2025, files audited accounts with the Charity Commission, names donors in its 2025 report, and lists its trustees.
Runs cultural centres in Ramallah and Gaza and lists the Mosaic Rooms in London among its facilities; it founded the Rooms in 2008 and they are now an independent charity.

f: Riwaq NGO: EU, Sweden, Germany/KfW, UNDP, UNESCO, ALIPH, British Council CPF, Ford, Open Society, Prince Claus, Doen, Arab Fund, OPEC Fund.
w: OPEC Fund for International Development (oil-state money) is on Riwaq's donor list. Last full biennale 2014; 2019 Chicago edition.
x: FY2025 revenue USD 1.86M: about 82 percent donor-restricted grants released, 5 percent unrestricted donations, 12 percent other revenues (audited statement of activities 2025).
Riwaq posts annual reports for 2010 to 2025, an auditor's report in 2025, an undated named donor list, and its board in each report.

The biennale belongs to the NGO RIWAQ, which is a founding member of ICOMOS Palestine and works jointly with Bethlehem University, Oxford Brookes, Columbia GSAPP and the University of Arizona. Member of Arts Collaboratory. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

n: Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Panamá
f: Private non-profit funded by companies and art lovers. Naturgy, a gas and electricity group, signed a sponsorship in April 2023 covering upkeep and operations.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Naturgy is a gas utility group; its Panama arm distributes electricity. Donor logos on the museum's site carry no names.
x: Publishes annual reports for 2018 to 2025 and a named board; donor logos carry no names or date, and no financial statements are posted.
Founded by the Instituto Panameño de Arte (Panarte) in 1962 and host venue of the Panama Art Biennials.

f: Private foundation museum (Escobar, Salerno); 2026 sponsors page names Banco Itaú, Citibank, French embassy, a law firm and named friends.
w: Bank money named: Itaú (sponsor) and Citibank (supporter). No sponsor controversy found.
x: Its sponsors page names a bank sponsor, supporters and named friends, but the site posts no annual reports, accounts or foundation board.
One of three museums in the Centro de Artes Visuales, backed by the Fundación Carlos Colombino Lailla, beside the Museo de Arte Indígena and the Museo Paraguayo de Arte Contemporáneo.

f: Private museum in Barranco. Sponsors include UTEC, Fundación Telefónica Movistar, Fundación BBVA, Credicorp, Bloomberg and the EU delegation. The Getty Foundation gave $64,000 in 2022 for a works-on-paper show.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. The Getty Foundation belongs to the J. Paul Getty Trust, endowed with Getty Oil stock. The Getty rule adds Fossil fuels. Bloomberg is also listed.
x: Its Auspicios page shows ten sponsor logos with no date; the site posts no annual reports, accounts or board, and no Peruvian register was found.

f: KPMG-audited 2025 revenue S/17.1M: tuition 38%, donations and memberships 37%, services 25%. Donors named: Fundación Telefónica, JOMA, THOMA, Smurfit Kappa. Camisea gas consortium funded free Thursdays.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Camisea, operated by Pluspetrol, sponsored free Thursday entry from August 2022 to March 2025. Alberto Rebaza chairs the board.
x: FY2025 income PEN 17.1M: about 38 percent tuition, 37 percent donations and memberships, 25 percent rentals and services; a government capital grant of PEN 987k was released (audited statements).
Posts audited accounts for 2003 to 2025, committee annual reports for 2007 to 2021 and a named board; its partners page shows an unnamed banner.
Governed by the Patronato de las Artes, founded in 1954. The mayor of Lima, the archbishop and the culture minister sit on it ex officio. Member of CIMAM, Gallery Climate Coalition.

n: Museum of Contemporary Art and Design (MCAD)
f: Part of De La Salle-College of Saint Benilde. It relies on Art Circle patrons and benefit auctions (Funding the Future, 2018 and 15 November 2025). Donors are not named.
w: Free, non-collecting museum. Leon Gallery is the auction partner and artists donate the works.
x: Its Support, About and Downloads pages post no reports, accounts, named donors or board; it sits under De La Salle-College of Saint Benilde.
The external face of De La Salle-College of Saint Benilde, on whose Design and Arts Campus it sits.

f: University museum of Ateneo de Manila University, founded 1960 on Fernando Zobel's gift of his collection; later donors, including artists, added works.
w: Zobel gave his artwork collection. No operating funder, sponsor, protest or censorship flag is documented.
x: The gallery's own site, read from 2025 archive copies, posts no reports, accounts, funder list or board; any financials sit with the university.
A unit of Ateneo de Manila University, housed in the Arts Wing of its Areté arts centre.

f: Formerly central-bank subsidised; now a non-profit foundation (1979, Imelda Marcos, Bienvenido Tantoco Sr.). Founding benefactors include Campos family firms NutriAsia and Del Monte Philippines; Metrobank and NCCA back programmes.
w: NutriAsia, named a benefactor in 2021, saw police break up its 2018 Marilao strike: at least 30 people injured, 19 arrested.
x: Its site describes a non-government, not-for-profit foundation and posts no annual reports, accounts, funder list or board; no Philippine register was readable.

n: KALEKTAR research platform on Belarusian contemporary art
f: German Federal Foreign Office (Civil Society Cooperation programme) and Rönne-Stiftung, per the platform's own about page
w: Online archive, index and journal founded in 2015. Co-founder and editor-in-chief Sergey Shabohin lives in Białystok, the map point, because the platform publishes no address.
x: Its About and Partners pages name funders, undated; the site posts no annual reports, accounts or board, only an editorial team and advisory council.
Based in Poznań, it lists DOMIE, Gray Mandorla Studio, Galeria Arsenal Białystok, Ambasada Kultury, InshyJA and I-DZE-JA as partners, and Minsk's Gallery Ў as its main partner until 2020.

f: Municipal museum of the City of Kraków. Its partners page names Strabag as museum sponsor, with Remondis, RE-Bau, Tribe Hotels and the Ministry of Culture.
w: Sponsor Strabag's minority shareholder Rasperia was controlled by Oleg Deripaska, sanctioned by the US, EU and UK. Strabag keeps the stake frozen (2025).
x: Partner logos are undated and the Museum Council is named, but no reports are posted; the city bulletin with accounts timed out.
A cultural institution of the City of Kraków whose About page states membership of the International Council of Museums (ICOM).

f: European Union (ArtPower Belarus, €2M over 28 months, delivered with the Danish Cultural Institute); Danish Cultural Institute; listed partners ABBA, RESET!, Forum of National Platforms, NDF
w: Founded Oct 2020 as the Belarusian Culture Solidarity Fund. Belarus's interior ministry designated it 'extremist' on 7 Jun 2022 and again on 24 Apr 2026.
x: FY2025 income EUR 705,000 in the Council's Estonian association: EUR 704,027 donations and grants, not split by payer, and EUR 973 own revenue (annual report 2025, p. 5).
It posts activity reports 2021 to 2025 and files accounts in Estonia; partners appear as undated logos, and the site names staff but no board.

Registered in Estonia, it implements the EU-funded ArtPower Belarus programme with the Danish Cultural Institute as lead partner, and lists ABBA, RESET! and the Eastern Partnership Forum of National Platforms.

f: Ticket sales; an actor says funding is zero (2025). Polish Ministry of Culture award (March 2025); Latushka's foundation backs two projects; Council of Culture passes on EU money.
w: Belarus declared its channel and social media extremist in February 2024, the troupe itself in December 2024. Exiled in Poland.
x: The troupe has no website of its own, only social media and press coverage, so it publishes no reports, accounts, funders or board.

f: Project of Pavel Latushka's National Anti-Crisis Management. Warsaw municipality gave 367 m2 of premises; Polish Ministry of Culture co-financed Digital Culture 2025; donors give by PayPal and crypto.
w: Belarus sentenced Pavel Latushka, head of the sponsoring National Anti-Crisis Management, to 18 years in absentia in March 2023.
x: A project of the National Anti-Crisis Management: no reports, accounts or funder list; the parent names its leadership and takes PayPal and crypto donations.

A project of Pavel Latushka's National Anti-Crisis Management, with preliminary cooperation agreements with Poland's NIMOZ, the Karta Foundation, the Hoover Institution and the Francis Skaryna Library and Museum in London.

f: National cultural institution financed by the Ministry of Culture and National Heritage; some projects co-financed from the state budget and the EU.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. A 2019 art-world petition opposed director Piotr Bernatowicz's appointment; crowds protested his 'Political Art' show in August 2021. The minister dismissed him in June 2024.
x: Publishes no annual reports or accounts that we found; the partners page shows logos with no dates and the board is not listed.
Its cinema lists Europa Cinemas, CICAE and the Polish arthouse cinema association Stowarzyszenie Kin Studyjnych as partners. No parent beyond the Ministry of Culture is named.

f: 2025 budget PLN 9.6M: 76% base grant including the city's, 13% earmarked grants, 8% national grant programmes (Ministry of Culture), 2% own revenue, 0% outside sponsors.
w: Municipal gallery network of the City of Wrocław. The Adam Mickiewicz Institute funded its Milan Triennale show in 2025.
x: Its public bulletin posts annual reports 2021 to 2025 naming grant funders; budget shares only, no full accounts, and no governing board is listed.
A municipal institution of four galleries that co-organises the WRO Media Art Biennale, the Nowe Horyzonty exhibitions and Studio Queer, and meets with the former BWA gallery network.

f: Cultural institution of the Łódź Voivodeship self-government, co-financed by the Minister of Culture and National Heritage. It seeks paying partners through its 'partner ms' programme.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment, Protest or boycott. Culture ministry dismissed director Jarosław Suchan in April 2022 with no explanation; Guggenheim, MoMA and Tate directors and Polish artists protested in letters.
x: Calendar 2023 income PLN 26.0M: about 94 percent public subsidies (budget subsidy 16.9M plus other grants 7.6M), 4 percent sales of goods; no donations line (profit and loss account).
Posts activity reports for 2016 to 2025, profit and loss accounts for 2016 to 2023 and its 15-member museum council; no named funder list.
Runs the Herbst Palace Museum as a branch, shares the Łódź Voivodeship parent with seven regional institutions, and has worked with MoMA's Post platform since 2013. Member of CIMAM.

f: Caixa Geral de Depósitos (state bank) gave EUR 6.45M in 2025, EUR 3.2M for operations. Own revenue of EUR 2.27M came from Fidelidade, EU funds, patrons, tickets and rentals.
w: Foundation instituted by CGD; it also manages the CGD art collection. Closed 2025 with a result of EUR 19,603.
x: FY2025 income EUR 8.64M: about 74 percent donation from founder Caixa Geral de Depósitos (state-owned bank), 14 percent other donations, 9 percent sales and services (audited accounts, note 17).
It posts reports and audited accounts for 2004 to 2025, a yearly funder table with amounts for 2009 to 2025, and its named board.
The cultural arm of Fundação Caixa Geral de Depósitos, with a Porto venue, care of the bank's 1,800-work art collection and a place in the Rede Portuguesa de Arte Contemporânea.

f: Ferré-Rangel and Fonalledas families, Fundación Ángel Ramos, 700+ individuals. Gala sponsors: Banco Popular, Genera PR (New Fortress Energy, 2023), Puma Energy (2019). 2024-25 Form 990: government grants 58%, earnings <1%.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. New Fortress Energy's subsidiary Genera PR runs Puerto Rico's thermal power plants. The sponsors page also lists Puma Energy, a fuel company (2019).
x: FY2024-25 income USD 16.2M: about 58 percent government grants, 37 percent other donations and gifts, under 1 percent earned; investment income is 529k (Form 990, Part VIII).
Posts annual reports for 2022-23 and 2023-24 and a named sponsor list with 2019 gala tiers; no accounts on its site, but the operating foundation's Form 990 is public.
Founded by Luis A. Ferré's foundation in 1957 and accredited by the American Alliance of Museums since 1987.

n: Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Puerto Rico
f: FY2025 revenue $4.9M. Funders on the 2026 sponsor page: NEA, IMLS, Mellon, Ford, Luce, Wallace, Teiger, Banco Popular, Walmart and The Macallan. Getty Foundation co-funded a 2023 curator grant.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Walmart paid over $282M in 2019 to settle US foreign-corruption charges. Mellon, Ford, Getty and Terra funded the 2023 grant together.
x: FY2024-25 income USD 4.95M: about 18 percent government grants, 56 percent donations and gifts, 4 percent earned, 22 percent rents, event income and other revenue (Form 990, Part VIII).
Form 990 filings for 2020 to 2024 are on ProPublica; its sponsorship page shows three undated logos, and its board and team pages return 404.

f: 2023: no permanent private or state funding and no annual budget, per its programme director. In 2017 patron Rinat Mardanov and landlord Yakov Margulis paid for launch and reconstruction.
w: The Goethe-Institut was a partner on Unsound in 2017, and the Tatarstan culture ministry backed the book festival. Neither is a current funder.
x: No reports, funder list or board on its site; statutory accounts for 2017 to 2025 are public in the Russian state accounting register.

f: Krasnoyarsk Krai: subsidy of 40-50m RUB a year, 70-80% of budget (2019). Rest from earnings, grants, local business. Mikhail Prokhorov Foundation co-created its library and funded a 2020 programme.
w: Foundation founder Mikhail Prokhorov has been on Ukraine's NSDC sanctions list since 19 Oct 2022; he is on no US, EU or UK list.
x: FY2024 income RUB 181.6M: about 80 percent Krasnoyarsk Krai subsidies (state task, other-purpose and capital), 20 percent own earnings, under 1 percent gifts (form 0503721, 2024).
A regional budget museum: its Documents page posts public reports 2016 to 2025 and balance sheets 2023 and 2024; no funder list or board.
It belongs to the Russian national committee of ICOM; its founder and owner is the Krasnoyarsk Krai Ministry of Culture, a government body that is skipped.

f: Private museum paid for by founder Natalia Opaleva's own money, including a $7.5M mansion (Forbes, 2016). She then held 20.36% of gold miner Vysochaishy and was vice-president of Lanta-Bank.
w: Lanta-Bank is under US, EU and UK sanctions; Vysochaishy under US and EU sanctions. Opaleva herself is on no list.
x: This private museum's site has no annual reports, accounts, funder list or board; press says its founder funds it from her own money.
Its one standing tie is the AZ/ART centre in the Maroseika chambers, founded by the same patron, Natalia Opaleva.

f: Self-funded from the Oktyabr technical-paper mill and studio rents, with the owner's support; no large outside investors (director Asya Filippova, 2016).
w: Free entry to exhibitions. Asya Filippova has led the centre since it opened in 2005.
x: This private creative cluster's site posts no annual reports, accounts, funder list or board; it describes tenants, studios and programmes only.

Its About page names one institutional tie, membership of the Trans Europe Halles network since 2008, and says its first show in 2005 belonged to the First Moscow Biennale. Member of Trans Europe Halles.

n: Moscow International Biennale of Contemporary Art
f: Private biennale foundation (Yulia Muzykantskaya); sponsor roster not published; 2022 edition hosted by the state Tretyakov Gallery.
w: The Ministry of Culture cancelled the 9th edition on 3 Nov 2022, citing 'controversial content'. It was due to open 7 Nov. No edition since.
x: No working site. The foundation's accounts for 2021, 2023 and 2025 are in the state register; it publishes no reports, funders or board.
Press names the State Tretyakov Gallery as host of its cancelled 2022 edition. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: Moscow city government, through the Department of Culture, since the 1999 opening. Founder Zurab Tsereteli died in April 2025. Patron and donor programme; no sponsor names published.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. Cancelled a student show in July 2022 over 'political subtext'; iStories says Culture Department orders reached curators, and artists' works were painted over.
x: Calendar 2025 income RUB 714.5M: about 94 percent Moscow city subsidies, 6 percent paid services, under 1 percent gratuitous receipts (plan execution reports, form 0503737).
Posts a 2025 results report and balance sheets for 2015 to 2025, but names no sponsors or board; only management is listed.
Runs the Sidur, Nalbandyan and Tsereteli museum-workshops as branches, and co-ran the ARCA project with Ruarts Foundation from 2019 to 2026.

f: Founded by Boris Mints (O1 Group), who cannot fund it as before. Trustee Vladimir Voronin (FSK Group) since Feb 2024. About 40% of budget is admissions (2023); rest partners, donors.
w: National Bank Trust, 99% owned by Russia's central bank, sues founder Boris Mints and sons for $850m in London; they deny fraud.
x: The site shows tiered partner logos without names or dates and no reports or board; accounts for 2024 and 2025 are in the state register.
Its About page states membership of ICOM since 2015; its owner entity is the company RUSIMP, which is skipped as a company.

n: Arsenal, Volga-Vyatka branch of the Pushkin Museum
f: Federal via the Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts (branch since 2020); three-year cooperation agreement with Nizhny Novgorod region signed 15 Nov 2024.
w: Founder-director Anna Gor became a Pushkin deputy director; Alexander Komarov now heads the branch. No local sponsor list.
x: Its parent museum posts reports and accounts for 2012 to 2025 on bus.gov.ru; the branch names its partners, undated, and the parent its trustees.
The Volga-Vyatka branch of the Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts, whose only other branch is in Tomsk; it co-organises a graphics festival with the Nizhny Novgorod State Art Museum.

f: Artist-run autonomous non-profit founded 2015 by Artem Filatov; grants, ticket/catalogue sales and donated artworks; a Garage Museum grant funds its archive.
w: Nine resident artists; collaborates with Garage on archiving the Nizhny Novgorod scene.
x: This artist-run studio's site names its team and takes donations but posts no annual reports, accounts, funder list or board.

f: Regional state (GKBUK; founder Ministry of Culture of Perm Krai); founded 2009 under governor Chirkunov with Marat Gelman and sponsor Sergei Gordeev; new building on Krisanova St since 2024.
w: FSB searched the museum and director Nailya Allakhverdieva's home on 21 Nov 2024 in a terrorism-justification case against founder Gelman. Allakhverdieva left.
x: FY2025 income RUB 124.6M: about 94 percent Perm Krai subsidies (state task 109.3M plus targeted funds 8.1M), 6 percent own earnings, no gifts recorded (form 0503721, 2025).
A regional state museum: its Documents page posts results reports 2019 to 2025 with a balance sheet; it names no funders and no board.

f: Perm Krai government; its Ministry of Culture is founder. Sber is general partner of the opening season and the Potanin Foundation backs a 2026-2028 programme.
w: Flags: Sanctions. Sber is on US, EU and UK sanctions lists. Vladimir Potanin, whose foundation backs the programme, is sanctioned by the US and UK.
x: Calendar 2025 income RUB 261.4M: about 98 percent Perm Krai subsidies (156M of it for other purposes), 1 percent paid services, 1 percent gratuitous receipts (2025 execution report).
Posts a 2025 results report and 2025 financial results report, with plans back to 2022; no sponsor list and no board.

f: Private: founded 2010 by Marina Varvarina (widow of Orimi tea-and-coffee group owner Dmitry Varvarin); the museum states it has never taken state support, grants or sponsors.
w: 12,000 sq m, c. 40 exhibitions a year; c. US$30–35m invested in the building. No sanctions match for Varvarina on OpenSanctions.
x: The museum states it takes no state money, grants or sponsors; its site posts no annual reports, accounts, funder list or board.

f: St Petersburg city budget institution under the Committee for Culture. Its site lists partners and sponsors including PhosAgro, VTB Bank, PSB, Rosseti Lenenergo and Bank Saint Petersburg.
w: Flags: Sanctions, Arms and defence, State censorship or punishment. Treasury sanctioned VTB and PSB in 2022; PSB finances Russia's defense industry. Artists told Novaya Gazeta Manege barred or retitled works in 2024.
x: Names partners and sponsors in text with no date and lists a four-member supervisory board; posts only a 2025 task report and a financial plan.
Its partnership page names the Hermitage, Russian Museum, Pushkin Museum, Tretyakov Gallery and ten more museums as cultural partners, plus the Repin Academy of Arts.

f: Self-managed artists' commune since 1989 under the Free Culture Fellowship. No funder list is published; it gave its collection of about 5,000 items to the state in 2023.
w: Founders Rybakov and Orlov told Novaya Gazeta that Manege barred one work and demanded a retitle for another in the 2024 show.
x: Its People page has a board (Pravlenie) group, but it posts no annual reports, accounts or funder list.
Grew from the Free Culture Fellowship, which set up its Museum of Nonconformist Art in 1998; a member of Trans Europe Halles and Res Artis since 1995. Member of Res Artis, Trans Europe Halles.

f: Founded 2013 by Alexander Mechetin, co-owner of the Novabev Group (spirits); Novabev lists Zarya in its corporate responsibility programme. Partners include the State Tretyakov Gallery.
w: Novabev is a spirits group; alcohol is not a flag category. OpenSanctions search shows no sanctions entry for Mechetin or Novabev.
x: Its partners page shows undated logos under three headings; the site posts no reports, accounts or board, and names no legal entity.
Its About page names the Tretyakov Gallery, MMOMA, the Shchusev and Mayakovsky museums, the Cinema Museum and ROSIZO as partners; residency partners include How Art Museum and HIAP.

f: State budgetary institution of Voronezh Oblast, run on annual state assignments. The federal 'Culture' national project paid for storage cabinets in 2023.
w: Governor Aleksandr Gusev heads the funding region; he is on US (2023), EU (2023) and UK (2024) sanctions lists.
x: FY2024 receipts RUB 69.6M, of which RUB 12.5M, about 18 percent, is the museum's own income from paid activity; the report does not itemise the rest.
It posts yearly reports 2020 to 2024 and annual financial plans 2022 to 2025, but names no funders and shows no board.

n: Ural Industrial Biennial of Contemporary Art
f: Ural branch of the National Centre for Contemporary Arts, part of the Pushkin Museum since 2020. 6th edition (2021) budget ~100m RUB. Residencies sought Presidential Fund for Cultural Initiatives grants.
w: The city administration announced the cancellation of the 7th edition in Apr 2023 without explanation. Founder-commissioner Alisa Prudnikova left to run GES-2 (V-A-C).
x: No records of its own were reachable, so this is its parent, the Pushkin Museum: yearly reports and accounts, logo-only sponsors, named trustees.

The biennial grew out of the Ural branch of the Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts, formerly the state centre for contemporary art, which ceased work in October 2025. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: City of Yekaterinburg: the Department of Culture of the city administration is founder of this municipal autonomous museum. Financial reports for 2014-2024 are published; no sponsor list.
w: Five sites including the Hermitage-Ural centre; a supervisory board oversees the museum. Financial reports are scanned images.
x: FY2024 income RUB 249.5M: about 79 percent city assignment and targeted subsidies, 1 percent private gifts, 19 percent own paid services and rent; expenditure RUB 273.4M (Form 0503721).
It posts yearly reports 2014 to 2023, financial results 2014 to 2024 and the supervisory board's composition orders, but no sponsor list.
Runs three branches, the Hermitage-Ural centre, the Museum of Naive Art and the Denisov-Uralsky stone-cutting centre; Hermitage-Ural hosts temporary shows from the State Hermitage Museum.

f: Financed by the Senegalese state through the culture ministry; its sponsors page names the Prime Minister's office, City of Dakar, UNESCO, ECOWAS, Ecobank, SUNU Group and Sococim (cement).
w: The 16th edition runs 19 November to 19 December 2026. The 2024 edition was postponed, drawing criticism from artists and curators; no sponsor flag.
x: It shows sponsor logos without names or dates and names its 20-member steering committee, but posts no annual reports or accounts.
Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: Senegalese state museum. China financed the building with a CFA 20 billion (over EUR 30M) grant. 2025 own revenue was CFA 353.9M.
w: China's grant paid for the building, not operations. No sponsor, protest or censorship found.
x: Its site did not open from here; a search listing shows a 2025 activity report, and nothing on accounts, funders or board was checked.

f: Founded 2008 by Koyo Kouoh. Partners listed for 2024: Arts Collaboratory, OSIWA, Mellon Foundation, Foundation for Art Initiative, Little Sun, Porticus and Sharjah Art Foundation.
w: Flags: Gulf state body. Sharjah Art Foundation sits under the Government of Sharjah's Department of Culture and Information and is already flagged Gulf state body on this map.
x: The site names five board members and shows five sponsor logos, undated; it posts no reports or accounts.
Took part in the Arts Collaboratory network from its 2013 phase and co-hosted its 2015 Dakar assembly. Founded in 2008 by Koyo Kouoh. Member of Arts Collaboratory.

n: NTU Centre for Contemporary Art Singapore
f: Co-funded by Nanyang Technological University and Singapore's Economic Development Board (2020 reports). SEA AiR residency funded by the European Union.
w: Closed its Gillman Barracks exhibition and residency space in March 2021 after financial restructuring; continues as an NTU research centre.
x: No records of its own; parent NTU posts annual reports 2016 to 2026 with audited accounts; the centre lists its Governing Council.
It belongs to Nanyang Technological University and runs a joint centre with the Max Planck Institute for the History of Science (2026 to 2031).

f: Singapore government base grant of S$1.2m a year, about 30% of costs, plus a rent-free state building (2016, per director). Rest from artwork sales and patrons.
w: Latest funding statement found is the director's 2016 interview. STPI publishes no donor list or accounts; patron tiers start at S$2,500.
x: Its About page names ten board members; it posts no annual reports, accounts or funder list, and the governance page is one paragraph.
A non-profit that its own About page places with National Gallery Singapore and Singapore Art Museum in the national Visual Arts Cluster.

f: FY23/24: state (Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth) plus Mapletree, Singapore Tourism Board, CHARLES & KEITH Foundation, New Carlsberg Foundation (alcohol).
w: Board member Pierre Lorinet is a director of oil trader Trafigura (joined 1 Jul 2024). Roster is from FY23/24; the FY24/25 report was not found.
x: FY2025-26 income SGD 35.5M: about 61 percent government grants, 13 percent donations, 24 percent other grants, 1 percent earned (audited statements p. 26, Singapore Biennale year).
Its About page posts audited annual reports for FY2015 to FY2025, a named board, and the FY2025 report lists donors and sponsors.

Singapore's first art museum, which STPI's page places with STPI and National Gallery Singapore in the national Visual Arts Cluster; SAM's own About page names no institutional partner. Member of CIMAM. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

n: MGLC International Centre of Graphic Arts
f: Public institute founded by the City of Ljubljana, funded from its budget. 36th Biennale (2025) backed by the Ministry of Culture, Pro Helvetia, Mondriaan Fund and Danish Arts Foundation.
w: Organises the Ljubljana Biennale of Graphic Arts. Its 2025 edition lists TBA21 and Schering Stiftung as partners, and Delo and Kaval Group among local backers.
x: It lists its Board of Trustees and a founding-supporters roll from its creation, posts no annual reports, and its AJPES filings were not opened.
Independent since 1985, when it took over the Graphic Biennale from founding supporter Moderna galerija; it belongs to IBA, ICOM, CIMAM and the Slovenian Museum Association. Member of CIMAM.

f: Slovenian Ministry of Culture: up to EUR 2.07m from the state budget for its 2022 programme, plus up to EUR 100,000 for the Venice Biennale pavilion.
w: Founded by government decree in 1947 as the national museum of modern art. Its site has no sponsor page.
x: FY2024 income EUR 2.69M; on the cash statement of EUR 2.64M, about 91 percent is state budget and EU funds, 8 percent other non-tax revenue (annual report pp. 57-58).
Its public-information page posts annual reports 2020 to 2024 in the AJPES finance format and names the council, but lists no sponsors.

Runs the Museum of Contemporary Art Metelkova as its second site, handed its Graphic Biennale to MGLC in 1985, and lists Slovenian museums, two universities and L'Internationale as partners. Member of L'Internationale.

f: National public entity, an agency of the Department of Arts and Culture (now Sport, Arts and Culture). No corporate sponsor is named on its site.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment, Protest or boycott. In December 2025 management covered 11 works in Steven Cohen's retrospective the night before opening. SWEAT and Sisonke protested Mthethwa's work in December 2016.
x: FY2025-26 revenue ZAR 239.6M for Iziko Museums of South Africa, the gallery's parent: about 54 percent government grants, 33 percent state property in kind, 3 percent sponsorship, 6 percent earned.
Posts annual reports from 2003/04 to 2025/26 with audited statements and donor sections, and names its nine-member council; the site itself lists no donors.
Part of Iziko Museums of South Africa, alongside the South African Museum, Slave Lodge, Bo-Kaap Museum, Bertram House and Koopmans-De Wet house.

f: Property investor Louis Norval financed it entirely at the 2018 opening and set up a capital fund. Sponsors include Schroders (art prize), Stonehage Fleming (2021 auction) and Sanlam.
w: A capital fund and earned income are meant to make it self-sustaining. No fossil, arms or gambling sponsor found.
x: It names its twelve trustees on the About page but posts no annual reports, accounts or funder list.
Norval's news page describes a multi-year collaboration with the Irma Stern Trust, which holds the artist's estate, on a four-part series of Irma Stern exhibitions.

f: Jochen Zeitz donated the collection he had loaned; sponsors include Gucci and BMW, the Mellon Foundation funds fellowships, and the board now pays.
w: Director Mark Coetzee resigned in 2018 amid misconduct allegations and sued; this concerns staff, not a funder or board figure.
x: Its supporters page names corporate members, founders and sponsors including the Mellon Foundation and BMW, undated, but it posts no reports, accounts or board.
An independent non-profit; its US supporting body, American Friends of Zeitz MOCAA, was founded in 2017 with the museum's opening. Its pages name no parent institution.

f: Owned and run by the City of Johannesburg; no corporate sponsor is named. Johannesburg Heritage Foundation and Friends of JAG back a fully funded rescue plan.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. Johannesburg Heritage Foundation and Friends of JAG sent the City a legal demand on 28 August 2024 and weighed an interdict on 25 January 2025.
x: Publishes no annual reports, accounts, funders or board of its own; the City of Johannesburg runs the gallery and the Heritage Foundation posts rescue updates.
Backed by the Johannesburg Heritage Foundation and Friends of JAG, whom the City of Johannesburg asked in 2025 to sign a formal partnership agreement over the gallery.

f: Wits campus museum, opened 2006; its Rock Art Research Institute is funded by the National Research Foundation, Wits' research fund and Anglo American's Chairman's Fund. No centre funder list.
w: No page names a donor or sponsor of the centre itself. The draft's Arcadia and arts-department funding has no source.
x: The centre has no records of its own; parent Wits University posts annual reports 2006 to 2025 with audited accounts and lists its Council.
A museum on the West campus of the University of the Witwatersrand, showing rock art from Wits's Rock Art Research Institute. Wits Art Museum belongs to the same university.

f: University of the Witwatersrand museum. Standard Bank has been collection partner since 1978 and 1979; early donors include Norman Herber, Jack Ginsberg, John Schlesinger and Gertrude Posel.
w: No fossil, arms or gambling sponsor named. The May 2024 Wits encampment concerned university policy, not this museum.
x: The museum has no records of its own; its parent Wits University posts annual reports 2006 to 2025 with financial statements and lists its Council.
A museum of the University of the Witwatersrand, set in its Cultural Precinct; it also hosts the Jack Ginsberg Centre for Book Arts, opened in 2019.

f: 2026 edition run by the Busan Biennale Organizing Committee for Busan Metropolitan City, with BNK Busan Bank, Shinsegae, Naver and Danish, Dutch and UK cultural funds.
w: Bank (BNK Busan Bank), retail (Shinsegae) and media (Naver) money named; no sponsor protest found in English or Korean searches.
x: It posts yearly public-interest settlement filings for 2023 to 2025 and names its officers and auditors, but no annual reports or sponsor list.
The 2026 edition is run by the Busan Biennale Organizing Committee and held at Busan Museum of Contemporary Art, a former school and a former warehouse. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: Municipal museum run by Busan Metropolitan City, reopened in 2026 after a 46.9bn-won rebuild; patrons' society members include BNK Busan Bank and Hwaseung Group.
w: Curatorial dispute, Sept 2026: Korea Economic Daily called its reopening exhibition on defector and socialist-affiliated artists one-sided.
x: One undated page names patrons' society members such as BNK Busan Bank and Hwaseung Group; it posts no reports, accounts or board.
Its own pages name one annex, Space Lee Ufan, and no parent body, network or partner museum. Member of CIMAM, Gallery Climate Coalition.

f: Busan Metropolitan City: its ordinance names the mayor as operator. Free entry except special shows, capped at 15,000 won. Opened June 2018.
w: Museum on Eulsukdo; second director Kang Seung-wan since June 2022. Its site menu has no sponsor page.
x: The museum site has no annual reports, accounts, sponsor list or board; it only shows an organisation chart and the governing ordinance.
The city's second municipal art museum after Busan Museum of Art, and a venue of the 2026 Busan Biennale. Member of Gallery Climate Coalition.

f: 2024: hosted by Changwon City and Changwon Culture Foundation; backed by Culture Ministry, Gyeongnam Province, KICOX, BNK Kyongnam Bank, Gyeongnam Mecenat Association. 2026 host unchanged.
w: 2024 edition drew 107,710 visitors. The 2026 edition runs 30 Sep to 15 Nov; its supporter list was not found.
x: Parent Changwon Culture Foundation posts accounts 2016 to 2025 and officer rosters, but no annual reports or funder list.
The Changwon Culture Foundation lists the biennale among its culture projects and posts its 2026 edition notice; Changwon City is the other host. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: Executive agency of South Korea's Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism since 2015. Its planning division builds and spends the state budget; the ACC Foundation shares operations.
w: Opened November 2015 in Gwangju. Its site menu has no sponsor or donor page.
x: Its site posts yearly introduction brochures and programme guides but no financial reports, funder list or board.
A responsibility operating agency of the culture ministry; the ACC Foundation, linked from its site, runs the ACC Children's Culture Centre and the culture shop.

f: Non-profit association (2019); 2026 shows supported by Arts Council Korea, supervised by Seoul Metropolitan Government, plus individual LOOP's Friends donors.
w: Dec 2025 Euljiro move drew a public gentrification inquiry from Cheonggyecheon-Euljiro Preservation Alliance and others.
x: Its Support page names its chairs, directors, auditor and 44 individual donors, undated, but it posts no reports or accounts.

f: Corporate museum run directly by Amorepacific Corp (site footer, 2026); cosmetics money. Current LeWitt show co-organised with MOT Tokyo.
w: Single funder: Amorepacific cosmetics. No sponsor protest found.
x: The museum posts nothing itself; its parent Amorepacific posts audit reports 2015 to 2024, sustainability reports 2017 to 2025 and its board.

f: Private museum founded by collector Kim Chang-il (CI Kim), funded by his Arario Corporation (bus terminal, retail, galleries).
w: Founder-funder Kim Chang-il got a 2-year sentence for breach of duty (Daejeon court, Feb 2021); the group said it would appeal.
x: The museum site shows only its philosophy, exhibitions and visitor information, with no reports, accounts, funders or board.
One of the Arario museums; the other site is Arario Museum Jeju, in the Tapdong Cinema, Tapdong Bike Shop and Dongmun Motel buildings.

f: State-run: operated by Arts Council Korea (national arts body, est. 1973) alongside its theatres and archive; no corporate sponsors listed.
w: Parent Arts Council Korea gave grant juries a political blacklist of artists in 2015; exposed in a National Assembly inspection.
x: No records of its own; parent Arts Council Korea posts reports 2019 to 2025, lists its council and files accounts on ALIO.
Run by Arts Council Korea, which also runs the Arko and Daehangno Arts Theatre, Arko Arts Archive, Artists' House and a training institute. Member of CIMAM.

f: Private museum founded 1998. Its site links the Daewoo Foundation, funded mainly by Daewoo chairman Kim Woo Choong since 1978, and invites corporate sponsors but names no funders.
w: No source ties the Daewoo Foundation to the centre's budget, and no sponsor list is published.
x: Its site posts no annual reports, accounts, sponsor names or board; it links the Daewoo Foundation and invites corporate sponsors only.
Its parent is the Art Sonje Museum in Gyeongju, founded in 1991 by the same founder.

f: Run by the Ilmin Cultural Foundation, a non-profit founded in 1994 in memory of Dong-A Ilbo president Kim Sang-man; the newspaper entrusted works to the collection.
w: No budget, donor or sponsor list found. The draft's newspaper-family funds claim has no source.
x: Its site and foundation page carry history, awards and collection notes only: no annual reports, accounts, sponsors or board.
Run by the Ilmin Cultural Foundation, a non-profit founded in 1994 in memory of Dong-A Ilbo president Kim Sang-man.

f: State museum. Hyundai Motor sponsored its series from 2014 to February 2024; LG Electronics sponsors the OLED Series from 2025. The Lee Kun-hee estate gave nearly 1,500 works in 2021.
w: Flags: Forced or exploited labour. Hyundai Motor sponsored its series to February 2024. Reuters found children as young as 12 at Hyundai subsidiary SMART Alabama in 2022.
x: The state museum posts no annual report, accounts, sponsor list or board on its site; its sponsorship page points to a separate foundation site.
Runs four venues: Seoul, Gwacheon, Deoksugung and Cheongju. The pages read name no network, university or partner museum. Member of CIMAM, Res Artis.

f: Seoul Metropolitan Government museum; Hana Financial Group co-funds SeMA-Hana Art Award; patrons' association SeMA人[in] since 2014.
w: June 2025 censorship row (critic's martial-law essay cut from catalogue). Patrons' board includes SK Group and MBK Partners.
x: Its patrons' page names the SeMA人[in] directors, including Hana Financial and MBK Partners executives, undated; it posts no reports, accounts or board.
Runs eight branches: Seosomun main building, Buk-Seoul, Seo-Seoul, Nam-Seoul, Art Archives, Photography, Nanji Residency and Paik Ground. Member of CIMAM. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: Private museum run by the Whanki Foundation, set up by the artist's widow Kim Hyang-an. No funder list or accounts found; the museum site fails its certificate check.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. In May 2026 residents and the Seoul Environment Alliance protested after herbicide was injected into a 200-year-old ginkgo beside the museum. It apologised.
x: The site posts yearly donation-use statements for 2017 to 2024; it has no reports or donor list and names only a chair and director.

f: Gyeonggi Province, through the Gyeonggi Cultural Foundation. Hyundai Motor sponsors its Trans-Local exhibition series (KRW 600M over three years, announced 2025). Free admission.
w: Flags: Forced or exploited labour. Hyundai subsidiary SMART Alabama hired children as young as 12 (Reuters, 2022). Same Hyundai ruling as MMCA applies.
x: Its parent foundation posts yearbooks for 2012 to 2025, settlement papers and a named board; the centre shows sponsor logos only, undated.
Run by the Gyeonggi Cultural Foundation, which also runs the Gyeonggi Museum of Modern Art, Gyeonggi Museum, Silhak Museum, Jeongok Prehistory Museum and children's museums.

f: 2025 grants EUR 2.76m: Spanish Ministry of Culture 1.17m, Generalitat de Catalunya 0.88m, Barcelona City Council 0.52m, Diputacio de Barcelona 0.15m. Budgeted income EUR 3.50m.
w: Grants are 79% of 2025 budgeted income. Trustees include the artist's family and Generalitat and city appointees.
x: FY2024 activity income EUR 2.87M: about 69 percent public grants, 6 percent donations and sponsors, 26 percent earned (audited accounts 2024, lines 1 and 6).
It posts annual reports of activities for 2025 and 2026, audit reports 2015 to 2024, a grants table to 2025 and names its trustees.
Shares the Articket BCN pass with five Barcelona museums: Museu Picasso, MNAC, MACBA, CCCB and Fundació Joan Miró. Its pages name no parent body. Member of CIMAM.

f: Private foundation; Generalitat, Barcelona council and Culture Ministry sit on its board. Strategic allies: Fundación BBVA, Fundació la Caixa, Puig. Also Fundació Banc Sabadell, Abertis, Sorigué, Damm.
w: la Caixa's holding Criteria is the largest shareholder of gas utility Naturgy, which paid 23% of Criteria's 2025 dividends.
x: FY2025 income EUR 12.0M: about 31 percent official grants, 15 percent other grants, donations and sponsorship, 54 percent earned from tickets, shop, services and rentals (audited accounts, income statement).
It posts annual reports for 2023 and 2024 and audited accounts, naming funders and trustees inside the 2024 report.

f: Private museum run by the Chillida family. Hauser & Wirth, which represents the estate, gave financial support for the 2019 reopening. Gipuzkoa council lent storage during works; no sponsors named.
w: Corporate sponsor page lists tiers from EUR 2,000 a year but no names. Partial closure from 2011 over a recurring deficit; full reopening April 2019.
x: Its site shows sponsorship tiers from 2,000 euros a year but names no funders, and posts no reports, accounts or board.
Part of a four-museum visitor alliance with Centro Botín, the Bilbao Fine Arts Museum and the Museum of the University of Navarra; the artist's estate holds the site copyright.

f: State museum. Corporate patrons: Inditex, Fundación la Caixa, Fundación Mapfre, Fundación Mutua Madrileña. Partners include Estrella Damm, HP, Iberia, Madrid city and region.
w: la Caixa's holding Criteria is the largest shareholder of gas utility Naturgy, 23% of its 2025 dividends. No Repsol, Endesa or Iberdrola listed.
x: FY2025 income EUR 42.6M excluding capital transfers: about 68 percent state transfers and EU, 3 percent named corporate and foundation gifts, 22 percent tickets and services (accounts 2025, note 14.1).
It posts annual activity reports 2002 to 2025, yearly accounts, a named sponsors page and the Real Patronato members.

Runs the Palacio de Velázquez and Palacio de Cristal in Retiro Park; the Museo Reina Sofía Foundation lends it a collection and a separate friends foundation supports it. Member of Bizot group, CIMAM, Gallery Climate Coalition, L'Internationale.

f: 3.5M visitors (2025). Benefactors Fundación BBVA (2025) and Fundación AXA (2024); Fundación Iberdrola España funds fellowships to 2027; Fundación Endesa, Rassini and la Caixa (to 2025) fund projects.
w: Utilities Iberdrola (66% renewable capacity) and Endesa fund programmes; both sell gas. la Caixa's holding Criteria owns 28.5% of gas utility Naturgy.
x: The Prado posts yearly reports since 2002, audited accounts, its Royal Board of Trustees and sponsor logos by tier, undated.

n: CA2M Centro de Arte Dos de Mayo
f: Comunidad de Madrid, as a museum of its Culture, Tourism and Sport department: 2024 budget EUR 1.45m for programming plus EUR 500,000 for art purchases.
w: Staff are employees of the regional culture department. Holds the Comunidad de Madrid collection and the Fundacion ARCO collection. No sponsor list published.
x: Its transparency page holds only a 2024 organigram and budget; it posts no reports, accounts, funder list or board.
A museum of the Comunidad de Madrid that houses the ARCO Foundation Collection alongside the regional CA2M Collection.

f: Govern balear, Consell de Mallorca, Palma council and Fundació d'Art Serra form the foundation. Sponsors: Fundació Baleària, Caixa Colonya, El Corte Inglés, Summum Hotel Group, Hotel Saratoga.
w: Sponsor names come from the collaborators page. No energy, tobacco, arms or gambling name appears. No protest or censorship found.
x: FY2025 income EUR 3.27M: about 78 percent public (Govern, Consell de Mallorca, Palma, state), 3 percent private sponsors and grants, 19 percent earned (audited accounts, notes 13 and 15).
It posts annual reports 2007 to 2025 and accounts 2004 to 2025 with audits, a sponsor logo page, and names its Board of Trustees.
Governed by the Es Baluard Foundation, whose board brings together the Balearic government, Consell de Mallorca, Palma council, the culture ministry and the Fundació d'Art Serra. Member of CIMAM.

f: Public company owned by Donostia city council, Gipuzkoa council and the Basque Government, five board seats each. 2025 income EUR 1.87m; Basque culture department nominal grants.
w: Former state tobacco factory (1913-2003), bought by the three bodies. Its 2025 annual report names no tobacco company.
x: FY2025 own income EUR 1.87M against spending of EUR 7.45M; the owners' contribution that covers the gap is not itemised in the report (memoria 2025, p. 64).
It posts annual reports 2020 to 2025 with income and spending tables, a 2024 budget and its named board, but no funder list.
A public cultural centre in Donostia; its cinema pages list the Elías Querejeta Zine Eskola film school and carry the Basque Film Archive's programme. Member of European Media Art Platform.

f: 2024: Diputacion Foral de Alava EUR 2.53m, Basque Government EUR 1.72m, Spanish Ministry of Culture EUR 150,000, Vitoria-Gasteiz city EUR 130,000.
w: Run by a foundation; the Alava council owns the building. The Basque Government gave EUR 200,000 in 2024 for Shared Collection purchases.
x: FY2024 operating income EUR 4.53M, of which EUR 4.40M is activity income (grants, donations, sponsorship; not split in the registry) and EUR 0.12M commercial sales.
It posts activity reports 2019 to 2025, audited accounts 2019 to 2025, sponsor logos without dates, and names its Patronato.

f: Run by the independent Fold Media Collective. Named: founding partners Goethe-Institut, British Council and Alliance Française, plus individual Friends. The page's 33 partner and patron logos carry no names.
w: Cinnamon Hotels was title sponsor in the 2010s. The Gujral Foundation is a long-term partner. The ASAP grant in the old text is not found.
x: Its Partners page names founding partners and eleven Friends in text, undated; most patron logos have no names, and no reports, accounts or board.
Its founding partners are EUNIC Sri Lanka's members, the Goethe-Institut, British Council and Alliance Française de Kotte.

n: Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art Sri Lanka
f: Non-profit set up in 2019, with no fixed venue. Founding Patrons are individuals; the John Keells Foundation was named primary sponsor in March 2020.
w: John Keells Holdings, the foundation's parent, developed the City of Dreams Sri Lanka resort (opened August 2025); Melco manages the casino with JKH.
x: FY2024-25 income LKR 102.7M: about 99.8 percent donations and sponsorship (founder patrons 27.2M, other sponsorship 75.2M); no government or earned income line (audited statements, pp. 3, 11).
It posts its 2025/26 audit report, names its board, and lists Founding Patrons for 2026; no earlier annual reports are linked.

f: Run by Lund municipality's culture and leisure committee. The municipal council approved an SEK 86M rebuild in Aug 2026, with the hall closed for 18 months.
w: No sponsors or private funders are listed. The site states it is part of Lund municipality. No funder controversy found.
