x: No records of its own; parent Lund municipality posts annual reports 2024 and 2025 and lists its culture committee; no funder list.
A municipal konsthall that works regularly with Skissernas Museum, Kulturen i Lund and Galleri Aura, and is supported by the independent association Lunds konsthalls vänner.

f: Part of Malmö stad's culture department and funded by the city. The Swedish Inheritance Fund (Allmänna Arvsfonden) gave SEK 6M for the Studio Syd artist centre, 2025-27.
w: Free entry. No sponsors are listed on its site. No funder controversy found.
x: No records of its own; parent Malmö stad posts its 2025 annual report with accounts; no funder list, no board found.
Part of the City of Malmö's culture department; it runs Studio KOAS for artists with disabilities, and Skånes Konstförening's members started the 1931 foundation behind the gallery.

f: Run non-profit under the Bonnier Group. The Jeanette Bonnier Foundation, set up after her death in 2016, supports its financing and development.
w: Grew out of the Maria Bonnier Dahlin Foundation, founded 1985 by Jeanette Bonnier. Its site lists no outside sponsors.
x: No records of its own; parent Bonnier posts annual reviews 2015 to 2025, accounts 2016 to 2025 and its board; the konsthall lists no funders.
Grew out of the Maria Bonnier Dahlin Foundation, set up in 1985 by Jeanette Bonnier; its pages name no network or partner institution. Member of Gallery Climate Coalition.

f: Robert Weil Family Foundation, funded by the Weil family office Proventus. No outside sponsors or public funders are named on the museum or foundation sites.
w: Founded 1987 by David Neuman and Robert Weil. Runs a Jaffa branch since 2018. No protest or censorship found.
x: The museum posts nothing; its funding Weil Foundation names four board members but no reports, accounts or outside donors.
Works under the Robert Weil Family Foundation, runs the satellite Magasin III Jaffa, and backs Accelerator and the Curating Art master's programme at Stockholm University. Member of CIMAM.

f: SEK 271M income (2025): state 70%, sponsors SEK 1.07M. Sponsors: Bank of America, Bloomberg, PwC, Jung, Patriksson, a wine and spirits supplier; partners Hotel Skeppsholmen, Panasonic Connect.
w: Sponsor Bloomberg: more than 260 UK artists asked five London theatres to drop Bloomberg Philanthropies in May 2026. Moderna Museet was not named.
x: FY2025 income SEK 271.4M: about 75 percent public (state appropriation 70 percent), 3 percent private including sponsorship, 22 percent earned (annual report 2025, pp. 40, 47-48).
It posts annual reports 2015 to 2025 with accounts, names sponsors and partners on its support page, and lists its Board of Trustees.
A state museum with a Malmö branch, born from Nationalmuseum's modern collection in 1958; ArkDes and the Public Art Agency are to be merged into it. Member of CIMAM.

f: 2022 income SEK 37.3m: Umeå University 22.6m, Umeå municipality 5.0m, Fort Knox 3.0m, Culture Ministry 0.8m, Region Västerbotten 0.5m.
w: University museum of Umeå University. Umeå municipality gave SEK 5.0m in both 2019 and 2022; Fort Knox is credited on named exhibitions.
x: FY2024 income SEK 35.7M: about 95 percent public (Umeå University 26.0M, Umeå municipality 5.0M, state, region and Nordic bodies), 1 percent private foundations, 2 percent earned.
It posts annual reports 2012 to 2022; parent Umeå University posts annual reports 2024 and 2025 and lists its board; no funder list.
A part of Umeå University and the public heart of its Arts campus, beside the Academy of Fine Arts, Institute of Design and School of Architecture.

f: Canton Basel-Stadt CHF 950k a year for 2024-27 (32% of budget); third-party grants about CHF 660k (30%); restaurant and property rent 22%; members 8%.
w: In November 2023 an SVP member of the cantonal parliament demanded subsidy be cut over director Almusibli's ceasefire letters; the canton did not act.
x: FY2025 income CHF 2.92M: about 33 percent canton grant, 9 percent memberships, 24 percent grants not split by funder, 27 percent earned (annual report 2025, p. 161).
It posts annual reports 2014 to 2025 with financial statements, names members and corporate supporters in the 2025 report, and lists its association board.
Run by the Basler Kunstverein, which founded it and built the hall in 1872; its membership also covers entry to the S AM Swiss Architecture Museum.

f: Canton Basel-Stadt and the Emanuel Hoffmann, Christoph Merian and Laurenz foundations. UBS is partner; Novartis, KPMG, Trafina and the Federal Office of Culture are sponsors.
w: UBS paid a $100M Federal Reserve fine in 2004 over dollar dealings with sanctioned states. Novartis paid $678M in 2020 over kickbacks to doctors.
x: FY2025 spending CHF 30.55M: about 69 percent met by the canton's global budget, 19 percent admissions and sales, 12 percent other income and transfers (annual report 2025, p. 62).
It posts annual reports 2010 to 2025 with accounts, names its partner and sponsors undated, and lists its Board of Trustees.

Part of the city's public art collection, with Neubau and Gegenwart as its other venues; the Emanuel Hoffmann Foundation lends contemporary works and co-created Gegenwart in 1980. Member of Gallery Climate Coalition.

f: Roche has paid all operating costs since the museum opened in 1996 as a gift for its centenary; Roche built it and funds collection additions.
w: Roche pleaded guilty in 1999 to a worldwide vitamin price-fixing conspiracy and paid $500M in US criminal fines.
x: The museum has no records of its own; funder Roche posts annual and finance reports 2020 to 2025 and its board; no donor list.
Shows a permanent loan from the Emanuel Hoffmann Foundation; its own pages name no parent institution, network or partner museum. Member of CIMAM, Gallery Climate Coalition.

f: Made possible by the Laurenz Foundation, founded in 1999 by Maja Oeri and Hans U. Bodenmann. The foundation does not give grants; no other funders are named.
w: Herzog & de Meuron built it in 2002-03. The Emanuel Hoffmann Foundation collection is its core.
x: It posts no reports, accounts or donors; its Laurenz Foundation pages name the foundation board and say the foundation makes Schaulager possible.
Run by the Laurenz Foundation; it holds the Emanuel Hoffmann Foundation's collection, which is on loan to the Öffentliche Kunstsammlung Basel, whose delegates sit on that foundation's board.

f: City of Bern pays CHF 1.05M a year (83% of 2025 income). Foundations back shows: Scherbarth, Guggenheim, Gubler-Hablützel. Burgergemeinde Bern and the canton's lottery fund supported building work.
w: 2023: two city-council factions asked about the incoming director's signed Palestine letter. The city grant stayed CHF 1.05M.
x: FY2024 income CHF 1.16M: about 90 percent City of Bern operating grant, 8 percent membership contributions; donations of CHF 96k listed separately (annual report 2024, p. 72).
It posts annual reports 2016 to 2025 with balance sheet and audit report, names funders in the 2025 thanks pages, and lists its board.
Run by an association founded in 1912, backed by the Bernische Kunstgesellschaft, Stiftung Kunsthalle Bern and Berner Kunstfonds; a member pass covers its 24 listed partners.

f: Canton Bern and the Burgergemeinde's museum foundation fund it. UBS is main sponsor; Mobiliar and UNIQA sponsor exhibitions; eight funding foundations include Hansjörg Wyss's Stiftung GegenwART.
w: UBS paid a $100M US Federal Reserve fine in 2004 for dollar trading with Iran and other sanctioned countries.
x: FY2025 operating income CHF 9.14M: about 72 percent public contributions (Canton Bern and the Burgergemeinde's museum foundation), 16 percent earned, 12 percent received gifts and sponsorship (annual report 2025, Betriebsrechnung).
Annual reports 2016 to 2025 with full accounts, an undated partner page naming UBS, sponsors and foundations, and a listed foundation board.
Shares a sponsoring office with Zentrum Paul Klee and works with the Verein der Freunde, Bernische Kunstgesellschaft, Berner Kunstfonds and Stiftung Kunsthalle Bern, which also serve Kunsthalle Bern.

f: Canton of Fribourg, City and Agglomeration of Fribourg, Loterie Romande, Banque Cantonale de Fribourg, the Sandoz family foundation and the Friends association.
w: Loterie Romande is a public lottery, no flag. Partners include the University of Fribourg and Fribourg Tourisme. No protest or censorship found.
x: No annual reports or accounts found; the about page names backers and partners without a date and lists the association committee.
An association-run kunsthalle whose members get free entry at 18 Swiss institutions; it names the museum associations of Fribourg and Switzerland and Université de Fribourg as partners.

f: Logo strip on its 2026 site: a canton BL logo, Münchenstein, Muttenz, Novartis, Basellandschaftliche Kantonalbank, Habasit, Jenzer Fleisch + Feinkost and a hotel. Novartis lists it as a long-standing partner.
w: Novartis paid $678M in July 2020 to settle US claims that it bribed doctors through speaker programmes. No protest at the Kunsthaus found.
x: FY2025 income CHF 1.27M: about 51 percent Canton Basel-Landschaft, 36 percent sponsors, donations, members and the building foundation, 12 percent earned (annual report 2025, Erfolgsrechnung).
Annual reports 2020 to 2025 carry full accounts and a named partner and supporter list; the association board and foundation council are listed.
Founded by the Kunstverein Baselland in 1944 and run under it; Kunstverein members get free entry at 21 named Swiss art institutions.

f: CHF 30M budget. Basel-Stadt and Riehen give about 9%; the Beyeler Foundation covers a 27% deficit. Sponsors include UBS (Artist Talks) and Globus.
w: UBS paid a $100M US Federal Reserve fine in 2004 for dollar trading with Iran and other sanctioned countries.
x: No annual reports or accounts found; sponsors appear as unlabelled undated logos, and the team page does not list a foundation board.
Grew from the Beyeler Foundation, set up in 1982 to hold the collection; the new Wyss Museum building joined the ensemble in 2026. Member of CIMAM.

f: 2024 income CHF 684k: Stadt St.Gallen 208k, Kanton 196k, other grants 165k (Swisslos, Pro Helvetia, foundations), members and Club der 20 CHF 105k, with UBS and Julius Bär listed.
w: UBS paid a $100M US Federal Reserve fine in 2004 over dollar dealings with sanctioned states. Swisslos is a public lottery.
x: FY2025 income CHF 668k: about 63 percent City and Canton of St.Gallen, 16 percent membership fees, 17 percent other grants (mixed), 3 percent earned (annual report 2025).
Annual reports 2016 to 2025 with full accounts, a funder page naming backers year by year to 2026, and a listed board.

Member of the Swiss museums association (VMS) and the association of Swiss contemporary art institutions (VSIZK); Architektur Forum Ostschweiz and Literaturhaus St. Gallen are partners for its new foyer.

f: Funded by members and patrons, City of Zürich and Canton Zürich subsidies, the Ernst Göhner, Foksal Gallery, Gubler Hablützel and Luma foundations, and Ringier AG.
w: Swiss Re and Bloomberg, named in the old note, are not on the 2025 supporter list. No controversy found among the funders listed.
x: FY2025 income CHF 2.42M: about 51 percent City and Canton of Zurich subsidies, 28 percent members, private donors and the Kunsthalle foundation, 3 percent earned (annual report 2025, Erfolgsrechnung).
Annual reports 2015 to 2025 include audited accounts; a dated 2025 supporter list and the full board are on the about page.
Governed by the Verein Kunsthalle Zürich; its members get free entry at 24 named partner institutions, from Kunsthalle Basel and Bern to the Whitney Museum in New York.

f: Institution of the Migros-Kulturprozent, carried by the Migros cooperative federation, which pays a turnover-based sum into culture since 1957. The sheet lists CHF 12 tickets and no public funder.
w: Migros owns fuel supplier Migrol: CHF 1.3bn of CHF 31.9bn group sales in 2025, about 4%. Fuel is not its main line.
x: The museum publishes nothing itself; parent Migros-Genossenschafts-Bund publishes reports 2020 to 2025, audited accounts and its board. No donor list.
An institution of the Migros-Kulturprozent, the culture arm of the Migros Group; its pages name no network, sibling museum or partner.

f: Kaohsiung City administrative corporation since 2017; 2025 donors: Applied Materials Taiwan, Rotary 3510, art foundations, shipping, King's Town Bank foundation.
w: Allowed money to name: Applied Materials Taiwan, King's Town Bank charity foundation, Fulong shipping. Only row: 2024 sketching ban.
x: Annual records for 2016 to 2025 and yearly donation ledgers 2017 to 2025 are on its site; no accounts or board list found.
Run since 2017 by the Kaohsiung administrative corporation with the Kaohsiung Museum of History and Film Archive; its director sits on C-LAB's board.

f: Ju Ming Culture and Education Foundation (net assets NT$446M). 2023 revenue NT$210M: donations 63%, services 22%, shop 10%, grants 5% (Ministry of Culture NT$8.85M for 2023-24).
w: The report names 13 small firms and 68 individual donors, none flagged. NT$132M of donations is not itemised.
x: FY2025 income NT$151M: about 11 percent government subsidies, 40 percent donations, 37 percent sales and services, 12 percent investment and property income (annual report 2025, p. 60).
It posts annual reports for 2016 to 2025 with CPA-audited statements, a donor thanks page and a named board of nine.
Run by the Ju Ming Culture and Education Foundation, which founder Ju Ming set up to keep the museum going.

n: National Taiwan Museum of Fine Arts
f: Funded by the Ministry of Culture. 2025 gifts of NT$5.64M came from property and building-materials firms, the E.SUN Foundation (bank), France's CCAC and individuals.
w: The filing masks some donor names. In Aug 2026 the Gwangju Biennale renamed its Taiwan Pavilion 'NTMoFA', a row the museum did not cause.
x: FY2025 income about NT$700M: about 97 percent central government transfers, 2.5 percent earned from fees, concession royalties and course fees; donated property is excluded (final accounts 2025, p. 102).
Annual reports 2017 to 2025, audited final accounts and dated donation lists are on its site; as a state agency it has no board.
Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: Founder Chiu Tsai-hsing's private money through Chew's Culture Foundation. No admission fee; running cost about NT$14M a year (2006). No outside sponsors are named.
w: Chiu's money is from electronics firms, among them Jiye Enterprise. The 2006 Global Views article is the latest funding account found.
x: Its site publishes no annual reports, accounts, funder list or board; it names only founder Andrew Chew and Chew's Culture Foundation.
A private museum founded by Andrew Chew, who also set up Chew's Culture Foundation; a member of the Ministry of Culture's Local Cultural Museums network since 2003.

f: Owned by Taipei City, run by the Taipei Culture Foundation since 2008. Sponsors: Epson Taiwan, Lord Hotels, Contemporary Art Foundation, Sony, Thermos; five more logos unnamed.
w: In 2020-21 director Lo Li-chen cancelled Jun Yang's show, then it was shortened after he threatened legal action. Taipei Times did not call it censorship.
x: The support page shows five undated sponsor logos with no alt text; no annual reports, accounts or board list found.
Owned by Taipei City and run by the Taipei Culture Foundation since 2008; the Contemporary Art Foundation ran it from 2001 to 2007.

f: Artist-run space founded 2010. In 2013 its director said most money came from sales of donated artworks, plus a small government subsidy (about 15%). No current funder list found.
w: JUT Land Development gave the building 2009 to 2012. The centre's own site fails its certificate check; no 2025 or 2026 programme found.
x: Publishes annual reports for 2015 to 2017, 2010 to 2011 income charts, benefactors named and dated 2017, and board lists; the live site is down.

f: Taipei City agency; 2025-26 sponsors incl. CTBC Culture & Education Fdn (bank), Chanel, Friends of TFAM, Winsing Arts Fdn, Luce Fdn.
w: Dec 2021: Venice pavilion paused over Sakuliu assault claims; victim's lawyer said TFAM's name was used to pressure her. No sponsor row.
x: FY2025 income about NT$1.09B, about 97 percent Taipei City and ministry funds, 2.5 percent earned; much of it is capital for a new building (final accounts, p. 54).
Annual reports 2006 to 2024, yearly budget and final accounts 2014 to 2025 and a dated sponsor directory are on its site; no board.
Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: Ministry of Culture, through its Taiwan Living Arts Foundation. The phase 2 plan (2022-25) totals NT$1.02B, with NT$269M set for 2025. No private sponsors are listed.
w: Run by a foundation under the Ministry of Culture. In 2021 the Executive Yuan cut its public-works plan to about a third.
x: FY2025 income NT$237M of the foundation running C-LAB: about 88 percent Ministry of Culture and other public bodies, 8 percent earned, 2 percent corporate foundation (final accounts).
Its operator, Taiwan Living Arts Foundation, posts annual reports 2018 to 2025, financial statements, a donations and subsidies list and its trustees.
Operated by the Taiwan Living Arts Foundation; the Kaohsiung Museum of Fine Arts and Asia University Museum of Modern Art hold board seats; IRCAM partners on its Sound Lab.

f: BAB Foundation, chaired by ThaiBev CEO Thapana Sirivadhanabhakdi; ThaiBev is main partner, with Siam Piwat and Central Group (2018). Venice 2026 show adds Bangkok city, TAT, BEM, Ch. Karnchang, Generali.
w: Alcohol money (ThaiBev, Fraser and Neave, SABECO) is no flag. Bangkok city, a partner, censored a July 2025 BACC show, not the biennale.
x: No reports or accounts found; sponsors show as undated logos without names, and the BAB Foundation page lists its board members.

Run by the BAB Foundation, whose board includes ThaiBev executives; its venues include BACC, Museum Siam, the National Museum Bangkok, Silpakorn University's art centre and three temples. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: Run by the James H.W. Thompson Foundation, which says it relies entirely on its own funding. The page names its trustees and no outside donors or sponsors.
w: The foundation also supervises the Jim Thompson House Museum. The claim that house-museum income pays for the centre is not on its page.
x: The art centre publishes nothing itself; its parent foundation lists seven trustees, says it funds itself, and shows no reports, accounts or donors.
Run by the James H.W. Thompson Foundation, which also operates the Jim Thompson House Museum; the two sell a combined ticket.

f: Privately held by the Beurdeley-Bunnag family: Jean Michel Beurdeley, the late Patsri Bunnag and son Eric Bunnag Booth. Shows the family collection; no sponsors or public funders are named.
w: Converted warehouse in Chiang Mai, opened 2016. Admission was planned at about 150 baht. No censorship or protest found.
x: The site publishes no annual reports, accounts, funder list or board; it names only the Beurdeley-Bunnag family as founders.

f: Organised by the Ministry of Culture's Office of Contemporary Art and Culture with Phuket's provincial government, which budgeted THB 59M for 2025-26. Foundations co-fund commissions; none are named.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. 2018 Krabi edition: its organiser, the state OCAC, excluded Chulayarnnon Siriphol's film Birth of Golden Snail unless he cut it.
x: State-run by the Culture Ministry's OCAC; the site has no reports, accounts, board or named funders, and its Partners page shows placeholder images.
Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: Togolese state paid the XOF 2.2bn renovation and funds operations. Director Sonia Lawson sought sponsors in 2019. CFAO and Toyota Tsusho hosted an award show in June 2026.
w: No current budget or sponsor list is published. No censorship, cancelled show or protest found.
x: No reports, accounts or board are published; the patrons thank-you page says its content will be available soon.

c: Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago
f: Mellon Foundation USD 150,000 over 36 months (awarded February 2024). Nordic Culture Fund and OCA support residencies; co-rd Ltd and Basso Leonard Architects are listed supporters.
w: Artist-run space in Belmont, Port of Spain, 20 years old in 2026. Trinbagonians for Palestine supported a 2025 screening.
x: The blog's sidebar names two supporters, co-rd Ltd and Basso Leonard Architects, with no date; no reports, accounts or board are published.

f: Kamel Lazaar Foundation (created 2005 by Swicorp founder Kamel Lazaar) opened B7L9 in 2019. Partners: German Federal Foreign Office, EU delegation, Goethe-Institut, Pro Helvetia, Institut Français, Tunisair, Tunisian Education Ministry.
w: Swicorp is a Riyadh-based investment bank, not a state body. Lazaar once sat on the board of Creative Energy Resources, a power-sector holding.
x: No reports or accounts found; the parent Kamel Lazaar Foundation names 18 partners and funders on an undated page and its founders and staff, but no board.
Run by the Kamel Lazaar Foundation, which also runs the Jaou Tunis biennale and the IBRAAZ platform; the Foundation lists the University of Applied Arts Vienna among its partners.

f: Suna and İnan Kıraç Foundation. 2025 income TL 369M, 94% donations; the report says the founders' gifts sustain the museum. Chair İpek Kıraç, a founder, sits on Koç Holding's board.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Arms and defence. Koç Holding owns Tüpraş (oil refining) and Otokar (military vehicles). The report text does not name Koç Holding as a donor.
x: The Suna and Inan Kirac Foundation posts a 2025 activity report and names its six-member board; no donor list or audited accounts found.
Founded and owned by the Suna and İnan Kıraç Foundation, which also runs the Istanbul Research Institute.

f: Founded in 2011 by Garanti BBVA (bank), which runs it as a social investment programme. Garanti executive Ebru Taşcı Firuzbay sits on SALT's board. Entry is free.
w: Global Energy Monitor lists Garanti coal-plant loans (2017 sources). In 2023 350 Turkey asked it at its AGM about financing coal-linked firms.
x: SALT publishes no reports or board itself; parent Garanti BBVA posts reports 2000 to 2025, accounts and a board list; SALT names supporters.
Founded in 2011 by the bank Garanti BBVA; a member of L'Internationale since 2013 and of the International Confederation of Architectural Museums since 2024. Member of L'Internationale.

f: Self-funded by founder Smita Prabhakar, who directs AMS International, a Dubai HR and events firm. Based at Alserkal Avenue; Abdelmonem Alserkal is honorary chairman of the trustees.
w: The National (2024): 'completely self-funded'. A 2017 profile also lists her at Lazer Capital (infrastructure, oil and gas); no source links it to Ishara.
x: The site lists its trustees and advisory board; it publishes no annual reports, accounts or funders.
A self-funded foundation based at Alserkal Avenue and presented in partnership with Alserkal, whose founder Abdelmonem Alserkal sits on its board.

f: Privately funded by Art Jameel, the cultural arm of the Saudi group Abdul Latif Jameel. Not financed or run by the UAE state. No outside sponsors named on its site.
w: Opened November 2018. Abdul Latif Jameel won a 2005 libel appeal against the Wall Street Journal Europe. No protest or censorship found.
x: Neither the centre's site nor parent Art Jameel's site publishes annual reports, accounts, a funder list or a board.
Founded and funded by Art Jameel, which also runs Hayy Jameel in Jeddah.

f: Creative Scotland, Heritage Lottery Fund, Angus Council, Scottish Government (£5.5M Tay Cities Deal); trusts include Foyle, Robertson, Garfield Weston, William Grant Foundation, Pilgrim Trust, Historic Environment Scotland.
w: Robertson Trust and William Grant Foundation are whisky-endowed; alcohol is not a flag category. No protest found.
x: FY2025 income GBP 834k: about 19 percent public (Creative Scotland), 18 percent trusts and donations, 35 percent earned, 23 percent unnamed restricted project grants (consolidated accounts 2025, note 4).
No annual reports; OSCR holds accounts for 2020 to 2025, the Future Plan page names funders without a date, and the board is listed.
Runs a long-standing residency partnership with the Royal Over-Seas League and co-hosts a 2026 residency with TRACS, Traditional Arts and Culture Scotland.

f: £3.9M income (FY2025). Arts Council England, Durham County Council, National Lottery Heritage Fund £250k, Wolfson Foundation, Swire Charitable Trust, Art Fund, about 20 other trusts; Darlington Building Society, Global Radio.
w: Arms and Armour Heritage Trust is a heritage charity, not an arms maker. No flagged funder or protest found.
x: FY2025-26 income GBP 4.20M: about 29 percent public (Arts Council England, Durham County Council), 17 percent private gifts and trusts, 36 percent earned (accounts, notes 3 to 6).
No annual report on its site; accounts 2021 to 2025 are on the Charity Commission register, a supporters page names donors, trustees are listed.
Delivers the Durham Creative Community Fellows programme with Derby Museums and NAS, as a strand of the county-wide Into the Light initiative. Listed in the Art Fund directory.

f: Public funders are the National Lottery Heritage Fund and Community Fund. Trusts include Garfield Weston, AKO, Clore Duffield and the Blavatnik Family Foundation; Bloomberg Philanthropies backed the website.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Len Blavatnik's fortune includes the TNK-BP oil venture (Bellingcat, 2019). The map counts such money as fossil-fuel money.
x: Calendar 2025 income GBP 3.73M: about 64 percent gifts and legacies, mostly one 1.55M Schroder donation, 24 percent earned; public funding is not separated in the accounts (SOFA p. 14).
Posts trustees' reports and signed accounts for 2016 to 2024, names its eleven directors and keeps a named supporters list with no date.
Works with Bath Spa University, the University of Bath and Bath College on student placements and live briefs. Member of Gallery Climate Coalition. Listed in the Art Fund directory.

f: Arts Council of Northern Ireland and Belfast City Council, per its support page. A 2024 interview adds trusts and foundations, unnamed.
w: Both bodies are on the Arts Council NI 2025/26 funding lists. No controversy, protest or censorship found.
x: FY2024-25 income GBP 423k: about 44 percent public (Arts Council NI, Belfast City Council), 23 percent unnamed grants, 32 percent project and conference receipts (accounts, note 5).
The NI charity register holds its annual reports 2023 to 2024 and accounts to 2025; funders show as logos and no board is listed.
Works with Ulster University as a key member of its CHOICE health research programme and partners each year with the Northern Ireland Mental Health Arts Festival.

f: £400k income (FY2025); Arts Council NI, National Lottery, Belfast City Council, Art Fund, Gulbenkian, Ireland Funds, Ampersand, Future Screens NI.
