f: 2026 partners include Inpex (Major), Beetaloo Energy and BW Offshore (Star) and Mindil Beach Casino Resort (Distinguished). Santos sponsored for almost 30 years until Dec 2022.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Gambling, Sponsor dropped under pressure, Protest or boycott. Santos left after a campaign. In June 2022 almost 200 artists and Traditional Owners sent the festival an open letter demanding it drop Santos.
x: Calendar 2024 income AUD 7.18M: about 31 percent government revenue, under 1 percent donations, 68 percent goods and services, not split further (ACNC 2024 return).
Posts annual reviews for 2016 to 2025 and names its board; the 2026 partners page shows logos only and accounts sit with the charity regulator.
Lists the Museum and Art Gallery of the Northern Territory, Brown's Mart and the AANT Centre as 2026 venue partners.

f: Woodside sponsored through the 2023 season. The 2026 partners are Lotterywest, Tourism WA, City of Perth and local firms; none is a flagged industry.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Sponsor dropped under pressure, Protest or boycott. Fringe World ended Woodside for the 2024 season after a five-year campaign of protest performances, a petition and a rival fossil-free festival.
x: FY2023-24 Artrage (Fringe World) income AUD 19.9M: about 25 percent government, under 1 percent donations, about 75 percent goods and services (ticketing and sponsorship not split; ACNC AIS).
Artrage, Fringe World's organiser, posts its 2025-26 annual report, files accounts with the ACNC, shows 2026 partner logos, and lists its board.
Presented by ARTRAGE Inc, the not-for-profit that also produces Rooftop Movies.

f: Qatar Museums is Major Strategic Partner of the 2026 edition; Fondation Cartier is Visionary Partner. Transfield, a sponsor for 41 years, left in 2014.
w: Flags: Gulf state body, Sponsor dropped under pressure, Prison or detention, Protest or boycott. Nine artists withdrew in 2014 over Transfield's offshore detention contracts, and on 7 March the board ended the sponsorship.
x: The State Department gave $110,000 for US artists at the 2008 Biennale. The embassy objected to works with "politically partisan messages" and urged cutting future support. (Cablegate 09CANBERRA221)
FY2024 income AUD 6.6M: about 52 percent government, 9 percent donations and bequests, 36 percent goods and services including sponsorship; expenses 8.7M, a deficit of 2.2M (ACNC AIS 2024).

Kuba Szreder, Productive Withdrawals: Art Strikes, Art Worlds, and Art as a Practice of Freedom (e-flux, 2017): Szreder argues that art strikes, boycotts and occupations are productive withdrawals that generate collective creativity and new commons-based institutions. He surveys the 2014 boycotts of Manifesta, the São Paulo and Sydney biennials, Poland's art workers' strike and Gulf Labor actions at the Guggenheim. Ahmet Öğüt, CCC: Currency of Collective Consciousness (e-flux, 2015): Öğüt describes how artists withdrew from the 2014 Biennale of Sydney to protest its founding sponsor's role in Australian asylum-seeker detention, and how that pressure led to the sponsor being dropped and the chair resigning. See the What the field says case study.
Biennale of Sydney posts a report per edition for 2018 to 2024, files accounts with the ACNC, names main funders undated, and lists ten directors.
Hosts editions at the Museum of Contemporary Art Australia, the Art Gallery of New South Wales and the University of Sydney's Chau Chak Wing Museum. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: Produced by the Samdani Art Foundation, founded in 2011 by Rajeeb and Nadia Samdani. Their Golden Harvest group has sponsored it. Over 500,000 visitors in 2023.
w: Bonik Barta (September 2024) reported a regulator probe of Golden Harvest, including spending on the foundation, and alleged Hasina-family ties. The foundation denies them.
x: No annual reports or accounts found; its producer Samdani Art Foundation shows undated partner logos and names only a president and one trustee.
Produced by the Samdani Art Foundation since 2012 and hosted every two years at Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy; Delfina Foundation is partner in the Samdani Art Award.

f: Belgazprombank started and runs the gallery and its corporate collection; its Art-Minsk festival has run since 2018. Gazprom and Gazprombank own 49.8% each; Gazprom's chairman greets the project.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Sanctions. EU transaction ban in February 2025 over Russia's SWIFT alternative. Canada and Ukraine listed the bank in 2023. Co-owner Gazprombank is UK-listed since 2022.
x: A BelTA report in Stratfor's emails says Gazprom and Gazprombank each owned 49.02% of Belgazprombank after a $75 million capital increase, and the Belarusian state 0.52%. The report does not mention the gallery, which the atlas lists as the bank's collection. (news item forwarded in a leak)
A project site run by Belgazprombank that names its partners and mentions an expert council.
The Art-Belarus project names the National Art Museum of the Republic of Belarus and the Belarusian Union of Artists as partners.

n: National Art Museum of the Republic of Belarus
f: State museum. Sber Bank (Belarus) is general partner of the Chagall exhibition lent by the State Russian Museum, open 8 Apr to 21 Sep 2026.
w: Flags: Sanctions. Sber Bank Belarus is the former BPS-Sberbank, on the US SDN list since 6 Apr 2022 and linked to Sberbank of Russia.
x: The museum's site lists administration and documents but no annual report, accounts, sponsor list or governing board.
Runs three branch museums: the Vankovich House in Minsk, the Museum of Belarusian Folk Art and the Byalynitsky-Birulya museum in Mogilev.

f: Minsk hub launched in 2017 by Belgazprombank under Viktar Babaryka; authorities closed it after 2020. The Warsaw relaunch is seeking funding (Aug 2026) and names no funders.
w: Art director Maria Kalesnikava. Persecution came from a state that did not fund the hub: no flag. Belgazprombank is listed only by Canada and Ukraine.
x: The same BelTA report shows Gazprom and Gazprombank held 98% of Belgazprombank in 2009. The atlas lists that bank as launching OK16 in 2017. The atlas flags Art-Belarus Gallery for the same ownership; OK16 carries no flag. The report does not mention OK16. (news item forwarded in a leak)
The Warsaw relaunch has no website and no named funders; Zerkalo (Aug 2026) says the team is formed and funding is being sought.
A sibling of the Art-Belarus Gallery under Belgazprombank; its Warsaw relaunch is to work with an unnamed Polish partner.

f: M HKA's 2026 partner page lists V-A-C among its foundations. V-A-C was set up by Novatek founder Leonid Mikhelson, on the UK sanctions list since 6 April 2022.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Sanctions. Present Continuous, an annual scheme for young Russian artists, is run jointly by M HKA and V-A-C. The 2020 winner's work joins M HKA's collection.
x: FY2025 income EUR 10.2M: about 80 percent Flemish Community subsidy of 8.17M, no city or province money; loss of 579,191 (annual report 2025, pp. 85 and 88).
M HKA posts annual reports for 2020 to 2025, files accounts with the National Bank of Belgium, names partners undated, and lists its board.
Part of the Flemish Community's cultural heritage institutions; lists L'Internationale among its research collaborations. Member of CIMAM, L'Internationale.

f: Instituto Cultural Vale is Mantenedora Master. Shell is a master sponsor and Ultra (Ipiranga fuel) a gold sponsor; CEMIG, Itaú, Nubank, Vivo and IBM also give.
w: Flags: Mining disaster, Fossil fuels. Vale's Brumadinho dam collapse killed 270 people in January 2019, near the park.
x: A US Embassy Abuja cable records Shell's Nigeria head Ann Pickard saying Shell had seconded staff to all the relevant Nigerian ministries and so had access to everything done in them. The atlas lists Shell as a master sponsor of Inhotim.
Mainly Rouanet funded: R$45.1M of company money came through the law in 2025. Inhotim calls its plan the largest in Rouanet history; Vale routes half of R$400M through it.
FY2025 net revenue BRL 99.6M: about 78 percent donations, partnerships and restricted corporate project funds, 24 percent tickets, shop and rentals; surplus 9.7M (audited statements 2025, note 11).
Inhotim posts institutional reports from 2012 to 2025, audited financial statements for most years, sponsor logos by tier with no date, and its full council.

f: Rio de Janeiro state cultural centre, renamed Casa Brasil in 2025. Petrobras is official sponsor, chosen through its Novos Eixos call; the 2026 page lists Petrobras as presenter.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. The rename came from a curatorial repositioning, not a sponsor exit. Protests target Petrobras's Amazon-mouth drilling; none found aimed at this venue.
x: State-run space in Rio that takes exhibition requests through an open scheduling form. No Rouanet project, PRONAC, sponsor or budget share found for it in open sources.
Casa França-Brasil's site has no reports, accounts or board, only a sponsor logo bar that names Petrobras and state government bodies.

n: Museu de Arte Moderna do Rio de Janeiro
f: Petrobras becomes official sponsor in 2026, after sponsoring since 1999, funding the school block, school-visit programme and Espaço Petrobras. Rio city and the federal government are also listed.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Petrobras's Petrobras Cultural programme pays for the permanent collection show due August 2026.
x: Corporate sponsorship runs mostly through incentive laws: in 2021, R$10.27M of R$11.18M, of which R$8.39M was federal Rouanet (PRONAC 203998). Free-money sponsorship was R$0.90M.
MAM Rio posts activity reports for 2020 and 2021 only, no accounts, sponsor logos by tier without a date, and its board and fiscal council.

f: Master sponsors of the 36th Bienal: Bloomberg, Bradesco, Petrobras, Instituto Cultural Vale, Citi Brasil and Vivo. Itaú is strategic partner; Open Society Foundations also supports.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Mining disaster. Vale's Brumadinho dam collapse killed 270 in 2019. Bloomberg Philanthropies faces a May 2026 UK artists' letter to London theatres; not targeted here.
x: A US Consulate Rio cable summarises opposition charges that Petrobras gave 609 million reais of unreported sponsorship to unions and cultural and social institutions tied to the ruling party. It names no atlas institution. Petrobras is a master sponsor of the Bienal.
Runs mainly on Rouanet: R$21.9M raised via the law in 2024 from 45 company groups (87% São Paulo-based) and R$30.5M in 2025. Brazil Journal calls it the law's second-largest beneficiary.

FY2025 revenue BRL 72.4M: about 77 percent donations and sponsorship (mostly under culture-incentive laws), 5 percent direct government grants, 11 percent space rental and services (audited statements 2025, note 19).

Kuba Szreder, Productive Withdrawals: Art Strikes, Art Worlds, and Art as a Practice of Freedom (e-flux, 2017): Szreder argues that art strikes, boycotts and occupations are productive withdrawals that generate collective creativity and new commons-based institutions. He surveys the 2014 boycotts of Manifesta, the São Paulo and Sydney biennials, Poland's art workers' strike and Gulf Labor actions at the Guggenheim. See the What the field says case study.
The Fundação posts two-year reports from 2010-11 to 2024-25, financial statements for 2013 to 2025, a named partner list with no date, and its councils.
Lists Sesc as its cultural partner. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: Partners page lists Itaú, Nubank, Bradesco, Citi, Google, Instituto Votorantim, Klabin, Bloomberg and Ultra (Ipiranga fuel distributor), among others.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Bloomberg Philanthropies faces a May 2026 UK artists' letter to five London theatres; no action aimed at MASP found.
x: Top Rouanet raiser in 2024 (R$47.2M received) and second in 2025 (R$49.2M) behind IDG, per Prosas. Incentive projects were 52% of 2024 operating revenue, up from 34% in 2023.
FY2024 revenue BRL 95.3M: about 76 percent donations and incentive-law projects, 21 percent tickets, shop and rentals, 1 percent municipal subsidy; surplus 27.4M (audited statements 2024, note 20).
MASP posts annual reports and financial statements for 2015 to 2024, fiscal council opinions, partner logos by tier without a date, and its full board.

n: Museu de Arte Moderna de São Paulo
f: Master sponsors (R$500k to R$2M): Grupo Ultra (Ipiranga fuel), Goodstorage, Unipar and Tiffany. Itaú and Pro Matre Paulista are strategic partners.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Grupo Ultra owns Ipiranga fuel stations and Ultragaz, a leading Brazilian fuel and LPG distributor.
x: Incentive laws are its largest income line. Federal Rouanet sponsorship booked R$18.3M in 2024 and R$12.7M in 2025, next to smaller state ProAC ICMS and city ProMAC lines.
FY2025 income BRL 35.5M, 11.3M of it non-cash gratuities and volunteer services: about 44 percent incentive-law sponsorship, 11 percent donations, 10 percent activity income (statements 2025).
MAM São Paulo posts annual reports for 2018 to 2025, audited statements for the same years, sponsor logos by tier undated, and its boards.

f: Privately funded by founders Jim and Susan Hill; rent from commercial tenants in its building pays operating costs. Admission is free.
w: Privately funded by Jim and Susan Hill. Their fortune comes from Pason, which supplies oil-drilling equipment; suppliers are not counted as fossil-fuel funders.
x: No annual reports, donor list or board found in archived pages of its site; its charity accounts could not be checked.

f: Donors to 31 March 2025: governments and Shaw Family Foundation $35M+; BMO, RBC and Palmer Family Foundation $1M+; Power Corporation $500k+. Chevron Canada Resources gave $1,000-$4,999.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Chevron's gift sits in the second-lowest tier of the published list. Suncor, Shell, Cenovus, Enbridge and Imperial are not listed.
x: FY2025-26 operating revenue CAD 5.1M: about 58 percent Alberta government and public grants, 39 percent donations, sponsorships and memberships; operating deficit 1.7M (audited statements, p. 4).
Glenbow posts yearly reports and financial statements from 2016-17 to 2025-26, a named donor list to March 2025, and its 19-member board.
Its library and archives sit at the University of Calgary on long-term loan, as the Glenbow Western Research Centre. Member of AAMD.

f: Provincial Crown corporation. In 2024-25 Chevron Canada gave C$185,000, completing a C$492,226 school-programme deal that ended June 2025; Cenovus gave C$20,000 for an Edukit; BMO gave C$100,000.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Chevron's sponsorship concluded at term. In March 2025 The Rooms asked BP Canada for C$30,000 for the renamed Curious Minds programme.
x: FY2025-26 revenue CAD 11.2M: about 78 percent provincial and federal government, 21 percent commercial operations, 1 percent corporate sponsorship; deficit 486,495 (audited statements, PDF p. 88).
The Rooms' annual reports for 2017-18 to 2025-26 sit on the ministry site with audited statements and donor names; its own site lists the board.
Governs three regional sites: the Demasduit Regional Museum, the Provincial Seamen's Museum and the Labrador Interpretation Centre.

n: Mansudae Art Museum / Mansudae Art Studio Gallery, 798
f: Owned by Beijingyuan Mansudae Cultural Company, a joint venture with North Korea that China says became wholly Chinese-owned in 2018. It sells works from the Mansudae Art Studio.
w: Flags: Sanctions. OFAC listed the group in December 2016, the UN on 5 August 2017 and the EU on 10 August 2017 (alias Mansudae Art Studio).
x: No official website, report, accounts, funder list or board turned up for the state-run Mansudae studio gallery in Beijing, which is under international sanctions.
Beijingyuan Mansudae Cultural Company, a China-North Korea joint venture until 2018 and wholly Chinese-owned since, per China; it sells works from the Mansudae Art Studio (Government of North Korea).
Owned by Beijingyuan Mansudae Cultural Company, a joint venture with North Korea until early 2018, per China. It sold works from the Mansudae Art Studio in Pyongyang and kept the Mansudae signage.

f: Private museum founded by the family behind appliance maker Midea, who commissioned the Tadao Ando building and built its collection of about 500 works.
w: Flags: Forced or exploited labour. TBIJ, the New York Times and Der Spiegel (May 2025) found Midea-run factories took part in China's Uyghur labour-transfer programme. Midea did not respond.
x: He Art Museum's site shows exhibitions, collection and visiting details, but no reports, accounts, donor list or board.

f: Run by the West Kowloon Cultural District Authority, a Hong Kong statutory body. Lead partner HSBC, major partner Chanel; patrons Bloomberg Philanthropies, Citadel, Morgan Stanley, Peak Re; sponsors include UBS.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. In 2021 M+ left out an Ai Weiwei work and pulled its image after pro-Beijing complaints. Citadel's Griffin was targeted at the Whitney, not here.
x: M+ posts yearly Reviews for 2019 and 2021 to 2025, shows undated supporter logos, and lists its 16-member board; accounts sit with its parent authority.
Governed by the West Kowloon Cultural District Authority, which also runs the Hong Kong Palace Museum and Xiqu Centre; M+ takes part in CIMAM and BIZOT. Member of CIMAM, Gallery Climate Coalition.

f: The Hong Kong Jockey Club, the city's betting operator, committed HK$3.8 billion to restore the site. Its Charities Trust set up the not-for-profit company that runs Tai Kwun.
w: Flags: Gambling, State censorship or punishment, Protest or boycott. In 2018 Tai Kwun cancelled two talks by writer Ma Jian, then reversed. Twelve artists protested on site and handed over a petition.
x: Tai Kwun publishes no annual report or accounts; it names its Jockey Club funder and individual donors undated, and lists its company board.

f: Run by Macao's Cultural Affairs Bureau, co-organised by the Government Tourism Office and six casino operators: Galaxy, Melco, MGM, Sands China, SJM and Wynn Macau.
w: Flags: Gambling. Each operator presented a special exhibition in the 2025 edition, which ran July to October with nearly 30 exhibitions.
x: Art Macao is run by the Cultural Affairs Bureau, which names six casino operators as co-organisers for 2025 but publishes no report, accounts or board.

f: Founded by Liu Yiqian and Wang Wei. Liu, a former taxi driver, chairs Guohua Life Insurance. Sotheby's said the 2023 sale of about 40 works would fund museum initiatives.
w: Guohua Life reported half-year 2023 losses of $23.3M to $28.7M.
x: No annual reports, accounts, donor list or board found; archived pages name only the founders Liu Yiqian and Wang Wei.
A private museum founded by Liu Yiqian and Wang Wei with three venues in two cities: West Bund and Pudong in Shanghai, and one in Chongqing.

f: Private museum founded by collector Budi Tek and run by the non-profit Yuz Foundation, separate from LACMA and Qatar Museums. Hyundai sponsored a 2019 show.
w: Qatar Museums co-organises exhibitions with Yuz and LACMA in a six-year partnership. LACMA says this is unrelated to the collection foundation.
x: No annual reports, accounts or board found; a standing partners page names LACMA, Qatar Museums, Hyundai and the Yuz Foundation, without a date.
Founded by Budi Tek in 2014; its About page presents the Yuz Foundation, set up in 2007, which also works through Yuz Museum Jakarta.

n: Museo de Arte Moderno de Bogotá
f: Private non-profit museum. Its 2025 gala donor list includes Fundación BAT, the Colombian foundation of British American Tobacco.
w: Flags: Tobacco, Protest or boycott. In February 2026 the board ended curator Eugenio Viola's contract; 170 people signed a letter seeking an explanation. Director Martha Ortiz left amid harassment claims.
x: MAMBO publishes no annual report, accounts or board; its gala page shows sponsor logos grouped by year, 2023 to 2025.

f: State-sponsored show organised since 1984 by the government-supported Wifredo Lam Center of Contemporary Art.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. In October 2021 an open letter with over 400 signatures called for a boycott of the 14th edition; at least five participants withdrew.
x: Two Dutch government-funded foundations stopped funding the Biennial in 2003: the Prince Claus Fund over Cuba's March 2003 jailing of 75 dissidents, and Hivos over censorship in the programme. (Cablegate 03THEHAGUE2114; IPS, 4 November 2003)
The Biennale's site, run by the Wifredo Lam Centre, lists past editions, a catalogue and staff, but no annual report, accounts, funder list or board.

Ministry of Culture, Consejo Nacional de las Artes Plásticas and the Wifredo Lam Centre (state). 2000 edition: Prince Claus Fund and Hivos (Netherlands, 70 percent of external funds), Art for the World (Switzerland), AFAA (France), FONCE. Both Dutch funders withdrew in 2003.
8th edition, 2003: Dutch foundations withdrew over US$200,000; the Cuban government gave US$156,000, the National Council for the Plastic Arts president said (IPS, 4 November 2003).

Organised by the Wifredo Lam Contemporary Art Centre, with the Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes and Casa de las Américas among its host venues. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory. The Consejo Nacional de las Artes Plásticas and the Ministry of Culture announced the 2024 edition with it.

n: Kunsten Museum of Modern Art Aalborg
f: Det Obelske Familiefond pledged DKK 10M over five years from 2025. The foundation owns C.W. Obel A/S, which holds over 10% of Scandinavian Tobacco Group.
w: Flags: Tobacco.
x: FY2023 income DKK 51.8M: about 39 percent public grants, 23 percent foundation grants and business-club memberships, 36 percent entry, shop, cafe and rentals (annual report 2023, accounts images).
Kunsten posts annual reports from 2016 to 2025 with accounts, names its funding foundations in the 2021 report, and lists its six-person board.
The Utzon Foundation appoints the chair of Kunsten's board. Member of ODM.

f: Augustinus Fonden gave DKK 2.5M in 2024 for exhibitions, architecture and new works. Its investment arm, Chr. Augustinus Fabrikker, holds over 25% of Scandinavian Tobacco Group.
w: Flags: Tobacco.
x: FY2025 income DKK 40.6M: about 48 percent state appropriation and public programme funds, 19 percent private foundation grants, 33 percent sales (annual report 2025, PDF pp. 18 and 30).
Ordrupgaard, a state museum, posts its 2024 and 2025 annual reports with full accounts, but names no funders and lists no board.

f: 2023 report names Augustinus Fonden, A.P. Møller Fonden, Ny Carlsbergfondet, Ole Kirk's Fond, Beckett-Fonden; Herning Municipality and the culture agency give operating grants.
w: Flags: Tobacco. Augustinus Fonden gave three grants in 2025. Its investment arm holds over 25% of Scandinavian Tobacco Group.
x: FY2023 income DKK 16.9M: about 96 percent grants and support (state, Herning Municipality, foundations, sponsors), about 4 percent admissions and shop contribution (audited statements 2023, p. 10).
HEART posts annual reports from 2009 to 2023 with audited accounts, lists six board members, and names its foundation funders in the 2022 report.
Sells a combined ticket with the Carl-Henning Pedersen & Else Alfelt Museum. Member of ODM.

f: Augustinus Fonden, Louis-Hansens Fond, Villum Fonden and Kolding Kommune committed DKK 102.4M in 2025 to expand Trapholt. Augustinus's investment arm holds over 25% of Scandinavian Tobacco Group.
w: Flags: Tobacco.
x: Trapholt posts annual reports and audited accounts for 2020 to 2025, names the funders of its 2025 rebuild, and lists its six-person board.

c: Santiago de los Caballeros, Dominican Republic
f: Private museum run by Fundación E. León Jimenes, a non-profit that belongs to Grupo León Jimenes, the León family group founded on the La Aurora cigar factory in 1903.
w: Flags: Tobacco. Founder-family tobacco money. The group sold La Aurora in 2011 and now holds beer, consumer, telecom and health stakes.
x: Centro León posts no annual report, accounts, donor list or board; its Amigos page describes membership fees but names no supporters.
Run by Fundación E. León Jimenes, which also runs the Pabellón de Helechos.

f: State museum. Saudi Arabia pledged €50M in 2024 toward the €262M renovation. Le Monde reports Hanwha pays €20M over four years to use the Pompidou name in Seoul.
w: Flags: Gulf state body, Arms and defence, Protest or boycott. More than 100 artists signed a 27 May 2026 open letter calling for a boycott of Centre Pompidou Hanwha over Hanwha's Elbit Systems ties.
x: Pompidou posts activity reports from 1973 to 2025 with a finance summary and a named 2025 patron list, but no accounts and no named board.
Runs Centre Pompidou sites with partners in Metz, Málaga, Shanghai, Seoul and Brussels, and houses the Bpi library and Ircam in its building. Member of Bizot group, CIMAM.

f: Corporate foundation of LVMH (Bernard Arnault). The group took €518.1M in tax relief on the building over its first eleven fiscal years.
w: The Cour des comptes (November 2018) said the donations could amount to sponsorship promoting LVMH. Anticor challenged the secrecy of its accounts.
x: No annual reports, accounts, donor list or board found; the Conseil d'Etat ruled in 2022 that its accounts cannot be released to third parties.
Corporate foundation created by the LVMH group, a company, as part of the group's patronage.

f: 2025 patron lists name Deloitte, DS Automobiles, Bloomberg, CMA CGM, EDF, Stellantis, Dior and Louis Vuitton. TotalEnergies funded exhibitions for two decades; the Louvre says no direct partnership since 2018.
w: Flags: Opioids, Fossil fuels, Campaigned name, Protest or boycott, Sponsor dropped under pressure. Sackler name came off in July 2019, after a PAIN protest; the Louvre cites a 20-year limit. Total faced a 2017 campaign here.
x: Prince Sultan bin Salman told the US ambassador that Saudi Arabia's heritage campaign would open with a Louvre show, Roads of Arabia (2010). Saudi cables show the cabinet praising it. (Cablegate 10RIYADH31; Saudi Cables)
A Fars News item forwarded in Stratfor's emails says Iran froze cooperation with the Louvre over a reciprocal show it says was promised for 2009–10. (Stratfor emails (Fars News item))

T. J. Demos, Accumulation (from The Great Transition: The Arts and Radical System Change) (e-flux, 2017): Demos argues that oil and gas sponsorship (BP, Total, Eni, Shell) buys cultural institutions public legitimacy and makes them complicit in climate harm. He treats Liberate Tate, BP or Not BP and allied campaigns as a movement that makes museums sites of political action. Hito Steyerl, Duty-Free Art (e-flux, 2015): Steyerl argues that contemporary art screens how war, tax havens and deregulated finance fracture time and space. She calls freeport vaults secret extraterritorial museums, presents a Syrian heritage foundation as regime public relations, and criticises the Louvre's franchising in autocracies. See the What the field says case study.
The Louvre posts activity reports for 2018 to 2025, a named 2025 donor list, and its 19-member board; no separate accounts page was found.
Runs Louvre-Lens, the Conservation Centre and the Delacroix museum, lends to Louvre Abu Dhabi, and partners with the Petit Palais in Avignon and Musée Bonnat in Bayonne. Member of Bizot group.

f: French public establishment. LVMH sponsored the €43M Caillebotte purchase in 2023 under a 90% tax deduction; the annual acquisition budget is about €3M.
w: A September 2025 analysis says taxpayers bore about 90% of LVMH's gift. Epstein's 2012 visit and Leon Black's 2014 loan are not flagged.
x: In an 18 March 2012 email in the DOJ's January 2026 release, Epstein wrote that "the govt is going to open the musee dorsay for me and woody alien at 4", "alien" being his typo for Woody Allen. He later bragged about the visit in emails, including one to Eva Dubin. The Musée d'Orsay did not respond to ARTnews and has not confirmed the visit.

Black lent his Van Gogh "Quarry near Saint-Rémy", valued at $60 million in 2016, to the Orsay's 2014 show "Van Gogh/Artaud: Le Suicidé de la Société". The Art Newspaper reports that the Epstein files indicate his Van Goghs were collateral for large bank loans around 2016. Epstein gave Black "extensive financial advice" for fees of at least $158 million, and Black denies wrongdoing and says he knew nothing of Epstein's crimes until 2019.
FY2025 income EUR 98.7M: about 32 percent state and other public subsidies, 68 percent own revenue, of which EUR 9.6M patronage collected (activity report 2025, pp. 79, 134).
Activity reports 2006 to 2025 with an aggregated income statement are on the EPMO site, patrons are undated logo clouds, and the board is listed.
Governed with the Musée de l'Orangerie by one public body, the Établissement public du musée d'Orsay et du musée de l'Orangerie. Member of Bizot group.

f: Non-profit company owned by the City of Bielefeld, Kulturstiftung Kunsthalle Bielefeld and Sparkasse Bielefeld. The Oetker family paid for the 1968 building and ended its support in 1998.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. Students, artists and citizens protested from 1968 against the Oetker-funded building and its Nazi-linked name. The city council dropped the name in 1998.
x: Kunsthalle Bielefeld names its three shareholders (the city, a foundation and Sparkasse) undated, but posts no reports or board; accounts sit in a German register.
Co-owned by the Kulturstiftung Kunsthalle Bielefeld and works with Hochschule Bielefeld on teaching projects. Member of Deutscher Museumsbund.

f: Its sponsor page lists RWE, E.ON, Evonik, Stadtwerke Essen, Allbau, Sparkasse Essen and several banks.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. RWE made 58% of its 2025 electricity from gas and coal. E.ON sells natural gas.
x: Museum Folkwang names 11 sponsors and 29 donors undated and lists its Board of Trustees, but posts no annual report or accounts.

Co-owned by the City of Essen and the Folkwang-Museumsverein, which the citizens founded in 1922; the Karl Ernst Osthaus Foundation also sits on its Board of Trustees. Member of Deutscher Museumsbund.

f: documenta und Museum Fridericianum gGmbH is a non-profit supported by the City of Kassel and the State of Hesse as shareholders.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. The Merz foundation cancelled a planned 2025 show over the code's IHRA antisemitism definition. The director says the code binds staff, not artists.
x: Fridericianum posts no reports or funder list and names only its supervisory board chair; its imprint names the city of Kassel and Hesse as owners.

Run by documenta und Museum Fridericianum gGmbH, the same non-profit company that stages documenta; the City of Kassel and State of Hesse are its shareholders. Member of Deutscher Museumsbund, Gallery Climate Coalition.

f: The City of Stuttgart approved €15,000 for the March 2026 symposium, then withdrew it. A donation drive covered the shortfall within days.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment, Protest or boycott. The German-Israeli Society Stuttgart sent an open letter demanding the cut. The Kunstverein says the city cited professional objections.
x: Württembergischer Kunstverein lists its administrative board and members but posts no annual report, accounts or funder list.

f: Private museum financed by Kunststiftung Volkswagen, mostly from the Asta and Christian Holler foundation. Volkswagen gave start-up money and Volkswagen Financial Services gives project support.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. The board ended director Ralf Beil's contract in December 2018, before his oil show. CIMAM condemned it; the museum denies any link.
x: Kunstmuseum Wolfsburg names Kunststiftung Volkswagen and other backers undated but posts no annual report or board; its team page lists staff only.

Member of the Deutscher Museumsbund; the museum describes itself as privately sponsored and supported by the Kunststiftung Volkswagen, a funder. No parent or branch named. Member of Deutscher Museumsbund.

f: Funded by Kerala state grants and private donors. Its 2025-26 site names no sponsors; a December 2025 headline records philanthropist Minal Bajaj's support.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. In December 2022, 47 artists and six collectives published an open letter citing poor communication and opaque finances. Founder Bose Krishnamachari resigned in January 2026.
x: Kochi-Muziris Biennale names benefactors, patrons and supporters for its 2025 edition and lists ten trustees, but posts no annual report or accounts.
Organised by the Kochi Biennale Foundation, a charitable trust set up in 2010; the Government of Kerala is its principal supporter. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: Private museum founded and chaired by collector Kiran Nadar, free to visit. Its home page names no funders.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott, State censorship or punishment. In July 2023 it fired Sandip K Luis over a post criticising Nadar's role in a state exhibition. Shahidul Alam pulled his show.
x: KNMA posts FCRA financial statements for 2014-15 to 2024-25 and lists its trustees and advisers, but no annual report or donor list.
Supported by the Shiv Nadar Foundation, whose trustees sit on KNMA's board; it names no parent, network or university. Past collaborators include the Met, Barbican and Qatar Museums. Member of CIMAM.

f: Private museum founded by Haryanto Adikoesoemo, president director of AKR Corporindo, which trades and distributes fuel oil, chemicals and lubricants. The museum sits in AKR Tower.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels.
x: Museum MACAN names its individual patrons undated but posts no annual report, accounts or board; its leadership page names only the foundation chair.
Founded by Haryanto Adikoesoemo and tied to Yayasan Museum MACAN, a non-profit foundation whose first initiative is the museum. The museum sits in AKR Tower.

f: Iraqi non-profit founded in 2012 that says it relies on donations. Its sponsor page lists Nechirvan Barzani, Khalid Khoshnaw, Prince Claus Fund, Rabee Securities, Miran Group and a KAR logo.
w: The sponsor list is undated and its events run 2013 to 2018. No later funder list is published, so the KAR link is not current.
x: Its About page lists sponsors and supporters, mostly as logos, undated, but posts no annual reports, accounts or board.
Commissioned the Iraq Pavilion at the Venice Biennale in 2013, 2015 and 2017; its pages name no parent or network.

f: Hennessy Art Fund has bought works for the collection since 2016. A September 2025 petition asks IMMA to suspend Hennessy and Soho House and drop BNP Paribas.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott, Campaigned name. Petition names all three over Israel-linked and fossil-fuel ties. BNP's partnership ended in 2019. It had 500 signatures by 16 September 2025.
x: FY2025 income EUR 12.4M: about 69 percent Oireachtas grant, 17 percent deferred pension funding, 10 percent commercial, 3 percent sponsorship; deficit 54,587 (audited statements, p. 12).
IMMA posts annual reports from 2006 to 2025 and signed financial statements from 2016 to 2025, shows 2025-26 supporter logos, and lists its board.

f: Run by the Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation. Institutional patron EFG; corporate sponsors include Swatch, Mapei, Rubelli, Florim, Roberto Coin and Villa Sandi.
w: Guggenheim Intrapresæ, its corporate membership programme, has run since 1992. EFG has been an institutional patron since 2001.
x: The Venice site names its corporate sponsors undated; its parent, the Guggenheim Foundation, posts consolidated financial statements and 990s and lists its trustees.
Part of the Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation, alongside the Guggenheim museums in New York, Bilbao and Abu Dhabi.

n: Russian Pavilion at the Venice Biennale
f: Artist Savchenkov withdrew in 2022 and the pavilion stayed shut. Its 2026 return drew a 10,000-signature letter, a culture-minister boycott and an EU cut of 2 million euros.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. Commissioner Karneeva co-runs a firm with Ekaterina Vinokurova, who is under US and UK sanctions. The source of the pavilion's funding is unpublished.
x: The Russian Pavilion has no own site, reports, accounts, funder list or board; its commissioner is named in press but its funding is unpublished.
Hosted by the Venice Biennale in the Giardini. The Russian state owns the pavilion; strategic management sits with the consultancy Smart Art, a company, skipped.

f: Last full festival was in 2015. Oita Gas, a city-gas supplier, is among about 30 sponsors of the committee's ALTERNATIVE-STATE project opened in December 2025.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. No protest found. The flag rests on the fossil-fuel rule alone.
x: FY2014 income JPY 3.97M for the committee's Beppu Art Month: about 35 percent city and prefecture grants, 46 percent foundation and sponsors, 13 percent fees (project report).
Beppu Project posts festival reports for 2012 to 2014 with income and spending, a named 2025 sponsor list of about 30, and no board.
Run by the Konyoku Onsen Sekai executive committee, whose secretariat sits inside the arts non-profit BEPPU PROJECT, which produces the current ALTERNATIVE-STATE project.

n: 21st Century Museum of Contemporary Art, Kanazawa
f: Gold member Kanazawa Energy sells city gas and runs hydro plants; Hokuriku Electric owns 48% and Toho Gas 43%. Iwatani Central Hokuriku (LPG) is a standard member.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. No protest found.
x: Kanazawa 21 posts its 2025 annual report and names its supporting members by tier undated, but publishes no accounts or board.
Partners with Kanazawa College of Art and the Oku-Noto Triennale committee under 2019 agreements, and with the Kanazawa Noh Museum and Yuwaku Sousaku no Mori since 2006. Member of CIMAM.

n: Kyoto City KYOCERA Museum of Art
f: Kyocera bought 50-year naming rights in 2017 for about 5 billion yen, half the renovation cost. About 15 citizens and artists rallied against the sale on 16 November 2019.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. Kyoto City owns the museum and was the first public art museum in Japan to sell its name. Citizen groups objected from 2016.
x: Kyoto City Kyocera Museum names 19 corporate supporters and the Kyocera naming-rights deal undated, but posts no annual report, accounts or board.

f: Agency for Cultural Affairs refused the full 78 million yen subsidy in September 2019, then agreed to pay 66 million yen. 2025 sponsors include Toho Gas, a gas utility.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Protest or boycott, State censorship or punishment. ReFreedom_Aichi gathered over 100,000 signatures against state censorship. Sponsor Nagoya Horse Racing leases Chukyo Racecourse to the JRA and runs no betting.
x: FY2025 budget JPY 1.29 billion: about 88 percent public contributions (Aichi Prefecture, Seto City), 10 percent tickets, 2 percent sponsorship and grants (2025 report, budget).
Aichi Triennale posts event reports for 2019 and 2025, the 2025 one with committee income and spending and named sponsors; it names only its chair.
Organised by the Aichi Triennale Organizing Committee and held at the Aichi Arts Center and other venues across Aichi Prefecture. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: Bloomberg is a current funder (Students Day, Oct 2026). In July 2015 the museum and Tokyo officials asked the Aida family to change or remove two political works; they stayed.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott, State censorship or punishment. Name to know: Bloomberg Philanthropies, which about 250 UK creatives asked five London theatres to drop in May 2026. Not targeted here.
x: MOT posts annual reports for fiscal 2008 to 2025; its operator foundation posts financial statements for 2015 to 2025 and names directors. No sponsor list.
Operated by the Tokyo Metropolitan Foundation for History and Culture, which also runs Tokyo Arts and Space, the Metropolitan Art Museum, Photographic Art Museum and Teien Art Museum.

f: Funded by Kairat Boranbayev, whose fortune comes from oil and gas, real estate, retail and pharmaceuticals. Convicted of embezzlement in 2023, he gave assets to the state.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Sentenced to eight years and released on probation. The director says the case has no implications for the centre's funding.
x: Tselinny names its patrons by tier undated and lists an advisory board, but posts no annual report, accounts or governing board.

f: 2025 roster: benefactors Marwan T. Assaf and Peter and Nathalie Hrechdakian; patrons include Foundation for Arts Initiative, Institut Francais and British Council; supporters include Al Mawred and the Arab Fund.
w: Sharjah Art Foundation appears only in 2018 and Qatar Foundation only in 2020. Neither is listed from 2021 to 2025.
x: FY2025 income USD 385k: about 69 percent private (donors, sponsors, fundraising events), 19 percent institutions of mixed origin, 12 percent earned; expenses USD 312k (annual report 2025, p. 37).
Annual reports 2009 to 2025 with financial statements are on its site, donors are named by year to 2025, and the board is listed.

f: Fondation Engie is an energy sponsor in the 2026 supporter list. Engie sells natural gas and runs coal plants. Other energy sponsors: Energy Assistance, CMA CGM, Dammous & Partners.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. No protest found.
x: Sursock posts its 2025 annual report, named supporter lists for 2024 to 2026, and its board of trustees, but no financial statements.

f: JTI is named among exceptional supporters, with Cargolux, Clearstream, A&O Shearman and the Leir Foundation. ArcelorMittal and Banque de Luxembourg are listed as further supporters.
w: Flags: Tobacco. The page gives only the initials JTI. It lists Clearstream, whose partnership began in March 2024, so the list dates from 2024 or later.
x: Mudam posts activity reports for 2007 to 2025, names its patrons undated, and lists its board, but shows no financial statements.

Primary partner with Serralves, Bozar, CAC Vilnius, TEA Tenerife and Triennale Milano Teatro in the PIT performance-art initiative, and co-creator with Casino Luxembourg of the Roundtables series. Member of CIMAM.

f: UNAM's contemporary art museum. Its benefactors page lists Bloomberg and Fundación AXA as corporate members; FEMSA, Fundación Televisa and Fundación Alfredo Harp Helú also appear. No amounts or years.
w: Page names only 'Bloomberg', added between 2021 and 2024. In May 2026, 260+ UK artists urged theatres to drop Bloomberg Philanthropies; MUAC was not named.
x: MUAC has no records of its own; parent UNAM publishes audited 2025 accounts and lists its Junta de Gobierno; MUAC's benefactors page names donors undated.
A museum of UNAM run by its Dirección General de Artes Visuales; its site names a close collaboration with Tate Modern, MACBA, Fundación Proa, Reina Sofía and MFAH. Member of AAMD, CIMAM.

f: Supported by the Fundación Olga y Rufino Tamayo. Patrons include Carlos Hank Rhon and Eugenio López Alonso; sponsor logos include Bloomberg, FEMSA, AXA and Aeroméxico.
w: Patron Carlos Hank Rhon paid a $40M Federal Reserve fine in 2001 over his Laredo bank stake, admitting no wrongdoing.
x: No annual reports or accounts found; the foundation page names its board and international council, while corporate sponsors appear as undated logos.
Listed under INBAL in its own directory, and backed by the Fundación Olga y Rufino Tamayo, formed in 1989 by the museum's founders.

f: ING has been a main sponsor since 2005. Extinction Rebellion altered paintings there in February 2024 and rallied in March 2024 demanding the museum end the ING deal.
w: Flags: Campaigned name, Protest or boycott. Saudi Aramco ended in 2017 with no protest at the museum. Vriendenloterij and KPN are also partners.
x: A US Embassy The Hague cable says the Dutch government decided on 6 February 2006 to return 202 paintings to the heirs of Jacques Goudstikker, affecting several Dutch museums including the Rijksmuseum, which would receive no compensation.

FY2025 income EUR 115.3M: about 37 percent OCW and other public subsidy, 13 percent sponsorship and private gifts, 50 percent tickets, shop and indirect income (jaarverslag 2025, exploitatierekening).
It posts Dutch annual reports for 2021 to 2025 with financials, names main partners ING, KPN and Vriendenloterij, and has pages for its boards.

Runs fellowship programmes with the Louvre, Bard Graduate Center and the Museum of National History at Frederiksborg. The Ministry of Education, Culture and Science is its founder. Member of Bizot group, Museumvereniging.

f: Shell sponsored research at the museum for 18 years until August 2018. Fossil Free Culture NL staged 'Drop the Shell!' protests there in 2017 and 2018, including arrests.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Sponsor dropped under pressure, Protest or boycott, Campaigned name. The museum says the partnership ended naturally when the research on its paintings was finished.
x: FY2025 income EUR 77.7M: about 14 percent OCW subsidy, 11 percent sponsorship and private funds, 75 percent tickets, shop and other earned income (annual report 2025, p. 62).
It posts annual reports with a financial section (2024 on its own page), lists corporate patrons by name, and names its supervisory board.
Shows the core collection owned by the Vincent van Gogh Foundation and leads the Van Gogh Europe programme with affiliated museums and sites. Member of Museumvereniging.

f: GasTerra and Gasunie sponsor the museum, which says they back the energy transition. Fossil Free Culture NL protested there on 31 October 2025 and in earlier actions from January 2022.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Protest or boycott, Campaigned name. The group calls it the last major Dutch museum with fossil sponsors. GasTerra sells gas; Gasunie runs the gas grid.
x: FY2025 income EUR 10.4M: about 67 percent public subsidy, 15 percent private funds and lotteries, 19 percent tickets and other; sponsor income was only EUR 20k (jaarverslag 2025, p. 67).
It posts annual reports from 2005 to 2024 with a financial section, names GasTerra and Gasunie among sponsors, and names its supervisory board.
Member of the Netwerk Kunst en Cultuur Groningen, and cooperates with Museum aan de A and Groninger Archieven on a planned new museum and shared exhibitions. Member of Museumvereniging.

f: Shell partnered with the museum for six years until the contract lapsed in July 2018. Main partner since 2016: NN Group, with the Friends Lottery and the culture ministry.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Sponsor dropped under pressure. Fossil Free Culture attacked the Shell link and claimed the end as a win. The museum gave no reason for not renewing.
x: The same cable names the Mauritshuis among the Dutch museums losing paintings to the Goudstikker heirs. The State Secretary for Culture said the museums would get no compensation, calling the decision morally correct despite the "bloodletting" for museums.
It posts annual reports from 2013 to 2024, with financial reports for 2016 to 2018, names partners including NN Group, and names its supervisory board.

f: Todd Energy, New Zealand's leading natural gas provider, is Founding Corporate Partner of the Len Lye Centre and a perpetual Foundation partner. It names the foyer and learning centre.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. No protest found. New Plymouth District Council owns and mainly funds the gallery.
x: FY2024-25 operating funding NZD 5.9M: about 85 percent New Plymouth District Council rates, 10 percent fees and charges, 5 percent other operating grants (NPDC annual report 2024/25, p. 44).
The gallery has no reports of its own; owner New Plymouth District Council posts audited annual reports for 2013 to 2025. Partners show as logos.
Houses and shows the Len Lye collection owned by the Len Lye Foundation, which shares a joint committee with the council; Ngā Taonga is a listed Len Lye partner. Member of CIMAM.

f: The Fletcher Trust sponsored the 2019 Theo Schoon show. Students called a boycott and protested at the gallery on 1 August 2019 over Schoon's use of Maori motifs.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. The protest targeted the exhibition, not the sponsor. The gallery scheduled public talks on Schoon for 16 and 17 August.
x: City Gallery has no records of its own; its operator Wellington Museums Trust posts a 2025-26 annual report and trustees page. Partners show as logos.
Run by the charity Experience Wellington for Wellington City Council, alongside Capital E, Wellington Museum, Space Place, the Cable Car Museum and Nairn Street Cottage.

f: State-run museum in Kaesong with over 1,000 Koryo-dynasty artefacts in four halls and an open-air stone collection; 20,000 m², 12 main buildings.
w: Flags: Sanctions. Hall 3 is left off the foreign-visitor route unless a guide opens it. The Government of North Korea is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
x: A North Korean state museum; searches found no website, report, accounts, donor list or board.

Government of North Korea (state budget, announced only as yearly percentage changes, plus part of visit revenue set aside for heritage upkeep); Kaesong People's Committee manages the site; gift-shop sales.
Occupies the Songgyungwan academy, one of 12 components of the UNESCO World Heritage property Historic Monuments and Sites in Kaesong, managed by the Kaesong People's Committee.

f: State library and Juche study centre: 100,000 m², 600 rooms, claimed capacity 30 million books. A 1989 broadcast claimed over 10 million visits a year; budget unpublished.
w: Flags: Sanctions. North Korea's Library Law treats libraries as essential for promoting ideology. The Government of North Korea is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
x: The library's site, read from archive copies, posts no reports, accounts, funders or board; it lists only past presidents.
Government of North Korea (state budget, announced only as yearly percentage changes); the Asia Foundation, a US nonprofit that has sent donated books since 1996.

f: National fine-art museum with 22 display rooms; KCNA claimed 6 million cumulative visitors by 2020. Budget unpublished.
w: Flags: Sanctions. The Government of North Korea is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
x: The national arts portal's page on the museum, read from an archive copy, gives its history only; no reports, accounts, funders or board are posted.
Government of North Korea (state budget, announced only as yearly percentage changes); sales of artworks and souvenirs in the museum store.

f: Collection of about 100,000 relics; its 19 halls show over 4,000 objects (Koryo Tours). The museum claimed 10 million cumulative visitors by 2015. Kim Il Sung founded it in 1945.
w: Flags: Sanctions. Kim Jong Un's 2014 speech called it a model for history museums. The Government of North Korea is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
x: A North Korean state museum; no official website, report, accounts, donor list or board turned up.
Government of North Korea (state budget, announced only as yearly percentage changes, plus part of visit revenue set aside for heritage upkeep); sales of ceramics and celadon in the museum shop.

f: Pyongyang studio listed as Mansudae Overseas Project Group of Companies (alias Mansudae Art Studio) by the US in 2016 and by the UN and EU in 2017.
w: Flags: Sanctions. The listing cites exporting workers to build statues and monuments abroad to earn revenue for the North Korean state.
x: No site of the studio's own exists: the archived mansudaeartstudio.com was an Italian dealer's sales site, now parked, with no reports, accounts, funders or board.

Government of North Korea (state studio); foreign governments that pay for monuments through its overseas group; art sales abroad, including through an Italian dealer who told Reuters the revenue goes direct to the studio.

Its foreign commercial division is the Mansudae Overseas Project Group of Companies. The studio is not under the Ministry of Culture; it had Kim Jong Il's guidance until 2011. Its Beijing gallery in the 798 art district ran under Beijingyuan Mansudae Cultural Company until early 2018, and an Italian dealer sold its work abroad until December 2017.

n: Mansudae Overseas Project Group of Companies (Mansudae Overseas Projects)
f: Builds monuments abroad, including the African Renaissance Monument in Dakar. Listed by the UN, US, EU and UK for exporting workers to raise revenue for the DPRK government.
w: Flags: Sanctions. The UN listed it on 5 August 2017; the Panel of Experts had urged covering all subsidiaries worldwide. Its US and EU listings are separate.
x: President Wade's architect told the embassy Senegal would give North Korea about $30M of land in Dakar to build the African Renaissance Monument. A 2009 cable calls the financing murky and the price $16M. (Cablegate 08DAKAR649, 09DAKAR288)
A sanctioned North Korean overseas construction group, listed by the US (2016), the UN, the EU and the UK; it has no website, report, accounts or board of its own.

Foreign governments that hire it (Namibia, Angola, Botswana, Mozambique, Senegal in land); the Government of North Korea and the Workers' Party, named by the UN, US and EU listings as recipients of its revenue.

A UN Security Council diplomat said Mansudae's business earned tens of millions of dollars worldwide (Reuters, October 2017); the AP put North Korea's income from statue sales abroad near US$10 million a year (December 2016). Senegal's monument: US$25 million on its plaque, about US$70 million per foreign officials (Bloomberg Businessweek, 2013).

The overseas division of the Mansudae Art Studio, Pyongyang. UN Panel-linked firms: MOP Architectural and Technical Services (Namibia), Mansudae Group Construção Civil Publicas (Angola), Mansudae New Tech (Cambodia). Sites: Independence Memorial Museum (Namibia), Angkor Panorama Museum (Cambodia), African Renaissance Monument (Senegal).

n: Sinchon Museum of American War Atrocities
f: Memorial to the 1950 Sinchon massacre. The museum claims over 35,000 deaths and blames US forces; South Korean historians attribute the killings to both communist forces and anti-communist vigilantes.
w: Flags: Sanctions. A larger building opened in July 2015; closed to foreign visitors since 2018. The Government of North Korea is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
x: A North Korean state museum; no official website, report, accounts, donor list or board turned up.
Government of North Korea (state budget, announced only as yearly percentage changes).

f: Equinor and the festival renewed their agreement in 2025 after nearly 40 years, now as a local sponsorship. DNB is main partner.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Protest or boycott, Campaigned name. A Greenpeace activist protested at the 2023 opening, and Folk mot Fossilmakta petitioned for Equinor out of the festival.
x: A Reuters report forwarded in Stratfor's emails says Statoil, now Equinor, agreed in 2006 to pay a $10.5 million US penalty over a 2002 Iran consulting contract, and US bribery charges were dismissed in 2009. Executives lost their jobs over the case. (news item forwarded in a leak)
FY2025 operating income NOK 70.5M, of which sales revenue NOK 10.2M (about 14 percent); the register gives no split of the other NOK 60.3M between grants and sponsorship (Regnskapsregisteret).
The festival posts no annual report, but its foundation files annual accounts in Norway's register; it names its sponsors and seven board members.
Run by the Foundation Bergen International Festival; its Board of Representatives seats Bergen Kunsthall, KODE, Stiftelsen Harmonien, Den Nationale Scene, Grieghallen and the University of Bergen.

f: INPEX Idemitsu Norge, an oil and gas company, renewed its sponsorship in February 2023 for five years and has given over NOK 100 million since 1991.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Protest or boycott. A November 2021 projection of Idemitsu, Aker BP and Equinor logos on the facade protested the museum's oil ties.
x: The museum posts a 2024 annual report, shows seven sponsor logos with no date, and names no board; it is a unit of Oslo municipality.
Member of CIMAM. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: Corporate sponsors. Engro, which owns the Thar coal power plant, gave Rs 75 million as lead partner of KB22 in 2022.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, State censorship or punishment, Protest or boycott. Police shut Adeela Suleman's installation in October 2019 and the Biennale disowned it; over 100 artists and curators signed an open letter.
x: It posts a trustee list of ten names and sponsor logos by edition (KB24 partners), but no annual report and no accounts.

Hosts its biennales at recurring venues such as NED University, Alliance Française Karachi, Sambara Art Gallery and Indus Valley School, with cultural institutes and Teesside University as listed partners. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: ORLEN, an oil and gas group, is named as the gallery's patron on its own sponsorship page. The Culture Ministry sets the director's term.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, State censorship or punishment, Protest or boycott. In July 2021 the culture minister ended director Hanna Wróblewska's tenure; over 1,000 art professionals signed an open letter against it.
x: FY2024 income PLN 25.5M: about 87 percent Ministry of Culture operating subsidy and targeted grants, 13 percent own revenue, not split further (Raport 2024, p. 90).
The gallery posts annual reports from 2011 to 2024 and yearly financial statements in its public bulletin; its partner page names ORLEN, but no board.
Supervises and organises exhibitions in the Polish Pavilion at the Venice Biennale and works with the Museum of History of Photography in Cracow on poster digitisation. Member of CIMAM.

f: Run by Fundação EDP, the cultural foundation of utility EDP, which opened the museum in October 2016.
w: EDP made about 90% of its 64 TWh of 2025 generation from renewables; gas and coal plants supply the rest.
x: FY2025 EDP Foundation income EUR 15.9M: 76 percent the EDP Group's regular grant, 17 percent sales and services; MAAT has no accounts of its own (annual report 2025).
MAAT has no records of its own; its operator Fundação EDP posts annual reports and audited accounts 2021 to 2025 and lists its boards.
Opened and run under the cultural patronage of Fundação EDP, which owns the art and energy heritage collections shown at MAAT.

f: Galp Energia is listed as a Patron Founder in the Annual Fund every year from 2021 to 2024, alongside Sonae, Inditex, Mota-Engil and others.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. REN Portgás Distribuição, a gas distributor, is also a Patron Founder in each of those four years.
x: FY2024 income EUR 16.9M: about 39 percent public subsidy, 24 percent patronage (2.5M of it under the residence-permit law), 36 percent sales and services (Relatorio e Contas 2024, note 15).

Academics, curators, artists and educators (100 signatories), Open letter to museums and galleries in support of education and other essential workers (e-flux, 2020): Signatories criticise museums for cutting freelance and part-time education staff during COVID-19, naming MoMA, MOCA Los Angeles, MASS MoCA and the Serralves Foundation. They demand reversed layoffs and secure, fairly paid contracts for all cultural workers. See the What the field says case study.
Serralves posts yearly reports with audited accounts from 1989 to 2020 and names founders, but its directors are not named on the governing bodies page.
Primary partner with Mudam, Bozar, CAC Vilnius, TEA Tenerife and Triennale Milano Teatro in the PIT performance-art initiative. The Portuguese State is a founder since 1989.

n: Mathaf: Arab Museum of Modern Art
f: Owned by Qatar Museums, chaired by Sheikha Al-Mayassa Al Thani; the collection came from Sheikh Hassan bin Mohamed Al Thani. Opened 2010 in Education City.
w: Flags: Gulf state body.
x: A Reuters piece in Stratfor's emails says Doha "last year opened a museum of contemporary Arab art", in a passage on the Qatari leadership's talk of an Arab renaissance through its wealth. The item does not name Mathaf. (news item forwarded in a leak)
Mathaf has no records of its own; its parent Qatar Museums posts no reports, accounts or sponsor names but lists eight trustees.
A member of Qatar Museums, which also oversees the Museum of Islamic Art, the National Museum of Qatar, the 3-2-1 Olympic and Sports Museum and Fire Station.

f: Owned and run by Qatar Museums, a Qatari state body; Shaika Nasser Al-Nassr has been director since 2024.
w: Flags: Gulf state body.
x: Two items in Stratfor's emails tie the museum to the Qatari state. Reuters says analysts hear the leadership talk of an "Arab renaissance" through its wealth, and notes Doha's Islamic art museum. Hugh Eakin's essay says "the emirate inaugurated" the I.M. Pei building. (news item forwarded in a leak)
The Museum of Islamic Art has no records of its own; parent Qatar Museums posts no reports, accounts or sponsors but lists eight trustees.
Overseen by Qatar Museums since its founding, with Mathaf, the National Museum of Qatar, the 3-2-1 Olympic and Sports Museum and Fire Station under the same body.

f: Qatari government entity founded in 2005 and chaired by Sheikha Al-Mayassa bint Hamad Al Thani; it oversees the state's museums and heritage sites.
w: Flags: Gulf state body. HRW's 2026 Qatar chapter documents wage theft and kafala abuse but does not name Qatar Museums.
x: In a worker-rights cable, the authority's security chief says he was fired with no reason given; staff were barred from contacting Sheikha Al Mayassa without approval. 15 expatriates resigned and 8 were fired in April 2008. (Cablegate 08DOHA393)
Qatar Museums posts no annual report or accounts and names no sponsors, but lists its board of eight trustees by name.
Oversees the Museum of Islamic Art, Mathaf, the National Museum of Qatar, the 3-2-1 Olympic and Sports Museum, Fire Station and two QM galleries; four more museums are planned.

f: V-A-C, set up by Novatek founder Leonid Mikhelson, runs GES-2; he spent at least $300M on it. The UK has listed him since 6 April 2022.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Sanctions. Ragnar Kjartansson cancelled his Santa Barbara show in February 2022 over the war. Artistic director Francesco Manacorda resigned in March 2022.
x: GES-2 posts no annual report, accounts, donor or sponsor list, or board; the site names only the founder Leonid Mikhelson.
GES-2 is the Moscow platform of the V-A-C Foundation, which Leonid Mikhelson established in 2009. The pages read name no partner museum, network or university.

f: Non-profit project of the IRIS Foundation, founded by Roman Abramovich and Dasha Zhukova. Endowment page lists Abramovich's gifts from 2018 to 2023. He is on UK and EU sanctions lists.
w: Flags: Sanctions. Garage paused exhibitions in February 2022 and showed its collection again in 2024. Security services searched its offices in April 2024.
x: The same cable says Abramovich paid to build the Bakhmetevsky garage exhibition space, Garage's home from 2008, as a gift for Darya Zhukova. (Cablegate 08MOSCOW2700)

An AFP report in Johnson's Russia List, forwarded in Stratfor's emails, says Dasha Zhukova, "Roman Abramovich's partner", would move Garage to Gorky Park. It calls the park's new director Sergei Kapkov "a close ally" of Abramovich, appointed by Moscow's mayor. (news item forwarded in a leak)
FY2025 income RUB 919M: about 81 percent donations, 12 percent earned revenue, 4 percent interest, 4 percent other income (statutory filing 2025, thousand-rouble tables).
The Garage endowment fund posts reports and statutory audit results for 2019 to 2025 and a named donor list by year; two trustees are named.

A non-profit project of the IRIS Foundation, founded by Dasha Zhukova, which offers a joint master's programme with the Higher School of Economics. No network or partner museum is named. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: Partners page lists VTB Bank, Sberbank, SAFMAR foundation, Severstal and Metalloinvest, with Rosneft as an exhibition partner. Founding donors in 2012 to 2014 included Vekselberg, Abramovich and Blavatnik.

The museum shows partner logos with no date and posts no annual report, accounts or board list; a news item mentions a board meeting.
Founded on the idea of the Federation of Jewish Communities of Russia (FEOR); no branches or networks named on its own pages.

f: Founded by the Moscow Government in 1996, director Olga Sviblova. Partners page lists Nornickel as corporate trustee, Alfa-Bank as strategic partner, plus Live Sound and Priorov Center.
w: Flags: Sanctions. Alfa-Bank is on the US (Apr 2022), UK (Mar 2022) and EU (Feb 2023) sanctions lists. Nornickel itself is not blocked.
x: FY2025 cash income RUB 485M: about 73 percent Moscow city subsidies (state task and targeted), 27 percent own income from paid services and rent (plan execution report 2025).
The museum posts 2025 results and financial reports and plans, names Nornickel and Alfa-Bank as partners without a date, and lists no board.
Contains the Rodchenko School of Photography and Multimedia; the Sphere and Still Art foundations hold seats on its Board of Trustees. Member of CIMAM.

n: Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts
f: VTB is general sponsor of the museum, and PSB partnered the Diamond Chariot Buddhist art exhibition. LG and Yandex Eda are also partners.
w: Flags: Sanctions, Arms and defence. Marina Loshak left in March 2023; Ekaterina Pronicheva is director now. The board of trustees includes Sberbank, Gazprombank, PSB and Transneft.
x: The museum and the Culture Ministry first refused, then allowed, the US envoy for Holocaust issues to see two works claimed by American families. (Cablegate 09MOSCOW774)
FY2018 cash receipts RUB 1.34B: about 43 percent federal state-task subsidy, 57 percent paid services and other own income (results report 2018, the only year the museum site posts).
The museum posts activity reports and Treasury financial forms for 2012 to 2025, shows four undated sponsor logos, and names its board of trustees.
Runs the Arsenal branch in Nizhny Novgorod and a Siberian branch in Tomsk, plus the Tsvetaev museum, Richter apartment, Steinberg workshop and Private Collections venue.

f: Private foundation founded in 2003 by collector Marianna Sardarova, named as the wife of oil and gas owner Rashid Sardarov. It publishes no donors.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Sardarov's South Ural Industrial Company processes Kazakh gas condensate at Gazprom plants; he is not on a sanctions list.
x: A Bosnian weekly quoted in Stratfor's emails says Russian businessman Rashid Sardarov, via Comsar Energy, planned two thermoelectric plants at Ugljevik and sought coal concessions. The atlas names his wife as the foundation's founder; the item mentions neither her nor the foundation. (news item forwarded in a leak)
The foundation posts no annual report, accounts, donor list or board; its About page names founder Marianna Sardarova and art director Catherine Borissoff.
Founded by collector Marianna Sardarova, who also set up the separate RuArts Gallery; it states it works with state museums but names no standing partner.

f: Corporate partners include VTB, Sberbank, PSB, Gazprombank, Transneft, LUKOIL, Surgutneftegas and NOVATEK. Private patrons include Leonid Mikhelson and Alisher Usmanov; the V. Potanin Foundation also gives.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Sanctions, Arms and defence, State censorship or punishment. The Ministry of Culture declined to renew director Zelfira Tregulova in February 2023 after a complaint of destructive ideology and a letter demanding exhibit changes.
x: Embassy Moscow followed the criminal trial of former Tretyakov curator Andrei Yerofeyev over the 2007 Forbidden Art show. (Cablegate 09MOSCOW1688)
The gallery posts annual reports (2015 to 2020 seen), fund reports to 2025, a named trustees list and a named thanks list for corporate supporters.
Runs the Samara branch, a Vladivostok public space, the Tretyakov family museum and the two Vasnetsov memorial museums in Moscow.

f: Private centre founded in 2007 by Roman and Sofia Trotsenko. Their Winzavod Foundation, led by Sofia, funds its programmes; they put their 2021 artist support at 15-20 million roubles.
w: Flags: Sanctions. Roman Trotsenko is on the EU list (June 2024) and the UK list (Feb 2025). His son Gleb is on the US list.
x: Winzavod posts no annual report, accounts or board; its documents page holds policies and safety assessments, and partners show as logos with no date.
Governed through its own Winzavod foundation, which initiated the Association of Galleries; a gallery of the HSE School of Design sits on site.

f: VTB Bank co-authored the idea with architects SPEECH and backs the centre as its philanthropic project; it opened in 2022 in the former Khlebozavod No. 5.
w: Flags: Sanctions. VTB Bank has been under US full blocking sanctions since February 2022.
x: It names patrons and partners, VTB as general partner, but posts no annual report, accounts or board; the legal page holds only registrations.

f: Private gallery in Samara founded in 2005 by Leonid Mikhelson, chairman of gas producer Novatek. Kommersant calls him its owner; the UK has listed him since 6 April 2022.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Sanctions. The rebuilt gallery held its reopening ceremony in March 2026 under new general director Sergey Balandin.
x: The gallery posts no annual report, accounts, partner list or board; its About page names founder Leonid Mikhelson and three managers.

f: Roman Abramovich's Millhouse won the 2010 tender. Works paused in June 2022; a 2026 court filing puts the project at 80% complete.
w: Flags: Sanctions, Fossil fuels. Abramovich built his fortune on oil firm Sibneft. Fontanka tied the June 2022 stop to his sanctions; the project gave no reason.

The site posts no reports, accounts, sponsor list or board; its project page names Millhouse and the Iris Foundation as builders and creative partners.

f: St Petersburg charitable foundation. Its 2025 report lists programme backers: the city's Committees for Culture and Social Policy, Friends of BDT Foundation and the Vladimir Potanin Foundation.

Works mainly with the State Hermitage Museum, the Bolshoi Drama Theater, the Alexandrinsky New Stage, the Museum of the History of St Petersburg and St Petersburg State University.

f: Its 2025 sponsor list includes VTB, Sberbank, Gazprom, Rosneft, Gazprom Neft and the Gazprombank foundation, plus Vladimir Potanin and his foundation. Potanin chairs the Board of Trustees.
w: Flags: Sanctions, Fossil fuels, Protest or boycott. Hermitage Amsterdam cut ties on 3 March 2022. Canada sanctioned director Piotrovsky in 2023 and the EU listed him on 23 April 2026.

The Hermitage posts yearly reports for 2009 to 2018 and a sponsor list by year (2022 seen); its reports name a board of trustees.
Runs exhibition centres in Kazan, Vyborg, Yekaterinburg, Omsk and Orenburg, and has worked with the PRO ARTE Foundation since 1999. Member of Bizot group.

Has branches in Kemerovo and Kogalym and runs Cultural and Exhibition Centres inside museums in Kazan, Yaroslavl, Murmansk, Saransk, Yoshkar-Ola and Kogalym.

f: Run by the OMK-Uchastie charity foundation with support from steel-pipe maker OMK and the Vyksa administration since 2011. Irina Sedykh chairs the trustees.

Run by the OMK-Uchastie Charitable Foundation, which also runs Art Residency Vyksa and the Volna Cultural Centre; Tsaritsyno Museum-Reserve advises its education programme.

The centre posts yearly accounting statements and names its trustees and board; it has no annual report and its partners page lists no sponsors.
Houses a branch of the Yeltsin Presidential Library, with which its charter provides for cooperation.

n: King Abdulaziz Center for World Culture (Ithra)

f: Operated within the Marina Bay Sands casino resort, which Las Vegas Sands owns.

The museum has no records of its own; owner Marina Bay Sands posts annual reports and parent Las Vegas Sands files 10-Ks with the SEC.

Works with Centre Pompidou, Musée d'Orsay, Tate Britain, MOMAT and MMCA, co-runs Articulation with Singapore Art Museum and the National Gallery, and seats the National Heritage Board's chief. Member of ASEMUS, Bizot group, CIMAM.

w: Flags: Fossil fuels. RGE also owns pulp, palm oil and viscose businesses. The foundation publishes no donors.

The foundation lists its trustees and auditors by name, posts audited financial statements (2020 and 2021 seen), and shows past sponsors as logos.

Governed by the Gwangju Biennale Foundation, whose board seats the directors of the Gwangju Museum of Art and Gwangju Media Platform and the artistic director of SONGEUN. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

The foundation posts yearly donation disclosures for 2022 to 2025, with a 2024 audit report, but no annual report, donor list or board.
Partners with the Delfina Foundation on residencies and with the Stedelijk Museum on a video series; its artistic director sits on the Gwangju Biennale board.

MACBA posts its 2025 general accounts and audit reports for 2011 to 2018 and names its trustees, but no annual report or donor list.
A member of L'Internationale; it is run as a consortium in which the private Fundació MACBA sits beside the city, Catalan and Spanish governments. Member of CIMAM, L'Internationale.

f: Trustees include the Basque Government, Bizkaia, the Guggenheim Foundation, Iberdrola, BBK, Fundación BBVA and Petronor, an oil refiner.

Part of the Guggenheim network with the New York, Venice and Abu Dhabi museums; the Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation is a founding trustee. Member of Gallery Climate Coalition.

f: Zurich city and canton paid half the 2021 extension. The Emil Bührle Collection foundation, built on an arms fortune, lends about 200 works on a 20-year loan.

FY2025 operating income CHF 36.5M: about 37 percent City of Zürich grant, 21 percent members and donors, 28 percent earned, 14 percent from a Monet sale (annual report, p. 102).
Its 2024 annual report carries full accounts with an audit report and a logo image of funding partners, but names only the board chair.
Governed by the Zürcher Kunstgesellschaft and holding long-term loans from the Bührle and Giacometti foundations, the Kunstfreunde patrons' society and others.

x: It names its donors and supporters with funding years but posts no annual reports or accounts, and describes its board without naming anyone.

x: Annual reports for 2013 to 2024 are online, supporters are named without a date, and the Foundation Committee is listed; accounts could not be read.

f: Run by the Vehbi Koç Foundation. Koç Holding supports its 2026 show Work in Progress; Tüpraş was main sponsor at the 2019 reopening. Koç Holding owns Tüpraş and Otokar.

x: Arter has none of its own; parent Vehbi Koç Foundation posts reports for 2012 to 2025 without audited accounts. Arter names sponsors, lists its board.
Arter is the contemporary art institution of the Vehbi Koç Foundation, which also runs the Meşher arts venue in Arter's former Istiklal Street building.

f: Owned by the Abu Dhabi Department of Culture and Tourism. Abu Dhabi pays France €400M for the Louvre name and €190M for loans under the 2007 agreement.
w: Flags: Forced or exploited labour, Gulf state body. Human Rights Watch documented passport confiscation, unpaid wages and unsafe conditions on Saadiyat Island, including the Louvre site, in a 2015 report.

It posts annual reports for 2018 to 2023 and names partners and patrons; the site blocked fetches, so accounts and board could not be checked.

f: A Sharjah government body: its parent is the emirate's Department of Culture and Information, and the ruler's daughter Hoor Al Qasimi founded it in 2009.
w: Flags: Gulf state body, State censorship or punishment. In April 2011 the ruler dismissed director Jack Persekian after complaints about a biennial artwork. Other works were then removed or put under review.
x: Ghalya Saadawi, Post–Sharjah Biennial 10: Institutional Grease and Institutional Critique (e-flux, 2011): Saadawi argues that the fallout from Sharjah Biennial 10 should widen into a critique of how institutions and capital shape art, beyond boycotts alone. She questions the Sharjah Art Foundation's conduct and state funding, and the Guggenheim's censorship of Hans Haacke in 1971. See the What the field says case study.
Its site has no annual reports, accounts, funder list or board list; the sponsors page names no one.

Shares its director, Hoor Al Qasimi, with the Sharjah Architecture Triennial and The Africa Institute, and has staged joint exhibitions with the Institute and Sharjah Museums Authority. Member of CIMAM. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: Dropped Baillie Gifford as a sponsor in March 2024, weeks after Arts Workers for Palestine Scotland launched a campaign against the firm's arts ties.
