x: FY2024-25 income GBP 802k: about 35 percent public grants (Creative Scotland), 11 percent trusts and donations, 48 percent earned from trading, 5 percent tax relief (Companies House accounts, p. 17).
It posts no annual reports, files returns with the Scottish charity regulator, shows three funder logos with no names or date, and lists its trustees.
Member of Gallery Climate Coalition. Listed in the Art Fund directory.

f: Ended its 20-year Baillie Gifford partnership in May 2024 after several authors withdrew and activists threatened disruption.
w: Flags: Campaigned name, Sponsor dropped under pressure, Protest or boycott. Greta Thunberg withdrew in August 2023 over the sponsorship. Fossil Free Books gathered over 200 author signatures by May 2024.
x: FY2025 income GBP 3.77M: about 15 percent public core grants, 49 percent trusts, donors and sponsors, 25 percent earned from tickets and commission, 11 percent project grants (Companies House accounts).
It posts impact reports for 2024 and 2025, files accounts with the Scottish regulator, names funders and sponsors undated, and lists its trustees.
Hosted at the University of Edinburgh's Edinburgh Futures Institute under a long-term partnership, and runs the Paper Trails project with Edinburgh Libraries and Streetreads.

f: Dropped Baillie Gifford in June 2024 after six years and £25,000 a year, after activists targeted the gallery over the firm's Israel links.
w: Flags: Campaigned name, Sponsor dropped under pressure. Arts Workers for Palestine Scotland praised the decision. The gallery cited its values, ethics and funding policy.
x: FY2024-25 income GBP 2.13M: about 31 percent Creative Scotland core grant, 15 percent donations, 36 percent earned from cafe, shop and hire, 17 percent other grants and income (Companies House).
It posts no annual reports, files returns with the Scottish charity regulator, names current supporters without a date, and lists its board.
Member of Gallery Climate Coalition, Plus Tate. Listed in the Art Fund directory.

f: Scottish Government funds it, about £26 million a year. Baillie Gifford stayed a main sponsor after a July 2024 review. BP's Portrait Award tie ended in November 2019.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Campaigned name, Sponsor dropped under pressure, Protest or boycott. More than 800 cultural workers asked national galleries to refuse Baillie Gifford money. BP or not BP? protests preceded the BP exit.
x: FY2024-25 income GBP 32.6M: about 71 percent Scottish Government grant in aid, 6 percent donations and memberships, 16 percent earned, 6 percent unnamed grants (annual report, p. 43).
It posts audited accounts for 2023-24, names corporate supporters and donors on site pages, and OSCR lists its 12 trustees.
Member of Gallery Climate Coalition, NMDC.

f: Announced on 7 June 2024 that it would no longer seek Baillie Gifford funding. Current funders include Creative Scotland, City of Edinburgh Council and Bloomberg Connects.
w: Flags: Campaigned name, Sponsor dropped under pressure. Artists and cultural workers campaigned against Baillie Gifford's arts sponsorship. Bloomberg Connects is a current supporter and has not been targeted here.
x: Nine months to December 2025 income GBP 494k: about 33 percent public grants (Creative Scotland, City of Edinburgh), 19 percent trusts, 44 percent earned (OSCR accounts, p. 7).
It posts no annual reports, files accounts with the Scottish regulator, names 19 funders and supporters undated, and lists three board members.
Takes part in Creative Carbon Scotland's Green Arts Initiative; no parent, branch or standing partner is named on its own pages. Member of Gallery Climate Coalition.

f: Suspended Baillie Gifford sponsorship on 24 May 2024, citing claims from campaigners and intense pressure on artists to withdraw.

x: FY2025 income GBP 6.9M: about 68 percent earned from tickets, books and fees, 25 percent trusts, donors and sponsors, 7 percent public grants (Companies House accounts, p. 14).
It posts no annual reports, files accounts at Companies House, names Airbnb and other partners without a date, and lists 12 trustees.

f: Arts Council England, Liverpool City Council, National Lottery Heritage Fund and Bloomberg Philanthropies sit under 'Funded by' on its 2026 homepage; Culture Liverpool is under 'Supported by'.

x: FY2024-25 income GBP 2.35M: about 30 percent named public revenue grants (Arts Council England, Liverpool City Council), 41 percent earned (catering, rents, hires), almost no donations (audited accounts p. 17).
No annual reports found; accounts are on the Charity Commission register, the homepage Funded by block is undated logos, and board members are listed.

f: BP gives £50M over ten years for the masterplan, announced 19 December 2023. The Sackler name came off its rooms and endowments in 2022.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Campaigned name, Protest or boycott. Trustee Ahdaf Soueif resigned over BP in 2019; 80 signed a 2023 open letter. The Sackler name left by agreement in 2022.
x: The same item says Iran's National Museum cut ties with the British Museum in early 2010 over the delayed Cyrus Cylinder loan, and restored them once the cylinder went to Tehran. (Stratfor emails (Fars News item))

FY2025-26 income GBP 149.8M: about 54 percent grant-in-aid, 10 percent donations and legacies, 32 percent earned from charitable activities and trading, 4 percent investments (annual report, p. 47).

T. J. Demos, Accumulation (from The Great Transition: The Arts and Radical System Change) (e-flux, 2017): Demos argues that oil and gas sponsorship (BP, Total, Eni, Shell) buys cultural institutions public legitimacy and makes them complicit in climate harm. He treats Liberate Tate, BP or Not BP and allied campaigns as a movement that makes museums sites of political action. See the What the field says case study.
It posts reports and audited accounts for 2022 to 2025, names donors in its 2022-23 review, and lists 21 trustees on its governance page.
Member of ASEMUS, Bizot group, NMDC. Listed in the Art Fund directory.

f: Earns income from event hire. Lord Mandelson chaired its trustees from 2017 to June 2023. Arms maker Leonardo hired it for a July 2018 reception.

Bellingcat's #ItalianArms team found Leonardo helicopters and Oto Melara naval guns in Turkmenistan's forces, some without export authorizations. Leonardo held a private reception at the Design Museum in July 2018, and artists pulled work from its exhibition in protest.
FY2024-25 income GBP 17.2M: about 70 percent earned from admissions, programmes and trading, 18 percent donations and memberships, 8 percent public grants (Companies House accounts, p. 40).
It posts no annual reports, files group accounts at Companies House, names corporate partners with a few exhibition years, and lists its trustees.

Has a three-year strategic partnership, from March 2025, with Shenzhen Bay Culture Square (D-Bay); its founder Terence Conran is a person. Member of Gallery Climate Coalition. Listed in the Art Fund directory.

f: The Dr Mortimer and Theresa Sackler Foundation endowed the director fund, valued at £3.5m in March 2021. The Sackler Trust finances part of the gallery's education work.

It lists annual reviews from 2011-12 to 2018-19 and files group accounts at Companies House for 2022 to 2025; its site blocked page fetches.
Listed in the Art Fund directory.

Eva Andersson-Dubin is Epstein's ex-girlfriend, and Virginia Giuffre alleged that Epstein trafficked her to Dubin in 2001, when she was 16, which the Dubins categorically deny. f: Non-profit founded 2011 by Aida Mahmudova, niece of First VP Mehriban Aliyeva; says no state money (2015), no funder list published.
w: Co-partnered a March 2026 exhibition with bp, SOCAR Midstream and PASHA Holding; funder roster itself not published.
x: An embassy profile of the First Lady's Pashayev family: it controls PASHA Holding and runs the Heydar Aliyev Foundation. YARAT's founder is the First Lady's niece, and PASHA Holding co-partnered a 2026 YARAT show. (Cablegate 10BAKU54)
No reports or accounts found; the partners page shows eight unnamed, undated logos, and the team page lists staff but no board.
Its About page lists four further venues under YARAT: ARTIM Project Space, YARAT Studios, YAY Gallery and the Painting Museum.

f: A US$250M Azerbaijani state project opened in 2012; its main contractor was tied to the Aliyev family's offshore network. No sponsor roster is published.
w: Zaha Hadid building named for Heydar Aliyev; site cleared by forced evictions
x: The centre's site carries no annual reports, accounts, sponsor list or board; it publishes only a statute and structure page for this state body.
Member of four events and convention trade associations since 2013 and 2014; its site names no parent institution, sibling or museum network.

n: Armenian Center for Contemporary Experimental Art (ACCEA/NPAK)
f: US 501(c)(3) NGO. Benefactors listed in February 2022: Balassanian Fund, Cafesjian Museum Foundation, Boghossian Foundation, Hovnanian Fund, JHM Charitable Foundation, Carolyn Mugar and Rouben Avanessian.
w: Flags: Gambling. Benefactor JHM Charitable Foundation: a 2011 California Gambling Control Commission filing ties its trustees to Commerce Casino shareholders.
x: Its site posts no reports; it lists major benefactors as of February 2022 and its board, and its US arm files Form 990-EZ.

f: City of Yerevan museum, founded 1972 with the mayor's backing. The municipality and Eduardo Eurnekian supported its 2022 anniversary exhibition.
w: Eurnekian was charged with aggravated tax evasion in 2010, upheld on appeal. In 2017 the Supreme Court ruled against him on the tax owed.
x: No annual reports, accounts, funder list or board found on the museum site; the team page lists the director and staff only.

f: Small NGO museum (founded 2017) in Stamba Hotel; funded by Swiss SDC, Adjara Group/Stamba, Prince Claus Fund, OSGF, MG Law, MagiC Carpets.
w: Moved some operations to a Lithuanian NGO after Georgia's 2024 foreign-agent law
x: No annual reports or accounts found; a Donors and Partners footer block shows seven named-in-alt logos with no date, and no board is listed.

n: State Museum of Arts of the Republic of Karakalpakstan (Savitsky Museum)
f: State museum with about 70,000 visitors in 2025; the government-backed ACDF paid for its renovation, restorers and digitisation.
w: Savitsky's collection of banned Soviet avant-garde art; refurbished by the state ACDF
x: The museum site has no annual reports, accounts or funder list; it names the director and a deputy for finance but no board.

n: A. Kasteyev State Museum of Arts
f: State museum under Kazakhstan's Ministry of Culture and Information. Samruk-Kazyna and its Trust backed the 2025 renovation; Samruk-Kazyna and Rosatom fund the October 2026 Tretyakov exhibition. Budget not disclosed.
w: Flags: Arms and defence. Rosatom, Russia's state nuclear and weapons-complex corporation, backs the Tretyakov show. Its head Likhachev and deputy Komarov are on US and UK sanctions lists.
x: Its old site posted narrative annual reports for 2017 to 2019 without accounts; the new site was unreadable.

n: Gapar Aitiev Kyrgyz National Museum of Fine Arts
f: Underfunded national museum (about 18,000 works) paid for by Kyrgyzstan's Ministry of Culture; no sponsor roster published.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment, Protest or boycott. In December 2019 a Culture Ministry commission confiscated works from the Feminnale. Director Mira Dzhangaracheva left after death threats.
x: A state museum; its site has no reports, accounts, donor list or board, and a search found none from the ministry.

n: Savannah Centre for Contemporary Art (SCCA Tamale)
f: Founder Ibrahim Mahama pays for everything from sales of his own art, he told Contemporary And in 2021. The centre's site lists individual collaborators and no institutional funders.
w: Artist-run since 2019. Its site thanks individuals, not companies or governments.
x: No reports, accounts or funder list found; the site lists individuals who collaborated and supported it, in no order or date, and names no board.
Its site names blaxTARLINES KUMASI as the only institution among the individuals who collaborated with and supported it.

f: Lagos non-profit founded 2007, behind LagosPhoto. Its 2024 collaborators page shows Open Society, Ford Foundation, Mondriaan Fund, Vontobel, Deutsche Bank, Canon, Nigerian Breweries, Goethe-Institut and National Geographic.
w: No tobacco funder or funder campaign found. Nigerian Breweries makes beer. The Keystone Bank row is a property eviction, not funding.
x: No reports or accounts found; the collaborators page shows undated logos, mostly without alt text; the team page lists staff, not a board.
Its Collaborators page names SCCA Tamale and Les Ateliers Coffi; LagosPhoto Festival is its own programme.

f: University museum opened 2019, endowed by collector Prince Yemisi Shyllon; free entry from June 2026 paid by Aisha and Gbenga Oyebode.
w: On the Pan-Atlantic University campus. Its 2026 free-admission funder chairs a palm-oil firm in a land dispute.
x: Annual reports 2020 to 2025 give income shares but no accounts; sponsor logos are undated; the supervisory council and advisory board are named.
Belongs to Pan-Atlantic University as its teaching museum and announced a 2025 knowledge-exchange partnership with the Toledo Museum of Art.

f: Founder Barthélémy Toguo pays from his own money, with coffee grown on the project's land since 2010 and the Amis de Bandjoun Station association; Apollo reports no government support.
w: The Amis de Bandjoun Station association backs young artists with fully paid residencies, per Africultures (2015).
x: The live site is down; its January 2025 archived copy has no reports, accounts, funder list or board, only project text and press.
Bandjoun Station holds a signed convention with the Université de Picardie Jules Verne.

f: Small art centre founded 2012 by Bill Kouélany, funded project by project: Fondation Almayuda (since 2018), Institut français, EU/OACPS (Popul'Art 2023).
w: The only contemporary art centre in this research for the Republic of the Congo. Almayuda is a Geneva foundation registered in 2023.
x: No site of its own found, only Facebook; no reports, accounts, funder list or board; funder Almayuda names it on its own site.

f: State museum under Mali's culture ministry; 10,937 visitors in 2025. Spain's AECID backs the 2026 'Repenser le Musée national du Mali' project; the amount was not disclosed.
w: Project launched 21 April 2026 with minister Mamou Daffe. It covers staff training, conservation, security and youth outreach.
x: No annual reports, accounts, funder list or board on the museum's old site; its web address now redirects to an unrelated site.
Founded in 1953 as the Sudanese Museum of Bamako by IFAN, later a state museum.

f: The state commits to counterpart and running costs. A €16M concessional AFD (French development agency) loan, signed 30 Mar 2026, covers rehabilitation and extension of nearly 8,000 m2 plus equipment.
w: The museum becomes a public administrative body. AFD's director called the loan unprecedented for the cultural sector.
x: No site of its own found; the culture ministry's site has only a March 2026 news item on the AFD loan, nothing else.
State museum under the culture ministry; since September 2026 it has a digitisation memorandum with the national archives and the national library.

f: State public body since 2002, under the culture ministry. An April 2026 site improvement drive involved Agence Faso Mɛbo, the Ouagadougou commune, Salif Sanfo and gifts from unnamed companies.
w: A friends' association president appealed to volunteers, companies and media for support in April 2026.
x: Documents page is empty and no accounts or funders are posted; the site says a board exists under a 2002 decree but names no one.

Its 2021 to 2025 strategic plan names partners in France, Switzerland, Germany and Benin, a local university, and ICOM Burkina Faso, the national museum-professionals association and the West African Museums Programme as supporting associations.

f: Founded 2005 by Elisabeth Piskernik. Residency artists pay their own travel, lodging and supplies, per TransArtists. No funder roster published.
w: Independent exhibition and residency space in Rabat with a Vienna branch; still programming in 2025. No supporters page found.
x: Le Cube names partners only for single exhibitions and publishes no annual reports, accounts, funder list or board.
Runs Le Cube Vienna and the nomadic Le Cube Expanded alongside its Rabat space, founded in 2005 by Elisabeth Piskernik.

n: Musée Mohammed VI d'Art Moderne et Contemporain (MMVI)
f: State museum run since 2014 by the Fondation Nationale des Musées, built with Ministry of Culture and Fonds Hassan II money; partners include Royal Air Maroc.
w: Morocco's first national museum of modern and contemporary art, opened October 2014 by the king; FNM president Mehdi Qotbi.
x: The museum has no site of its own; its parent foundation FNM publishes no annual reports, accounts or funder list and names no board.
Run by the Fondation Nationale des Musées, which lists it among 22 museums across Morocco, including the Musée National de la Photographie in Rabat.

f: Jardin Majorelle ticket profits (almost 700,000 visitors a year) and the Fondation Pierre Bergé-Yves Saint Laurent, which owns the garden. Bergé's 2015 sale of Moroccan art also helped pay.
w: Run by the Fondation Jardin Majorelle, president Madison Cox. The foundation reinvests its earnings in cultural, educational and social projects in Morocco.
x: The museum site and the Jardin Majorelle site publish no annual reports, accounts, funder list or board; the parent foundation's own site returned unreadable code.
Holds the Fondation Pierre Bergé – Yves Saint Laurent collection, sits beside Jardin Majorelle and its Berber museum, and shares its name with the Paris museum.

n: Musée Public National d'Art Moderne et Contemporain (MAMA)
f: Public body (EPA) under the Ministry of Culture since 2007, with little budget beyond its opening; collection built mostly from private and artist donations.
w: In a 1909 neo-Moorish department store on rue Larbi Ben M'hidi; opened for Algiers Capital of Arab Culture 2007.
x: Its old site, now offline, showed no reports, accounts, funder list or board in an archived copy; only mission, publications and a support link.

n: Darb 1718 Contemporary Art and Culture Center
f: Small non-profit founded 2008 and mainly funded by artist Moataz Nasr; 2022 Moleskine Foundation grant; 2025 artist-donated auction at Tarathuna.
w: Fustat headquarters bulldozed in January 2024; working from temporary space and raising money for a new home.
x: The live site is suspended; its archived copy has no reports or accounts, shows six unlabelled collaborator logos with no date, and lists no board.

n: Arete Foundation for Arts and Culture
f: Founded 2012 in Tripoli. AFAC grants in 2012, 2016 and 2019 (North Africa Cultural Program national fund). No full funder list found.
w: Hosted a 2 March 2023 symposium at Dar Al Funoon, Tripoli. No annual report or supporters page found.
x: No Arete website was located; the only records are AFAC's grantee page and an events listing, with no reports, accounts, funders or board.

f: Developed and funded by Art Jameel, founded and chaired by Fady Jameel, vice chairman of the Saudi business group Abdul Latif Jameel. Opened December 2021.
w: Opened 6 Dec 2021 to mark 75 years of Jameel family arts patronage. Separate from Jameel Arts Centre in Dubai.
x: Hayy Jameel and its parent Art Jameel publish no annual reports, accounts or funder list; the site lists staff and the founder but no board.
Developed and managed by Art Jameel, sister to the Jameel Arts Centre in Dubai, with the V&A, The Met and Delfina Foundation as named Art Jameel partners.

f: Founded 2008, paid for privately by founder Sheikha Lateefa bint Maktoum plus project partners such as Van Cleef & Arpels (luxury) and Dubai Culture
w: Non-profit studio, residency and gallery that also runs a commercial consultancy. ENOC, Dubai's state oil company, commissioned work through it for Expo 2020.
x: No annual reports, accounts, funder list or board; the about page names founder Sheikha Lateefa bint Maktoum and the team page lists staff only.

f: Parent is the Salama bint Hamdan Al Nahyan Foundation, founded by the UAE president's wife. Partners: Abu Dhabi education department, NYU Abu Dhabi, Zayed University. No budget published.
w: Flags: Gulf state body. Its parent foundation is the UAE president's wife's royal foundation, treated as a Gulf state body. No donor list or accounts are published.
x: It posts a 2021 to 2022 review and a 2023 study but no accounts; its partners page names sponsors from older projects without a date.
Works with NYU Abu Dhabi and Zayed University on learning programs and names the Salama bint Hamdan Al Nahyan Foundation on its partners page.

f: Founded 1998 by Bayan Kanoo, who owns it; non-profit with income from courses, rentals and a shop. No sponsor or grant list is published.
w: Bahrain's culture authority attended the February 2022 reopening at the Bank House; its news item states no grant.
x: Al Riwaq publishes no annual reports, accounts, sponsor list or board; its partnerships page names only an events collaborator.

f: Founded 2011 by Amer Huneidi. Co-hosted a 2024 Lebanon show with the Lebanese Embassy, UNHCR, Lebanese Business Council Kuwait and Lebanese Ladies Society. No funder list published.
w: No supporters page, annual report or sponsor credits found on capkuwait.com, in the 2025 newsletter or in Al-Jarida coverage.
x: CAP Kuwait publishes no annual reports, accounts, funder list or board; its about page calls it a non-profit private organization.

f: Private museum opened in 1988 by the Zubair family. Forbes Middle East lists it as a Zubair Corporation project; the group owns oil and gas firms including ARA Petroleum.
w: Zubair Corporation's nine sectors include ARA Petroleum (oil exploration and production). It publishes no revenue split, so oil is not shown as its largest line.
x: A cable on Oman's leading business families says the Zubair fortune grew from the founder's closeness to Sultan Qaboos; Zubair Corporation holds 10% of Sohar Power and makes offshore oil-and-gas products. (Cablegate 09MUSCAT851)
The foundation's site publishes no annual reports, accounts, funder list or board; it names the founder and managers and posts only a commercial registration certificate.
Managed by the Bait Al Zubair Foundation, which the Zubair family set up in 2005 as the cultural arm of the family business.

f: Qatar Museums' artists-in-residence programme in a former civil defence base, open since March 2015; Wael Shawky has been artistic director since November 2024.
w: Flags: Gulf state body.
x: Part of Qatar Museums, which posts no annual reports, accounts or sponsor names; its board is named only in state press.
Qatar Museums runs it as a Creative Hub project, alongside Mathaf, the Museum of Islamic Art, the National Museum of Qatar and other Qatar Museums bodies.

f: Anchorage Museum Association spent about $12.6M in 2023 (IRS 990). Its 2022 contributor list names ConocoPhillips Alaska, Chevron and Alyeska Pipeline; ConocoPhillips has a named gallery.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Oil majors are current donors. No campaign or protest aimed at the museum or its oil gifts found.
x: FY2024 income USD 13.2M: about 44 percent government grants, 31 percent donations and gifts, 18 percent earned, 4 percent investment income (Form 990, Part VIII).
It posts its 2023 Form 990 and names nine directors; a 2026 Gratitude Report exists but was not opened.

Hosts the Smithsonian Arctic Studies Center, a Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History program that opened an Anchorage office with the museum in 1994. Member of AAMD, Gallery Climate Coalition.

f: Municipal museum owned by Kommuneqarfik Sermersooq. A large Augustinus Fonden donation bought the Melting Barricades collection in 2024. Its residency runs with the Danish Arts Foundation.
w: Flags: Tobacco. Augustinus Fonden's investment arm holds over 25% of Scandinavian Tobacco Group.
x: A municipal museum; its site links one annual report, for 2015, and names only staff, with no accounts or donors.

f: About 33.6k cinema visits in 2023. Funded by Greenland's Self-Government and Kommuneqarfik Sermersooq (2M DKK each extra in 2026), plus GrønlandsBANKEN and Air Greenland.
w: A self-owning foundation; its board is appointed by the Self-Government, the municipality, Visit Greenland and EPI. Bank (not under campaign) and state airline as sponsors.
x: Annual management reports 2018 to 2023 give results without full accounts; two unlabelled undated sponsor logos; the board is named in the 2023 report.

f: Run by the public agency ADCK of the New Caledonia government; centre budget about 400M XPF in 2026. The French State pays 68% of the renovation under development contracts (2025).
w: Renzo Piano building from 1998. Renovation runs to 2027 under State and New Caledonia development contracts.
x: The centre's site carries no annual reports, accounts, funder list or board; the 2026 budget and State renovation share come only from press coverage.

n: Musée de Tahiti et des Îles – Te Fare Iamanaha
f: Government of French Polynesia: 158.8M XPF operating and 30.8M XPF capital subsidy in 2024. The 844M XPF renovation was financed under the Contrat de projets.
w: Public establishment set up in 1980. 2024 revenue was 421.7M XPF. A friends' association, Amis du Musée, supports it.
x: FY2024 operating receipts XPF 258M: the government of French Polynesia subsidy of XPF 158.8M is about 62 percent; capital-section receipts of XPF 163.7M are excluded (provisional account).
No annual reports or funder list; the government's public-bodies report carries a one-page 2024 financial summary; no board is named.

n: Papua New Guinea National Museum and Art Gallery
f: A state statutory body funded by the PNG government. Australia paid for its 2015–2018 refurbishment, which reopened on 12 Oct 2018.
w: Australia paid for the building in the 1970s and for its pre-APEC refit in 2018. No corporate sponsor was found.
x: Its site is down; archived copies show no reports, accounts or funder list, and a Board of Trustees page that names no one.
Runs the J.K. McCarthy Museum in Goroka, Haus Independens and three Kokoda Track community museums, and has a Friends of the Museum Association.

f: Fiji Government grant: F$697,525 operating and F$500,000 capital in 2018/19. US Ambassadors Fund has paid for digitisation since 2021; it runs out in Sept 2026.
w: A statutory body under the Fiji Museum Act. It needs $300,000 more to finish digitising by Dec 2028.
x: FY2016-17 revenue FJD 1.45M, including a government operating grant of FJD 354k, about 24 percent; the capital grant of FJD 233k is not counted (committee report).
No reports, accounts or funders on its site; annual reports for 2015 to 2017 went to Parliament, later ones lapsed; no trustees named.

n: Oceania Centre for Arts, Culture and Pacific Studies (USP)
f: A unit of the University of the South Pacific, owned by 12 Pacific governments including Fiji. Its 2026 residency is run with Creative New Zealand and Creative Australia.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. Fiji, USP's host and an owner, halted its grant in 2020 and deported the vice-chancellor in 2021. It restored funding after the 2022 election.
x: The centre has no records of its own; parent USP posts annual reports, audited statements for 2005 to 2025 and names its Council.

n: IAIA Museum of Contemporary Native Arts
f: Part of IAIA, a federally chartered college: federal funds cover 75% of operating costs, with a $13.48M appropriation confirmed. Ford Foundation (2020) and Art Bridges (2025) granted the museum funds.
w: Trump's FY2026 budget proposed eliminating IAIA; the Senate funded it anyway.
x: Parent IAIA posts financial statements and a trustee list; ProPublica carries its Form 990s for 2012 to 2024; no annual report or donor list found.
Part of the Institute of American Indian Arts, a college that calls itself and MoCNA one entity in two locations; the museum grew from IAIA's student collection.

n: Eiteljorg Museum of American Indians and Western Art
f: 2023 revenue $11.5M; Lilly Endowment leads, plus Capital Group, Fifth Third, PNC, OneAmerica and Citizens Energy Group (gas utility), all on its corporate partners page.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Citizens Energy Group delivers natural gas in Indianapolis. No sponsor withdrawal or protest aimed at the museum found.
x: FY2024-25 income USD 13.6M: about 69 percent donations and grants, no government grants, 7 percent earned, 20 percent investment income (Form 990, Part VIII).
It posts annual reports from 2019 to 2024 with a 2024 donor list, a financial summary and board; Form 990s are on ProPublica.

f: Small artist-run centre; Canada Council gave $280k over two years (2017-18); also Manitoba Arts Council, Winnipeg Arts Council and Province of Manitoba.
w: Indigenous artist-run centre founded in 1996 in the Exchange District.
x: FY2023-24 income CAD 503k: 76 percent federal, provincial and municipal grants, 7 percent gifts and charity grants, under 1 percent earned sales (T3010, Schedule 6).
T3010 returns sit on the CRA charity listing; the site names three directors and shows nine undated, unlabelled supporter logos; no annual reports.

f: Small community art centre; core IVAIS support since 1998-99, plus NT Government, Ian Potter Foundation and Cotton On Foundation (retail).
w: Yolŋu community-controlled art centre, founded 1976. A local landowner corporation that earns bauxite royalties gave money in 2017.
x: FY2023-24 income AUD 10.2M: 10 percent government revenue, under 1 percent donations, 76 percent goods and services, 14 percent other revenue (ACNC annual information statement).
ACNC holds annual reports for 2017 and 2018 and financial reports for 2013 to 2025; the centre's own site lists no funders or board.
Consists of two divisions, the Yirrkala Art Centre and the Mulka Project, which includes the Mulka Museum; its pages name no outside partner or network.

f: Small Aboriginal-run trust at Federation Square. Its 2022-23 report lists Creative Victoria, First Peoples-State Relations and City of Melbourne, plus Viva Energy (oral history), Lendlease and ANZ.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Viva Energy, which supplies about a quarter of Australia's fuel under the Shell brand, is a key sponsor. No protest aimed at the Trust found.
x: FY2023-24 revenue AUD 8.2M: about 62 percent government, 2 percent donations and bequests, 30 percent goods and services, 3 percent investments (ACNC annual information statement).
It posts annual reports from 2008 to 2023 with full financial statements, a partners and sponsors section and the board.

f: Very small First Nations artist-run space; Australian Government Indigenous Languages and Arts, Creative Victoria and Merri-bek Council.
w: First Nations-led gallery in Brunswick, founded in 2011. Hosted the 2014 '18C' protest show against Racial Discrimination Act changes.
x: FY2023-24 income AUD 178k: 99.8 percent government revenue; expenses AUD 212k, of which AUD 183k is grants and donations paid out (ACNC annual information statement).
ACNC holds financial reports for 2021 to 2026; the about page names three government funders, undated; no annual reports and no named board.
Member of Contemporary Art Organisations Australia and home to Blakademy, its own critical Indigenous learning space. Member of CAOA.

n: Sámi Center for Contemporary Art (Sámi Dáiddaguovddáš)
f: Sámi Parliament direct grant of NOK 6.09M in 2025 (NOK 5.88M in 2024), against total operating revenue of NOK 7.92M.
w: Foundation in Karasjok led by Monika Anti. The other NOK 1.8M of 2025 revenue is not itemised in the sources read.
x: FY2025 operating revenue NOK 7.92M against operating costs of NOK 8.15M; the register shows no grant breakdown, so the public share is not stated (Brønnøysund accounts register).
Audited accounts for 2023 to 2025 are in Norway's accounts register; the site lists the full board but no annual reports or funders.
Member of Kunstsentrene i Norge, the national association of 15 regional art centres.

f: Creative New Zealand gives core funding and is the principal funder. Total revenue in 2025 was NZ$1.16M.
w: Māori arts charitable trust founded in 1996. Its 2025 annual report, published June 2026, names Creative New Zealand as principal funder.
x: FY2025 group income NZD 1.16M: 88 percent goods-and-services revenue including Creative New Zealand funding (not split out), 5 percent member fees and donations, 7 percent interest (annual report 2025).
Annual reports 2018 to 2025 carry financial statements; the 2025 report names Creative New Zealand as core funder with partner acknowledgements and lists the trustees.

f: Small photo museum (193k visitors 2019); City of Amsterdam, tickets, VriendenLoterij, VandenEnde Foundation, Garanti BBVA International (bank), Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation.
w: Roster read via a Dec 2025 archive of its partnerships page; a lottery and a bank are the corporate names to know.
x: FY2025 income EUR 5.15M: 24 percent public subsidy (AFK and City of Amsterdam), 24 percent private contributions and sponsorship, 52 percent earned (annual report 2025, pp. 41-42).
Annual reports for 2024 and 2025 carry the accounts, named funders and the supervisory board; an undated partnerships page names four major partners.
Member of the Dutch network Musea Bekennen Kleur; its 2024 report lists Fotomuseum Winterthur, The Photographers' Gallery, Le Bal and FOMU among education partners. Member of Museumvereniging.

f: City of Winterthur gives CHF 738k a year for 2025-2032; also Canton of Zurich, Verein, Volkart Stiftung, Ringier, Monterosa and about 20 foundations.
w: Name to know: the Krupp foundation, a funder that holds 10% of warship builder TKMS and 21% of thyssenkrupp.
x: FY2024 income CHF 2.17M: 57 percent City of Winterthur and Canton of Zurich, 14 percent the Verein, 2 percent earned; the rest names no funder (annual report 2024, p. 44).
Annual reports 2019 to 2024 include accounts and named partners and patrons; the Stiftungsrat is named on the About page.
Runs the Fotozentrum (Center for Photography) jointly with Fotostiftung Schweiz, and through it belongs to the Art Museums of Switzerland group.

f: €8.6M budget in 2024, 68% from the Ministry of Culture; Jaeger-LeCoultre, CHANEL, Fondation Neuflize OBC, Louis Roederer and Swiss Life also fund it.
w: 2013 censorship row: after a complaint from the CRIF, the culture ministry made it add visitor notices to Ahlam Shibli's show.
x: Activity reports 2019 to 2025 are posted, but without financial statements; the patrons page shows undated logos, and the governance page lists the association's members.
Member of the d.c.a and Tram networks; its board and general assembly include Centre Pompidou, Musée d'Orsay, Rencontres d'Arles, BnF and Le Point du Jour. Member of Réseau Tram.

f: About $8M revenue and $15M expenses (FY2023 Form 990); corporate supporters are Fondation d'entreprise Hermès, Select Equity, Harlowe, Paramount Global, MPB and Hearst.
w: 2020 open letter from about 150 community members over students' protest photos; ICP refused to make students take them down.
x: FY2025 income USD 7.53M against expenses of USD 15.18M: about 2 percent government grants, 49 percent other contributions, 53 percent earned, mostly tuition (Form 990, Part VIII).
Form 990s for 2021 to 2024 are posted on its site and in ProPublica; corporate supporters show as undated logos, and the board is listed.
Runs education programmes with Pace University, Hunter College, Barnard College, St. John's University, Ringling College and the Centro Italiano per la Fotografia in Milan.

n: ZKM Center for Art and Media
f: About 250k visitors in 2023; the City of Karlsruhe and Baden-Württemberg are founders and split core funding. EnBW is its partner, with BBBank and dm as project sponsors.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. EnBW owns about 84% of gas group VNG and still burns coal. No protest or petition aimed at ZKM or its EnBW tie found.
x: It posts no annual reports or accounts; partners show as logos, and its board of trustees is named as of September 2026.

A foundation under public law set up by Baden-Württemberg and the City of Karlsruhe; it shares its building with the HfG art university and the Kunstmuseum Karlsruhe. Member of Deutscher Museumsbund, European Media Art Platform.

f: City of Linz and Linz AG, the city's wholly owned utility (core partners); Land Oberösterreich, Siemens, KUKA, Dorotheum, ORF and others as supporting partners.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Gas fuelled 81.30% of Linz AG's own electricity generation. Bloomberg Philanthropies, under campaign in London, is a current project partner. Ars Electronica is not targeted.
x: 2023 total revenue about EUR 25M, a record: about two thirds self-earned, the remainder public funds for public-service tasks, mainly the City of Linz as owner (company press release).
It posts no annual report; accounts are filed in the Austrian company register, partners show as logos, and an advisory board is named.
Operated by Ars Electronica Linz GmbH & Co KG, which also runs the Festival, the Prix Ars Electronica and the Futurelab. Member of European Media Art Platform.

f: Private foundation financed by tickets, books, sponsors, donations and its Friends, and funded by the Berlin Senate culture department. Corporate members: DKB, GASAG and Pfizer Deutschland.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. GASAG, Berlin's gas supplier founded in 1847, is a current corporate member. No protest or boycott aimed at C/O Berlin found.
x: It posts no annual report or accounts; sponsors show as logos, and its advisory board is named.
Co-awards the Ulrike Crespo Photography Prize each year with the Crespo Foundation and is supported by its Friends association. Member of Deutscher Museumsbund.

f: Ville de Paris is main partner. Patrons include ADAGP, Fondation BIC, Fondation Hermès and Rubis Mécénat, the endowment fund of fuel and gas distributor Rubis.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Rubis distributes fuels, heating oils, lubricants, liquefied gases and bitumen, and holds a stake in a Caribbean refinery.
x: Its partners page names backers without an overall date; it posts no reports or board, and its register accounts were not checked.

A non-profit association whose standing partners include EHESS for its autumn seminar, the CNAP for talks and the Carnets du BAL series, and the Cinéma des cinéastes for film cycles. Member of Réseau Tram.

f: Opened 12 Sep 2025 for about US$100M (building and collection); Astana Motors (cars, malls) pays running costs, and Halyk Bank has been Lead Partner since Mar 2026.
w: Private museum of Nurlan Smagulov. Its lead bank partner is majority-owned by Nazarbayev's son-in-law Timur Kulibayev.
x: US embassy cables say Timur Kulibayev, the president's son-in-law, controlled Halyk Bank: a 2005 cable reports a controlling interest; a 2008 note says he and Dinara Kulibayev each own half of Almex, which owns Halyk. The atlas lists Halyk as the museum's lead partner.
FY2024 receipts KZT 14.1bn: 79 percent founder contributions, 21 percent unnamed other receipts, all spent on building the museum, which opened in September 2025 (report on targeted use of funds).
Targeted-use-of-funds reports for 2021 to 2024 are posted; the partners page names only Halyk Bank, undated; the team page lists staff, not a board.
Long-term partner of the Centre Pompidou, and of MMCA in Seoul under a memorandum signed in September 2026.

f: Produced by the state Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation. Lead partners: Tourism Committee, Chamber of Commerce and Bukhara Oil. Partners include ACWA Power, Agrobank, Uzcard and Yandex Uzbekistan.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. First edition opened 5 September 2025. ACWA Power sponsored the display of the AlMusalla Prize design.
x: Its own site would not open; parent ACDF posts no reports or accounts, and an advisory board was announced publicly.
Organised by the Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation, whose chair Gayane Umerova commissioned it. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: State museum network under the Ministry of Culture, whose minister appointed its management. BP paid for pipeline rescue archaeology in the 2000s (2010 book); no current corporate sponsor found.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. In May 2022 ministry-appointed managers fired about 40 staff; sacked curators cite critical posts and a new union.
x: It posts annual reports from 2005 to 2017 only; no accounts, donor names or board were found on its site.

A national museum group that includes the Museum of Georgia, the National Gallery, the Tbilisi History Museum, regional museum-reserves such as Dmanisi and Vani, house museums and two research centres.

n: Center of Contemporary Art Tbilisi (Tbilisi Triennial)
f: Key benefactors: Peter Moening Foundation, Modern Ancient Brown Foundation, Swiss SDC, ERTOBA Georgia, DVV International, German Foreign Office, Danish Cultural Institute, New Democracy Fund (Denmark), Hastings Audio Network.
w: Lists 100+ international partners and donors. Georgian Dream's grants laws target foreign funding of arts groups (Freemuse, 2026). No action against CCA found.
x: No annual reports or accounts found; the supporters page names nine key benefactors and individual donors with no date; no board is listed.
Its Tbilisi Triennial is named as the only regional member of the International Biennial Association (2018). Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: State non-commercial organisation under Armenia's culture ministry, set up by ministry order in 2002. The ministry bought a Gorky work for it. Lincy Foundation helped pay the 2004 renovation.
w: The Lincy Foundation's help with the 2004 renovation is 22 years old; no current corporate sponsor is named in the sources.
x: The gallery's site carries no annual reports, accounts, funder list or board; it lists branches, collection, visits and education only.
Runs 13 branch galleries and house-museums across Armenia, from Etchmiadzin to Jermuk; the culture ministry above it is skipped.

f: Opened 20 Mar 2009 with about 800 works; founded by First Lady Mehriban Aliyeva and funded by the Heydar Aliyev Foundation, which she heads.
w: A ruling-family foundation is its only known funder; the director since 2012 is Aida Mahmudova, founder of YARAT.
x: A US Embassy Baku profile says the First Lady's art collection became the base of Baku's new Museum of Modern Art, which "opened quietly last fall". It writes that her family is believed to exert control over the culture ministry.
The museum's site, live copy down, shows no annual reports, accounts, funder list or board; it carries only about, visit, library and what's-on pages.

n: National Museum of the Republic of Kazakhstan
f: A state museum opened in 2014 with about 175,000 objects, run by the Ministry of Culture and Information; its budget is not published and no corporate sponsors are listed.
w: Aug-Sep 2026 show co-organised with sanctioned oligarch Vladimir Potanin's Olympic Collection.
x: The museum's site posts legal acts and anti-corruption pages but no annual reports, accounts, funder list or board.
Joint laboratory with the China National Silk Museum, cooperation with the Louvre, and an in-house Halyk Kazynasy research institute. Member of ASEMUS.

n: State Museum of Arts of Uzbekistan
f: State museum founded in 1918. The state Art and Culture Development Foundation runs a museum renovation programme that includes it. No budget or funder list is published.
w: 2023: RFE/RL reported the museum withheld Vyacheslav Akhunov's 1987 Bukhara painting from a show; it issued no statement. ACDF also runs the Bukhara Biennial.
x: The museum and its renovation sponsor, the Art and Culture Development Foundation, publish no reports, accounts or funder list, and name only a chairperson.

f: University museum of IFAN and Cheikh Anta Diop University. Its partners page lists Senegal's arts and heritage directorates, Fondation TOTAL Sénégal, Fondation SOCOCIM, Fondation Volkswagen and the Goethe-Institut.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Fondation TOTAL Sénégal is listed with no gift year. Sococim renovated the museum in 2010 and 19M renovated one of its two buildings.
x: The museum sits inside IFAN at Cheikh Anta Diop University and posts no reports, accounts, donors or board of its own.
The museum belongs to IFAN Cheikh Anta Diop, the research institute integrated into the University of Dakar (now Cheikh Anta Diop University) in 1960.

f: About 1.3-1.5bn FCFA executed in 2025 (~US$2.3M), nearly 80% from the Burkina state; EU 195M FCFA, plus the UN, OIF, LONAB lottery and telecoms.
w: Pan-African film festival, held every two years since 1969. The 2025 edition was nearly 80% state-funded under the military transition.
x: No reports, accounts or board posted; partners and media partners blocks show undated logos, and the sponsor slot shows the organiser's logo.

f: Terra Foundation for American Art gave $150,000 (2023) and $100,000 (2025). The 2024 edition also thanked Open Society Foundations, Pro Helvetia, Goethe-Institut, Institut Français and Lagos State.
w: Run by Àkéte Art Foundation. The 5th edition is titled The Museum of Things Unseen.
x: No reports or accounts found; the supporters page shows about 40 logos, mostly without alt text, and the site names six advisory board members.
Runs under the Àkéte Art Foundation; its partners page shows the Centre for Contemporary Art Lagos, Omenka Gallery and Foto Factory Lagos. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

f: Tiny association with project grants: Fondation Langlois (2001) and EU ACPCultures, EUR 399,409 (2009 award). No funder list for the 2020s found.
w: Own site ker-thiossane.org refuses connections and the Wayback Machine rate-limited; the Partcours profile lists projects, not funders.
x: The site is a script-only app that no archive copy renders, and no register is open, so nothing could be checked.
Runs Afropixel, which became the African node of the Pixelache network in 2008. Member of Arts Collaboratory.

f: State subsidy of 327M CFA francs a year; tickets cover about a third of costs (AFP, 2021). China National Petroleum funded the oil exhibition, Orano the uranium show.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. CNPC is China's state oil company. Its oil exhibition at the museum includes a large model of the Zinder refinery.
x: No official site was found for this national museum, and nothing from it or its ministry on reports, accounts, donors or board.

f: Founder Vitshois Mwilambwe Bondo says he funds it from his art sales and sponsors, mostly for the Congo Biennale. Works with Fondation Montresso. Sited in the TEXAF concession.
w: He says the Congolese government gives no support. Sponsors are unnamed. Pro Helvetia reported a 2024 artist residency there.
x: Kin ArtStudio's biennale site shows 28 unnamed partner logos with no date, and posts no reports, accounts or board; it lists curators and advisers.
Works in partnership with the Montresso Art Foundation, according to its founder Vitshois Mwilambwe Bondo.

f: Cameroon's culture ministry. AFD gave EUR 1M through a debt-reduction contract from 1 October 2019; Expertise France ran the 2020 to 2024 modernisation.
w: National museum since 1988, in the former presidential palace; it reopened in 2015 after renovation.
x: It has no site of its own found and publishes no reports, accounts, funder list or board; its funders appear only on AFD project pages.

f: ACCRA [dot] ALT festival. 2023 supporters: Ghana's tourism and culture ministry, Ghana Tourism Authority, Korle Klottey Municipal Assembly, Ghana Museums and Monuments Board, Citi FM/TV, Institut Français.
w: The organiser's own press release lists the supporters. The 2023 edition moved from James Town to Osu; no reason was given.
x: The organiser's site posts no reports, accounts or board, and names supporters only inside festival announcements, not on a standing funder page.
Organised by the ACCRA [dot] ALT arts organisation.

f: Small independent non-profit founded 1998 by William Wells, now a foundation; no funder list found and its website no longer resolves.
w: Egypt's first independent contemporary art space; closed after a state raid in 2015, then ran from a converted factory.
x: Its archived site names no board, reports, accounts or funders; it says it is a Swedish foundation and relies on donors, grants and sponsors.
Tied to the Rawabet performance space, which it supported from 2006 until that space closed in 2020.

f: Cultural association funded by private Tunisian patrons who are not named, per its director. Partner: African Culture Fund. No budget or donor list published.
w: Renovation was handled by Mamia Taktak (director Camille Lévy, 2022). 32bis.org lists no supporters, partners or accounts.
x: 32bis.org lists no annual reports, accounts, partners, funders, board or team.

f: State museum. 2001 World Bank loan (~24M TND) and state money (9.5M TND) funded the 2009–12 expansion. TOTAL Tunisie, Loukil, ATUGE and Dar El Marsa backed a 2017 Louvre partnership.
w: Tunisia's largest museum, known for its Roman mosaics; closed July 2021 to Sept 2023.
x: The museum site published no reports, accounts, sponsor list or board; it is now a blank hosting page, and the ministry was not checked.
Partner of the Louvre since 2009, through agreements signed with Tunisia's Institut national du patrimoine for the Bardo.

f: Algerian State. Its 1985 statute makes it a public administrative establishment under the culture minister, funded by State, local and public-body subsidies, gifts and entry fees.
w: State oil firm Sonatrach handed over 174 Guccione paintings in 2012, a one-off gift. The museum site names no sponsor.
x: The museum's old site posts no reports, accounts, funder list or board; it is a state establishment under the culture minister.

f: Private foundation and residency (opened 2009) funded entirely by its founder, the French businessman Jean-Louis Haguenauer; no other sponsors are named.
w: Residency on a 10-hectare olive grove 20 km outside Marrakech, hosting about 40 artists a year; visits by appointment.
x: The foundation's site posts no reports, accounts, funder list or board; it names only collaborating institutions and its Amis de Jardin Rouge association.
Works with the Musée Mohammed VI in Rabat and runs its education programme through the friends association Les Amis de Jardin Rouge.

f: Run by Fondation Al Mada, the corporate foundation of Al Mada, the royal family's holding company. Le360 (10 May 2023) says it manages the Casablanca and Rabat villas.
w: Al Mada's Nareva holds 50.7% of the Safi coal plant (two 693 MW units). Al Mada also owns Attijariwafa Bank, Inwi, Managem and Marjane.
x: The Villas' site, read from archive copies, names Fondation Al Mada as its corporate patron but posts no reports, accounts, funder list or board.
Run by Fondation Al Mada, which also runs the sister Villa des Arts de Rabat.

n: Museo de Arte Moderno de Medellín (MAMM)
f: Mid-size private museum founded 1978; pillars are Medellín city hall, national Culture Ministry, Comfama, SURA, Bancolombia, EPM, Fundación Fraternidad and Fundación MUV.
w: Roster read on its own Pilares y aliados page. Public utility EPM is a pillar; Celsia (an energy firm) is credited for website support.
x: FY2024 income COP 9.45bn; the museum's own table gives 42 percent own income, 27 percent sponsorship and donations, 23 percent public bodies (informe de gestion 2025, p. 26).
The museum posts annual reports for 2022 to 2025, 2024 financial statements, a named list of pillars and allies, and its 12-member board.
Lists Fundación Montechico, El Boga Casa Taller and Minkalab as institutional allies.

n: Museo Nacional de Etnografía y Folklore (MUSEF)
f: State museum (60 years in 2022) funded through the Fundación Cultural del Banco Central de Bolivia, a public body under the central bank.
w: Holds more than 33,000 cultural objects. Its director was pushed out in 2020 after a change of government and reinstated in 2021.
x: MUSEF has no records of its own; parent Fundación Cultural del BCB posts reports 2019 to 2025, statements 2018 to 2025 and its council.
Part of the Fundación Cultural del Banco Central de Bolivia since 1995, sister to Museo Nacional de Arte de Bolivia and Casa Nacional de Moneda; has a Sucre branch.

f: State national museum; the government has budgeted about US$100M for a new building, with a state-owned enterprise managing construction.
w: The government overturned the jury's choice of design for the new building in July 2026.
x: The ministry lists a preliminary 2022 accountability report for the National Museum; its own site is blocked, so funders and board are unread.

f: Ministry of Culture museum with a 2021 budget of about COLONES 1.77bn (about US$3M), 48% of it salaries; about 37,000 visitors in 2018.
w: Public collection museum in La Sabana. Its board approved lending works to the presidential offices in Sep 2026 without saying which works.
x: 2021 national budget line CRC 1.745bn, all state money (no external resources), of which CRC 1.427bn was spent; CRC 839M of that was salaries (execution report 2021, p. 1).
The MAC posts leadership reports for 2018 to 2022, budget and execution reports, and board minutes, but no funder list or board roster.
The MAC runs the Escuela Casa del Artista.

n: Museo Nacional de Arte Moderno Carlos Mérida (MUNAM)
f: State museum of the Ministerio de Cultura y Deportes, which spent over Q16M (about US$2M) on roof and museography works in 2023-25.
w: Closed since Nov 2022, with no reopening date as of Oct 2025.
x: The museum has only a page on its ministry's site with no reports, funders or board; the ministry posts budget execution for the whole ministry.

n: Fundación Casa de los Tres Mundos
f: Small cultural foundation built with German, Austrian, Swiss and Dutch government grants and the City of Granada; closed by the Nicaraguan state in 2024.
w: Founded 1987-89 by Ernesto Cardenal and Dietmar Schönherr. Ran art and music schools and Radio Volcán.
x: The foundation's archive site names its 2022 board but posts no annual reports, accounts or funder list; closed in 2024.

f: Corporate sponsorship programme for its eight rooms. Pillar companies on its site: Pollo Campero, Pepsi and CMI, from the 2019 roster. Part of Universidad Francisco Marroquín.
w: The sponsors page still shows the 2019 roster. OpenSanctions has no match for CMI, Pollo Campero or Dionisio Gutiérrez.
x: The museum has no records of its own; its parent university posts audited statements and annual reports, and its sponsor page shows three 2019 logos.
Part of Universidad Francisco Marroquín, on whose Guatemala City campus it stands.

f: Privately owned museum founded in 1926; a foundation was set up in 1959 to maintain it. No funder list, annual report or accounts found.
w: Pre-Columbian collection of about 45,000 objects. Led by president and CEO Andrés Álvarez Calderón Larco.
x: Larco publishes no annual reports, accounts or sponsors; its directory names only an executive president and a director, not a board.

f: A small state-backed museum: most of its money comes from Finland's Ministry of Education and Culture, plus a yearly grant from Inari Municipality.
w: Owned by the Sámi Museum Foundation, whose board must be at least half Sámi. Its exhibition renewal was paid for by Finnish foundations.
x: Siida's site posts no annual reports, accounts, funder list or board names; it says only that the foundation board has eight members.
Founded by Sámi Litto in 1959; runs the Skolt Sámi Heritage House and has cooperation agreements with the University of Lapland and the Sámi Education Institute. Member of Suomen museoliitto.

f: 2023: about NOK 15M in public operating grants, NOK 13.1M of it from the Sámi Parliament (Sametinget), plus Finnmark county and four municipalities.
w: A Sámi museum foundation running several sites. It had 14,467 visitors in 2023 and has no corporate sponsors.
x: FY2025 income NOK 26.1M: the six named public grants total NOK 22.8M (about 87 percent), NOK 20.4M from the Sámi Parliament; sales NOK 1.0M (annual report 2025, p. 5).
RDM posts annual reports for 2014 to 2025 and names its eight board members, but no donor list; its accounts are in Norway's register.
A Sámi museum foundation made up of De Samiske Samlinger, Kautokeino bygdetun, Porsanger museum, Kokelv sjøsamiske museum and the Samisk Kunstmagasin art collection.

f: About NOK 32M a year (2022). 96% is public grants and the rest comes from non-profit foundations; it has no commercial sponsors.
w: The regional art museum for Northern Norway, with a strong Sámi programme. It opened a Bodø venue in 2025 and programmes Nordover in Longyearbyen.
x: FY2025 income NOK 48.4M against costs of NOK 45.7M; the register shows totals only, with no split between grants and earned income (Regnskapsregisteret).
The museum names its 2024 to 2027 board and files accounts in Norway's register, but posts no annual reports and no funder list.
Runs Nordover kunstsenter in Longyearbyen and is key partner of the Artica Svalbard residency; two artists' associations appoint a board member.

f: 2023 revenue US$21.5M (IRS 990), from state and federal agencies, Hawai'i foundations such as Kamehameha Schools, and Hawai'i corporate sponsors.
w: Hawai'i's state museum of natural and cultural history, founded in memory of Princess Bernice Pauahi Bishop.
x: FY2024-25 revenue USD 28.1M: about 52 percent government grants, 33 percent donations and memberships, 13 percent earned, 2 percent other items (Form 990, Part VIII).
The museum posts annual reports for 2020 to 2025, audited statements and Form 990s, named corporate and foundation donors, and its board of directors.

n: Greenland National Museum and Archives (Nunatta Katersugaasivia Allagaateqarfialu)
f: DKK 13.6M operating grant from Greenland's 2024 budget. Augustinus Fonden gave DKK 4.5M for a 2025-27 research project and funds two others. Beckett-Fonden also gave.
w: Flags: Tobacco. Augustinus Fonden's investment arm holds over 25% of Scandinavian Tobacco Group.
x: It posts activity reports from 2001 to 2024 without accounts; its site names managers and no board or donors.

n: Listasavn Føroya (National Gallery of the Faroe Islands)
f: Public grants from the Faroese parliament and government. Augustinus Fonden gave DKK 17M in 2022 for building development, after co-funding the 1993 extension with Tórshavn, Fossbankin and Danish foundations.
w: Flags: Tobacco. Augustinus Fonden owns Chr. Augustinus Fabrikker, which holds over 25% of cigar and pipe-tobacco maker Scandinavian Tobacco Group.
x: It posts no reports, accounts or donor list, says it runs on public funds, and names four board members.
Formed in 1989 by merging the collection of the Faroe Islands Art Association, founded in 1941, with the Faroese parliament's art collection.

f: Vanuatu statutory body. Its 2025 newsletter lists government grants, international donors, corporate sponsors and museum income, all unnamed. UNESCO's Heritage Emergency Fund paid for post-quake repairs to May 2026.
w: The fund's donors include the Qatar Fund for Development, Norway, Canada, the UK and France. Online fundraising followed the Dec 2024 quake.
x: The centre's site posts no annual reports, accounts, named funders or board; its 2025 newsletter names funding types only.
The umbrella body for the National Museum of Vanuatu, the National Archives and the Port Vila Public Library.

f: Solomon Islands Government (department of the Ministry of Culture and Tourism). Its 2024 virtual museum was funded by Australia's Digital Pasifik project, with British High Commission support.
w: Virtual museum launched Oct 2024 with both national libraries of Australia and New Zealand; the museum now owns and sustains the site.
x: The ministry's pages for the museum carry a brochure and a staff directory only; no reports, accounts, funder list or board were found.
It is a division of the Ministry of Culture and Tourism, alongside the National Art Gallery and the National Archives; the ministry itself is skipped.

f: Small foundation-run house (2025); carried by the Christoph Merian Stiftung, Basel-Stadt, Basel-Landschaft and the Federal Office of Culture.
w: Building is at Freilager-Platz 9 in Münchenstein. Education is funded by Göhner and Binding; the Pax Art Awards by Art Foundation Pax, an insurer's foundation.
x: HEK posts annual reports for 2021 to 2025 and names its foundation board, but shows funders as logos and publishes no accounts.
Partner of the European Media Art Platform (EMAP) since 2018. Member of European Media Art Platform.

f: Small art-and-tech centre (2025) with structural funding from Fédération Wallonie-Bruxelles, Flanders and VGC, plus the National Lottery and the ERDF.
w: Canal-side centre and fablab in Molenbeek. Its private partners are Fondation Orange (telecom) and Selligent (software).
x: iMAL names its board and shows public and private partners as logos, but posts no annual reports or accounts.
Member of the European Media Art Platform; its partners page lists V2_, LABoral, FACT, Ars Electronica, Bozar, Waag, LIMA and Gaîté Lyrique, among many others. Member of European Media Art Platform.

n: V2_ Lab for the Unstable Media
f: Small foundation (2025–2028 plan) with structural funding from the Creative Industries Fund NL and the City of Rotterdam, plus EU project grants.
w: Founded 1981. Dutch arts cuts after 2012 forced a reorganisation and ended DEAF, last held in 2014.
x: FY2025 income EUR 1.26M: earned EUR 83,878 and private funds EUR 5,000 are named; the rest is described as Rotterdam city and Stimuleringsfonds subsidy (bestuursverslag 2025, section 7).
V2_ posts annual reports for 2007 to 2025, annual accounts for 2019 to 2023, its funders for 2025 to 2028 and its supervisory board.
One of seven sponsoring partners of the Summer Sessions residency network, with Sardegna Teatro, Metamedia, PiNA, Schmiede Hallein, Marginal and the Academy for Theatre and Digitality.

f: Slovenian Ministry of Culture and City of Ljubljana, plus European Commission programmes (Creative Europe, Horizon 2020, ERDF, Interreg) and the Swiss Contribution, per the institute's supporters list.
w: Kersnikova Institute runs Kapelica Gallery, the Rampa Lab and BioTehna. Slovenia's culture portal lists it as an EU Creative Europe funding recipient.
x: Kersnikova lists 21 supporters by name but posts no annual reports, accounts or board; its Crew page names a director and staff.

Run by the Kersnikova Institute, founded by the University of Ljubljana's student organisation; a member of EMAP with LABoral, iMAL, Ars Electronica and Onassis. Member of European Media Art Platform.

f: Corporate cultural facility (2026) run and paid for by NTT East, a telecom operator, in Tokyo Opera City Tower.
w: Opened in 1997 to mark the centenary of Japan's telephone service. A non-profit art and science venue, not a commercial attraction.
x: ICC publishes nothing itself; its operator NTT East posts annual financial results and names its directors, and ICC lists no funders.

f: Annual festival (2026) funded since 2004 by the Kulturstiftung des Bundes. Berlin Senate, bpb, Medienboard and Creative Europe funding was listed for 2020–21.
w: Coordinates mark central Berlin, because festival venues change each year. Its 2026 partner programmes include the Schering Stiftung and HAU.
x: transmediale names no board and posts no reports or accounts; its old partner page shows funder logos and its about page names two funders.
Listed among the current partners of the European Media Art Platform (EMAP). Member of European Media Art Platform. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

n: LABoral Centro de Arte y Creación Industrial
f: Public foundation (budget about €1.3M in 2014) governed by Asturias, Gijón city and the Gijón Port Authority. Project sponsors in 2023 included the Onassis Foundation's Ariona Hellas.
w: Housed in the Universidad Laboral building. Fundación EDP, an energy group's foundation, co-funded the Eco-Visionarios exhibition in 2018–19.
x: FY2025 income EUR 1.29M excluding capital-grant releases: about 89 percent public operating grants (Asturias EUR 857,000), 8 percent earned, 3 percent sponsors and collaborations (audited accounts 2025).
LABoral posts activity reports for 2018 to 2025, audited accounts for 2014 to 2025 and its trustees, but no list of named funders.
Member of the European Media Art Platform with iMAL, Kersnikova Institute, Ars Electronica and Onassis; the Gijón Port Authority sits on its board. Member of European Media Art Platform.

f: Small nonprofit (revenue $1.63M in 2023), funded by Atlantic, Ford, Jerome and Arison Arts foundations, the NEA, NYSCA and NYC DCLA.
w: Art-and-technology nonprofit registered in Brooklyn as Eyebeam Atelier Inc. Arison Arts Foundation is Arison-family money.
x: FY2024-25 revenue USD 0.92M: about 17 percent government grants, 75 percent other donations, 4 percent earned, 4 percent investment income (Form 990, Part VIII).
Eyebeam's support page names its institutional funders, individual donors and seven board members; its Form 990s are public, but it posts no annual reports.

f: Donors, October 2023 to September 2024: Adobe, Luce Foundation, NYC Cultural Affairs and Smithsonian initiatives at $100k+; Bloomberg Philanthropies, Apple, PwC Charitable Foundation and NYSCA at $25k to $49,999.
w: Bloomberg Philanthropies gave $25,000-$49,999 in 2023-24. In May 2026, 260+ UK artists urged five London theatres to drop it; not aimed here.
x: Democracy Now!, citing the Wall Street Journal, reported a White House plan for a far-reaching review of Smithsonian exhibitions to align them with Trump's interpretation of U.S. history. It followed the removal of references to his impeachments.
Its parent Smithsonian posts annual reports 2015 to 2025 and audited accounts; the museum itself names donors for 2023-24 and its trustees.
A Smithsonian museum that runs a master's programme in design history and curatorial studies with Parsons School of Design.

f: 2023: about two-thirds own earnings and under one-third state grant; Danish foundations pay for buildings and shows, Augustinus Fonden among them.
w: Flags: Tobacco. Augustinus Fonden, which part-owns Scandinavian Tobacco Group, funds its buildings and shows.
x: FY2025 income DKK 75.4M: about 68 percent own earnings (tickets, shop, cafe, rentals), 24 percent state grants, 7 percent non-public grants (annual report, p. 74).
It posts Danish annual reports from 2012 to 2025 with an income and expense account, names its funders for 2025 and lists its board.

A self-governing institution whose Representative Office, which chooses the board, includes seats for the Royal Danish Academy (KADK), the National Museum, C. L. Davids Fond & Samling and its Friends. Member of ODM.

f: 2024: EUR 16.1M income, EUR 11.7M of it federal base funding; sponsors Porsche Holding Salzburg, Wienerberger, Wiener Städtische, Swarovski and others.
w: Porsche Holding Salzburg, a Volkswagen firm, began a multi-year partnership in 2024 and backed free-entry days in December 2024 and December 2025.
x: FY2024 income EUR 16.1M: about 73 percent federal base funding, 22 percent sales (admissions, rentals, sponsoring), 1 percent donations, 3 percent grants (annual report 2024, p. 44).
The MAK posts annual reports for 2017 to 2025, audited accounts, a named 2024 sponsor thank-you list and its Kuratorium members.
Runs branches in Vienna (Geymüllerschlössel, MAK Tower), the MAK Center in Los Angeles, and the Josef Hoffmann Museum in Brtnice with the Moravian Gallery.

f: Private foundation founded 1989 by Vitra and Rolf Fehlbaum, with a Vitra subsidy. The 2026 Jongerius show is backed by Maharam, Camper and IKEA Stiftung, with the Design Circle.
w: IKEA Stiftung, founded by the German IKEA companies in 1981, backs the 2026 show. Disclose reported forced prison labour at IKEA's Belarus suppliers (November 2022).
x: The museum posts no annual reports, accounts, donor list or board; sponsors appear only as credits on individual exhibition pages.
Member of ICOM, the Deutscher Museumsbund and the Museumsverband Baden-Württemberg; its friends association Design Circle is a named cooperation partner. Member of Deutscher Museumsbund.

f: 2023: US$42.5M revenue, US$25.1M of it contributions. Founder Corning Incorporated is the main funder. FY2025 Form 990 fills no government-grant line, so press-named New York State grants are not separable.
w: Founded 1951 by Corning Glass Works; budget is large but attendance (about 400k, 2012) is under the 500k line.
x: FY2025 revenue USD 59.9M: about 66 percent contributions, 27 percent earned (admissions, shops, education), 7 percent investment returns; no government-grant line is filled (Form 990, Part VIII).
The museum posts annual reports from 2010 to 2024, audited statements, a named Business Alliance list and its trustees.
Works with UrbanGlass on New Glass Review and sits with Fondazione Giorgio Cini, Pentagram Stiftung and two Venice universities on the Committee for Glass Scholarships. Member of AAMD.

n: Die Neue Sammlung - The Design Museum
f: Bavarian state museum under the Bavarian Ministry of Science and the Arts. Its 2025 centenary show was funded by the ministry, PIN. Freunde der Pinakothek der Moderne and Allianz.
w: Allianz's US unit, AGI US, pleaded guilty to securities fraud in 2022 and agreed to pay $5.8bn. PIN. Freunde lists Allianz as partner in 2026.
x: This Bavarian state museum posts no annual reports, accounts, funder list or board; sponsors appear only as credits on exhibition pages.
Housed in the Pinakothek der Moderne, with an affiliate museum in Weiden, a cooperation with the Neues Museum Nürnberg and the friends association PIN. Member of Deutscher Museumsbund.

Ghalya Saadawi, Post–Sharjah Biennial 10: Institutional Grease and Institutional Critique (e-flux, 2011): Saadawi argues that the fallout from Sharjah Biennial 10 should widen into a critique of how institutions and capital shape art, beyond boycotts alone. She questions the Sharjah Art Foundation's conduct and state funding, and the Guggenheim's censorship of Hans Haacke in 1971. See the What the field says case study.
Its site blocks automated reads; searches found no reports, accounts or board. State-owned TDIC owns it and the Guggenheim Foundation runs the programme.
Developed with the Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation, which sets its programme, and the newest member of the network with the Guggenheim museums in New York, Venice and Bilbao.

n: John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts
f: Congress pays for the federally owned building; programmes run on ticket sales and private gifts. Trump became chair in February 2025; a $100M FY2026 revenue shortfall was projected.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment, Protest or boycott. Trump fired the president and board in February 2025. Hamilton, Issa Rae, Renée Fleming and Philip Glass pulled out of the Center.
x: After Trump made himself Kennedy Center chair in February, new leadership fired at least seven Social Impact staff, including artistic director Marc Bamuthi Joseph, who said the takeover is destroying a sanctuary for creative expression.
The Kennedy Center board, hand-picked by Trump after he named himself chair, voted to rename the venue for Trump and Kennedy. Democratic lawmakers said any name change needs an act of Congress.

Judge Christopher Cooper ruled Trump's rebranding of the Kennedy Center illegal and temporarily barred its closure. Trump had announced a two-year closure after a wave of artists and performers resigned or canceled.
Trump's Kennedy Center board voted to close the center immediately, citing financial shortages and renovations, hours after a judge again blocked adding Trump's name without congressional approval.

Dozens of artists and organizations, including the San Francisco Ballet and the Martha Graham Dance Company, pulled out of Kennedy Center performances after Trump appointed himself chair. Fired programmer Mallory Miller co-founded Hands Off the Arts.

Drag performers led a protest outside the Kennedy Center against Trump's takeover. Organizer Lord Henry demanded the board reinstate queer programming after Trump fired the president, replaced the board and named himself chairman.
FY2024 income USD 306.9M: about 18 percent government grants, 41 percent donations and memberships, 34 percent earned (programming receipts and fees), rest parking, investments and other (Form 990).
Its annual reports run 2017 to 2023 with financial reports for 2021 to 2023; Form 990s are on ProPublica; funders and board were not checked.
Listed in the Artist Communities Alliance directory.

f: A Smithsonian museum. About two-thirds of the Smithsonian's money comes from Congress; the rest is private gifts, endowment and earned income.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. In August 2025 the museum removed a reference to Trump's two impeachments from its presidency exhibit, and the White House put it under content review.
x: Democracy Now!, citing the Wall Street Journal, reported a White House plan for a far-reaching review of Smithsonian exhibitions to align them with Trump's interpretation of U.S. history. It followed the removal of references to his impeachments.

The National Museum of American History removed references to Trump's two impeachments from an exhibit. A person told the Washington Post the review came under White House pressure to remove an art museum director; the museum said the label was temporary.
FY2025 enacted operating resources USD 41.5M: about 69 percent federal appropriations and public grants, 21 percent donor and sponsor designated, 10 percent general trust (budget request, p. 39).
No records of its own: parent Smithsonian posts a 2025 annual report naming donors, audited statements for 2011 to 2025, and 17 Regents.

f: A Smithsonian museum; Congress supplies about two-thirds of the Smithsonian's money. David H. Koch, a board member, backed the Hall of Human Origins, which carries his name.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment, Fossil fuels, Campaigned name, Protest or boycott. The White House named it in its August 2025 content review. In 2015, 15 groups campaigned to remove Koch from the board.
x: Democracy Now!, citing the Wall Street Journal, reported a White House plan for a far-reaching review of Smithsonian exhibitions to align them with Trump's interpretation of U.S. history. It followed the removal of references to his impeachments.

Democracy Now! reported scientists' call for museums to cut ties with Koch money. It said David Koch sat on the Smithsonian natural history museum's board and that a Koch-backed Smithsonian installation drew criticism.

The New Yorker profile quotes Joseph Romm of ClimateProgress saying the Koch-funded Hall of Human Origins "whitewashes the modern climate issue". A ThinkProgress item in a Podesta-archive email says Koch's donations will name a Smithsonian wing. (news item forwarded in a leak)
FY2025 enacted operating resources USD 80.2M: about 73 percent federal appropriations and public grants, 21 percent donor and sponsor designated, 7 percent general trust (budget request, p. 49).
No records of its own: parent Smithsonian posts a 2025 annual report naming donors, audited statements for 2011 to 2025, and 17 Regents.

f: A Smithsonian museum; Congress supplies about two-thirds of the Smithsonian's money, the rest from private gifts, endowment and earned income.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. Trump said in May 2025 he was firing director Kim Sajet, who then resigned. Amy Sherald cancelled her show in July 2025 over a painting.
x: Democracy Now!, citing the Wall Street Journal, reported a White House plan for a far-reaching review of Smithsonian exhibitions to align them with Trump's interpretation of U.S. history. It followed the removal of references to his impeachments.
The Portrait Gallery removed text on Trump's two impeachments when it replaced his photo in the “American Presidents” exhibition. The Smithsonian told NPR it was a planned update of labels.

A Washington Post column forwarded in Sony's emails says Smithsonian Secretary Wayne Clough removed a Wojnarowicz video from a 2010 National Portrait Gallery show after a Catholic League complaint, exploited by conservative congressmen. A WSJ column in Stratfor's emails also reports the removal. (news item forwarded in a leak)
FY2025 enacted operating resources USD 13.9M: about 55 percent federal appropriations, 27 percent donor and sponsor designated, 18 percent general trust (budget request, p. 54).
No records of its own: parent Smithsonian posts a 2025 annual report naming donors, audited statements for 2011 to 2025, and 17 Regents.

f: The art museum of Indiana University, a public university. Sidney and Lois Eskenazi gave $15M in 2016 for the renovation and the name.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment, Protest or boycott. Indiana University cancelled the Samia Halaby retrospective in December 2023. PEN America urged reinstatement and a petition drew 8,000 signatures.
x: Indiana University canceled Samia Halaby's first U.S. retrospective after three years of work, and that she was told her Gaza posts were the reason. The university cited concerns about the exhibit's integrity.
It posts annual reviews for 2020 to 2023; parent Indiana University posts audited annual financial reports and names its nine trustees; no donor list online.
The art museum of Indiana University Bloomington, which uses IU Auditorium for event booking and management.

n: Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts
f: Campus Fund supporters (June 2026) in the top Leader tier: Bloomberg Philanthropies, Kenneth Griffin and Citadel, American Express, JPMorganChase, Hearst. David Koch pledged $100M in 2008 for the theater.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Campaigned name, Protest or boycott. Activists disrupted the Met Opera's Carmen on 21 November 2025, demanding Lincoln Center remove Koch names. Griffin was targeted at the Whitney, not here.
x: Democracy Now!, discussing Jane Mayer's New Yorker article, reported that David Koch funded modernization of Lincoln Center's New York State Theatre, which now bears his name. Guest Charles Lewis called Koch Industries “the Standard Oil of our time.”

A New Yorker profile that Sidney Blumenthal forwarded to Hillary Clinton says David Koch gave $100 million in 2008 to modernise Lincoln Center's New York State Theatre, which now bears his name. It says the Kochs operate oil refineries and pipelines. (news item forwarded in a leak)

FY2025 income USD 235.0M: about 2 percent government grants, 45 percent donations and memberships, 43 percent earned (mostly facility rentals and services), 9 percent investments (Form 990, Part VIII).
It posts Form 990 and audited statements, a named Campus Fund supporter list of June 2026, 67 directors, and archived annual reports to 2017.
Home to eleven resident arts organizations, including the Metropolitan Opera, New York Philharmonic, New York City Ballet, Juilliard, Lincoln Center Theater and Jazz at Lincoln Center.

f: A Ukrainian city museum until 2022. Under Russian occupation the culture ministry of the so-called Donetsk People's Republic runs it. The US, EU and UK list that republic as sanctioned.
w: Flags: Sanctions. Its Kuindzhi paintings were taken to a museum in Donetsk after the city fell in 2022.
