The Rwanda Cultural Heritage Academy manages it with seven other national museums, including the Ethnographic Museum in Huye and Kandt House Museum in Kigali.

f: Artist-run centre founded in 2012 by painter brothers Innocent Nkurunziza and Emmanuel Nkuranga. It runs a gallery, classes, tours, memberships and a café; no funders or sponsors are named.
w: Ten resident-artist slots at KG 563 St, Kacyiru. A funder list is not published.
x: Inema's site names its two founders but no funders, reports, accounts or board; a Support Inema page exists but was not readable.

f: Funded privately by founder Hassanein Hiridjee, Axian's chief executive, who chairs it. Partners: Air France, Cité internationale des arts, Ravinala Airports, Fondation Axian, Interreg Océan Indien.
w: Name to know: founder's Axian group. Axian Energy (USD 510M, 18.5% of USD 2.75bn in 2024) runs 135 Jovena and Eydon fuel stations. Telecom leads.
x: Shows 20 partner logos with no names or date; posts no annual reports or accounts, and names only its president and staff.
Fondation H runs its Paris artist residencies and exhibition space through a partnership with the Cité internationale des arts, in place since 2020. Member of Gallery Climate Coalition.

f: Won Culture Resource's Abbara Program grant (round 7, 2022). The Australian Government and Creative Australia support its Qubit fellowship (2026). The Spanish Embassy is a named partner.
w: Opened Muse Gallery in Khartoum in 2022; since the April 2023 war it works between Sudan and Egypt and runs the Sudan Art Archive.
x: Posts narrative year reviews for 2023 to 2025 with no figures; no accounts, no standing funder list, and only its five staff are named.
The Muse Multi Studios runs a fellowship with Qubit Incubator in Australia and lists Muse Gallery, Bait Alnisa and the Sudan Art Archive as affiliated studios.

n: Institute of Contemporary Art Indian Ocean (ICAIO)
f: Founded in 2015 by Salim Currimjee, a painter, architect and collector. No funder or sponsor list is published.
w: Exhibitions change each quarter, showing Mauritian, Indian and South African artists, at 51 Sir Seewoosagur Ramgoolam Street, Port Louis.
x: The institute's domain now redirects to an unrelated site and its archived pages hold no readable text, so nothing could be checked.

f: Operates under the Women's Gallery Arts and Research Trust. Its March 2023 show had support from the Swiss and Australian embassies and UN Women. No funder list is published.
w: Gallery Delta was founded in 1975 by Derek Huggins and Helen Lieros, who died in 2021; Nhaka presents itself as continuing that legacy.
x: No Nhaka Gallery website was found; the only named backers are for one 2023 show, and no reports, accounts or board appear.
Maintained since 2008 by the Gallery Delta Foundation for Art and the Humanities, a trust.

f: Founder Victor Mutelekesha's household paid for the building. Pro Helvetia paid for shelving; OCA, a Norwegian arts body, part-financed the 2023 opening show; the late artist Jan Groth donated.
w: Opened 6 January 2023 in New Chamba Valley with a gallery, library and artist residency; first show Prospice, Kwacha!
x: Names its eleven-member advisory board; publishes no annual reports, accounts or funder list.

f: Artists' association with over 100 members. State funding ended in the civil war; a late-1990s profile names Hivos as donor. No current funder list is published.
w: Official foundation 1948; reopened in 1993 by young artists. Maputo's council and the CTA led a 2021 mural project with 40 of its members.
x: The association's only page found is a late-1990s profile naming Hivos; it publishes no reports, accounts, funder list or board.

f: Funded by Wissam and Hiba Nesr. Wissam is chief executive of Webcor Group, a Swiss-based food importer and distributor with most African revenue in Angola. No outside funders named.
w: Opened in 2021 with a residency for Angolan and Lusophone African artists; the artistic committee is chaired by Paula Nascimento.
x: Names its eight-member advisory board and three-member artistic committee; publishes no annual reports, accounts or funder list, being paid for by its founders.

f: Binational centre under Namibian law, funded by the French government. Namibia gave the land and France paid for the building; foundation stone laid in 1998.
w: Has a large multipurpose gallery and hosts exhibitions at 118 Robert Mugabe Avenue, Windhoek.
x: Publishes no annual reports, accounts or funder list; its Team page names the director and staff but no board.

n: Botswana National Museum and Art Gallery
f: Statutory museum set up by Act of Parliament in 1967 and run by the Department of National Museum and Monuments. Government funded its P33 million refurbishment, begun in 2020.
w: Includes the National Art Gallery and the Octagon Gallery. Opened to the public in 1968.
x: The museum's own site is down and the government portals have expired certificates, so its publications could not be read.

n: Musée des Cultures Contemporaines Adama Toungara (MuCAT)
f: Built on the initiative of Adama Toungara, then mayor of Abobo; the director says it was built from own funds. No funder, cost or sponsor list is published.
w: Stands opposite Abobo town hall on 3,500 m², designed by architect Issa Diabaté. Opened with the pan-African show Prête-moi ton rêve.
x: MuCAT's site lists a team but no board, partners, reports or accounts; it says the museum is private, foundation-owned and gets no state subsidy.

n: Festival International des Arts du Bénin (FInAB)
f: Run by Groupe Empire's events arm with Benin government support through its arts fund (FDAC). MTN partnered the 2026 edition, Canal+ Impact 2025. Other partners unnamed; no budget published.
w: Festival in Cotonou, Porto-Novo and Ouidah. The fourth edition closed in early March 2026, with days for Nigeria, Togo, Lebanon and Morocco.
x: No FInAB website was found; press names organiser Groupe Empire, the culture ministry and different sponsors each year, with no reports, accounts or board.

f: Founded by Andrew Munuwa with Valentin Rudloff. The National Arts Council (BASATA) says it is keen to support it; no funder or sponsor list is published.
w: Launched in 2023. The 2025 edition showed 15 artists from Congo, Sudan, Kenya and Tanzania in Dar es Salaam and Zanzibar.
x: No reports, accounts, funder list or board are published; the About page names founder Andrew Munuwa and producer Tanzania Foto Collective Company Limited.
Held its 2025 Coexistence exhibition at DARCH in the Old Boma building.

f: Texaf, listed on Euronext Brussels, is founder and head sponsor of the centre. Its income is 85% Kinshasa real estate, 12% a sandstone quarry and 3% digital.
w: Texaf is 62.9% held by Société Financière Africaine and 10% by the Cha family. Bilembo covers over 1,000 m² of exhibition and workshop space.
x: Posts a 2025 activity report and an undated partner logo strip; no accounts or board named, though founder Texaf publishes its own audited accounts.
Texaf Bilembo links the Institut des Musées Nationaux du Congo and the Académie des Beaux-Arts de Kinshasa as partners; its founder Texaf is a company.

f: Burkina Faso's culture ministry organises it and pays professional artists' fees, flights and stay, per its 2024 call for applications. No other funder is named.
w: Founded 1989 by Siriki Ky, 35 km from Ouagadougou. The 15th edition runs 2 to 23 November 2026 under President Traoré's patronage.
x: The culture ministry organises and pays for the symposium, per a 2024 call and a 2026 programme article; the ministry's site is down.

f: Eastern Cape government, Sarah Baartman District Municipality, National Lottery Commission, Standard Bank. National government gave R5.5 million for 2022 to 2024, nothing in 2025, a smaller grant in 2026.
w: Minister McKenzie says it lost an open call. A January 2026 petition of 302 artists cites the cut among his refusals to renew funding.
x: Names its eleven-member board and management, and two presenting sponsors in text with logos for the rest; no annual reports or accounts found.
The National Arts Festival works in tandem with the Grahamstown Foundation, shares its CEO, and co-produces Scifest Africa and school festivals.

n: Javett Art Centre at the University of Pretoria (Javett-UP)
f: University of Pretoria gave the land and funding. The Javett Foundation funded construction and pledged ten years of annual gifts for running costs and an endowment.
w: Opened September 2019. An independent trust runs it. Michael Javett founded the Unisec Group, later sold to Standard Bank, and Tolux, now Brait.
x: Posts one annual artistic report, for 2023, with no figures; no accounts, funder list or board names on its site.
Javett-UP is a partnership between the University of Pretoria and the Javett Foundation.

f: Private firm of Nadine Abdel Ghaffar. Egypt's foreign and tourism ministries and UNESCO sponsor Forever Is Now. Partners: LMD, Suez Canal Bank, BMW (2026); TotalEnergies, Afreximbank (2024).
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Protest or boycott. In October 2026 a petition of 500 to 700 signatories made it drop sculptor Bernar Venet over Israeli ties; artists and galleries withdrew.
x: It posts no reports or accounts; the site shows four logos of ministries and UNESCO, undated, and lists a three-person team but no board.
Art D'Égypte lists UNESCO among its partners; its other named partners are Egyptian ministries.

f: Primarily funded by the Yinka Shonibare Foundation at its 2019 launch. Donors include Terra Foundation, Deutsche Bank, Afreximbank, Still Earth Holdings, British Council and Pro Helvetia.
w: Founded 2019 by Yinka Shonibare, who started the London residency Guest Projects. Patron Still Earth Holdings owns drilling contractor Tirex, an oil-services supplier.
x: Posts two impact reports (2022 to mid-2025), a named donor list and its trustees; accounts are filed by its UK parent, the Yinka Shonibare Foundation.
G.A.S. Foundation was set up with the Yinka Shonibare Foundation, partners with Yale School of Art and Spelman College on residencies and internships, and joined TheMuseumsLab network in 2025.

f: Art network and incubator tied to the KNUST painting and sculpture department in Kumasi. No funders, sponsors or budget appear in any source opened.
w: Ranked 69 in ArtReview's 2025 Power 100 and invited to the 2026 Venice Biennale main exhibition.
x: No blaxTARLINES website was found; Wikipedia lists none and no source names a funder, report, accounts or board.
Works from KNUST's Department of Painting and Sculpture; co-runs Kelas Bareng with Gudskul, Städelschule and Nordland, and co-organises the Wintanworks exchange with Art Hub Copenhagen.

f: Trust founded in 1995. Swedish NGO donor Forum Syd commissioned a 2016 audit. Robert Devereux's African Arts Trust aimed to become a patron in 2012. No current funder list.
w: Closed its offices in September 2016 for a donor audit after multi-million shillings went missing; artists kept the centre running.
x: Annual reports for 2012 to 2014 sit on its old site; the 2012 one names four trustees and 2011 funders, and none carries accounts.

Its archived 2013 site says it has hosted the Arterial Network's East African secretariat since February 2012; its 2014 annual report lists Triangle Arts Trust, the GoDown Arts Centre, Goethe-Institut and nine other cultural partners.

f: Founded with private money by Boubacar Koné and actress CCH Pounder; Koné gave it to the Senegalese state in December 2014. No budget or sponsor list is published.
w: Ngor museum of contemporary African art with artist studios and a residency. A conservator from the Ministry of Culture took office in March 2015.
x: The ministry page on Boribana gives its history and 2014 state handover but no budget, reports, accounts, funders or board.
It has been a state museum since the founder donated it in December 2014 and sits with the Dak'Art Biennale and other state sites under the culture ministry.

n: Contemporary Art Museum of the Kasbah
f: Run by the National Foundation of Museums. Restoration and design cost 13 million dirhams; the Wilaya of Tangier supervised it, with the Ministry of Culture, APDN and the Foundation contributing.
w: Opened in December 2021 in the former Kasbah prison to mark the Foundation's tenth anniversary. Opening show: The School of the North.
x: Publishes nothing itself; its operator, the National Foundation of Museums, posts laws and an org chart image but no reports, accounts, donors or board names.
The Fondation Nationale des Musées runs the Kasbah museum and its sister museums, among them the Musée Mohammed VI in Rabat, and Dar Niaba and Villa Harris in Tangier.

n: Museo Casa sobre el Arroyo (Casa del Puente)
f: The national state bought the house in 2012 and passed it to the city. The Ministry of Public Works paid over ARS 72M for the restoration, reopened April 2023.
w: Amancio Williams's house of 1943 to 1945 over the Las Chacras stream. Its restoration won the 2024 World Monuments Fund/Knoll Modernism Prize.
x: Ministry of Public Works (national government) paid over 72 million pesos for the 2023 restoration. The Municipality of General Pueyrredon (local government) holds the house.
No accounts or funder list found; press reports give the restoration cost.
Municipal museum of Mar del Plata, with its page on the city's site. The national Comisión Nacional de Monumentos oversaw the restoration. Member of Iconic Houses.

f: Lothar Trierenberg, of an Upper Austrian paper family, bought the house for EUR 5M and spent twice that restoring it. Stadt Wien gave EUR 700k, the Monuments Office about 200k.
w: Josef Frank and Oskar Wlach's 1930 villa, open since March 2026. Lothar Trierenberg co-owns delfortgroup, a specialty paper maker whose lines include cigarette paper.
x: Lothar Trierenberg (co-owner of delfortgroup, a paper maker with cigarette paper lines), Stadt Wien (city government) and Bundesdenkmalamt (federal monuments office).
Names its managing directors, sole shareholder and sponsors (Bundesdenkmalamt, Stadt Wien Kultur, Beijerstiftelsen) on its site; it publishes no accounts there.

Run by Villa Beer Foundation gemeinnützige GmbH, wholly owned by the XELAOS Private Foundation. Villa Beer Betriebs GmbH runs the rentals and guest rooms. Member of Iconic Houses, and cooperates with MAK, Wien Museum and DOCOMOMO Austria.

f: Owned by the NSW Government and run by Museums of History NSW (successor to the Historic Houses Trust), a statutory body with a 2024-25 budget of A$73.6M.
w: Harry Seidler's 1950 house for his parents, handed to the state in 1988 and open to the public since 1991.
x: Run by Museums of History NSW, a NSW state government statutory body with an A$73.6M budget in 2024-25.
Part of Museums of History NSW, a statutory body of the NSW Government; no separate accounts or funder list for the house found.
Run by Museums of History NSW, a NSW Government body with 13 sites, on a lease from the state. Member of Iconic Houses.

f: Robin Boyd Foundation revenue AUD 435k in 2023-24: donations 137k, grants 36k, partnerships 30k. Partners include Brickworks, Maddocks and Arup; donor trusts include Mori Provan and Isaacson Davis.
w: Robin Boyd's own 1959 house in South Yarra. A private ancillary foundation, unnamed, lent AUD 1.8M interest free against the title.
x: Revenue AUD 435,438 and expenses AUD 400,191 in the year to June 2024 (annual report). Donations 137,130, grants including government 35,741, partnerships 30,000, programmes 115,207, tours and venue hire 72,457.
Brickworks (brick maker, merged into Soul Patts in 2025), Arup (employee-owned engineers), Maddocks (law firm), and the Mori Provan and Isaacson Davis foundations (donors, origin of funds not found).
Publishes annual reports for 2011 to 2024 with reviewed accounts, its board, and named donors, Boyd Circle members and partners.

Owned and run by the Robin Boyd Foundation, a company limited by guarantee and ACNC charity (ABN 50 111 119 807), set up in 2004 with support from the Boyd family and the National Trust of Australia (Victoria). Member of Iconic Houses.

f: Verein Margarete Schütte-Lihotzky Club is funded by Stadt Wien, Bezirk Margareten, the federal arts ministry, GESIBA and arching. ORF named Wertinvest, the building's owner, a financial backer in 2021.
w: The architect's flat, open since October 2022. Wertinvest's Heumarkt tower put Vienna's historic centre on UNESCO's red list, 2017 to 2026.
x: Stadt Wien (city government), the federal arts ministry (state), Wertinvest (investment company of Michael Tojner, the building's owner), GESIBA (city-owned housing company), Bezirk Margareten (district) and arching (architects' chamber).
Names its funders and cooperation partners, with roles, on a page of its site; no accounts or amounts found.
Run by Verein Margarete Schütte-Lihotzky Club (ZVR 854118344), which ORF calls a publicly funded association. Member of Iconic Houses since December 2022.

n: Das Rote Wien im Waschsalon Karl-Marx-Hof
f: Run by Verein Sammlung Rotes Wien. Stadt Wien gives an annual subsidy and the insurer Wiener Städtische supports it. Wien Tourismus shows as a partner logo.
w: Exhibition on Red Vienna, 1919 to 1934, in a laundry of the 1930 Karl-Marx-Hof, open since 2010. Students and volunteers guide.
x: Stadt Wien (city government) pays an annual subsidy. Wiener Städtische (insurance premiums) supports the museum.
Names its six-member board, curators, guides and partner logos on its site; no accounts or subsidy amounts found.
Run by Verein Sammlung Rotes Wien (ZVR 988113764), chaired by Wolfgang Maderthaner. Member of Iconic Houses.

f: The Bulgarian state bought the house in 1975 and runs it as the Bulgarian Cultural Institute, the embassy's cultural department. Both countries' culture ministries backed its 2024 Wittgenstein exhibition.
w: Paul Engelmann and Ludwig Wittgenstein's house of 1928, a protected monument since 1971. It hosted a Wittgenstein exhibition in November 2024.
x: The Bulgarian state (national government, owner since 1975) runs the house as the Bulgarian Cultural Institute. The Bulgarian and Austrian culture ministries backed its 2024 exhibition.
No accounts or funder list found; the house belongs to the Bulgarian state, which bought it in 1975.
Owned by Bulgaria and run as the Bulgarian Cultural Institute within the Bulgarian Embassy's cultural department. Member of Iconic Houses.

f: STEINHAUS Günther Domenig Privatstiftung receives subsidies from Land Kärnten (culture) and the Federal Ministry for Arts, Culture, the Civil Service and Sport. Gemeinde Steindorf and HTL Villach give in-kind sponsoring.
w: Günther Domenig's own house. In 2008 he put it into the foundation with his artistic, legal and material estate.
x: Land Kärnten (state government) and the federal arts ministry pay subsidies. Gemeinde Steindorf (municipality) and HTL Villach give in-kind sponsoring.
Names its four-member board, two co-opted members, public funders and in-kind sponsors on its site; the foundation is in the Firmenbuch (FN 218529 t). No accounts or visitor figures found.
Run by the STEINHAUS Günther Domenig Privatstiftung, with the Land Kärnten culture department as beneficiary; STEINHAUS Betriebsgesellschaft mbH manages operations. Member of Iconic Houses.

f: The commune of Saint-Gilles bought the house in 1961. The museum's EUR 800k renewal is paid by Urban Brussels, the commune, Fonds Baillet-Latour, museum resources and an unnamed patron.
w: Victor Horta's house and studio of 1898 to 1901, a museum since 1969. The first phase of facade and reception works ends in November 2026.
x: Commune of Saint-Gilles (local government), Urban Brussels (Brussels-Capital Region) and Fonds Baillet Latour (dividends on an InBev brewing stake) pay for the EUR 800,000 renewal, with an unnamed patron.
No accounts, board or funder list found; the commune of Saint-Gilles owns the buildings, and the 2026 renovation funders were named in the press.
Municipal museum of the commune of Saint-Gilles, part of the UNESCO-listed Major Town Houses of the Architect Victor Horta. Member of Iconic Houses.

f: Run by the Boghossian Foundation, created in 1992 by the jewellers Robert Boghossian and his sons, which bought and restored the villa. The Circle of the Villa adds donors.
w: Michel Polak's villa of 1930, an art centre since 2010. Circle donors include Jan-Leonard Moortgat (Duvel) and Claude Moët (Moët & Chandon).
x: Boghossian Foundation (Boghossian jewellery family). Circle of the Villa donors include Jan-Leonard Moortgat (Duvel brewery) and Claude Moët (Moët & Chandon). The King Baudouin Foundation holds the Friends fund.
Names its board, staff and Circle donors on its site; it files annual accounts with the National Bank of Belgium, 2016 to 2024.

Operated by the Boghossian Foundation, a Belgian foundation (0888.046.579) created by Robert Boghossian and his sons. Its Friends fund sits under the King Baudouin Foundation. Member of Iconic Houses.

f: Owned by the Arthur Erickson Foundation, a charity that takes donations and tour fees. Canadian Heritage gave CAD 17,800 in 2024. Patrons include Michael Audain and Yosef Wosk.
w: Garden tours run April to October and the house interior is closed. Phyllis Lambert chairs a board of 16 directors.
x: Canadian Heritage grant of CAD 17,800 for the AE100 centennial in 2024 (open.canada.ca). Annual income is filed with the CRA under charity number 888354842RR0001. No total is cited.
Canadian Heritage (federal government, CAD 17,800 in 2024), Michael Audain (Polygon Homes builder) and Yosef Wosk (family retail and property fortune), both named patrons.
Names its directors and patrons on its governance page and gives its charity number, 888354842RR0001, on its donate page.

Owned and run by the Arthur Erickson Foundation, a British Columbia society registered since 1993. Member of Iconic Houses. Its Stewardship Council, formed in 2016, advises owners of other Erickson buildings.

f: Donations were CZK 4.48M in 2025: CZK 4.40M from founder Bata Schuh Stiftung, CZK 30k from Continental Barum. Subsidies: City of Zlín CZK 195k, Zlín Region CZK 35k.
w: Thomas J. Bata recovered the villa by restitution and donated it to the foundation. Rosemarie Bata Blyth chairs the board, which includes Zlín's mayor.
x: 2025 annual report: donations CZK 4,477,465 and subsidies CZK 230,000 (IČO 65822374).
Bata Schuh Stiftung (Swiss foundation serving the Bata footwear group, CZK 4.40M), Continental Barum (tyre maker, CZK 30k), City of Zlín (CZK 195k) and Zlín Region (CZK 35k), all in 2025.
Publishes annual reports for 2015 to 2025, the 2025 one with donor and subsidy tables, and names its board and supervisory board.

Run by the Thomas Bata Foundation (Nadace Tomáše Bati), started by Thomas J. Bata in 1996 and based in the villa. Its 2025 report lists Bata Schuh Stiftung as founder. Member of Iconic Houses. The chancellor of Tomas Bata University sits on its supervisory board.

f: The National Heritage Institute runs it. Transfers, mostly from the Ministry of Culture, were 69 percent of 2024 revenue. EU's ERDF paid 85 percent of a CZK 179M restoration project.
w: Built 1927 to 1929 for textile owner Alfred Stiassni and later used for state visits, including Fidel Castro's. Opened to the public in December 2014.
x: National Heritage Institute revenue CZK 2,557.6M in 2024: transfers CZK 1,772.0M, sales of services and goods CZK 724.2M (annual report 2024). No villa-only figure. The villa had 16,350 visitors.

National Heritage Institute (Czech state body under the Ministry of Culture) runs the villa. The European Regional Development Fund (EU budget) paid 85 percent of a CZK 179M restoration project, the state budget 15 percent.
NPÚ reports the villa inside its annual report, which gives income by source and visitor numbers by site.

A site of the National Heritage Institute (NPÚ), a Czech state heritage body funded through the Ministry of Culture. NPÚ has run the villa since 2009. Member of Iconic Houses. Also a partner of the Adolf Loos interiors in Pilsen.

f: The Brummel family owns the house. Plzeň - TURISMUS, a City of Pilsen organisation, runs the tours. The Adolf Loos Plzeň project credits Ministry for Regional Development state-budget money.
w: Jan and Jana Brummel commissioned Loos to remodel the house in 1929. Their nephew Michal took it over in 1991.
x: City of Pilsen proposed a CZK 240,000 grant to the owner in 2016 for furniture repairs (archiweb, 6 May 2016). No income figure for the tours is published.

Brummel family (private owners). Plzeň - TURISMUS and the City of Pilsen (city government) proposed a CZK 240,000 repair grant in 2016. Ministry for Regional Development (national government) is credited on the tours project.
Names the organiser and its company number (00075361) on its contacts page and credits the state programme. No budget for the tours is published.

Privately owned by the Brummel family. Tours are organised by Plzeň - TURISMUS under the Adolf Loos Plzeň project, with the Gallery of West Bohemia, Villa Tugendhat and Villa Stiassni as partners. Member of Iconic Houses.

f: Herita vzw, a heritage non-profit, runs it with the City of Antwerp. The Flemish Government set EUR 6.3M for Herita's 2025 operating year under a one-year agreement.
w: Renaat Braem left the house to the Flemish Community in 1999. Herita has worked since 2024 to open it to the public.
x: Flemish Government figure of EUR 6.3M for Herita's 2025 operating year (decision of 13 December 2024). No figure for the Braemhuis alone.
Flemish Government (regional government) funds Herita vzw, the non-profit that runs the house, with EUR 6.3M for 2025. The City of Antwerp (local government) works with Herita.
Herita lists its 11 board members and 17 sites on its site, and the Flemish Government announces its funding decisions on vlaanderen.be.
Run by Herita vzw, a non-profit that manages 17 heritage sites in Flanders and has been Flanders' first recognised heritage network since 1 May 2024. Member of Iconic Houses.

f: Lombard Odier is the structural partner. urban.brussels, Loterie Nationale and Uccle are institutional partners. Friends pay EUR 150 a year, patrons from EUR 2,000.
w: Belgium's National Lottery, a public-law company, has run Scooore sports betting since January 2013.
x: Lombard Odier (Geneva private bank), Loterie Nationale (state lottery), urban.brussels (Brussels-Capital Region) and Uccle (municipality), plus Friends from EUR 150 and patrons from EUR 2,000 a year.
Lists its eight directors on its site, matching the Belgian company register (KBO 0407.561.930).
Run by the Musée et Jardins Van Buuren public-utility foundation, created by Alice van Buuren in 1970. Member of Iconic Houses. Its gardens are on the European Route of Historic Gardens.

f: Branch of the Moravian Gallery, founded by the Ministry of Culture, which paid CZK 140.9M of its CZK 168.0M 2025 income. A Norwegian Financial Mechanism grant supported the villa.
w: Dušan Jurkovič's own villa of 1906 in Brno-Žabovřesky, with a permanent exhibition on the architect and seasonal shows. Tickets must be booked in advance.
x: Gallery-wide, not the villa, 2025 (annual report): income CZK 168.0M, of which Ministry of Culture contribution 140.9M, local government grants 2.4M, own revenue 13.7M including tickets 4.8M, reserve funds 11.0M. 185,284 visitors.

Czech Ministry of Culture (national government), founder of the Moravian Gallery that runs the villa, paid CZK 140.9M of the gallery's CZK 168.0M income in 2025. The Norwegian Financial Mechanism (Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway) also supported the villa with a grant.
The Moravian Gallery's 2025 annual report prints a gallery-wide income table as an image; the villa has no separate accounts.
Branch of the Moravian Gallery in Brno, a state museum founded by the Ministry of Culture. Member of Iconic Houses (house page on iconichouses.org), with the gallery's Josef Hoffmann Museum.

f: Plzeň Region owns the building and gave the Gallery of West Bohemia CZK 37M of its CZK 39M 2024 budget. Region and EU funds helped pay the EUR 4.5M restoration.
w: Apartment of Oskar Semler, remodelled 1932 to 1934, with interiors by Heinrich Kulka to a concept by Adolf Loos. Fully open since September 2022.
x: Gallery-wide 2024 (annual report): revenue CZK 46.4M, of which operating subsidies 41.4M (Plzeň Region 37.0M, other contributions 1.7M, other transfers 2.6M) and tickets 2.5M. 44,506 visitors, over 8,000 at the residence.

Plzeň Region (regional government) owns the building and gave the Gallery of West Bohemia CZK 37.0M of its CZK 39.0M 2024 budget. The European Union (IROP programme) helped pay the EUR 4.5M restoration.
Budget, founder contribution and visitor numbers are in the Gallery of West Bohemia's 2024 report; the residence has no separate accounts.

Owned by Plzeň Region and run by the Gallery of West Bohemia (Západočeská galerie v Plzni), a regional contributory organisation. Plzeň-Turismus co-operates on tours. Member of Iconic Houses (house page on iconichouses.org and plaque on its site).

f: Ministry of Culture paid CZK 38.4M in 2025 for the villa and furniture; the Museum of Decorative Arts runs it. An EEA grant covered EUR 348k of the earlier restoration.
w: Josef Gočár's 1914 cubist villa, bought from the Czech Cubism Foundation, which had restored it and opened it. Tours since July 2025.
x: Museum-wide 2024 (annual report), before the villa joined: income CZK 138.9M, of which operating subsidy 97.0M, project grants 16.2M, own revenue 25.7M.

Czech Ministry of Culture (national government) bought the villa and furniture for CZK 38.4M, handed over in August 2025. The Museum of Decorative Arts, a state organisation, runs it. EEA and Norway Grants (Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway) paid EUR 347,820 toward an earlier project.
The Museum of Decorative Arts posts annual reports with income lines; the villa joined it in 2025 and has no separate accounts.

State property managed by the Museum of Decorative Arts in Prague (UPM), a state contributory organisation of the Ministry of Culture; owned by the Czech Cubism Foundation until 2025. Member of Iconic Houses (house page on iconichouses.org).

f: Run by the Prague City Gallery, which the City of Prague founded and pays: CZK 122.8M operating contribution in 2024, against CZK 10.8M own revenue. Four patrons gave CZK 360,000.
w: František Bílek's home and studio, built 1911 to his own design. A new permanent exhibition opened in June 2022; about 8,000 visitors in 2024.
x: Gallery-wide 2024 (annual report): City of Prague non-investment contribution CZK 122.8M and investment contribution CZK 164.5M. Own revenue CZK 10.8M, of which tickets 8.1M. Costs CZK 135.8M.

The Prague City Gallery, a City of Prague organisation, runs the villa. The city (municipal government) gave it CZK 122.8M in 2024, against CZK 10.8M own revenue. Four patrons, not named, gave CZK 360,000.
Budget commentary, city contributions, revenue and patron income are in the Prague City Gallery's 2024 report; the villa has no separate accounts.
Managed since 1963 by the Prague City Gallery (GHMP), a contributory organisation of the City of Prague. Member of Iconic Houses (house page on iconichouses.org).

f: Owned by the City of Prague and run by the Museum of Prague, a city organisation that received a CZK 227.9M city subsidy in 2024.
w: Adolf Loos's 1930 villa. Closed in February 2025 for failed terrace waterproofing, it reopened in 2026 after a reconstruction costing about CZK 20M.
x: Museum-wide 2024 (annual report): city subsidy CZK 227.9M, revenue besides the subsidy CZK 23.1M, costs CZK 254.9M. The villa had 8,001 visitors.
City of Prague (municipal government) owns the villa. The Museum of Prague, a city organisation, runs it on a CZK 227.9M city subsidy (2024).
The Museum of Prague's 2024 report gives budget results, the city subsidy and visitors per building; the villa has no separate accounts.

Owned by the City of Prague and run by the Museum of Prague, a municipal contributory organisation that also runs Villa Rothmayer. Member of Iconic Houses (house page on iconichouses.org and the museum's report).

f: Run by the Museum of Prague, which the City of Prague funds with a CZK 227.9M subsidy (2024). The museum site also names the Education Ministry and Erasmus as supporters.
w: Architect Otto Rothmayer's own villa of 1929 in Prague 6, with 3,558 visitors in 2024. Its garden opened free to the public in May 2026.
x: Museum-wide 2024 (annual report): city subsidy CZK 227.9M, revenue besides the subsidy CZK 23.1M, costs CZK 254.9M. The villa had 3,558 visitors.

City of Prague (municipal government) funds the Museum of Prague, which runs the villa, with a CZK 227.9M subsidy (2024). The museum's site also names the Czech Ministry of Education and the EU's Erasmus programme as supporters, with no amounts.
Covered by the Museum of Prague's 2024 report, which lists the villa's visitors and the city subsidy; the villa has no separate accounts.
Run by the Museum of Prague, a municipal contributory organisation of the City of Prague, together with Villa Müller. Member of Iconic Houses (house page on iconichouses.org and the museum's report).

f: Brno City Museum, funded by the City of Brno: CZK 108.3M of CZK 199.2M income in 2025. State budget and funds CZK 4.6M, South Moravian Region CZK 0.35M.
w: Mies van der Rohe's 1930 villa, on the UNESCO list since 2001, with 57,036 tour and exhibition visitors in 2025.
x: Museum-wide 2025 (activity report): income CZK 199.2M, costs CZK 199.0M. Transfers CZK 118.0M, of which City of Brno 108.3M; sales of services CZK 50.3M. The villa had 57,036 tour and exhibition visitors, 193,156 counting its free grounds.

City of Brno (municipal government) gave the Brno City Museum CZK 108.3M of its CZK 199.2M income in 2025. State budget and funds gave CZK 4.6M and South Moravian Region CZK 0.35M. EEA and Norway Grants backed a CZK 639,378 museum project.
Income, costs, transfers and visitors per building are in the Brno City Museum's 2025 activity report; the villa has no separate accounts.
Department of the Brno City Museum (Muzeum města Brna), a contributory organisation of the City of Brno, which also runs Špilberk Castle. Member of Iconic Houses (house page on iconichouses.org).

f: Foundation set up by owner Čestmír Vančura. 2025 income CZK 4.2M: gifts 2.1M (including his foundation, NAVI CZ, ZULIP, MEJTA, Edhouse, PSG Construction), grants 1.0M, mainly EEA and Norway Grants.
w: Traveller Miroslav Zikmund owned the villa from 1953 until he sold it to Čestmír Vančura in 2020. The foundation opens it for guided tours.
x: Income CZK 4,164k and costs CZK 1,982k in 2025 (annual report): operating grants 1,000k, gifts 2,149k, sales 1,021k. Grants: EEA and Norway Grants 735k, Zlín Region 80k, State Culture Fund 65k.

Gifts of CZK 2.1M in 2025 included Čestmír Vančura's foundation (forging firm Kovárna VIVA, sold 2023), PSG Construction (building), NAVI CZ (machining), Edhouse (software), Juráš a partneři (law), ZULIP, MEJTA and private donors. EEA and Norway Grants gave CZK 0.735M.
The foundation files annual reports for 2022 to 2025 and accounts for 2020 and 2021 in the public court register; its site names its board and director, and the 2025 report lists donors and grants.

Run by Nadační fond Zikmundova vila, founded in 2020 by the owner Čestmír Vančura, who chairs its board; the vice-chair, lawyer Jaroslav Juráš, is tied on the foundation's site to the law office Juráš a partneři, also a donor. Member of Iconic Houses (house page on iconichouses.org).

f: The Akseli Gallen-Kallela Museum Foundation runs it. 2024 income EUR 0.80M: state subsidy 39%, municipal grants 26% (Espoo is a named supporter), tickets 21%, services and sales 14%.
w: Akseli Gallen-Kallela's studio at Tarvaspää, completed 1913 and protected as built heritage. Espoo's cultural committee granted EUR 70,000 for its restoration in 2024.
x: Income EUR 803,643 and costs EUR 785,923 in 2024 (Finnish Heritage Agency museum statistics): state subsidy 39%, municipal grants 26%, tickets 21%, services and sales 14%.
Finnish state museum subsidy (national government), 39% of 2024 income of EUR 0.80M. City of Espoo (municipal government), 26% in grants, including EUR 70,000 for the 2024 restoration.
Board and founders are listed on the foundation page. Its income and costs for 2024 are in the Heritage Agency's museum statistics.
Run by the Akseli Gallen-Kallela Museum Foundation, registered in 1958. Member of Iconic Houses, the Artist's Studio Museum Network, Small Art Museums Helsinki, Seaside Museums and CultureEspoo.

f: The City of Järvenpää, owner since 1998, runs it. The first restoration phase, budgeted at EUR 425,000, drew on city investments and a EUR 105,000 culture ministry grant.
w: Alvar Aalto's 1969 home for the composer Joonas Kokkonen. Open May to September on guided tours. A 2024 city paper proposed a second phase.
x: No separate figure for the villa. The city's Järvenpää Art Museum reported 2024 costs of EUR 1.68M, state share EUR 103,872, further state grants EUR 660,205 and tickets EUR 118,539 (Finnish Heritage Agency statistics).
City of Järvenpää (municipal government), owner since 1998. Ministry of Education and Culture (national government), EUR 105,000 toward the first restoration phase.
The city's council papers give the restoration budget and the ministry grant. The villa has no separate accounts.
Owned and run by the City of Järvenpää as one of four city museum sites with the Art Museum, Ahola and Suviranta. Iconic Houses member.

f: The Didrichsen Art Foundation, set up by the founders in 1963, runs it. 2024 income EUR 1.30M: tickets 50%, state subsidy 17%, other grants 16% (grantors not named), services 15%.
w: The founders' home, designed by Viljo Revell and completed in 1957. The site shows partner logos for Transmeri, Grano and hs.fi, with no role stated.
x: Income EUR 1,301,716 and costs EUR 1,393,289 in 2024 (Finnish Heritage Agency museum statistics): tickets 50%, state subsidy 17%, other grants 16%, services and sales 15%, sponsorship 2%.

Didrichsen Art Foundation, set up in 1963 from the founders' collection, estate and building (Gunnar Didrichsen founded the importer Transmeri). Finnish state museum subsidy (national government), 17% of 2024 income. Other grants, 16%, name no grantor.
Publishes its foundation by-laws and no donor list. Income and costs for 2024 are in the Finnish Heritage Agency's museum statistics.
Run by the Didrichsen Art Foundation, set up in 1963 by Gunnar and Marie-Louise Didrichsen. Member of Iconic Houses, Small Art Museums Helsinki and the Seaside Museums network.

f: State money. A site of the National Museum of Finland, a department of the Finnish Heritage Agency under the Ministry of Education and Culture. Adult ticket EUR 15.
w: Studio home of the architects Gesellius, Lindgren and Saarinen, completed 1903. Open May to September. The National Museum names no corporate partners online.
x: No separate figure. The National Museum of Finland, with ten sites, had costs of EUR 21.4M in 2024 against tickets of EUR 2.38M, services and sales of EUR 1.54M and other income of EUR 0.46M (Finnish Heritage Agency statistics). The state appropriation is not itemised.

Finnish state (national government): Hvitträsk is a site of the National Museum of Finland, a department of the Finnish Heritage Agency under the Ministry of Education and Culture. No corporate partner is named.
The Finnish Heritage Agency's museum statistics give the National Museum's costs and income. Hvitträsk has no separate accounts.
A site of the National Museum of Finland, which operates within the Finnish Heritage Agency under the Ministry of Education and Culture. Iconic Houses member.

f: The Alvar Aalto Foundation runs it. The foundation's Alvar Aalto Museum reported 2024 income of EUR 2.73M: state subsidies 38%, tickets 19%, services and sales 19%, municipal grants 14%.
w: Alvar and Elissa Aalto's self-designed studio and summer home, built 1952-54. Open for guided tours in summer. Tickets are sold through Aalto2.
x: Alvar Aalto Museum, run by the foundation: income EUR 2,734,704 and costs EUR 2,765,205 in 2024 (Finnish Heritage Agency statistics, which do not say which sites it covers): state subsidies 38%, tickets 19%, services and sales 19%, municipal grants 14%.

Finnish state museum subsidy and grant, EUR 1.04M in 2024 (national government). Municipal grants, EUR 393,000 (local government, municipalities unnamed). Both are listed under the foundation's Alvar Aalto Museum.
Board listed on the foundation page. Income and costs for its Alvar Aalto Museum are in the 2024 Finnish Heritage Agency statistics.

A site of the Alvar Aalto Foundation, which also runs the Aalto House and Studio Aalto in Helsinki and the Alvar Aalto Museum in Jyväskylä. Iconic Houses member and part of the UNESCO Aalto Works series.

f: The Villa Mairea Foundation runs it. A. Ahlström Kiinteistöt Oy owns and maintains the building. No income, grant or donor list is published on the foundation's site.
w: Designed by Aino and Alvar Aalto and completed in 1939 for Maire and Harry Gullichsen. The foundation dates from 1980. Guided tours cost EUR 30.
x: A. Ahlström Kiinteistöt Oy (real estate arm of the Ahlström family group: forest and fibre companies, forests, property) owns and maintains the building and appoints two board members. No income or donor list is published.
Its board page lists the members and the four bodies that appoint them, and the staff page names three staff. The site carries no accounts or funder list.

Run by the Villa Mairea Foundation, in a building owned by A. Ahlström Kiinteistöt Oy. Iconic Houses member, part of the UNESCO Aalto Works series, the Alvar Aalto Route and the Ahlström in Society platform of family foundations.

f: The Christine and Göran Schildt Foundation owns and runs it, and Christine Schildt sits on its board. Tickets cost EUR 22. No accounts or donor list is published.
w: Alvar Aalto's last and smallest house, built 1969-70 for his friends Christine and Göran Schildt. Open to the public since December 2020, on guided tours.
x: The Christine and Göran Schildt Foundation, named for the author and his wife, owns and runs the villa. No accounts, donor list or other funder is published.
A board of six trustees and an executive director are named on the site. It carries no accounts or funder list.
Owned by the Christine and Göran Schildt Foundation, which works with the Friends of Villa Kolkis. Iconic Houses member.

f: The City of Nancy, owner since 2003, runs it through the Musée de l'École de Nancy. With the Fondation du patrimoine it has opened an appeal for the 2026-28 restoration.
w: Henri Sauvage's house of 1901-02 for the cabinetmaker Louis Majorelle, a listed monument. Open Wednesday to Sunday by booking.
x: City of Nancy (municipal government), owner since 2003. Fondation du patrimoine (private foundation living on donations, corporate patronage, the heritage lottery and unclaimed estates) runs the public appeal for the 2026 to 2028 restoration.
The city publishes a press kit and a patronage leaflet for the villa. It has no separate accounts.

Owned by the City of Nancy and run by the Musée de l'École de Nancy. Iconic Houses member since 2014, Maison des Illustres label (Ministry of Culture, 2011), and the city is in the Réseau Art nouveau Network.

f: A public-utility foundation created by decree in 1994 runs it. No funder is named on its site. Its subsidiary HB Projet hires the site out for events and filming.
w: Home and studios of the painters Hans Hartung and Anna-Eva Bergman, open to the public since May 2022. Closed until the spring 2027 exhibition.
x: The Fondation Hartung-Bergman, a public-utility foundation created in 1994, holds the painters' works and archives and runs their Antibes villa and studios. No outside funder is named on its site.
Its team page names a president, a director and staff, and its presentation page gives the 1994 decree. The site shows no accounts or funders.
Public-utility foundation (decree of 16 February 1994) with a subsidiary, HB Projet. Iconic Houses member.

f: The City of Le Havre bought the flat in 2005 for EUR 220,000 and fitted it out for EUR 150,000. The Pays d'art et d'histoire service runs the guided visits.
w: A reconstruction of the model homes Auguste Perret showed in 1947 and 1949-53, inaugurated in 2006. Guides took 24,000 visitors through it in 2025.
x: City of Le Havre (municipal government) bought the flat in 2005 for EUR 220,000 and fitted it out for EUR 150,000. Le Havre Seine Métropole (inter-municipal authority) plans the guided visits.
The service gives a visitor count on its site. No accounts for the flat are published.
Guided by the Pays d'art et d'histoire of Le Havre Seine Métropole, in the national label network since May 2019. Part of the UNESCO-listed rebuilt centre of Le Havre. Iconic Houses member.

f: The Association Alvar Aalto en France, founded in 2006 to buy and manage the house, runs it. The Finnish and French culture ministries and the Île-de-France Region are named supporters.
w: Aalto's only French work, made for the art dealer Louis Carré. Weekend guided tours from March to November. Hired out for shoots and events.
x: Association Alvar Aalto en France (non-profit that bought and runs the house); Friends of the Maison Carré (association); Finnish Ministry of Education and Culture, French Ministry of Culture (DRAC) and Île-de-France Region (public funds). No amounts are published.
The history page lists the seven-member board, the administrator and three public supporters. The site publishes no accounts.
Run by the Association Alvar Aalto en France, founded 2006. The Friends of the Maison Carré, founded 2004, back its programme. Iconic Houses member.

f: Patrons Cassina and Chanel and institutional partners DRAC Île-de-France (Ministry of Culture) and Région Île-de-France support the Fondation Le Corbusier, which runs it. Adult ticket EUR 10.
w: Le Corbusier's home and studio in the Molitor building, 1931-34. A restoration campaign ran in 2017-18. Cassina supported the latest one.
x: Fondation Le Corbusier, which runs the apartment: operating income EUR 1,532,514 in 2019, of which other income EUR 1.03M, services EUR 414k, goods EUR 35k and operating grants EUR 52k, with a surplus of EUR 266k (Grant Thornton accounts, Journal officiel).

Fondation Le Corbusier (licence contracts, paid loans of works); Cassina (furniture maker owned by Haworth, US); Chanel (Wertheimer family fashion house); Ministry of Culture through DRAC Île-de-France (state); Île-de-France Region (regional government).
Board, patrons and institutional partners are listed on its site. Audited accounts for 2017 to 2019 are in the Journal officiel, none later found.
Run by the Fondation Le Corbusier, which also runs Maison La Roche in Paris. UNESCO World Heritage site, Maison des Illustres label and Iconic Houses member.

f: CMN, the State's monuments body, runs it: State operating subsidy near EUR 45M in 2024, ticket sales EUR 91.6M in 2023, patrons EUR 3M to 4M yearly across 110 sites.
w: Le Corbusier's 1931 villa, sold by Poissy to the State in 1959. Listed by UNESCO in 2016 with 16 other Le Corbusier sites.
x: Operator-wide, not the villa alone: Centre des monuments nationaux resources rose 157% in ten years to EUR 220M in 2023, State funding a little over half, tickets EUR 91.6M (Senate finance committee report, September 2024).

French State through the Centre des monuments nationaux: State subsidy near EUR 45M in 2024, ticket sales EUR 91.6M in 2023, patronage EUR 3M to 4M a year across 110 monuments. The villa's page names no sponsor.
The villa's supporters page is empty and no accounts for the villa were found. The operator's figures come from a 2024 Senate finance committee report.

Run by the Centre des monuments nationaux (renamed Monuments Nationaux in 2026), a public body under the Ministry of Culture. The State owns the villa. Member of Iconic Houses and part of the Le Corbusier UNESCO listing.

f: CMN, the State's monuments body, runs it: State operating subsidy near EUR 45M in 2024 across 110 sites. Villa patrons: Neuflize OBC, Printemps Lille, AG2R La Mondiale foundation, Rolex.
w: Robert Mallet-Stevens' 1932 villa for the textile manufacturer Paul Cavrois. The State bought it in 2001. A EUR 23M restoration ended in 2015.
x: Operator-wide, not the villa alone: Centre des monuments nationaux resources rose 157% in ten years to EUR 220M in 2023, State funding a little over half, tickets EUR 91.6M (Senate finance committee report, September 2024).

French State through the Centre des monuments nationaux (subsidy near EUR 45M in 2024). Villa patrons: Neuflize OBC (private bank), Printemps Lille (department stores; Qatari investors bought the group in 2013), AG2R La Mondiale foundation (mutual insurer), Rolex (watchmaker).
The villa's site names four supporters (Neuflize OBC, Rolex, Printemps Lille, Fondation AG2R La Mondiale) without amounts. No accounts for the villa were found.
Run by the Centre des monuments nationaux (renamed Monuments Nationaux in 2026), a public body under the Ministry of Culture. The State has owned the villa since 2001. Member of Iconic Houses.

n: Cap Moderne (Villa E-1027 and Le Cabanon)
f: Restoration cost EUR 5.5M: 55% from regional authorities and the state, 45% from private sponsors and fundraising, including Getty Foundation grants in 2016 and 2019 ($200,000 for the second).
w: Eileen Gray's 1929 villa and Le Corbusier's Cabanon stand on a site owned by the Conservatoire du littoral. The latest Getty grant came in 2019.
x: Public money paid 55% of the EUR 5.5M restoration: Ministry of Culture and Conservatoire du littoral (national), PACA Region, Alpes-Maritimes department. Sponsors and fundraising paid 45%, including the Getty Foundation (Getty Oil fortune). Porter Foundation (Tesco family wealth) is also named.
Association Cap Moderne names its trustees, partners and sponsors on its site and gave the restoration cost split in a 2021 press release. No accounts were found.

Site owned by the Conservatoire du littoral and managed by the Centre des monuments nationaux since 2018. Association Cap Moderne, a charitable association set up in 2014, led the restoration. Member of Iconic Houses, which lists Villa E.1027 and Le Cabanon.

f: Dutch education and culture ministry grant EUR 34,000 a year. Dutch foreign ministry refunded EUR 29,168 of maintenance in 2025. Resident rent brought in EUR 24,000.
w: Theo van Doesburg's 1930 studio house, owned by the Dutch State and let to resident artists. Open to registered visitors on the first Saturday monthly.
x: Income EUR 90,321 and costs EUR 87,833 in 2025 (financial report, VAT included): resident rent 24,000, ministry grant 34,000, foreign ministry maintenance refund 29,168, tours 1,145, interest 1,908, gifts 100.

Dutch education and culture ministry (national government), EUR 34,000 a year. Dutch foreign ministry (national government), EUR 29,168 of maintenance refunded in 2025. Functionals, a Goirle furniture maker, supplied furniture.
Publishes its board, a multi-year budget for 2025 to 2028 and a 2025 financial report (in Dutch). Its colophon names the ministry subsidy and a furniture supplier.
Run by Stichting Van Doesburghuis, a Dutch public benefit charity (ANBI since 2018) set up in 1980. The Dutch State owns the house and a ministry official observes the board. Member of Iconic Houses.

f: Klassik Stiftung Weimar, 2024: federal EUR 14.6M, Thuringia 14.6M, Weimar 5.6M, own income 2.0M. LOTTO Thüringen, the state lottery, sponsored the Stiftung's 2023 and 2024 theme years.
w: Bauhaus model house of 1923, passed from Weimar to the Stiftung in 2019. LOTTO Thüringen is Thüringer Staatslotterie AöR, a state public body.
x: Klassik Stiftung Weimar, the operator, had institutional funding and own income of EUR 36.8M in 2024: federal 14.6M, Thuringia 14.6M, City of Weimar 5.6M, own income 2.0M. A further EUR 30.6M came as project funds (Jahresbericht 2024).

Klassik Stiftung Weimar (public-law foundation): federal government EUR 14.6M, Thuringia EUR 14.6M, City of Weimar EUR 5.6M in 2024. LOTTO Thüringen (the state's own lottery operator) sponsored its 2023 and 2024 theme years.
Publishes annual reports, the 2024 one with an income and spending summary, and names its public funders and its main sponsor on its site.

Run by the Klassik Stiftung Weimar, a public-law foundation funded by the federal government, Thuringia and Weimar, which took the house over from the city in 2019. Member of Iconic Houses and part of the Bauhaus UNESCO listing.

f: Klassik Stiftung Weimar, 2024: federal EUR 14.6M, Thuringia 14.6M, Weimar 5.6M, own income 2.0M. LOTTO Thüringen, the state lottery, sponsored the Stiftung's 2023 and 2024 theme years.
w: Henry van de Velde's own 1907 house, closed for renovation, reopening due in the 2027 summer season. Bought in 2012 with help from the Ilse-Burghardt-Stiftung.
x: Klassik Stiftung Weimar, the operator, had institutional funding and own income of EUR 36.8M in 2024: federal 14.6M, Thuringia 14.6M, City of Weimar 5.6M, own income 2.0M. A further EUR 30.6M came as project funds (Jahresbericht 2024).

Klassik Stiftung Weimar (public-law foundation): federal government EUR 14.6M, Thuringia EUR 14.6M, City of Weimar EUR 5.6M in 2024. LOTTO Thüringen (state lottery operator) sponsored its theme years. Ilse-Burghardt-Stiftung helped buy the house in 2012.
Publishes annual reports, the 2024 one with an income and spending summary, and names its public funders and its main sponsor on its site.
Run by the Klassik Stiftung Weimar, a public-law foundation funded by the federal government, Thuringia and Weimar, which has used the house as a museum since 2003. Member of Iconic Houses.

f: Stiftung UAA, founded 1990, names no sponsor or donor, and no accounts were found. Early-2025 repairs were backed by Deutsche Stiftung Denkmalschutz, NRW's heritage programme and the federal culture commissioner.
w: O.M. Ungers' own 1959 house and library, open by guided tour. No accounts or sponsor list were found.
x: Stiftung UAA, a charitable foundation, names no sponsor and no accounts were found. Repairs finished in early 2025 were backed by Deutsche Stiftung Denkmalschutz (donations and lottery), North Rhine-Westphalia (state) and the federal culture commissioner.
Names its board, a friends circle (founded 2011) and sponsorship options on its site. No accounts, annual report or donor list were found.
Run by the Stiftung UAA, a charitable foundation under civil law in Cologne. Member of Iconic Houses. The 1958/59 house is a listed monument.

f: Kulturstiftung Landkreis Leipzig, set up by the district, bought the house with federal money. Its Supported by logos show the federal culture commissioner, Kulturraum Leipziger Raum and Zwenkau town.
w: Adolf Rading built it in 1929 and 1930 for physicians Erna and Erich Rabe, with Oskar Schlemmer's art inside. Visits by reservation only.
x: Kulturstiftung Landkreis Leipzig, set up by the district (local government), bought the house with federal money. Supported by the federal culture commissioner, Kulturraum Leipziger Raum (Saxon cultural region) and Zwenkau town.
Names its board, foundation council, friends circle and eight supporters on its site, with three funder logos. No accounts or annual report were found.
Run by the Kulturstiftung Landkreis Leipzig, a non-profit foundation under private law set up on a 2018 district decision and recognised in 2020. Member of Iconic Houses.

f: The Cragg Foundation, set up by the Cragg family in 2005, runs the park Tony Cragg bought in 2006. The site names no funders or accounts and asks for donations.
w: Franz Krause built the villa between 1947 and 1950; it now holds the foundation's archive and offices. The park opened in 2008.
x: Cragg Foundation, set up by the Cragg family in 2005, runs the park that sculptor Tony Cragg bought in 2006. No funder list or accounts are published, and the site asks for donations.
Names the Cragg Foundation as publisher in its legal notice; the site lists no board, funders or accounts.
Run by the Cragg Foundation, a non-profit foundation the Cragg family set up in 2005. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

f: Funders include Frankfurt's culture, monuments and parks offices, Hessen's science and arts ministry and monuments office, the Hessian Museum Association, Deutsche Stiftung Denkmalschutz, Wüstenrot Stiftung and Stiftung Polytechnische Gesellschaft.
w: Ernst May and Carl-Hermann Rudloff's 1927 to 1928 house in the Römerstadt estate. ABG Frankfurt Holding, a City of Frankfurt company, owns it.
x: Funders include the City of Frankfurt (city budget), Hessen's science and arts ministry (state budget), Wüstenrot Stiftung (stakes in Wüstenrot & Württembergische), Deutsche Stiftung Denkmalschutz (donations) and Stiftung Polytechnische Gesellschaft (sale of the Frankfurter Sparkasse). The city-owned ABG owns the house.
Lists its board, trustees and funders on its site, which carries no accounts or annual report.

Run by ernst-may-gesellschaft e.V., a charitable association founded in 2003 whose patron is Frankfurt's mayor. Member of Docomomo, Iconic Houses, the Gesellschaft für Designgeschichte and the Gesellschaft der Freunde des DAM.

f: The Friends of the Weissenhof Estate run the museum in a city-owned house. Stuttgart's culture office granted EUR 375,000 a year for 2024 and 2025. Wüstenrot Stiftung joined the restoration.
w: Le Corbusier's 1927 double house, a museum since October 2006 and a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2016.
x: City of Stuttgart grant to the association: EUR 375,000 a year for 2024 and 2025, of which EUR 75,000 is fixed-term to 2027 (council paper GRDrs 182/2024, 12 July 2024). It was EUR 220,000 a year in 2022 (GRDrs 365/2022).

The Friends of the Weissenhof Estate (members' dues) run the museum in a house the City of Stuttgart owns. The city budget pays them EUR 375,000 a year for 2024 and 2025. Wüstenrot Stiftung (stakes in Wüstenrot & Württembergische) helped restore the building.
Names its staff on its contact page; its site shows no accounts, sponsor list or board list. The city's council papers publish its grants.

Operated by the Friends of the Weissenhof Estate (Freunde der Weissenhofsiedlung e.V.) in a City of Stuttgart building. A UNESCO World Heritage site since 2016, with Le Corbusier's neighbouring single-family house. Listed in Iconic Houses.

f: GGG, a City of Chemnitz company, owns the villa. C3, another city company, has run events there since July 2023. Kunstsammlungen Chemnitz run the museum. Sponsors: PYUR, Adlatus.
w: Henry van de Velde's 1903 villa for the textile entrepreneur Herbert Esche, restored 1998 to 2001. It holds the Henry van de Velde Museum.
x: The City of Chemnitz (city budget) owns the villa through its housing company GGG and has run events there since 2023 through its company C3. Kunstsammlungen Chemnitz run the museum. Named sponsors are PYUR (internet and TV provider) and Adlatus (asset manager).
Names C3's managing director and register number in its legal notice and lists the villa's sponsors; C3's site carries no accounts for the villa.

Building owned by GGG, events run by C3 Chemnitzer Veranstaltungszentren GmbH, both City of Chemnitz companies. The municipal Kunstsammlungen Chemnitz run the museum. Member of the Route der Industriekultur in Sachsen and Iconic Houses.

f: Run by the Georg Kolbe-Stiftung. Land Berlin gave EUR 513,624 in 2023. The museum credits the federal culture commissioner, Ernst von Siemens Kunststiftung and Hermann Reemtsma Stiftung for research.
w: Flags: Tobacco. Hermann Reemtsma Stiftung, set up in 1988 by a son of cigarette maker Hermann F. Reemtsma, backed the sculpture catalogue launched in May 2024.
x: Land Berlin funding of EUR 513,624 in 2023 (Senate answer to the Berlin parliament, Drucksache 19/15 860, 5 July 2023). No museum accounts were found.

Georg-Kolbe-Stiftung (the sculptor's estate) runs the museum. Land Berlin (state budget) has contributed since 1978. Research is backed by the federal culture commissioner (federal budget), Ernst von Siemens Kunststiftung (Ernst von Siemens's wealth and Siemens AG capital) and Hermann Reemtsma Stiftung (Reemtsma cigarette family).
Names its two-member foundation board in its legal notice and credits research funders by name; its site carries no accounts.
Run by the Georg Kolbe-Stiftung, established in 1949 to administer the sculptor's bequest. The Freundeskreis Georg Kolbe Museum e.V. (2000) supports the museum. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

f: City of Hagen property, run by its Osthaus Museum. The museum names Freunde des Osthaus Museums, Dr. Michael Otto and the Osthaus & van de Velde Gesellschaft as funders.
w: Henry van de Velde's 1908 house for Karl Ernst Osthaus, open weekends at EUR 4; its garden was restored in 2022 and 2023.
x: The City of Hagen (city budget) owns the house and runs it through its Osthaus Museum. The museum's friends page lists Freunde des Osthaus Museums, Dr. Michael Otto (Otto Group, trade and services) and the Osthaus & van de Velde Gesellschaft as funders.
The museum's site carries no accounts or funder list for the house; its friends page names three funders.
Site of the Osthaus Museum Hagen, a City of Hagen museum, and an anchor point of the Route der Industriekultur. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

f: The Hungarian Academy of Arts, paid from the state budget, funds the Museum of Architecture (MÉM MDK) that runs the villa and financed its 2020 to 2022 renovation.
w: Under first head György Fekete the Academy took over the Műcsarnok-Kunsthalle in 2013 and named György Szegő its art director in 2014 (Artistic Freedom Initiative).
x: The Hungarian Academy of Arts, paid from the state budget, funds the Museum of Architecture (MÉM MDK) that runs the villa and financed its renovation, which began in autumn 2020. The villa opened to visitors on 18 May 2022.
Publishes no accounts or funder list; the villa's renovation page names the Academy as financer and the museum's site names it as its funder.

Exhibition space of the Hungarian Museum of Architecture and Monument Protection Documentation Centre (MÉM MDK), open to visitors since 18 May 2022 and funded by the Hungarian Academy of Arts. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

f: The Municipality of Bergeijk gave EUR 78,000 of EUR 112,473 income in 2025. Friends of the Cultuurhuis gave EUR 10,000 and Postcode Loterij Buurtfonds EUR 5,000. Operations earned EUR 16,518.
w: Runs a museum in Bergeijk and first-Friday tours, April to October, of Rietveld's Van Daalen House, which the Van Daalen family still owns.
x: Income EUR 112,473 in 2025 (accountant-compiled accounts): municipality 69%, operations 15%, Friends 9%, Postcode Loterij Buurtfonds 4%, other 3%. 2024 income EUR 91,052.

Municipality of Bergeijk (local government) EUR 78,000 of EUR 112,473 income in 2025. Friends of the Cultuurhuis (membership dues) EUR 10,000. Postcode Loterij Buurtfonds (charity lottery stakes) EUR 5,000. Operations EUR 16,518.
Publishes its annual accounts and reports for 2022 to 2025 and a 2024 to 2027 policy plan, and names its five unpaid board members.
Run by Stichting Cultuurhuis Bergeijk, a cultural ANBI formed in 2021 from three foundations. Listed in the Iconic Houses network for Rietveld's Van Daalen House.

f: Vestfoldmuseene IKS, its operator, got NOK 44.3M from the state, 31.5M from Vestfold county and 15.5M from owner municipalities in 2024. Sparebankstiftelsen DNB funds projects at other sites.
w: Edvard Munch's house in Åsgårdstrand, a museum since 1947 and protected since 2013. Its page shows it closed for the season in October 2026.
x: Vestfoldmuseene IKS 2024 (annual report): state grant NOK 44.3M, county NOK 31.5M, municipalities NOK 15.5M, sales NOK 14.7M. No separate figure for Munchs hus.

Operator Vestfoldmuseene IKS got NOK 44.3M from the Norwegian state, NOK 31.5M from Vestfold county and NOK 15.5M from its owner municipalities in 2024. Sparebankstiftelsen DNB (holds about 8% of DNB bank) funds its other projects.
Vestfoldmuseene's 2024 annual report gives grants by owner, sales and visitor counts, and its company agreement lists the owners' shares. Munchs hus is not reported separately.
A branch of Vestfoldmuseene IKS, owned by Vestfold county (36%) and seven municipalities. Part of the Munch network. Listed in the Iconic Houses network (house page on iconichouses.org).

f: Part of Kulturetaten, the City of Oslo's culture agency, and paid from the city budget. No sponsor list or separate museum accounts are published.
w: Gustav Vigeland's studio, where he also lived from 1924 until 1943. His 1921 contract left his works to the city; the museum opened in 1947.
x: City of Oslo, through its culture agency Kulturetaten, pays from the city budget. No sponsor list or separate museum accounts are published.
Kulturetaten's 2026 allocation letter gives the museum's visitor counts for 2023 and 2024; no museum accounts are online.
Operated by the City of Oslo's culture agency, Kulturetaten. Its house page on iconichouses.org places it in the Iconic Houses network.

f: A City of Sopot cultural institution. The city's operating subsidy was PLN 2.43M of PLN 2.59M revenue in 2023; own sales were the rest. No sponsors named.
w: Walter Schulz's 1904 villa opposite Sopot's beach entrance 29, under renovation. The museum runs outdoor exhibitions and holds lectures at partner venues.
x: Revenue PLN 2,588,252 and costs PLN 2,532,818 in 2023 (income statement on its public information site): organiser subsidy PLN 2,430,217, own sales PLN 158,035.
City of Sopot (local government) paid PLN 2.43M of the museum's PLN 2.59M revenue in 2023. Own sales were the rest. No sponsors are named.
Posts its balance sheet and income statement, statute and museum council on its public information site; the latest statements posted are for 2023.
Cultural institution of the City of Sopot; its statute dates from a 2021 City Council resolution. Listed in the Iconic Houses network (house page on iconichouses.org).

f: Branch of the Museum of Modern Art in Warsaw, run jointly by the City of Warsaw and the Ministry of Culture. Named supporters: Audi, EY, E.ON Polska, EFC Foundation.
w: B for partner E.ON Polska: the E.ON group sells gas and electricity; the Polish unit sells electricity. The museum has owned the house since 2017.
x: Parent museum: revenue PLN 54.9M and costs PLN 55.9M in 2025 (audited statement); the income statement does not split subsidy from sales. No separate figure for the house.

City of Warsaw and the Ministry of Culture and National Heritage (local and national government) run the owner museum. Its partners: Audi (Volkswagen Group), EY (audit network), E.ON Polska (energy group), EFC Foundation (glucose-device fortune).
Audited yearly statements, the statute and City of Warsaw resolutions are on the museum's public information site. Nothing is reported for the house alone.
Owned by the Museum of Modern Art in Warsaw since the end of 2017 and a branch of it since 2017. Member of Iconic Houses since 2014, per the museum's page.

f: Visits are run by the Município de Esposende's cultural heritage and museums service. No separate budget or sponsor is published; the municipality's 2025 budget was EUR 55.4M.
w: Viana de Lima's house of 1954-57, a Monument of Public Interest since 2012. Open by booking, with free open weeks in summer 2026.
x: Município de Esposende (local government; 2025 municipal budget EUR 55.4M) runs the visits through its cultural heritage and museums service. No separate house budget or sponsor is published.
The municipality posts its yearly budget; no figures for the house alone are published.
The Município de Esposende's house page states membership of the Iconic Houses Network and registration with Docomomo International.

f: The Museum and Galleries of Ljubljana, founded by the City of Ljubljana, runs it. In 2024 the city paid 31 of the museum's 60.5 posts, the Ministry of Culture 28.5.
w: Architect Jože Plečnik's home, a monument of national importance since 2009. Open by guided tour only, in Slovenian and English.
x: Museum and Galleries of Ljubljana 2024: income EUR 6,091,083, spending EUR 5,958,544, own revenue 15%, sponsors and donors EUR 31,670 (city culture strategy report). No separate figure for the house.

The Museum and Galleries of Ljubljana, founded by the City of Ljubljana, runs it. In 2024 the city paid 31 of the institute's 60.5 posts and the Ministry of Culture (national government) 28.5. No sponsor is named.
Names its board and expert council on its site; its yearly income and spending appear in the City of Ljubljana's culture strategy report.
One location of the Museum and Galleries of Ljubljana (MGML), a public institute. Its house page on iconichouses.org lists it in the Iconic Houses network.

f: The Fundació Rafael Masó, a public foundation, manages the house. The Ajuntament de Girona budgeted EUR 224,500 of the EUR 253,500 income for 2025.
w: Architect Rafael Masó's family house, ceded to the city by its last owners, his nephew and niece. The mayor of Girona chairs the foundation.
x: Budget EUR 265,500 for 2026: transfers EUR 237,500 (89%), fees and other income EUR 28,000. 2025 budget EUR 253,500: city EUR 224,500, other non-profits EUR 10,000, tickets EUR 15,000, shop EUR 4,000.
Ajuntament de Girona (city government) budgeted EUR 224,500 of the Fundació Rafael Masó's EUR 253,500 income for 2025. Non-profit transfers of EUR 10,000 are not named. No private sponsor is listed.
Publishes its yearly budgets for 2021 to 2026 on its transparency page and lists its full board on the site.

Fundació Rafael Masó, a public non-profit foundation created in 2006. Its board seats the Ajuntament de Girona, two architects' colleges, the University of Girona and the Masó and Aragó families. Listed in the Iconic Houses network (house page on iconichouses.org).

f: A site of the Barcelona History Museum, run by the Ajuntament de Barcelona. The Bon Pastor Neighbourhood Plan paid for the new space; museum-wide sponsorship was EUR 41,322 in 2024.
w: A block of sixteen workers' houses built in 1929, ten now museum spaces, free to enter. The neighbours' association AVV Bon Pastor is a partner.
x: MUHBA (all sites) 2024: income EUR 854,677 (tickets and activities 454,574, space rentals 84,651, grants 85,285, sponsorship 41,322, other 188,844), spending EUR 6,192,134 (total invoiced). No separate figure for Bon Pastor.

Ajuntament de Barcelona (city government) runs it through the Barcelona History Museum. The Neighbourhood Plan allocated EUR 2.3M to the project. Museum-wide sponsorship was EUR 41,322 in 2024, with no sponsor named.
MUHBA's yearly reports include an income and spending table and a resources summary; the Bon Pastor site is not broken out.
Part of the Museu d'Història de Barcelona (MUHBA), a municipal museum of the Ajuntament de Barcelona. Became a member of Iconic Houses in 2024, per MUHBA's 2024 report.

f: Rudolf Steiner Nachlassverwaltung income 2025 CHF 1.69M: project grants 948k, donations 445k, rent 167k. Donors over CHF 5,000 include Anthroposophical Societies of Switzerland and Germany, Humanus-Stiftung and Software AG Stiftung.
w: Reinforced-concrete house of 1916 by Rudolf Steiner and Hermann Ranzenberger, home of the Rudolf Steiner Archive since 2002. Reading room and shop open weekday afternoons.
x: 2025 income CHF 1,688,883, of which project grants 948,398, donations 444,967 and rent 167,481. Expenses CHF 1,731,576. Extraordinary income 236,500 (227,000 of it released bequest reserves) less extraordinary expense 65,000 left a surplus of CHF 225 (annual report 2025).

Rudolf Steiner Nachlassverwaltung, funded in 2025 by project grants (CHF 948k), donations (445k) and rent (167k). Donors over CHF 5,000 include Software AG Stiftung (software shares), Humanus-Stiftung and the Anthroposophical Societies of Switzerland and Germany.
The 2025 annual report gives the income statement, balance sheet, donors over CHF 5,000 and the board; reports for 2015 to 2025 are on its site.

Run by the Rudolf Steiner Nachlassverwaltung, an association from 1943 and a foundation since 2015, with two support associations: the Verein zur Förderung der Stiftung and the Internationale Fördergemeinschaft Rudolf Steiner. Its house page says it joined Iconic Houses in June 2015; iconichouses.org lists it as a member.

f: Fundació Mas Miró's 2024 report lists grants from Secretaría de Estado de Turismo (EUR 100k), Diputació de Tarragona (50k), Mont-roig council (20k), Generalitat (3k), Fundació la Caixa (6k, school visits).
w: la Caixa's holding Criteria is the largest shareholder of gas utility Naturgy, which paid 23% of Criteria's 2025 dividends.
x: 2024 income statement: turnover EUR 97,465 (tickets 64,699, shop 26,351), other operating income including grants EUR 76,215, capital grants EUR 14,169. Staff costs EUR 172,800, loss EUR 187,394 (Fundació Mas Miró accounts).

Fundació Mas Miró lists EUR 100k in 2024 from Spain's Secretaría de Estado de Turismo, 50k from the Diputació de Tarragona, 20k from the Mont-roig council, 6k from Fundació la Caixa (dividends of its holding Criteria) and 3k from the Generalitat.
Memòries for 2022 to 2024 are on its transparency page; the 2024 one lists grants by funder, visitors, the board and an income statement.

Run by Fundació Mas Miró, created in 2013 and entered as number 2,900 in the Generalitat's foundation register. Its board includes Joan Miró's heirs, Mont-roig council, Fundació Joan Miró, Fundació Miró Mallorca and the State Secretariat for Tourism. Joined Iconic Houses in 2024 (memòria); iconichouses.org carries its member page.

f: Fundació Catalunya La Pedrera, the owner, had EUR 46.3M income in 2025; La Pedrera earned EUR 28.5M against EUR 13.3M of costs. The report names no sponsor of the building.
w: Gaudí's 1912 apartment building, owned by the foundation created in 2012 from the savings bank CatalunyaCaixa. 909,061 visitors in 2025.
x: 2025: Fundació Catalunya La Pedrera income EUR 46,279,605 and expenses EUR 43,024,425, of which La Pedrera income EUR 28,463,935 and expenses EUR 13,322,438; group turnover EUR 66,631,925 (annual report 2025).

Fundació Catalunya La Pedrera owns the building. Created in 2012 from the savings bank CatalunyaCaixa, it had EUR 46.3M of income in 2025, EUR 28.5M of it from La Pedrera. The report names no sponsor.
Its 2025 annual report gives income and expenses by unit; it also posts bylaws and a 13-member board list.

Owned and run by Fundació Catalunya La Pedrera, a Catalan foundation under the Generalitat's oversight. Trustees include the RACC, Víctor Grífols i Lucas and Carulla foundations and the Barcelona and Tarragona provincial councils. Member of Iconic Houses; its page is on iconichouses.org.

f: FUNDOS, formed in 2015 from savings bank Caja España-Duero, runs the museum and lists the building as its asset. It spent EUR 1.16M on museum and collections in 2024.
w: Gaudí's 1891 building in León, run as a museum by FUNDOS since 2017. Over 150,000 visitors are projected for 2026.
x: 2024 audited accounts: museum and collections cost EUR 1,160,154 of EUR 3,687,683 total spend. Income from own activity was EUR 58,942 (collaboration agreements 22,719, donations and grants 36,223). Two EUR 100,000 capital grants for the facade came from an unnamed grantor, and the deficit on activity was EUR 402,777. The Junta de Castilla y León announced a further EUR 200,000 for the museum on 22 June 2026, pending approval (Diario de León).

FUNDOS, formed in 2015 from the savings bank Caja España-Duero, runs the museum and has its seat in the building. The Junta de Castilla y León announced a EUR 200,000 grant for the museum in June 2026.
Audited accounts for 2016 to 2024 and annual reports for 2018 to 2025 are listed on a transparency page; the 2024 accounts are a scanned PDF and the page shows no report downloads or sponsor list.

Run by FUNDOS (Fundación Obra Social de Castilla y León), created on 15 December 2015 by converting the savings bank Caja España-Duero; its seat is in the building. A member of Iconic Houses, whose logo is on the museum's site, and listed on iconichouses.org.

f: Barcelona's Institut de Cultura, through the Museu del Disseny, and the Generalitat's Institut Català del Sòl commissioned the apartment. Disseny Hub runs visits; the Generalitat owns the building.
w: Dwelling 1/11, a flat in the Casa Bloc social-housing block, open for guided visits since February 2012. Tickets EUR 5, Saturdays.
x: Barcelona City Council, through its Institut de Cultura and the Museu del Disseny, and the Generalitat's housing body INCASÒL commissioned the apartment. Disseny Hub Barcelona runs the visits. The Diputació de Barcelona signed a 1997 deal to rehabilitate the building.
It sits inside the city's Museu del Disseny, and no accounts, budget or visitor figures for the apartment were found.

Visits run by Disseny Hub Barcelona, part of Barcelona City Council, with the Museu del Disseny and the Institut de Cultura; building owned by the Generalitat de Catalunya. Iconic Houses member, with a page on iconichouses.org that links to the Disseny Hub visit listing.

f: Owned by the Ajuntament d'Eivissa, which received it from Gisela Broner, Erwin Broner's widow. The Govern balear part-funded its restoration from 2009, which cost nearly EUR 293,000.
w: Erwin Broner's 1960 home and studio in sa Penya, a museum since 2010. Closed since 10 August 2026 for ceiling repairs.
x: The Ajuntament d'Eivissa owns the house, a gift from Gisela Broner, Erwin Broner's widow. The Govern balear part-financed its restoration from 2009, which cost nearly EUR 293,000.
As municipal property it falls under the Ajuntament d'Eivissa's budget; no separate accounts or funder list were found.
Municipal house museum owned by the Ajuntament d'Eivissa. The iconichouses.org page for the house lists it as a member.

f: Verein Ein Haus WOBA funds a CHF 130,000 restoration from donations. Named supporters: Sulger-Stiftung, Kantensprung-Stiftung, Vitra, Embru, Horgen-Glarus, Buess AG, Wohngenossenschaft Eglisee and Freiwillige Basler Denkmalpflege.
w: Paul Artaria and Hans Schmidt designed the 1930 row house at Surinam 126, which an association formed in July 2017 preserves.
x: Verein Ein Haus WOBA names eight supporters: Sulger-Stiftung and Kantensprung-Stiftung (Basel foundations), furniture makers Vitra, Embru and Horgenglarus, Buess AG, Wohngenossenschaft Eglisee and Freiwillige Basler Denkmalpflege. Supporters' amounts are not published.
Names its three-member board, its supporters, a dated donor list without amounts and its tax-exempt status; its site has no accounts page.

Run by Verein Ein Haus WOBA, constituted in July 2017, which received the house from the Wohngenossenschaft Eglisee Basel. Iconic Houses member: its own site carries the network's logo and iconichouses.org lists the house.

f: Association Villa Le Lac runs it on support from the Commune de Corseaux, unnamed foundations, companies and individuals, and admission. The Fondation Le Corbusier owns the villa.
w: Le Corbusier's house of 1924 in Corseaux, on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 2016. Run by an association since 2013; weekend openings.
x: Commune de Corseaux supports the association that has run the villa since 2013, alongside unnamed foundations, companies and individuals. The Fondation Le Corbusier, a private foundation, owns the villa and handles its restoration and maintenance.
