The support page says the Commune de Corseaux, foundations, companies and individuals give but names only the commune; no accounts, annual report or donor list is shown.

Run by the Association Villa « Le Lac » Le Corbusier since 1 January 2013. Owned by the Fondation Le Corbusier, which handles restoration and maintenance under an agreement with the Commune de Corseaux. Member of Iconic Houses (iconichouses.org page for Villa Le Lac).

f: Structural funders: Amsterdams Fonds voor de Kunst, Stadsdeel Nieuw-West, Stimuleringsfonds Creatieve Industrie. EFL Stichting gives EUR 65k a year. Government subsidies were EUR 394k of EUR 609k income in 2025.
w: A 1952 museum apartment in the Slotermeer garden city, reached on guided tours from the museum at the Sloterplas. Residents founded the museum in 2010.

Amsterdams Fonds voor de Kunst and Stadsdeel Nieuw-West (city money) and Stimuleringsfonds Creatieve Industrie (Ministry of OCW) pay structural subsidies. EFL Stichting, a foundation that lives on investment returns, gives EUR 65k a year. Public subsidy was EUR 394k of EUR 609k in 2025.
Annual reports for 2020 to 2025, an ANBI form with its 2025 accounts, its board and a funder logo list are on its site.
Stichting Van Eesterenmuseum (ANBI) runs it. The ANBI form calls the museum apartment a joint project with De Alliantie. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

f: Subsidies were EUR 24.7k of EUR 60.6k income in 2025. Gemeente Amsterdam gives permanent subsidy. 2025 show funders: Amsterdam-Noord, Cultuurfonds Noord-Holland, Gifted Art, BPD, Jaap Harten Fonds, Kattendijke/Drucker Stichting.
w: Former studio and home of the sculptor André Volten (1925 to 2002), in the Poortgebouw, a 1927 building by Johannes Hendrik Mulder. Exhibitions open weekends.
x: Income EUR 60,565 in 2025 (accounts compiled by an accountant): EUR 24,740 subsidies, EUR 18,406 sales, exhibition and book income, EUR 13,685 gifts from funds and friends, EUR 3,734 image rights. Loss EUR 5,089.

Gemeente Amsterdam (city government) gives a permanent subsidy. Subsidies were EUR 24.7k of EUR 60.6k income in 2025. The 2025 show and catalogue took money from Amsterdam-Noord, Cultuurfonds Noord-Holland, BPD (owned by Rabobank) and the Gifted Art, Jaap Harten and Kattendijke/Drucker foundations.
Its site carries annual reports and accounts for 2020 to 2025, its board, ANBI status, permanent subsidy provider and project funders.
Run by Stichting André Volten, an ANBI foundation founded in 2006 with an unpaid board and volunteers. It rents the building, a municipal monument. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

f: Entry and workshops gave EUR 87k of EUR 138k in 2025. The municipality gave EUR 23.5k and RVO a EUR 3.7k landscape subsidy. Rabobank holds a EUR 180k loan.
w: Dune sculpture landscape begun in 1980 by R.W. van de Wint (1942 to 2006) on neglected inland dune ground. 7,584 regular visitors in 2025.
x: Income EUR 137,861 in 2025 (Stichting De Nollen accounts): EUR 87,019 entry and workshops, EUR 44,538 subsidies, EUR 6,305 gifts. Result EUR 1,264.
The municipality gave EUR 23.5k in 2025 and RVO, a national agency, EUR 3.7k. Rabobank, a Dutch cooperative bank, holds a EUR 180k loan and gave a EUR 35k solar grant earlier.
Annual accounts for 2012 to 2025, an ANBI form, a 2020 to 2027 policy plan and the unpaid board are on its site.
Stichting De Nollen (ANBI) runs it. R.W. van de Wint B.V., led by the artist's sons, manages the terrain. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

f: Income EUR 1.55M in 2025: Amsterdams Fonds voor de Kunst EUR 493k, Amsterdamse Federatie van Woningcorporaties EUR 110k, earned income EUR 710k. Mondriaan Fonds and Gemeente Amsterdam add project grants.
w: The 2025 deficit of EUR 357,517 took equity to minus EUR 9,098, after deficits in 2023 and 2024. The accounts name continuity a large concern.
x: Income EUR 1,554,612 in 2025 (accounts): EUR 710,074 earned income, EUR 554,289 public funds (Amsterdams Fonds voor de Kunst EUR 493,392), EUR 286,666 private funds (Amsterdamse Federatie van Woningcorporaties EUR 110,000), EUR 3,583 interest. Deficit EUR 357,517.

Amsterdams Fonds voor de Kunst (City of Amsterdam arts fund) paid EUR 493k of EUR 1.55M income in 2025, and the Amsterdam housing associations' federation paid EUR 110k. Mondriaan Fonds (national) and Gemeente Amsterdam add project grants.
Its site carries annual reports and accounts for 2020 to 2025, policy plans for 2021 to 2024 and 2025 to 2028, ANBI details, the supervisory board and a funder list.
Run by Stichting Amsterdamse School Museum Het Schip (ANBI), which also runs Museum De Dageraad. Iconic Houses lists both the Het Schip model home and Museum De Dageraad.

f: Het Nieuwe Instituut runs it. The Ministry of OCW paid EUR 13.2M of the institute's EUR 16.6M income in 2025. VriendenLoterij gave EUR 132k, other public subsidies EUR 1.3M.
w: Brinkman and Van der Vlugt's 1933 museum house. The institute counted 76,035 paying visitors in 2025 across the house and its main building.
x: These are Het Nieuwe Instituut's figures, not the house's. Income EUR 16,645,854 in 2025: EUR 13,185,015 OCW structural subsidy, EUR 1,290,844 other public subsidies, EUR 1,331,543 private funds (VriendenLoterij EUR 131,954), EUR 838,452 tickets, sponsors and other direct income. Deficit EUR 249,990.

Het Nieuwe Instituut runs the house. The Ministry of Education, Culture and Science (national government) paid EUR 13.2M of the institute's EUR 16.6M income in 2025. VriendenLoterij, a charity lottery, gave EUR 132k.

Publishes annual reports for 2013 to 2025, the 2025 one with a balance sheet and income statement, plus its supervisory board and a funder logo list. The 2025 report has no separate accounts for the house.

Managed by Het Nieuwe Instituut (called Nieuwe Instituut in its 2025 report), the national museum for architecture, design and digital culture, which holds the Rijkscollectie. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

f: The Park foundation runs it on admission fees and almost no operating subsidy. The Rijksvastgoedbedrijf pays the house's maintenance. 47 firms, including Pon and OHRA, sponsor the Park.
w: H.P. Berlage's country house for Anton and Helene Kröller-Müller, finished 1920. The interior opens on guided tours only, booked in advance.
x: No income total found. The figures here are the Park foundation's, not the house's: 570,000 paying visitors in 2025, and a 2025 to 2035 target that visitor income covers at least 80% of Park operating costs.

The Park foundation runs the house on admission fees with almost no operating subsidy. The Rijksvastgoedbedrijf (national government) pays its maintenance. Company sponsors of the Park include Pon (family-owned car and bicycle group) and OHRA (insurance brand of NN Group).
Publishes its supervisory board, management team and a 2025 to 2035 policy plan. No accounts for the house alone were found.
Managed by Stichting Nationale Park De Hoge Veluwe, a private non-profit foundation. Its paying-visitor target includes the visitors of the Kröller-Müller Museum. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

f: Income EUR 1.18M in 2025: Droom en Daad EUR 350k, VriendenLoterij EUR 212k, Gemeente Rotterdam EUR 205k, individual and company gifts EUR 216k, own income EUR 190k, Cultuurfonds EUR 2k.
w: Droom en Daad (Van der Vorm family) lends depot space free. Its 2019 gift offer to Boijmans failed after it asked for two board seats.
x: Income EUR 1,175,815 in 2025 (annual report): EUR 780,870 private funds (Droom en Daad EUR 350,000), EUR 204,650 subsidies (Gemeente Rotterdam structural EUR 160,900), EUR 190,295 own income. Surplus EUR 25,324.

Droom en Daad (asset fund of the Van der Vorm family, whose wealth began with the 1989 sale of Holland America Line) gave EUR 350k of EUR 1.18M income in 2025. VriendenLoterij, a charity lottery, gave EUR 212k and Gemeente Rotterdam EUR 205k.
Annual reports with accounts for 2021 to 2025, an ANBI form, policy plans for 2021 to 2024 and 2025 to 2028 and the supervisory board are on its site.
Run by Stichting Hendrik Chabot (ANBI, founded 1992). Stichting Volkskracht Historische Monumenten owns the Rijksmonument building. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

f: Museum Dr8888 runs it. In 2025 subsidy was EUR 884k of EUR 1.189M income. Subsidy from Smallingerland and the province of Fryslân is its essential base.
w: Reconstruction of Theo van Doesburg's first large De Stijl design, from 1921, with the story of the Rinsema brothers. Opened 2018.
x: EUR 1,189,000 income in 2025 for Museum Dr8888, which runs the house (annual report 2025): EUR 884k subsidies, EUR 188k public income, EUR 93k sponsorship and gifts, EUR 24k other. Result about zero.
Museum Dr8888, which runs the house, took EUR 884k in subsidies of EUR 1.189M income in 2025. Its base is subsidy from Smallingerland (municipality) and the province of Fryslân.
Museum Dr8888 publishes an annual report with an income table, ANBI documents, a 2026 to 2028 policy plan and board bios. The house has no accounts of its own.

Held by its own foundation and run by Museum Dr8888 (Stichting Museum Drachten), which is preparing to bring the house under its board and supervisory board. Part of the Iconic Houses network (2025 report; page on iconichouses.org).

f: Part of the municipality of Roermond, which subsidises its core tasks. Stichting Vrienden Cuypershuis Roermond backs acquisitions and exhibitions, and the museum takes donations and bequests.
w: Pierre Cuypers's 1853 building, home to his firm. A municipal museum opened there in 1932 and reopened as the Cuypershuis on 29 October 2011.
x: Municipality of Roermond (local government) is the museum's legal body and pays a subsidy for its core tasks. The friends' foundation Stichting Vrienden Cuypershuis Roermond backs acquisitions, exhibitions and projects with gifts and bequests.

States its legal name (municipality of Roermond, Chamber of Commerce number 14117104) and ANBI status online. No museum accounts were found. The friends foundation publishes a 2024 to 2028 policy plan.
Part of the municipality of Roermond, with Stichting Vrienden Cuypershuis Roermond (RSIN 813968501) as its support body. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

f: Not confirmed. The Het Blaakse Bos Foundation runs the show cube and charges EUR 3.50 admission. No accounts, funder list or ANBI number is published.
w: Furnished show cube in Piet Blom's 1984 Cube Houses, which are mostly private homes. Site names founder Ed R. de Graaf.
x: No funder is named. The Het Blaakse Bos Foundation runs the show cube, and the museum's page lists no sponsor or subsidy.
Publishes opening hours, ticket prices and contact details only. No accounts, funder list, ANBI number or board names.
Operated by the Het Blaakse Bos Foundation, as the museum's own contact page states. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

f: Owned by Vereniging Hendrick de Keyser, funded by rents and services (EUR 16.9M in 2025), bequests (EUR 4.3M), the VriendenLoterij (EUR 1.2M a year) and government subsidies (EUR 1.5M).
w: Jan de Jong's home and office, built in stages from 1956 to the 1980s. National monument since February 2019, restored by Hendrick de Keyser.
x: EUR 25.7M income in 2025 for the whole association (annual report 2025): EUR 16.9M rents and services, EUR 8.8M fundraising, including EUR 1.8M from lotteries and EUR 1.5M government subsidies.

Vereniging Hendrick de Keyser owns it and is funded by rents and services (EUR 16.9M in 2025), bequests (EUR 4.3M), the VriendenLoterij (EUR 1.2M a year, from lottery ticket sales) and government subsidies (EUR 1.5M).
Hendrick de Keyser publishes annual reports with accounts (2025 opened), ANBI details and a list of 29 named funds and subsidisers. The house has no accounts of its own.

Owned and run by Vereniging Hendrick de Keyser, a heritage association founded in 1918 and partner of the VriendenLoterij. The Jan de Jong Stichting uses the drawing room. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

f: Owned by the EFL Stichting, whose only 2024 income was a EUR 700k net investment result. Visitors' voluntary contributions pay for the house's maintenance and volunteers.
w: Cornelis van Eesteren's 1923 house with a colour scheme by Theo van Doesburg, restored by Bertus Mulder. Visits by appointment only.
x: EUR 700,437 net investment result in 2024 for the owning EFL Stichting, which committed EUR 252,026 to subsidies and projects (ANBI summary 2024). Nothing is itemised for the house.
The EFL Stichting owns the house. Its only 2024 income was a EUR 700k net investment result, and no other funder is named.
The owning EFL Stichting posts a 2024 ANBI summary with its income, expenses and subsidies. The house has no accounts or funder list of its own.

Owned by the Van Eesteren-Fluck & Van Lohuizen Stichting (founded 1975), which manages the archives and copyrights of Cornelis van Eesteren and Theodoor Karel van Lohuizen. Its partners include TU Delft's architecture faculty. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

f: Not confirmed. The volunteer-run Mart van Schijndel Foundation (set up 2008) runs visits for a EUR 45 donation. The house is still privately lived in and no owner is named.
w: Mart van Schijndel designed it for himself and finished it in 1993. Utrecht municipal monument since 1999. Tours by appointment, groups of up to 10.
x: No funder is named. The volunteer-run Mart van Schijndel Foundation runs the visits, and no page names the house's owner.
Publishes tour terms and donation rates only. No accounts, funder list or board names found.
Tours run by the Mart van Schijndel Foundation, which sells the house's book. Iconic Houses hosts its visiting page and members pay half. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

f: Not confirmed. Quakertown Studio Project, a New Jersey 501(c)(3) filing Form 990-PF, runs it on gifts of $166k in 2023 and $26k in 2024. Donors are not named.
w: Toshiko Takaezu's 1975 house and studio, now a working pottery studio with tours by appointment. States no tie to the Takaezu family or her foundation.
x: $26,292 revenue in 2024 and $166,122 in 2023; expenses $107,109 in 2024 (Form 990-PF, ProPublica).
No donor is named. Quakertown Studio Project runs the studio on gifts of $166,122 in 2023 and $26,292 in 2024, and ProPublica's summary of its Form 990-PF lists no donors.
ProPublica lists its Form 990-PF filings for 2022 to 2024 with three unpaid directors. The studio's site names no funders, board or accounts.
Operated by Quakertown Studio Project (EIN 87-4280049, exempt since March 2022), a New Jersey non-profit corporation. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

n: The Frank Lloyd Wright House in Ebsworth Park
f: Not confirmed. Contributions were $570k of $794k revenue in 2024 and no donor list is published. Board chair Clare Davis and David Obedin match roof gifts up to $100k.
w: Wright's 1958 house, bought from Russell Kraus by a nonprofit in 2001 and deeded to St. Louis County as a park.
x: $793,606 revenue in 2024: $569,522 contributions, $79,133 program revenue; expenses $326,120 (Form 990, ProPublica).

Clare Davis (board chair) and David Obedin match roof gifts up to $100,000 through 2026 and presented the 2025 benefit. No page states where their money comes from. Benefit patrons are listed by name only.
Files Form 990s (2001 to 2024 on ProPublica) with officer pay. Its site names the board, staff and the two roof matching donors but publishes no donor list.

Run by The Frank Lloyd Wright House in Ebsworth Park, a 501(c)(3). St. Louis County Parks and Recreation holds title and has an ex officio board seat. Partners with the Frank Lloyd Wright Building Conservancy on a roof case study. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

f: Contributions were $1.42M of $1.96M revenue in 2024. Suffolk County, Bloomberg Philanthropies and the Cordish Family Foundation each sit in the $10,000 to $24,999 band of the supporters list.
w: The list is undated. The Cordish Companies run casinos but publish no revenue split, so no Gambling flag.
x: $1,964,699 revenue in 2024: $1,420,823 contributions, $317,908 program revenue; expenses $2,249,339 (Form 990, ProPublica).

Suffolk County (county government), Bloomberg Philanthropies (Michael Bloomberg's Bloomberg L.P. wealth) and the Cordish Family Foundation (Cordish Companies: real estate and casinos) each give $10,000 to $24,999 on an undated list. Individuals fill the higher bands.

Files Form 990s (2003 to 2024 on ProPublica) with officer pay. Its site names trustees and staff, lists supporters by giving band with no date, and links 2024 and 2025 annual reports that list no donors.

Run by LongHouse Reserve, a not-for-profit (EIN 33-1058583) with a board of trustees; founder Jack Lenor Larsen is listed as an honorary trustee. Affiliate member of the National Trust's Historic Artists' Homes and Studios. The Garden Conservancy is a listed supporter. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

f: Owned and run by the University of Arkansas since the Jones daughters donated it. The Arkansas Natural and Cultural Resources Council, the university and private donors supported the 2015 restoration.
w: Fay Jones's own house of 1956, run as an architecture-school stewardship programme. Tours by reservation only, about 60 minutes.
x: The University of Arkansas (public university) owns the house through its architecture school. The Arkansas Natural and Cultural Resources Council (state grants paid from the real estate transfer tax) and private donors supported the 2015 restoration.
Publishes no accounts or donor list of its own. Its site names the university and the state council as supporters of the restoration.
Part of the Fay Jones School of Architecture and Design at the University of Arkansas, under a director of house stewardship. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

f: The National Trust for Historic Preservation owns and runs it. Contributions were $69.3M of its $104.9M revenue in fiscal 2025. Benjamin Moore supports its stewardship.
w: Mies van der Rohe's 1951 house. Bought at auction in 2003 for $7.5M with Landmarks Illinois, which holds the easement. About 10,000 visitors in 2024.
x: $104.9M revenue in fiscal 2025 (year ending June 2025) for the whole National Trust for Historic Preservation, which owns and runs the house: $69.3M contributions, $91.3M expenses (Form 990, ProPublica). No figures for the house alone.

The National Trust for Historic Preservation owns and runs the house; contributions were $69.3M of its $104.9M revenue in the year to June 2025, and federal funding ended in 1996. Benjamin Moore (paint maker, Berkshire Hathaway subsidiary) supports stewardship.
The National Trust files Form 990s. The house has no accounts of its own and no published donor list.

National Trust Historic Site owned and run by the National Trust for Historic Preservation. No separate non-profit operates it. Landmarks Illinois holds the preservation easement. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

f: The Western Pennsylvania Conservancy owns and runs Fallingwater on member gifts and tour and event tickets. Huntington Bank sponsored the Twilight Tour in 2018.
w: Edgar Kaufmann jr. gave Wright's house of 1936 to 1939 to the Conservancy in 1963. UNESCO inscribed it as World Heritage in 2019.
x: Whole Conservancy, not the house (Form 990, year to Dec 2025): revenue $41.6M, expenses $33.4M, contributions $29.0M, program service revenue $6.1M, net assets $147.6M. Fallingwater is not broken out.
The Western Pennsylvania Conservancy (member and donor gifts) owns and runs the house. Huntington Bank (an Ohio bank holding company) sponsored the Twilight Tour in 2018.
The Conservancy files a Form 990, posts audited statements and publishes an annual report. Fallingwater has no accounts or funder list of its own.

Owned and run by the Western Pennsylvania Conservancy, a 501(c)(3). Founding member of the Iconic Houses Network, per its own site. One of eight Frank Lloyd Wright sites on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 2019.

n: Frank Lloyd Wright Houses at the Currier Museum
f: The Currier Museum of Art runs both houses. The Zimmerman House came with an operating endowment in 1988. An anonymous donor paid for the Kalil House in 2019.
w: Moody Currier's bequest founded the museum in 1929. The Zimmerman House opened to the public in 1990.
x: Whole museum, not the houses (Form 990, year to June 2025): revenue $6.77M, expenses $7.28M, contributions $1.36M, program service revenue $539,117, net assets $103.0M.

The Currier Museum of Art, founded on Moody Currier's 1929 bequest, runs both houses. The Zimmermans left the Zimmerman House with an operating endowment in 1988. An anonymous donor paid for the Kalil House in 2019.
The museum files a Form 990 and publishes an annual report. Its corporate page describes sponsorship packages and names no sponsor in text.
Owned and run by the Currier Museum of Art, a non-profit in Manchester. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

f: Friends of Alice Austen House runs it on NYC Cultural Affairs, NYS Council on the Arts, NEA and NEH support, plus the Hillman Family, Auchincloss, Keith Haring and Teiger foundations.
w: NYC Parks owns the house and grounds. The house updated its designation to a national site of LGBTQ+ history in 2017.
x: Friends of Alice Austen House (Form 990, year to June 2025): revenue $550,244, expenses $772,873, contributions $465,999, program service revenue $64,622, net assets $704,151.

Friends of Alice Austen House runs the NYC Parks house on support from NYC Cultural Affairs (city), NYS Council on the Arts (state), NEA and NEH (federal), Hillman Family Foundations (coal, steel and real estate holdings) and Teiger Foundation (art collection sales).
Friends of Alice Austen House files a Form 990 and lists its government, foundation and institutional supporters on its support page; it names no corporate sponsor.

Operated by Friends of Alice Austen House, Inc. on a site owned by NYC Parks. Member of the Historic House Trust of New York City, the National Trust's Historic Artists' Homes and Studios group and the Iconic Houses Network, per its own about page.

f: The National Trust for Historic Preservation owns the house. The Rockefeller Brothers Fund, a Rockefeller family foundation, administers and maintains it and uses it for its programs and artist residencies.
w: The family fortune came from Standard Oil. In September 2014 the Fund announced it would cut fossil fuel holdings below 1 percent of its portfolio.
x: Fund-wide, not the house (Form 990-PF, 2024): revenue $76.1M, expenses $94.1M, net assets $1.37B. The house has no separate figure.

The Rockefeller Brothers Fund (Rockefeller family money, Standard Oil fortune) administers and maintains the house for its programs and artist residencies. The National Trust for Historic Preservation (members, private funds) owns it.
The Rockefeller Brothers Fund files a Form 990-PF; the house has no accounts or funder list of its own.
Owned by the National Trust for Historic Preservation and administered by the Rockefeller Brothers Fund. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

f: Founder Ernst Wagner gave the building to the Paul Rudolph Institute in 2023. Open-house tickets ($30), donations, memberships and design store sales fund it.
w: Paul Rudolph designed it as headquarters of the Modulightor lighting company. The Institute was gifted the company after Wagner died in December 2024.
x: Paul Rudolph Heritage Foundation, now the Institute (Form 990-PF, 2024): revenue $273,001, expenses $388,946, contributions $117,932, net assets $7.02M. In 2023 revenue was $7.31M, almost all contributions.

Ernst Wagner, co-founder of the Modulightor lighting company, gave the Paul Rudolph Institute the building in 2023. The company followed after his death in December 2024. Donations, memberships and design store sales also fund the Institute.
The Institute files a Form 990-PF and names its directors on its site. It publishes no donor list.
Run by the Paul Rudolph Institute for Modern Architecture, formerly the Paul Rudolph Heritage Foundation, a 501(c)(3) private operating foundation. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

f: Miami-Dade County owns and supports Vizcaya. The Florida Division of Cultural Affairs adds partial funding. Vizcaya announced a $20M gift from Ken Griffin on 7 November 2025.
w: Protesters targeted Griffin at the Whitney in November 2023, not at Vizcaya. His proposed Villa Serena donation and $5M endowment need county and city approval.
x: Vizcaya Museum and Gardens Trust (Form 990, year to Sept 2025): revenue $45.2M, expenses $25.5M, contributions $32.6M, program service revenue $11.8M, net assets $33.1M.

Miami-Dade County (county government) owns and supports Vizcaya. The State of Florida's Division of Cultural Affairs gives partial funding. Ken Griffin (Citadel hedge fund) announced a $20M gift on 7 November 2025.

The trust files a Form 990 and publishes an annual report. Its corporate partner page lists packages of $5,000 to $50,000+ and names PricewaterhouseCoopers, Coke Florida and TD Bank only in photo captions.
Operated by Vizcaya Museum and Gardens Trust, Inc., a 501(c)(3), on property owned by Miami-Dade County. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

f: The Liljestrand Foundation owns and runs it on donations and public tour and program revenue, with no endowment. Partners: Kaimana Beach Hotel, Aesop, OX Social, Honolulu Beerworks and Paiko.
w: A work of Hawai'i architect Vladimir Ossipoff. Howard Liljestrand's four children inherited it in 2004 and the Foundation took ownership in December 2015.
x: Liljestrand Foundation (Form 990-PF, 2024): revenue $602,205, expenses $583,317, contributions $140,619, net assets $3.80M.

The Liljestrand Foundation runs the house on Friends' donations and public tour revenue, with no endowment. Partners: Kaimana Beach Hotel, Aesop (skincare, owned by L'Oréal), Honolulu Beerworks (brewery), Paiko (florist) and OX Social (marketing agency).
The Foundation files a Form 990-PF and names its board, advisory board and staff on its site. It publishes no donor list.
Owned and run by the Liljestrand Foundation, created by the family in 2007. Listed in the Iconic Houses network; its site footer also shows Docomomo US and the Hawaii Museums Association.

f: The Annenberg Foundation Trust at Sunnylands owns and runs it on $691M in net assets and does no fundraising. Walter Annenberg's fortune came from Triangle Publications, sold in 1988.
w: Walter and Leonore Annenberg's winter estate. The Center & Gardens and the renovated estate opened to the public on 1 March 2012.
x: Annenberg Foundation Trust at Sunnylands (Form 990-PF, year to June 2025): revenue $40.5M, expenses $26.5M, of which charitable disbursements $19.0M, net assets $691.3M. No contributions received.
The Annenberg Foundation Trust at Sunnylands owns and runs it on $691M in net assets and does no fundraising. Walter Annenberg's fortune came from Triangle Publications, which he sold in 1988.
The trust files a Form 990-PF and names its President and nine trustees on its site. It publishes an annual letter, not accounts.
Owned and run by the Annenberg Foundation Trust at Sunnylands, governed by Annenberg descendants. Listed in the Iconic Houses network, which shows the trust's logo as a supporter.

f: The Conservancy raises gifts and endowments to run the city-owned house. The Annenberg Foundation gave operating support in 2022. A Getty Trust grant paid for its historic structure report.
w: Built in 1908 and open to the public since 1966, the house belongs to the City of Pasadena under a family gift agreement.
x: Gamble House Conservancy (Form 990, year to Sept 2025): revenue $2.29M, expenses $1.62M, contributions $682,173, program service revenue $476,503, net assets $13.9M.

The Gamble House Conservancy (investment income, gifts, program revenue) runs the City of Pasadena's house. The Annenberg Foundation (Walter Annenberg's publishing fortune) gave operating support in 2022. A J. Paul Getty Trust grant (Getty Oil bequest) supported its historic structure report.
The Conservancy links its latest Form 990 on its support page. Its site names no funders.
Operated by the Gamble House Conservancy, a 501(c)(3), for the City of Pasadena, which owns the house. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

f: The City of Los Angeles owns it and its Department of Cultural Affairs runs it on the city budget. The Barnsdall Art Park Foundation helps fund it.
w: Aline Barnsdall gave the house and park to the city in December 1926, and UNESCO inscribed the house on its World Heritage List in 2019.
x: City figure, not a filing: the council member's office put the cost of the house and Barnsdall park at about $1.36M a year (2025 budget talks). Barnsdall Art Park Foundation (Form 990, 2025): revenue $296,342, expenses $116,905.

The City of Los Angeles (city budget) owns the house and runs it through its Department of Cultural Affairs. The 2025 budget restored its staff funding. The Barnsdall Art Park Foundation (donations and events) helps fund it.
The city budget carries the house. The Barnsdall Art Park Foundation files its own Form 990.

Owned by the City of Los Angeles and operated by its Department of Cultural Affairs, with the Barnsdall Art Park Foundation as supporter. Listed in the Iconic Houses network. One of eight Frank Lloyd Wright sites on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 2019.

f: New York State parks office $200,186 (facade, 2023), State Council on the Arts $55,000 (2023), National Trust for Historic Preservation $18,000, Preservation League $3,680, Robert David Lion Gardiner Foundation $10,500.
w: Chaim Gross's Greenwich Village townhouse and studio, open to the public since 1994. Over two dozen friends funded its 1974 founding.
x: Revenue $248,604 and expenses $638,648 in 2024 (Form 990-PF): contributions $112,220, sales of assets $95,824, dividends $20,149. Year-end assets $7.34M. 2023 revenue $118,093.

Funders are the New York State parks office (state budget), the State Council on the Arts (state budget), the National Trust for Historic Preservation (members), the Preservation League (donations) and the Gardiner Foundation (set up by Long Island heir Robert David Lion Gardiner).
Files a Form 990-PF (on ProPublica for 2011 to 2024), lists named grants with amounts on a funders page, and names its seven trustees.
Run by the Renee & Chaim Gross Foundation, a 501(c)(3) (EIN 13-3490010) incorporated in 1989. Listed with Historic Artists' Homes & Studios and in the Iconic Houses network.

f: Tours and programs earn 58% of $5.5M income (2025). Funders include Illinois Arts Council, Institute of Museum and Library Services, JPMorgan Chase Foundation, Allstate, Google and Village of Oak Park.
w: Offers tours at four Wright sites: the Home and Studio, Robie House, Unity Temple and the Rookery. 115,000 visitors in 2025.
x: Income $5,457,368 and expenses $5,347,759 in 2025 (annual report): tours and programs 58%, merchandise 25%, contributions 5%, grants 4%. 2024 income $7.15M, grants $1.93M.

The 2025 report lists the Illinois Arts Council Agency (state budget), Institute of Museum and Library Services (federal budget), Village of Oak Park (local budget), JPMorgan Chase Foundation (bank), Allstate (insurance) and Google (advertising).
Publishes an annual report with financial statements, a 2025 contributor list by foundation and business, and its board and staff. Form 990s are on ProPublica to 2025.

Independent 501(c)(3), founded and incorporated in Illinois on 17 June 1974. Owns the Home and Studio, bought from the National Trust for Historic Preservation in 2012. Lists Iconic Houses as a member and partner.

f: Trust income $104,119 in the year to April 2025: contributions and grants $63,346, program services $40,143. Illinois Arts Council supports programming. The Village of Schaumburg is a named partner.
w: Paul Schweikher's 1938 home and studio. Alexander and Martyl Langsdorf lived there for nearly sixty years, Martyl until 2013.
x: Income $104,119 and expenses $45,667 in the year to April 2025 (Form 990-EZ): contributions $63,346, program services $40,143. Year-end assets $269,352. Income in the year to April 2024 was $58,671.

The Village of Schaumburg (municipal budget) owns the house, and the Illinois Arts Council Agency (state budget) supports its programming. Contributions of $63,346 made up most of the trust's $104,119 income in the year to April 2025.
Files a Form 990-EZ (on ProPublica for 2019 to 2025) and names its directors and executive director on its about page.

Run by the Schweikher House Preservation Trust, a 501(c)(3) the Village Board approved in 2009, whose board the village president appointed in 2010. The Village of Schaumburg owns the house, bought in 1999 from the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

f: Endowment from Suzy Frelinghuysen's 1988 bequest, built partly by selling the couple's New York apartment and Paris townhouse. Dividends $649,240 and gains $566,931 of $1.28M revenue in 2023.
w: Old inherited money, not a large industrial fortune, per her nephew. Her mother's father owned the Newark Daily Advertiser, her father led Mutual Benefit Life.
x: Revenue $4,309,123 and expenses $1,140,287 in 2024 (Form 990-PF), year-end assets $42.6M. In 2023 revenue was $1,276,904: dividends $649,240, gains $566,931, other income $57,251, gifts $3,482.

Suzy Frelinghuysen's bequest, old family money in her nephew's words, endows the house through the foundation she created. Her father led Mutual Benefit Life Insurance and her mother's father owned the Newark Daily Advertiser.
Files a Form 990-PF (on ProPublica for 2011 to 2024). Its about page names two co-trustees and links no annual report or funder list.

Run by the Frelinghuysen Morris Foundation (legal name George L. K. and Suzy F. Morris Foundation), a 501(c)(3) exempt since August 1988. Her nephew T. Kinney Frelinghuysen is director and co-trustee. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

f: Endowed by Stanley Picker, a cosmetics businessman, who set up the Trust in 1976 and left house, gallery and collection to it in 1982. Tour ticket sales go to conservation.
w: Kenneth Wood's 1968 house on Kingston Hill, with Picker's art collection and a 1976 pavilion gallery. Visits are by pre-arranged tour only.
x: Income £161,903 and spending £408,556 in the year to 5 April 2025 (Charity Commission data, charity 271185).
Stanley Picker's cosmetics business (Gala, Miners, Outdoor Girl) funded his collecting. The Stanley Picker Trust he set up owns and runs the house, which he left in trust in 1982.
Registered charity 271185 files accounts with the Charity Commission, whose data gives income, spending and four trustees. Its site names no trustees and links no annual report.
Run by the Stanley Picker Trust, a charity registered in 1976 that also pays for the Stanley Picker Fellowships at Kingston University's Stanley Picker Gallery. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

f: Donations and legacies £132,250 of £146,334 income in 2025 (individuals £19,581, other charities £6,328), rental income £12,237. Friends of 78 Derngate support the Trust. The accounts name no company funder.
w: Mackintosh's 1916 to 1917 remodelling for Bassett-Lowke. The Heritage Lottery Fund granted £999,000 towards the £1.4m 2002 to 2003 restoration.
x: Income £146,334 and spending £178,283 in 2025 (accounts): donations and legacies 90%, rental income 8%, interest 1%. Funds carried forward £3,430,207.

Friends of 78 Derngate raise money for the house. The Heritage Lottery Fund (lottery income) approved £999,000 for the £1.4M restoration in 2001, and Northampton Borough Council (local budget) bought a lease on the building in 1996.
Files accounts at Companies House (03495224) with a trustees' report and a full statement of financial activities. Its board is up to eight trustees.

Run by The 78 Derngate Northampton Trust, a charitable company (charity 1068270, registered 1998). West Northamptonshire Council holds the head lease on two of its three properties. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

f: Friends scheme, donations and sponsors: Community Chest, Haddenham Beer Festivals Trust and Haddenham and Waddesdon Community Board. Corporate friends: Allies and Morrison, Foster and Partners. Income £48,418 (2024).
w: Peter Aldington's 1967 house and garden, still the Aldington family home. He died in April 2026, and the Trust and family are planning its future.
x: Income £48,418 and spending £29,386 in 2024 (Charity Commission data, charity 1162076).

Turn End thanks the architecture practices Allies and Morrison and Foster and Partners as Corporate Friends. Sponsors are Haddenham Beer Festivals Trust (festival surpluses), Haddenham and Waddesdon Community Board (Buckinghamshire Council) and Community Chest.
Registered CIO 1162076 files with the Charity Commission, whose data gives income, spending and ten trustees. Its site lists its trustees and four patrons but links no accounts.
Run by the Turn End Trust, set up in 1998 and registered as a CIO in 2015. It joined the Iconic Houses network in July 2025.

f: Donations, shop sales and venue hire. Named supporters include Heritage Fund, Historic England, Royal Institute of British Architects, Vitra, Artek, Skandium, Paul Smith and Penguin. Income £48,894 in 2025.
w: Micro-museum in the former garage of Wells Coates's 1934 Isokon building, run wholly by volunteers since 2014.
x: Income £48,894 and spending £39,348 in 2025 (Charity Commission data, charity 1161069).

The support page names 30 organisations without amounts, among them the Heritage Fund (lottery), Historic England (UK government), the Royal Institute of British Architects (members), Vitra and Artek (furniture makers) and Paul Smith (fashion).
Registered charity 1161069 files with the Charity Commission, whose data gives income, spending and seven trustees. Its support page lists supporters and links no accounts.

Run by The Isokon Gallery Trust, a registered charity since 2015. Notting Hill Housing Association bought the building from Camden Council in 2003 and is the freeholder. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

f: The National Trust for Scotland, with 2024/25 income of £91.4M, owns and runs the house. National Lottery Heritage Fund gave £1.1M in late 2024, an anonymous donor £625,000 in 2026.
w: Mackintosh's 1904 house, enclosed in a protective box since 2019. The box stays until 2028.
x: These are the National Trust for Scotland's figures, not Hill House's: income £91.4M and spending £81.8M in the year to 28 February 2025. Shares: commercial activities 24%, membership 22%, legacies 13%, appeals 12%, property 11%, investments 8%, other 5%, grants 4%.

The National Trust for Scotland (membership, commercial activities and investments) owns and runs the house. The National Lottery Heritage Fund (lottery income) gave £1.1M in late 2024 and an anonymous donor gave £625,000 in 2026.
The National Trust for Scotland publishes audited annual accounts with grants by body and names its trustees. Hill House has no separate accounts.
Owned and run by the National Trust for Scotland, a charity (SC007410). Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

f: State museum founded 1948 as the National Central Liberation Struggle Museum and renamed 1960. KCNA claimed over 27 million visitors by 2008.
w: Flags: Sanctions. On Mansu Hill since April 1972. The Government of North Korea and the Workers' Party are blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
x: It is a state institution, and North Korea reports its state budget only as yearly percentage changes (spending up 3.8 percent in 2025, per the Korea Institute for National Unification).
KCNA describes it as an education institution of the Workers' Party of Korea.

f: Opened 1953; moved to Sosong in 1963 per Koryo Tours, rebuilt 1974 per Korean Wikipedia. Shows the USS Pueblo. KCNA claimed nearly 800,000 visitors in 2014.
w: Flags: Sanctions. The ship, seized in 1968, is still on the US Navy commissioned roster. The Government of North Korea is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
x: It is a state institution, and North Korea reports its state budget only as yearly percentage changes (spending up 3.8 percent in 2025, per the Korea Institute for National Unification).
Runs the display of the USS Pueblo, moored beside it on the Botong River since 2013.

f: State exhibition of North Korea's economic and technical work in six halls, with a planetarium. It opened in 1946 as a non-permanent industrial and agricultural exhibition, renamed 1983.
w: Flags: Sanctions. Open to foreign visitors. The Government of North Korea is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
x: It is a state institution, and North Korea reports its state budget only as yearly percentage changes (spending up 3.8 percent in 2025, per the Korea Institute for National Unification).
Runs a planetarium in its central building.

f: Opened 1978, this state museum holds gifts to Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il from foreign dignitaries. KCNA claimed hundreds of thousands of gifts from some 160 countries (1998).
w: Flags: Sanctions. Estimates of the gift count run from 60,000 to 220,000 (Wikipedia). The Government of North Korea is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
x: It is a state institution, and North Korea reports its state budget only as yearly percentage changes (spending up 3.8 percent in 2025, per the Korea Institute for National Unification).

f: State museum of Korean folk customs, opened February 1956 beside the Central History Museum. A 2014 reference book counts 7 rooms and 2,100 exhibits.
w: Flags: Sanctions. A state description mirrored on korea-dpr.com counts over 2,300 items in 7 halls. The Government of North Korea is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
x: It is a state institution, and North Korea reports its state budget only as yearly percentage changes (spending up 3.8 percent in 2025, per the Korea Institute for National Unification).

f: The state-owned Korea Stamp Corporation owns it, sells stamps and souvenirs in the building and prices its issues in US dollars for collectors abroad.
w: Flags: Sanctions. Opened April 2012 and renovated February 2019. The Government of North Korea, which owns the Corporation, is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
x: The Corporation publishes stamp release notes with US dollar prices and print runs, and North Korea reports its state budget only as yearly percentage changes (spending up 3.8 percent in 2025, per the Korea Institute for National Unification).
Korea Stamp Corporation (state-owned, earning from stamp and souvenir sales including to collectors abroad); Government of North Korea (owner of the Corporation).
Owned by the Korea Stamp Corporation, the state stamp issuer, which has offices in Beijing and Moscow.

f: Beside the Central Zoo, this state museum opened in mid-2016 (June per Newdaily, July per AP). Work began in late 2014 on Kim Jong Un's order, per Attractions Management.
w: Flags: Sanctions. Trade press called it the Nature Museum. Koryo Tours lists daily opening. The Government of North Korea is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
x: It is a state institution, and North Korea reports its state budget only as yearly percentage changes (spending up 3.8 percent in 2025, per the Korea Institute for National Unification).
Government of North Korea (state budget). Entry fees of 2 euros per person, per Koryo Tours.
Part of the Central Zoo leisure complex, which also holds an educational and science research centre (Attractions Management, 2016).

f: State museum at the site the state presents as Kim Il Sung's birthplace. Koryo Tours says it opened to the public in 1970.
w: Flags: Sanctions. Koryo Tours lists it with the Native House. The Government of North Korea is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
x: It is a state institution, and North Korea reports its state budget only as yearly percentage changes (spending up 3.8 percent in 2025, per the Korea Institute for National Unification).
Part of Mangyongdae, a historic site since 1947 and a listed Revolutionary Site (Wikipedia).

f: Mausoleum of Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il, run under a 2013 law. NK Insider says upkeep comes from donations to the Kim Il Sung-Kim Jong Il Fund.
w: Flags: Sanctions. Its plenary wing hosted Party conferences in 2010 and 2012. The Government of North Korea and Workers' Party are blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
x: Donation rules for its fund come from internal party documents seen by NK Insider, and North Korea reports its state budget only as yearly percentage changes (spending up 3.8 percent in 2025, per the Korea Institute for National Unification).

Kim Il Sung-Kim Jong Il Fund since November 2013, filled by donations from enterprises and organisations. Before that, a defector says, party dues and foreign-currency earnings. Owned by the Government of North Korea.

f: Opened in April 2002, the hall hosts flower festivals that began in the late 1990s. Wikipedia alone reports a 2020 rename to Okryu Exhibition Hall.
w: Flags: Sanctions. Open a few months a year, mainly around national holidays (Koryo Tours). The Government of North Korea is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
x: It is a state institution, and North Korea reports its state budget only as yearly percentage changes (spending up 3.8 percent in 2025, per the Korea Institute for National Unification).
Government of North Korea (state budget); seed and bulb sales at the hall (Koryo Tours).
Hosts the Kimilsungia and Kimjongilia festivals. A department director of the Kimilsungia-Kimjongilia Committee described the 2005 festival to KCNA.

f: Museum of the Workers' Party's founding on Haebang Hill, opened October 1970. KCNA said servicepersons and working people visit it.
w: Flags: Sanctions. Holds Kim Il Sung's preserved offices and meeting hall. The Government of North Korea and Workers' Party are blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
x: North Korea reports its state budget only as yearly percentage changes (spending up 3.8 percent in 2025, per the Korea Institute for National Unification).
Includes the nearby house where Kim Il Sung lived, which Wikipedia counts as part of the museum.

f: Museum of the Second Economic Committee, the state defence-industry agency, opened 11 October 2026 with the Hwasong-20 ICBM, missiles and drones on show. Kim Jong Un cut the ribbon.
w: Flags: Sanctions, Arms and defence. The Committee is listed by the US (August 2010), EU (December 2010), UN and UK (March 2016) and oversees ballistic missile production.
x: The state budget gives a national defence share, 15.7 percent for 2025 per Finance Minister Ri Myong Guk (Korea JoongAng Daily).
Second Economic Committee (state defence-industry agency, which runs the museum); Government of North Korea (state budget).

Belongs to the Second Economic Committee, which coordinates the defence industry and directs KOMID (EU Regulation 370/2013 text). EU texts of 2009 to 2011 call the Committee a body of the Workers' Party Central Committee, and Wikipedia says it was placed under the Cabinet in 2026.

f: Owned by the Government of North Korea. It earns foreign currency subcontracting animation for overseas clients; Italy's Mondo TV paid it about $538,000 between 2019 and 2021, per OFAC.
w: Flags: Sanctions. OFAC listed it on 10 December 2021, together with three Chinese front companies and a Chinese national who facilitated its wire transfers.
x: SEK Studio posts no accounts, and Treasury's 10 December 2021 release says its Chinese front companies received millions of dollars from foreign customers.
Mondo TV of Italy paid about $537,939 for animation work between May 2019 and November 2021 (OFAC settlement, 26 June 2024).

Government of North Korea (state budget, announced only as yearly percentage changes); overseas clients such as Mondo TV of Italy, which paid about $538,000 for subcontracted animation in 2019 to 2021 (OFAC).

Owned by the Government of North Korea. Founded in 1957 as the April 26 Children's Film Studio. OFAC's 2021 notice links it to three Chinese front companies: Nings Cartoon Studio, Moxing Cartoon and Shanghai Hongman Cartoon and Animation Design Studio.

f: State studio run by the Ministry of Culture and paid from the state budget. Koryo Tours says tourists and North Koreans can visit it.
w: Flags: Sanctions. Founded in 1947 as the National Film Studio, with around 1,800 staff on 1 million square metres. Completed films reach the public only with approval.
x: Government of North Korea (state budget, announced only as yearly percentage changes), through the Ministry of Culture.
Under the Ministry of Culture, according to Wikipedia. North Korea's other state studios include the Korean Documentary Film Studio, the April 25 Film Studio and SEK Studio.

f: Organised by a festival committee chaired by the head of the National Administration of Motion Picture Industry. The festival covers ground costs for filmmakers whose entries it accepts (Koryo Tours).
w: Flags: Sanctions. The 18th edition opened on 22 October 2025 at the Pyongyang International Cinema House, the first since 2019.
x: Koryo Tours, the festival's foreign coordinator, publishes entry forms and says accepted filmmakers' ground costs are covered; no accounts are posted.
Government of North Korea (state budget, announced only as yearly percentage changes); the festival itself pays accepted filmmakers' ground costs (Koryo Tours).

Its organising committee is chaired by the director-general of the National Administration of Motion Picture Industry. Koryo Tours has coordinated foreign entries since 2002; screenings are at the Pyongyang International Cinema House.

f: State publisher under the Workers' Party of Korea's Propaganda and Agitation Department, paid from party and state budgets. It publishes the Pyongyang Times and Korea Today for foreign readers.
w: Flags: Sanctions. KCNA marked its 50th anniversary on 4 December 1999. It is on no sanctions list; the flag rests on control by the blocked Workers' Party.
x: The publisher posts the Pyongyang Times and other titles online but no accounts.
Workers' Party of Korea (party budget), through its Propaganda and Agitation Department; Government of North Korea (state budget, announced only as yearly percentage changes).

Reports to the Propaganda and Agitation Department of the Workers' Party of Korea. KCNA listed its units in 1999: publishing houses for the Pyongyang Times, Korea Today and other titles, a printing plant and a school for translators. It runs the Naenara and Publications of the DPRK portals (Wikipedia).

f: Performing troupe run under the Workers' Party of Korea, the only Pyongyang troupe so placed (Korean Wikipedia). Paid from party and state budgets.
w: Flags: Sanctions. Wikipedia relays a claim of over 700 performances in more than 50 countries. Resident at the Mansudae Art Theatre since 1976.
x: Workers' Party of Korea (party budget); Government of North Korea (state budget, announced only as yearly percentage changes).

Operates under the Workers' Party of Korea (Korean Wikipedia). Successor to the Central Art Troupe formed in 1969; its Samjiyon Band began in 2009 and the Pochonbo Electronic Ensemble split off in 1985.

f: State theatre whose resident Mansudae Art Troupe runs under the Workers' Party of Korea. Used for revolutionary opera and Party assemblies (Korean Wikipedia). Paid from party and state budgets.
w: Flags: Sanctions. Completed in 1976 near the Grand People's Study House. It is a venue for the Samjiyon Band.
x: Government of North Korea (state budget, announced only as yearly percentage changes); the Workers' Party of Korea (party budget), which runs its resident troupe.
Home of the Mansudae Art Troupe, which operates under the Workers' Party of Korea. It stands in Mansudae, Chung District, near the Grand People's Study House.

f: State theatre, main stage of the Pibada (Sea of Blood) Opera Troupe, paid from the state budget. It reopened on 3 April 2009 after rebuilding (Korean Wikipedia).
w: Flags: Sanctions. Opened 13 August 1960 with 2,190 seats. North Korean media reported about 1,300 seats after the 2009 rebuild.
x: Government of North Korea (state budget, announced only as yearly percentage changes).
Home of the Pibada Opera Troupe, founded in 1946 as the North Korean Opera Troupe and renamed in 1971. The five revolutionary operas are staged here (Korean Wikipedia).

f: State circus company with its own theatre, paid from the state budget. Foreign visitors pay 20 euros a ticket through their guides (Koryo Tours).
w: Flags: Sanctions. Won top prizes at the Monte-Carlo and Figueres festivals in 2015 and visited Seoul in 2000, per Daily NK.
x: Government of North Korea (state budget, announced only as yearly percentage changes); foreign visitors, who pay 20 euros a ticket through their guides (Koryo Tours).

Its theatre on Kwangbok Street was built in 1989 for the World Festival of Youth and Students and renovated in 2012; a circus school stands on the grounds (Korean Wikipedia). It is one of the theatres of the April Spring Friendship Art Festival.

f: Organising committee housed in the Pyongyang International House of Culture. The April Spring Friendship Art Festival Fund, set up on 3 June 2011, sponsors it and promotes international fundraising.
w: Flags: Sanctions. KCNA announced the 34th edition on 25 March 2026. Wikipedia relays a claim of 2,090 troupes from 114 countries taking part in total.
x: The festival's fund lists its council directors (2021) but posts no accounts (Ministry of Culture's Korean Art site).
April Spring Friendship Art Festival Fund, set up on 3 June 2011, which sponsors the festival and promotes international fundraising for it (Ministry of Culture's Korean Art site).
Its organising committee has its office in the Pyongyang International House of Culture, and the Pyongyang Circus is one of its theatres (Wikipedia).

n: Kim Won Gyun Pyongyang University of Music and Dance
f: State university financed by the Government of North Korea, whose education system has been state-financed since 1959. It has a Workers' Party committee (Daily NK).
w: Flags: Sanctions. Dates from 1949; merged in 1972, split in 2004, and the music side took composer Kim Won Gyun's name in 2006 (Korean Wikipedia).
x: Government of North Korea (state budget, announced only as yearly percentage changes).
Runs a kindergarten course, a primary course and a preparatory course for young musicians and dancers (Wikipedia). Its Workers' Party committee sits inside the university.

f: State art university financed by the Government of North Korea, with its own art museum.
w: Flags: Sanctions. Founded in 1947 as a Pyongyang art specialist school and renamed in 1952 (Korean Wikipedia). It holds the Order of Kim Il Sung.
x: Government of North Korea (state budget, announced only as yearly percentage changes).
Many artists at the Mansudae Art Studio are its graduates. Faculties include graphic art, crafts, Korean painting and sculpture (Wikipedia).

f: State theatre, the main stage of the Mansudae Art Troupe, which operates under the Workers' Party of Korea (Korean Wikipedia). Paid from party and state budgets.
w: Flags: Sanctions. Built in 1989 for the Pyongyang world youth festival. The New York Philharmonic played here on 26 February 2008.
x: Government of North Korea (state budget, announced only as yearly percentage changes); the Workers' Party of Korea (party budget), which runs its main troupe.
Principal venue of the Mansudae Art Troupe (Korean Wikipedia), which Wikipedia says it hosted again on 1 January 2007 after reconstruction.

f: State studio of the Korean People's Army, paid from the state budget. It makes military-themed films about the army, navy, air force and special forces (Koryo Tours).
w: Flags: Sanctions. Founded in 1959 as the February 8 Cinema Studio. Not usually open to visitors, though tour groups have watched films in its cinema.
x: Government of North Korea (state budget, announced only as yearly percentage changes), through the Korean People's Army.
Run by the Korean People's Army (Wikipedia). One of North Korea's state film studios, beside the Korean Art Film Studio, the Korean Documentary Film Studio and SEK Studio.

f: State after-school palace managed by the Korean Children's Union (Koryo Tours) and paid from the state budget. Wikipedia counts over 500 teachers.
w: Flags: Sanctions. Opened on 2 May 1989 before the World Festival of Youth and Students, with 120 rooms and a 2,000-seat theatre that holds regular performances.
x: Government of North Korea (state budget, announced only as yearly percentage changes), through the Korean Children's Union.

Managed by the Korean Children's Union (Koryo Tours); Wikipedia names the Korean Youth Corps instead. It is the largest of the North Korean children's palaces and is separate from the Pyongyang Children's Palace.

n: North Hamgyong Provincial Revolutionary History Museum
f: Provincial museum on Chongjin's central square, funded and run by the North Korean state.
w: Flags: Sanctions. Stands beside the Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il statues. The Government of North Korea is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
x: No website, report, accounts, donor list or board is public for this state museum.
Government of North Korea (state budget, announced as yearly percentage changes; the 2025 plan was revenue +2%, spending +3.8%).
One of the provincial revolutionary history museums; the Koryo Tours guide says every province has one.

n: North Pyongan Provincial Revolutionary History Museum
f: State museum for North Pyongan Province, two storeys, in central Sinuiju.
w: Flags: Sanctions. Photos are not allowed inside. The Government of North Korea is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
x: This provincial state museum posts no report, accounts, donor list or board.
Government of North Korea (state budget, announced as yearly percentage changes; the 2025 plan was revenue +2%, spending +3.8%).
Provincial museum of North Pyongan Province, separate from the Sinuiju History Museum in the same city.

f: Founded on 30 November 1947; a state history museum holding antiquities excavated in North Pyongan Province.
w: Flags: Sanctions. Shows remains from prehistoric times to the modern era. The Government of North Korea is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
x: No report, accounts, donor list or board is public for this state museum.
Government of North Korea (state budget, announced as yearly percentage changes; the 2025 plan was revenue +2%, spending +3.8%).
Koryo Tours says it is not the North Pyongan revolutionary history museum, which is also in Sinuiju.

f: State museum in Hoeryong, two storeys, centred on the activities of Kim Jong Suk.
w: Flags: Sanctions. Photos are allowed inside, unlike many such museums, Koryo Tours says. The Government of North Korea is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
x: No website, report, accounts, donor list or board is public for this state museum.
Government of North Korea (state budget, announced as yearly percentage changes; the 2025 plan was revenue +2%, spending +3.8%).
Stands a short walk from the Native House of Kim Jong Suk, a site in the same city.

f: Museum in the Panmunjom building where the 1953 armistice was signed; military personnel check visitors there and a Korean People's Army guide gives the introduction.
w: Flags: Sanctions. The 1976 incident axe is on display at Panmunjom, Koryo Tours says. The Government of North Korea is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
x: A state museum with no website of its own; Koryo Tours describes it.
Part of the North Korean side of Panmunjom, where military personnel check visitors and a Korean People's Army guide gives the introduction, per Koryo Tours.

f: Provincial library opened in 2012 and run by the North Korean state.
w: Flags: Sanctions. In 2013 a guide told DW it had 301 computers. The Government of North Korea is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
x: No report, accounts or funder list is public for the library.
Provincial library of North Hamgyong Province, linked by the national intranet to other study houses and libraries, Koryo Tours says.

f: State science and technology library for South Hamgyong Province; state media reported its opening ceremony in December 2018.
w: Flags: Sanctions. Wikipedia dates the building to 2016 from Google Earth imagery. The Government of North Korea is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
x: No report, accounts or funder list is public for the library.
Provincial library of South Hamgyong Province, built on the site of the former South Hamgyong Cultural Exhibition House.

f: State theatre built in 1984, the largest in North Korea, used for major productions by a revolutionary opera troupe.
w: Flags: Sanctions. A Russian opera troupe staged Eugene Onegin here in 2010, Koryo Tours says. The Government of North Korea is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
x: No report, accounts, ticket revenue or funder list is public for the theatre.
Venue of a revolutionary opera troupe and of local bands, per Koryo Tours and Wikipedia.

f: Korea Paekho Trading Corporation, subordinate to the Ministry of People's Armed Forces, raises money for the state from art and construction contracts abroad; the studio also sells art in Pyongyang.
w: Flags: Sanctions. OFAC listed Korea Paekho Trading Corporation on 1 March 2023. Its parent ministry was listed by OFAC in 2017 and the UN in December 2017.
x: The studio has no site of its own and posts no report or accounts.

Supplies art and sculpture to the North Korean state and public and sells to foreign visitors in its Pyongyang gallery, per Koryo Tours; Korea Paekho Trading Corporation's art and construction projects abroad earn money for the North Korean government, per Treasury.

Trading arm: Korea Paekho Trading Corporation, based in the same building and subordinate to the Ministry of People's Armed Forces, per Treasury. Koryo Tours says the studio began as a military-run studio and is now a cooperative of more than 250 artists. A 2021 UN Panel of Experts report treats Congo Aconde SARL in the DR Congo as the corporation's front company.

f: Military venue opened on 7 October 1975 for military education; its April 25 Culture and Art Composition Office organizes the army's major cultural events.
w: Flags: Sanctions. Hosted the Workers' Party's 6th to 9th congresses. Both the Government of North Korea and the Workers' Party are blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
x: No report, accounts or funder list is public for the house.
Government of North Korea (state budget); Koryo Tours calls the house a military site.
Home of the April 25 Culture and Art Composition Office; stage of the Korean People's Army Ensemble and the Moranbong Band, per Koryo Tours.

f: Provincial gallery founded in 1968 and run by the state; sells local artists' paintings, posters and embroideries at prices below Pyongyang's.
w: Flags: Sanctions. Koryo Tours warns buyers off Mansudae Art Studio work, which is sanctioned. The Government of North Korea is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
x: No report, accounts or board is public for this provincial gallery.

Government of North Korea (state budget, announced as yearly percentage changes; the 2025 plan was revenue +2%, spending +3.8%); sales of paintings, posters and embroideries to visitors, per Koryo Tours.
Koryo Tours also lists it as the North Pyongan Provincial Art Gallery.

f: Mansudae built it with North Korean money, reported at US$24 million, and co-ran it with Cambodia's APSARA Authority. Its director said in 2016 Mansudae would take ten years' profit.
w: Flags: Sanctions. Shut since 4 December 2019; Mansudae's Cambodian subsidiary was deregistered that month (UN Panel). Mansudae is on US (2016), EU and UN (2017) lists.
x: The museum director gave the cost and profit terms to Al Jazeera on 22 February 2016; the museum publishes no accounts.

North Korea paid for the build, reported at US$24 million. Mansudae Overseas Projects ran the museum through a Cambodian subsidiary; the museum's director said Mansudae would take ten years' profit, then share it with APSARA, the Cambodian manager of Angkor, for ten more.

Run through Mansudae New Tech Corporation, a Cambodian subsidiary of the Mansudae Overseas Project Group of Companies, jointly with the APSARA Authority, the Cambodian body that manages Angkor; the deal returns it to the Cambodian government after the profit-sharing years.

f: Paid for by the Namibian government and built by Mansudae from 2009; it opened in March 2014. Entry is free and a culture ministry heritage official speaks for it.
w: Namibian press questioned the cost and the choice of Mansudae (2011). Namibia said in June 2016 it would end Mansudae's services (UN Panel S/2017/150).
x: The museum publishes no accounts or budget line.
Government of Namibia: the SWAPO government funded the build, per a 2024 Leiden thesis. Mansudae Overseas Projects of North Korea built the museum and designed its exhibitions as contractor.
Under Namibia's culture ministry, the Ministry of Education, Innovation, Youth, Sports, Arts and Culture.

f: Namibian government paid Mansudae N$60 million against a N$34 million budget; opened 26 August 2002. The National Heritage Council runs it; adult Namibians paid N$50 in 2024-25.
w: Insight Namibia's corruption tracker (March 2008) says the contract cost twice the first estimate. UN Panel report S/2017/150 lists the site among Mansudae's Namibian works.
x: The National Heritage Council gazettes the admission fees (Government Gazette No. 8206, September 2023); the site publishes no accounts.
Admission fees raised N$64,188 in 2006 against upkeep of N$500,000 a year (Van der Hoog, Leiden University thesis, 2024, p.147, citing The Namibian, 2002 to 2006).

Government of Namibia paid for the build. The National Heritage Council charges admission, and the Ministry of Works and Transport keeps up the site (New Era, 2017). Mansudae Overseas Projects built it as contractor.
Run by the National Heritage Council of Namibia, the statutory body under the National Heritage Act 2004 that sets admission fees for protected places.

f: Run by the Syrian Ministry of Defence, which lists it among its army museums. North Korea helped build it, per Wikipedia and Public Delivery.
w: Wikipedia, citing a visit video, says it was ransacked after December 2024. Opening is dated 1998 (Wikipedia) and 9 October 1999 (Frontline Club).
x: The Ministry's page describes the building and its exhibits but gives no budget, accounts or funder.
Syrian Ministry of Defence, which runs it. North Korea helped build it (Wikipedia, Public Delivery).
Part of the Syrian Ministry of Defence's military culture and museums section.

f: Zimbabwe's government commissioned it from North Korean builders in 1981 and it opened in 1982. The Department of Museums and National Monuments runs it.
w: Built 24 years before the UN's first North Korea sanctions (2006). UN Panel report S/2017/150 lists it among Mansudae's African works.
x: The National Museums and Monuments of Zimbabwe page on the Acre lists no budget, fees or accounts.
Government of Zimbabwe commissioned it; the state's Department of Museums and National Monuments runs it. North Korean builders (Mansudae Overseas Projects) worked as contractors.
Run by the Department of Museums and National Monuments of Zimbabwe, which the National Museums and Monuments of Zimbabwe site names as the manager of all heroes' acres.

f: The Senegalese State allocated CFA 300 million to the site, reported in 2020. Mansudae built it by 2010, paid in land, at a cost given as US$27 million.
w: President Wade claimed 35% of site revenue. Thousands protested against his regime and the statue in 2010; a 2009 US cable calls the financing murky.
x: The CFA 300 million State allocation comes from a 2020 press report (Au Sénégal); the site publishes no accounts.
CFA 300 million budget allocated by the State (Au Sénégal, 26 November 2020); the site administrator gave 120,000 to 140,000 visitors a year.

Government of Senegal (State allocation of CFA 300 million, reported 2020). Press accounts say the 2008 to 2010 build was paid in 30 to 40 hectares of land; a 2009 US cable calls the financing murky. Mansudae Overseas Projects built it as contractor.
Created by decree 2003-593 (16 July 2003) and placed under the Ministry of Culture and Tourism (Dakaractu); an administrator heads a State-funded staff of 40 or more (Au Sénégal, 2020).

n: Agostinho Neto Memorial (Memorial Dr. António Agostinho Neto)
f: State Budget transfers fund this public establishment under the Presidency, plus space hire, fees, publications and donations. Mansudae redesigned and built it from 2005; it opened in 2012.
w: UN Panel S/2017/150 saw Mansudae staff maintaining the complex in September 2016. Angola ended all Mansudae contracts in 2017 (S/2018/171).
x: Its statute, Presidential Decree 302/21, lists its revenue sources, puts its budget inside the State Budget and has the director submit annual accounts to the Tribunal de Contas.

Government of Angola (State Budget transfers; the President oversees it through the Casa Civil), plus space hire, fees, publications and donations. Wikipedia and Public Delivery say North Korea funded part of the US$40 million build, which Mansudae built.

A public establishment under the President of the Republic, supervised through the head of the Casa Civil (Presidential Decree 302/21); it holds Neto's sarcophagus, a museum, a library and an exhibition gallery, and works with the Fundação Dr. António Agostinho Neto.

f: Egypt's state commissioned it under President Mubarak and the National Military Museums Department runs it. North Korean architects helped build it; tickets cost 3 to 30 Egyptian pounds in 2010.
w: Opened 5 October 1989. Public Delivery names Mansudae Overseas Projects as co-builder.
x: Egypt Independent (October 2010) gives the ticket prices; the panorama publishes no accounts.

Government of Egypt, through the National Military Museums Department; President Mubarak commissioned it. North Korean architects helped build it (Wikipedia); Public Delivery names Mansudae Overseas Projects as co-builder.
Run by the Egyptian National Military Museums Department.

f: Created by law in April 1959 and attached to the Ministry of Culture since 1976. Publishes journals and the Casa de las Américas Prize.
w: EcuRed calls its activities non-governmental. Abel Prieto has led it since late 2019.
x: Its home page links departments, journals, prizes and a library catalogue; no budget, accounts or funder list is linked.
Attached to Cuba's Ministry of Culture. Co-publishes the journal Criterios with the Union of Writers and Artists of Cuba and holds the Haydée Santamaría collection of over 10,000 works.

n: Centro de Arte Contemporáneo Wifredo Lam
f: Art centre within the National Council of Plastic Arts (CNAP), a Ministry of Culture body. The Centre, CNAP and the Ministry co-sponsored the 15th Havana Biennial (2024 to 2025).
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. Dutch funders Hivos and the Prince Claus Fund withdrew funds from its 2003 Biennial. An October 2021 open letter asked artists to boycott the 14th.
x: Its site (2014 archive) carries bulletins and Biennial pages and credits the Ministry of Culture and CNAP; no budget, accounts or funder list is linked.
Ministry of Culture and National Council of Plastic Arts (Cuban state budget).
Institution of the National Council of Plastic Arts (CNAP). Organises the Havana Biennial with CNAP.

f: Created 12 December 1959 by decree of the Revolutionary Armed Forces Ministry (MINFAR) and housed in the former presidential palace since 1974. State sources claim over 300,000 visitors a year.
w: The Granma yacht stands in a memorial in its grounds. Decree No. 17 was signed by Raúl Castro as MINFAR minister.
x: Founded in 1959 by the Ministry of the Revolutionary Armed Forces (MINFAR).
Runs the Granma Memorial in its grounds, built in 1976 as an annex.

f: Run by the Office of the City Historian of Havana since 2005, which restored it by 2011. The collection began with sugar magnate Julio Lobo's Napoleonic pieces.
w: Princess Napoleon attended the 30 March 2011 reopening and gave Sèvres porcelain from her own collection (Fondation Napoléon).
x: The Historian's Office page describes the building and collection; no museum accounts or donor list is linked.
Office of the City Historian of Havana (state budget and other authorised sources, per Decree-Law 368 of 2018); Cuban government support for the 2011 restoration (Fondation Napoléon).
Museum of the Office of the City Historian of Havana, alongside the Museo de Arte Colonial, the Museo de la Ciudad and the Casa Oswaldo Guayasamín.

f: National museum listed among the institutions of the Cuban Music Institute, a Ministry of Culture body created in 1989. Founded 1971; its collections grew through musicians' donations.
w: The Odilio Urfé library and archive merged into the museum in 1997. The library joined IAML in 1995 and IASA in 1999.
x: Cuban Music Institute, Ministry of Culture (state budget); donations from musicians.
Institution of the Cuban Music Institute. Houses the Odilio Urfé library and archive, a member of the International Association of Music Libraries.

f: Its operator, the Office of the City Historian of Havana (Dirección de Patrimonio Cultural), runs on the state budget and other authorised sources (Decree-Law 368, 2018).
w: Opened 30 July 1969 in the 1720 Casa Bayona on Plaza de la Catedral.
x: The Historian's Office page describes collections and the annex; no museum accounts or donor list is linked.
Office of the City Historian of Havana (state budget and other authorised sources, per Decree-Law 368 of 2018).
Run by the Office of the City Historian of Havana, with an annex in the Palacio de Lombillo.

f: Directly subordinate to the National Council of Cultural Heritage (CNPC), a Ministry of Culture body. Opened 24 July 1964 in a mansion the state expropriated that year.
w: Spanish Wikipedia says it holds over 33,000 works, including French furniture and Sèvres, Limoges and English porcelain.
x: Ministry of Culture through the National Council of Cultural Heritage (state budget).
One of five institutions directly subordinate to the National Council of Cultural Heritage (CNPC), with the Museo Ernest Hemingway.

n: Museo Nacional de Historia Natural de Cuba
f: Under the Ministry of Science, Technology and Environment (CITMA) since 1992, after 1985 to 1991 under the Ministry of Culture.
w: Sits at Obispo 61 on Plaza de Armas in Old Havana. Its digital magazine Savia dates from February 2011.
x: Its site describes history, functions, collections and staff; no budget, accounts or donor list is linked.
Ministry of Science, Technology and Environment (Cuban state budget).
Under the Ministry of Science, Technology and Environment (CITMA), within its national science and technology system.

f: Answers to the National Council of Plastic Arts (CNAP), a Ministry of Culture body. Opened in 1986 as a photo archive, museum and gallery.
w: Runs the Noviembre Fotográfico month of photography since 2008 and offers creation and research grants to Cuban photographers.
x: Ministry of Culture through the National Council of Plastic Arts (state budget).
Part of the National Council of Plastic Arts (CNAP), with the Centro de Arte Contemporáneo Wifredo Lam and the Centro de Desarrollo de las Artes Visuales.

f: Non-profit created in 1995 by Peter and Irene Ludwig. The Ludwig Foundation, Aachen, supports it continuously; American Friends of the Ludwig Foundation of Cuba administers it.
x: The US arm files a public Form 990 listing its directors.
US arm, American Friends of the Ludwig Foundation of Cuba: revenue $215,263 for 2025, of which contributions $114,256 (Form 990, ProPublica).
Peter and Irene Ludwig Foundation, Aachen (ongoing support); American Friends of the Ludwig Foundation of Cuba (US donations).
Partner institution of the Peter and Irene Ludwig Foundation (Aachen) and its Ludwig network; administered by the American Friends of the Ludwig Foundation of Cuba.

n: Taller Experimental de Gráfica de La Habana
f: Print workshop founded 30 July 1962 and listed by the National Council of Plastic Arts (CNAP) among its institutions in 2013. It earns from print sales and commissions.
w: Moved to Callejón del Chorro in the 1990s; it has had nine directors since 1962, the latest Yamilys Brito (OnCuba, 2022).
x: Sales of prints and commissioned work, per CNAP's 2013 page. CNAP, a Ministry of Culture body, listed it as its institution in 2013.
Listed in 2013 among the institutions of the National Council of Plastic Arts (CNAP); hosts the practical engraving course of Cuba's art schools.

f: Under the National Council of Cultural Heritage (CNPC). The US Finca Vigía Foundation funds conservation: the Caterpillar Foundation announced $500,000 in 2016 and the US government gave $25,000 in 2023.
w: The US State Department and Treasury authorised the foundation's 2015 shipment of four containers for an on-site conservation workshop.
x: The US foundation files a public Form 990 naming its directors and paid staff.
Finca Vigía Foundation (US): revenue $368,460 for 2024, all contributions (Form 990, ProPublica).

Ministry of Culture through the National Council of Cultural Heritage (state budget). Finca Vigía Foundation, Boston, funded by US donors including the Caterpillar Foundation. US government fund of $25,000 (December 2023).
Directly subordinate to the National Council of Cultural Heritage (CNPC). Partner of the Finca Vigía Foundation of Boston, tax-exempt since 2004.

f: Opened 18 January 1992 by the Office of the City Historian of Havana with Oswaldo Guayasamín. Original works donated to the Cuban nation are on show.
w: Housed in an 18th-century house at Obrapía 111, where restoration uncovered colonial mural paintings.
x: The Historian's Office lists the house among its museums; no accounts or donor list is linked.
Office of the City Historian of Havana (state budget and other authorised sources, per Decree-Law 368 of 2018); Oswaldo Guayasamín financed the house's restoration (the Office's history page).
Among the museums of the Office of the City Historian of Havana.

n: Oficina del Historiador de la Ciudad de La Habana
f: Runs on the state budget and other authorised sources (Decree-Law 368, 2018). Its deputy director said in 2024 that large companies still hand over their historic-centre profits.
w: GAESA took over its business companies, led by Habaguanex, in 2016. Habaguanex, Hoteles Habaguanex, Fénix and GAESA are on the US Cuba Restricted List.
x: Its 2017 site describes its income sources without figures; Decree-Law 368 (Gaceta Oficial, 3 April 2019) sets its financing basis.
At least 7 million a year in hard currency for social projects, a 2024 claim by its deputy director (Diario de Cuba).

State budget and other authorised sources (Decree-Law 368, 2018). Museum tickets and shop sales. Foreign cooperation and donations. Profits that large companies still hand over, per its deputy director in 2024.

Runs Old Havana's museums and cultural centres, including the Museo de la Ciudad, Museo Napoleónico, Museo de Arte Colonial and Casa Oswaldo Guayasamín. Subordinate to the Council of Ministers. Restores the UNESCO-listed Historic Centre.

n: Museo de la Ciudad de La Habana
f: Housed in the Palace of the Captains General, the seat of the Office of the City Historian of Havana from 1938. The Office opened its first rooms in 1968.
w: Occupies the 1776 to 1791 palace on Plaza de Armas. The Historian's Office claims 40 permanent exhibition rooms.
x: The Historian's Office page describes the palace, the rooms and the Templete; no museum accounts or donor list is linked.
